Ghana News.title: Jospong Group supports 21 journalists to cover COP31 in Türkiye
Ghana News.content:
The Jospong Group of Companies has sponsored 21 Ghanaian journalists to attend the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, providing them with an opportunity to cover global climate negotiations and gain first-hand insights into international climate action.

The journalists, drawn from traditional and online media organisations, include reporters, editors, presenters, show hosts, bloggers and social media influencers.

COP31 opened on November 9 and is scheduled to end on November 20, 2026.

The Executive Chairman of the Jospong Group, Dr Joseph Siaw Agyepong, funded the journalists' flights, accommodation, local transportation and daily allowances.

The sponsorship is intended to strengthen media coverage of climate adaptation, resilience and Ghana's transition towards a greener and more circular economy.

It is the fourth consecutive time the Group has supported Ghanaian journalists to participate in the global climate conference, following previous sponsorships for COP28 in Dubai, COP29 in Azerbaijan and COP30 in Belém, Brazil.

Dr Agyepong believes the initiative will equip journalists with knowledge of emerging climate terminologies, practices and global concerns, which they can use to improve public understanding of climate change and its implications for Ghana.

Speaking in Antalya, some of the journalists welcomed the initiative, saying direct access to the negotiations would help them provide more informed coverage of global climate decisions and their implications for Ghanaian communities.

Alexander Adi, Assistant Manager for News at GBC News, said the sponsorship had enabled Ghanaian journalists to participate in negotiations that many would otherwise have had to follow remotely.

“Without that support, many Ghanaian journalists simply would not be here in Antalya to witness these negotiations, to pose the tough questions, and to tell Ghana’s climate story in our own voice rather than relying on foreign wire services to tell it for us,” he said.

He, however, stressed that the sponsorship did not compromise the independence of the journalists.

“Sponsorship does not equate to endorsement. My primary obligation remains to the public: to report accurately, to hold all actors, including sponsors, the government, and private corporations accountable, and to distinguish a company’s climate commitments from verified facts on the ground,” he said.

Mr Adi said participating in the conference had broadened his understanding of climate finance, carbon markets, waste-to-energy projects and the role of local authorities in climate action.

He added that the experience would inform his environmental reporting in Ghana, particularly in explaining how global climate decisions affect agriculture and urban communities.

Kwame Appiah Kubi, a journalist with Media General, said sponsorship initiatives of this nature contributed to journalists' professional development by deepening their understanding of climate change and the science behind it.

He said the knowledge gained would help reporters improve the accuracy of their coverage and explain complex climate issues more clearly to their audiences.

Mr Appiah Kubi added that attending COP31 had also provided an opportunity to examine how other countries were responding to climate change, allowing journalists to place Ghana's climate policies and interventions within a broader international context.

Kofi Ahovi, a journalist with Business Week, described the sponsorship as an investment in journalism and professional development.

He said attending the conference had given journalists direct access to policymakers, scientists, business leaders and development partners, whose perspectives could enrich reporting on climate change, waste management and green investment.

Mr Ahovi noted that the opportunity also came with a responsibility to maintain editorial independence, verify information and hold relevant stakeholders accountable.

He said the impact of the sponsorship would ultimately be reflected in the quality of independent and balanced reporting journalists produced to inform public debate and highlight practical solutions to climate challenges.

Benedicta Abekah, a radio and television host at Ignite Media, popularly known on air as Adjoah Nhyira, said her participation in COP31 had improved her understanding of the causes of climate change and the importance of reducing human activities that contribute to environmental degradation.

Ghana News.title: Ecobank Ghana’s Regina Ofori wins global award for Outstanding Contribution to Marketing
Ghana News.content:
Head of Marketing and Corporate Communications at Ecobank Ghana PLC, Regina Ofori.

Head of Marketing and Corporate Communications at Ecobank Ghana PLC, Regina Ofori, has received the Outstanding Contribution to Marketing (Brand) award at the 2026 Global Women in Marketing (WiM) Awards.

The recognition celebrates her more than two decades of experience and contributions to brand leadership, marketing innovation and corporate communications across the banking, telecommunications, consumer goods and beverages industries.

Ms Ofori was among seven African women recognised at the international awards, which celebrate outstanding achievements, leadership and innovation in the marketing profession.

Since joining the Ecobank Group in 2018, she has held progressively senior positions across Group and affiliate functions, contributing to the growth and visibility of the bank's brand through initiatives in cards, digital banking and digital marketing.

Her contributions include the introduction of virtual cards across Ecobank markets, the redesign of Ecobank's card portfolio and the launch of Ecobank Mobile 4.0.

Before joining Ecobank, Ms Ofori held senior marketing positions at Vodafone Ghana, where she contributed to the company's transition to its global brand identity and other strategic growth initiatives.

She also held marketing leadership roles at Reckitt Benckiser, Guinness Ghana Breweries and Unilever Ghana, building extensive experience in brand management, innovation, commercial strategy and consumer insight.

Her professional qualifications include an MBA, Associate of the Chartered Institute of Bankers (ACIB) and Chartered Marketer (MCIMG). She is also certified in Digital Marketing and Segment Marketing by Oxford Saïd Business School.

Ms Ofori's recognition places her among a growing number of African women making significant contributions to the global marketing industry.

The other African women shortlisted for the 2026 awards were Jean Okech of Diageo East Africa/East African Breweries PLC (Kenya); Olufunmilola ‘Funmie A. of Union Bank of Nigeria; Lola Soyebo Harris of Alpha Residential (USA/Nigeria); Nomsa Ngubeni of Europa Group (South Africa); Zandi Zinganto (Khwinana) of Revlon South Africa; and Dr Gillian Hammah of GradePoint AI (Ghana).

Ms Ofori was shortlisted in two categories, while Dr Hammah returned to the shortlist after winning the 2025 WiM AI for Impact Award.

The 2026 edition marked the 16th year of the Global Women in Marketing Awards, which recognise women whose professional achievements, leadership and ideas continue to shape the marketing industry.

The awards ceremony was held in London on November 11, 2026.

Ghana News.title: Government must listen to entertainers – Shatta Wale
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaian dancehall artiste Shatta Wale

Ghanaian dancehall artiste Shatta Wale has called on the government to pay greater attention to the concerns and contributions of the entertainment industry, arguing that musicians and other creatives can complement national development efforts.

He said although the government had its own policies and development agenda, authorities needed to engage entertainers and consider their perspectives when formulating interventions that affect the country.

Speaking in an interview on Afternoon Ride with Andy Dosty on Hitz FM, Shatta Wale stressed the need for collaboration between the creative industry and government, insisting that the two could work together to address issues affecting the country.

“What I am creating is not what government is creating. They also have their policies, but I believe sometimes they have to listen to us small. We can work together,” he said.

The musician argued that the music industry had several challenges and concerns requiring government attention, adding that the contribution of entertainment and social media to national life was often overlooked by policymakers.

He further credited social media and entertainment with playing a significant role in keeping the country engaged and functioning, suggesting that their influence extended beyond music and leisure.

“I can boldly tell you that it is social media that is making the nation function, entertainment. If not social media, forget politics. Social media and entertainment has made Ghana very sober, and politicians are not paying attention to that,” he stated.

Shatta Wale believes greater recognition of the entertainment industry, alongside meaningful engagement with creatives, could help government harness the sector's influence for national development.

Ghana News.title: Kwakye Ofosu challenges NPP’s criticism of new executive jet
Ghana News.content:
Government Communications Minister, Felix Kwakye Ofosu

Presidential Spokesperson and Minister of Government Communications, Felix Kwakye Ofosu, has cited former President Nana Akufo-Addo’s criticism of a previous government’s decision to acquire an executive jet to defend the Mahama administration’s purchase of a new Falcon 6X aircraft.

Speaking on JoyNews’ The Pulse on Tuesday, November 17, Mr Kwakye Ofosu said opposition to government decisions to acquire presidential aircraft was not new, pointing to comments made by Nana Akufo-Addo, then the Minority Ranking Member of Foreign Affairs in Parliament in February 2000.

He said Nana Akufo-Addo had criticised Jerry John Rawlings' administration’s planned purchase of a Gulfstream III aircraft, arguing that the expenditure was inconsistent with the country’s economic and social priorities.

Reading from the February 15, 2000 edition of the Parliamentary Hansard, Mr Kwakye Ofosu quoted Nana Akufo-Addo as saying that at a time when the country needed greater public investment in health and tertiary education, the government was considering spending $19 million over five years on an aircraft for the President.

“If anything demonstrates the need that has been consistently urged from this side of the House for us to review and prioritise public expenditure, this case justifies that call. I have no doubt, Mr Speaker, that if the priorities are spelt out properly, the purchase of an executive jet will come very low down on the scale of priorities,” Mr Akufo-Addo was quoted as saying.

"So, this is President Akufo-Addo assailing the Rawlings government for planning to buy the Gulfstream three aircraft," the Presidential Spokesperson added.

Mr Kwakye Ofosu said the opposition to the aircraft purchase continued after the New Patriotic Party (NPP) assumed office under former President John Agyekum Kufuor.

He claimed that former President Kufuor did not use the aircraft during his eight years in office and that a three-member committee was set up to investigate the purchase and found no evidence of wrongdoing.

"Indeed, they did not limit their opposition to that aircraft to just criticism. When they won power, and President Akufo-Addo became foreign minister, President Kufour refused to use that jet for eight years. They even went on and fabricated claims of corruption in the purchase of that aircraft."

"So, they set up a three-member committee chaired by the late J.H. Mensa, which had then Finance Minister Mr. Osafo Marfo and Kwabena Agyapong, then presidential spokesperson as members to look into the purchase. In fact, for eight years they found nothing.

"President Kuffour did not use that aircraft even once. So, it sat down, deteriorated, and then they exchanged," he said.

Mr Kwakye Ofosu argued that the historical opposition to the purchase of an executive jet by the NPP did not provide sufficient grounds to criticise the current administration over its acquisition of the Falcon 6X.

"So Honorable Ablakwa criticizing President Akufo-Addo for decisions that were inconsistent with the economic realities of the Ghanaian at the time is no basis upon which somebody sees to criticize this today," he said.

He also distinguished the circumstances surrounding the two purchases, saying the Mahama administration inherited an economy that had been severely weakened by the previous government.

According to him, the country was grappling with high inflation, a rapidly depreciating cedi and debt challenges, while government had struggled to meet its obligations to bondholders and pensioners.

According to him, the country was grappling with high inflation, a rapidly depreciating cedi and debt challenges, while government had struggled to meet its obligations to bondholders and pensioners.

He cited the participation of former Chief Justice Sophia Akuffo in demonstrations by pensioners demanding payment of their investments as an indication of the economic difficulties at the time.

"In that circumstance, we cannot say that you're going to buy a presidential jet. That also came on the back of a decision by the administration to rent expensive jets when the presidential jet was not available."

He criticised the previous administration's decision to rent expensive jets when the presidential aircraft was unavailable, saying that "If you needed to fly at a time when the jet was not available, there were other affordable options.

"So, you could rent a more modest jet or could go commercial as President Mahama has done."

Ghana News.title: Kwakye Ofosu challenges NPP’s principle on presidential jet purchase, cites 2000 parliamentary debate
Ghana News.content:
Minister of State in charge of Government Communications, Felix Kwakye Ofosu

Government Spokesperson Felix Kwakye Ofosu has questioned the New Patriotic Party's (NPP) consistency on presidential aircraft purchases, citing the party's opposition to the acquisition of an aircraft by the Jerry Rawlings administration in 2000.

He says the party cannot accuse the current government of abandoning its principles over the purchase of a new presidential jet without accounting for its own position when it was in opposition.

Speaking on JoyNews' The Pulse on Tuesday, November 17, Mr Kwakye Ofosu challenged the Ranking Member on Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, to explain what he described as the NPP's inconsistent position on the matter.

Reading from the February 15, 2000 edition of the Parliamentary Hansard, Mr Kwakye Ofosu quoted Nana Akufo-Addo as saying that at a time when the country needed greater public investment in health and tertiary education, the government was considering spending $19 million over five years on an aircraft for the President.

“When he [Samuel Abu Jinapor] speaks about principle, I also can challenge this principle. Where was his principle? Where was the NPP's principle? Where was President Akufo-Addo's principle? In the year 2000, they stood in Parliament and the parliamentary Hansard captures it, and attacked the Rawlings administration for buying an aircraft when they came to power. In fact, they ordered two aircraft. It was President Mills who cancelled one. Otherwise, we would have had two aircraft,” he said.

His comments follow criticism by Samuel Abu Jinapor, who challenged the government's position on presidential aircraft purchases, arguing that its current decision contradicts its earlier criticism of the Akufo-Addo administration.

The Government Spokesperson accused the NPP of selectively invoking the principle of consistency in the current debate while overlooking its own past positions.

He argued that the party was demanding accountability over the current government's aircraft purchase but did not want its historical position on presidential aircraft acquisitions brought into the discussion.

On the criticism of former President Akufo-Addo's use of expensive chartered aircraft, Mr Kwakye Ofosu said he stood by his comments and saw no reason to apologise.

“Absolutely not. People speak about an apology. Look, there is no apology to be had. Apologise for what? Calling out a president who chose to waste our money,” he said.

He maintained that the criticism was justified because of the economic conditions Ghana was experiencing under the previous administration.

“At a time when the president plunged all of us into hardship, he decided that he needed to live like an Arabian king,” he said.

Mr Kwakye Ofosu argued that the criticism was not about denying the President the right to travel safely but about the cost of the arrangements made for his official trips.

He said the previous administration could have opted for more affordable aircraft or commercial flights when the presidential jet was unavailable, rather than incur the cost of expensive chartered flights.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Iraqi PM heads to Lebanon amid push to explore oil routes beyond Hormuz
World.content:
Beirut, Lebanon – Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi is set to visit Lebanon on his latest regional visit aimed at boosting economic cooperation amid the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.

Al-Zaidi will hold a series of high-level meetings in Beirut, including with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam and Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri.

High on the agenda of Wednesday’s talks will be strengthening bilateral trade, customs exemption deals and coordination on security and countering drug trafficking.

Diversifying oil export routes via a pipeline linking the Iraqi city of Kirkuk, through Syria’s Mediterranean port of Baniyas, to Tripoli in northern Lebanon, is also expected to be discussed. The proposed project is aimed at potentially bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, a key energy waterway that has been severely disrupted since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran in late February.

“After the war in Iran and the story of Hormuz and exports in the Gulf, [Iraq] is looking for alternative routes to diversify their export routes,” Walid Marrouch, professor of economics at the Lebanese American University in Beirut, told Al Jazeera.

Iraq’s crude oil exports were badly hit following the start of the Iran war and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s energy passes in peacetime.

Last month, Iraq’s Ministry of Oil said crude oil exports reached about 2.7 million barrels per day (bpd), up from some 200,000 bpd in May. Before the war, Iraq was exporting about 3.5 million bpd. The increase has been boosted by the resumption of oil pumping this week through the Iraqi-Turkish pipeline at an initial capacity of 120,000 bpd.



Still, Iraq has been looking for alternatives to export its crude oil, primarily through Syria, which was previously difficult due to international sanctions under the leadership of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad, who was toppled in late 2024.

Tamer Badawi, an associate fellow with the Royal United Services Institute, said al-Zaidi’s visit to Lebanon was likely to be informed by US envoy Tom Barrack’s “efforts to diversify Iraq’s oil export routes across the region, particularly through Turkiye, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Lebanon”.

He added: “The broader ambition is to develop alternative export corridors connecting Iraq’s oil infrastructure to regional networks.”

‘Lebanon can benefit’

One of the potential proposed alternatives is Tripoli, in northern Lebanon.

The impoverished city has emerged as an option because of the long-defunct pipeline from Kirkuk and a local refinery that in 1940 filtered 21,000 bpd of crude oil from Iraq, according to the Lebanese Directorate General of Oil. The refinery shut down in 1992, shortly after the end of the 15-year Lebanese Civil War in 1990.

Industry insiders say Tripoli’s oil infrastructure has three legacy lines with a historical peak capacity of 900,000 bpd.

While it would need to be repaired and renovated, a report this year by the Basil Fuleihan Institute of Finance (BFIF), an autonomous agency under the tutelage of Lebanon’s Finance Ministry, said “the terminal infrastructure remains a goldmine of latent capacity” with a moderate flow scenario of 300,000 to 500,000 bpd that could gain Lebanon annual revenues in the region of $80m to $275m.

The revenues could be a boon to the Lebanese economy, which has been beset by a complex economic and banking crisis since 2019 that has seen its currency lose more than 90 percent of its value and the majority of its population living in poverty.

Al-Zaidi’s trip to Beirut comes weeks after he met with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa in Damascus. During the visit, the two countries signed a cooperation agreement to rehabilitate the pipeline running from Kirkuk to Baniyas, in a project to be carried out by US energy giant Chevron.

“Upon rehabilitation, this groundbreaking project will have an initial transport capacity of 2 million barrels per day of crude oil,” the US Department of State said in a statement at the time.

Experts said al-Zaidi’s visit on Wednesday was a big opportunity for Lebanon to ensure its place in a prospective tripartite agreement with Syria and Iraq – but warned that if Lebanese officials failed to act, the country could be left behind.



“Lebanon can benefit, but if Lebanon does not get a seat at the table, it [could be circumvented] because Iraq can already reach the sea from Syria,” said Marrouch.

Before reaching Tripoli, Iraqi crude oil would have to pass through some 250km (155 miles) of Syrian territory.

Syria also has its own ports in Tartous and Latakia, with a smaller port in Banias. According to BFIF, Syria is set up to handle about 350,000 to 500,000 bpd, between refineries at Banias and Homs, “a direct Mediterranean outlet that circumvents both the Suez Canal and the Strait of Hormuz”.

The flow of crude oil through Syria would also be a boost for the country, where domestic oil production is currently insufficient and energy costs have spurred protests. Syrian officials have also warned about attacks on the Homs refinery.

But experts believe including Lebanon in the deal could still be beneficial for all parties.

Tripoli’s deepwater quays allow it to handle larger vessels, reducing freight costs per barrel for Iraqi crude and making the oil competitive in European and North American markets, said the BFIF report, adding that Tripoli’s coastline is “naturally shielded from harsh southern winds and rough swells,” unlike in Banias in Syria.

“This makes the port accessible year-round, even during severe Mediterranean winter storms that frequently force the closure of offshore loading operations in Banias,” the report said.

World.title: Religious ruling revives memories in Israel of Rabin assassination
World.content:
As negotiations to form Israel’s next government continue, tensions across Israel have risen to an unprecedented high, evoking memories of the period leading up to the 1995 assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin.

In a letter published last week, Rabbi Gedalia Axelrod, a former head of Haifa’s rabbinical court, invoked a principle in Jewish religious law known as din rodef, issuing a religious ruling that could be used to justify the killing of politicians accused of facilitating a government backed by Arab-led parties. The same principle was invoked by Yigal Amir to justify his killing of Rabin because he had signed the Oslo Accords with the Palestinians.

“The Torah obliges me,” Axelrod later told the Israeli news website Walla. “I knew it was not easy, but if the Torah obliges, then we go. We are Jews, we make sacrifices.”

Axelrod’s ruling has prompted widespread condemnation and demands for a criminal investigation. The Chabad Hasidic movement that Axelrod belongs to has also distanced itself from his remarks.

Twenty former senior Israeli security, military and public figures, including former heads of the country’s intelligence agencies, have called on the authorities to investigate Axelrod. Separately, left-wing member of parliament Ofer Cassif and his fellow lawmaker Michal Rozin have also demanded an investigation, warning of the growing risk of political violence taking hold across Israel.

The controversy comes after Israel’s parliamentary election in late October, in which parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel won 19 of the parliament’s 120 seats. Parties opposed to caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu hold a majority in parliament, but several members of the opposition have refused to cooperate with the Arab parties.

History doesn’t repeat, it rhymes

For many in Israel, mention of din rodef, or the “law of the pursuer”, immediately evokes memories of the tensions and incitement that led up to Rabin’s killing on November 4, 1995.



Rabin’s widow, Leah, directly accused Netanyahu – who was then the leader of the opposition – of helping to foster that climate of hostility. She pointed to his presence at a rally a month before the assassination, at which protesters displayed an effigy of her husband dressed in a Nazi uniform.

Amir justified his assassination of Rabin by arguing that the prime minister’s pursuit of the Oslo Accords endangered Jewish lives, echoing the reasoning now employed by Rabbi Axelrod, who claims that an alliance with an Arab-led party would place Jewish lives at risk.

This conflation of politics and religion, while hardly unique to Israel, amounted to “political theology”, Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav-Shahrabani explained.

“By political theology, I mean the way ideas about God, sacred authority and the chosen people shape political life,” he said of the rules governing who is entitled to rule, who is allowed to belong and whose life must be protected. “Sometimes these ideas are explicit, as in a rabbi invoking divine law against an elected politician. But they can also survive in apparently secular ideas about the nation, sovereignty and historical destiny.”

“Someone who accepts Arab participation in government can then be portrayed as betraying a sacred community, and violence against them can become, in the eyes of a believer, a religious duty,” he said of the rationale behind Axelrod’s ruling.

A real threat

“The threat of political violence is really high,” Cassif told Al Jazeera. “We all remember what happened in 1995 and the atmosphere that preceded Rabin’s assassination. This time it’s worse. Then it was just a few extremists on the fringe; now it’s the mainstream. They’re being openly encouraged by a prime minister who, I think, is ready to consider or do anything to hold on to power.”

Cassif also pointed to far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s own role in the atmosphere of incitement before Rabin’s killing. In October 1995, the month before the assassination, Ben-Gvir was filmed brandishing the hood ornament torn from the prime minister’s car, telling journalists, “We got to his car, and we’ll get to him, too.”

Fears of far-right violence have grown as coalition negotiations have dragged on. Netanyahu and his right-wing Likud party have repeatedly sought to vilify Arab-led parties, both in their campaign ahead of the October 27 election and in their statements since.

Netanyahu has accused the parties of allying with foreign and hostile powers. And he used the swearing-in of the new parliament on November 10, anticipated to be largely ceremonial, to brand the incoming Palestinian politicians “terror supporters, haters of Israel” and denounce opposition politicians considering working with them.



Days earlier, right-wing protesters gathered outside the Herzliya home of Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader now tasked with forming a government, accusing the former general and chief of staff of being a traitor. One protester accused Eisenkot of having murdered his own son, Gal, who was killed in Gaza in December 2023. Turning his attention to Eisenkot’s wife, Hannah, the protester told her she would be joining her son.

“Obviously, this is a tense time,” said political psychologist Daniel Bar-Tal of Tel Aviv University, who has made a study of political violence.

“The ultra-rightists will try to stop the process of changing regimes,” he said, drawing parallels with the January 6, 2021, attack on the United States Capitol by supporters of President Donald Trump. “Thus, it is a dangerous situation.”

“What Netanyahu is doing now is what he’s been doing for years: taking the Arabs, [and] the democratic Jews who work with them, and presenting them to the Israeli public as an overwhelming threat,” Cassif said. “Using minorities and their supporters as a scapegoat has always been a cornerstone of nationalist right-wing policy, and so it is in present-day Israel.”

World.title: CAIR defends civil rights work against Trump’s ‘smear’
World.content:
The country’s largest Muslim advocacy group urges Trump to address rising hate crimes against Muslims instead of attacking its efforts.

The largest Muslim civil liberties organisation in the United States has condemned suggestions by President Donald Trump that it could face a blanket designation as a “terrorist” group.

The Council on American–Islamic Relations (CAIR) said the White House should be addressing violence against American Muslims, rather than attacking the rights group.

“The Trump administration should focus on addressing this surge in violent hate, not entertaining smears against the civil rights organisation that counters such hate,” CAIR said in a statement to Al Jazeera on Tuesday.

On Monday, Trump said he was considering giving a blanket “terrorist” designation to the Muslim Brotherhood and that his administration was also looking at CAIR, which is already classified as a “terrorist” group in Texas and Florida.

“CAIR is another one we are watching,” he said of the organisation.

When asked if he was considering naming CAIR as a foreign “terrorist” group, he responded: “I’m not going to say that yet, but it could happen.”

In its statement, CAIR said that it was “fully prepared to defend our civil rights work and the broader American Muslim community from any new attempts to censor free speech, punish dissent or otherwise undermine the rule of law”.

“Our advocacy for justice here and abroad is the real reason that anti-Muslim and anti-Palestinian extremists spend so much time obsessing over our work,” it said.

‘Clamping down’

Trump’s comments on Monday came during an exchange with reporters outside the White House, following a question about Egypt’s crackdown on the Muslim Brotherhood and whether Washington would consider a broader designation of the group.



Earlier this year, the Trump administration designated the Muslim Brotherhood chapters in Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt as foreign “terrorist” organisations.

Trump praised Egypt, where the Muslim Brotherhood originated, for cracking down on the group, indicating it did so at his request.

“Egypt has clamped down very hard on the Muslim Brotherhood, at my request,” he told reporters as he left the White House on Monday.

“Egypt did a great job,” Trump said.

World.title: Yemeni parliament approves law designating Houthis as ‘terrorists’
World.content:
The law targets the group’s financing and activities as renewed fighting threatens to derail efforts to end Yemen’s war.

Yemen’s parliament has unanimously approved a law designating the Houthis as a “terrorist organisation” and criminalising the group’s activities and financing, as fighting intensifies between the group and forces loyal to the internationally recognised government.

The vote, held over two sessions by videolink on Monday, comes seven years after the measure was first proposed. Parliament said it had deferred the bill, first tabled at a session in the city of Seiyun in April 2019, to give peace efforts a chance.

It noted that the Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, had attacked government-held areas of Yemen and Saudi Arabia, and accused the Iranian-backed group of brushing aside “all options for peace”.

Yemen’s cabinet approved the draft law on October 11. The country’s National Defence Council had designated the Houthis a “terrorist” organisation by executive decision in October 2022. The United States also lists the group as a “terrorist” organisation, and Saudi Arabia treats it as one.

What does the law say?

According to the state-run Saba news agency, the legislation was formally submitted to Rashad al-Alimi, head of the Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, on Tuesday to be signed into law.

It runs to 55 articles and designates the group – including all of its political, military and civilian formations – “a terrorist organisation” and a “rebellious faction”.

It also toughens penalties for offences including seizing state authority, besieging cities, attacking civilians, laying landmines and attacking international shipping. Certain offences would carry the death penalty.



The law also sets out procedures to identify, trace, freeze and confiscate assets linked to the group and its affiliated entities.

Renewed fighting

The vote comes amid months of renewed hostilities after several years of relative calm on Yemen’s front lines. In late June, the Houthis announced an escalation against government forces and Saudi Arabia, saying the move was aimed at lifting what the group describes as a “blockade”.

In early September, a Houthi ground offensive on the western coast gave the group control of parts of Taiz and Hodeidah governorates after government forces withdrew from the port city of Mocha and the strategic Bab al-Mandeb area.

Government forces launched an operation called “Dawn of Yemen” in early October to retake Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa. It initially made limited gains in recapturing territory lost on the Red Sea coast, but on Sunday, pro-government forces withdrew from those areas, allowing the Houthis to advance further.

Heavy fighting continues in Marib, al-Jawf and Lahij governorates, and the Houthis are pressing to take the city of Taiz, which the government and rights groups say is under a tight siege. The Houthis have also stepped up attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia, while the Saudi-led coalition says it is striking facilities that fund the group’s war effort.

The Houthis seized Sanaa in September 2014. United Nations-sponsored talks and regional mediation have failed to end the war since then.

Implications for peace and aid

Ismail al-Suhaili, a political science professor and senior researcher at the Mokha Center for Strategic Studies, said the law marks a shift towards a tougher government position after the failure of peace efforts. Moving the designation from an executive decision to parliamentary legislation gives it wider legal force, he said.

He said it could complicate future negotiations by shifting their focus from power-sharing towards restoring state institutions, disarmament and UN Security Council Resolution 2216.

Al-Suhaili warned that the law could put additional pressure on banks, traders and companies operating between government- and Houthi-controlled areas and deepen Yemen’s financial split. Donors and aid organisations could also become reluctant to work in Houthi-held areas, which could disrupt the delivery of essential supplies to civilians. The Houthis, he said, could respond with further military escalation or with countermeasures targeting government leaders.

Tawfiq al-Hamidi, head of the SAM Organization for Rights and Liberties, told Al Jazeera the law was “a late step” but provides a legal basis for holding those responsible for abuses to account and compensating victims.



While the law narrows the space for political negotiations in favour of military action, al-Hamidi said, it does not entirely rule out a future settlement.

World.title: Photos: Tens of thousands rally in France over living standards and wages
World.content:
Demonstrators have gathered across France after unions called a nationwide strike by public sector workers in a bid to secure pay rises, as protests over living standards and squeezed public services continue to roil the country.

France’s 5.8 million public sector employees were urged to mobilise on Tuesday after talks with Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Friday failed to satisfy union demands for across-the-board pay rises, following last week’s minimum wage boost for private-sector workers.

It is the third united day of strikes and protests in the public sector since September, after a previous mobilisation earlier this month drew hundreds of thousands of workers and saw police fire tear gas as clashes broke out in several cities.

More unions joined the call to strike after Lecornu’s meeting, saying the government’s proposed measures did not address what they describe as an urgent pay and cost-of-living crisis. In Paris, a major rally was taking place in the east of the city, with dozens of other demonstrations planned nationwide.

Police sources told AFP that between 40,000 and 80,000 people were expected to demonstrate in the capital, and up to 300,000 across France. In Paris, university professor Nicolas Prevot said he was marching to defend human rights, protect public services and keep the far right from power in next year’s presidential election.

World.title: Thousands demand cancellation of Nathan Cofnas talk at Oxford University
World.content:
Online petition with more than 32,000 signatures demands the university ‘cancel Nathan Cofnas’s invitation to speak’.

Thousands of people have signed a petition and protests are planned at the University of Oxford against the appearance of Nathan Cofnas, an American academic and self-described “race realist” accused of racism.

Cofnas, who had accused the late Professor Jason Arday of plagiarism last July, is due to give a talk at Oxford’s Oriel College on Tuesday evening at an event organised by the Oxford Reform student society, which is linked to the far-right Reform UK party.

Cofnas has drawn controversy for years with his eugenics-linked views tying race to intelligence, writing that Black people were less intelligent than others in an article which led to his dismissal from his position at a college at Emmanuel College, Cambridge.

He was suspended as a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University in Belgium in August after making plagiarism allegations against Arday, a Black Cambridge professor. Arday consistently denied allegations of plagiarism but acknowledged errors in his work.

Arday was later found dead in his home after resigning his post amid the ballooning scandal.

Cofnas was later allowed to resume some academic work at Ghent remotely, without teaching, while an investigation continued.

The Oxford Reform student society defended its event – titled “Is DEI Undermining Higher Education?”, referring to diversity, equity and inclusion – and said it is “committed to broadening participation in university life”.



In a statement, Oxford University said the event being hosted on its grounds “does not imply endorsement by the College of the views of its speakers”.

An online petition demanding the university “cancel Nathan Cofnas’s invitation to speak” has more than 32,000 signatures.

“Ideas platformed at Oxford do not stay in the lecture theatre”, the petition said.

World.title: Election-winning student movement enters Serbia’s new parliament
World.content:
Hundreds hail Student List lawmakers as the new parliament meets for the first time.

Following the October 25 vote that upended Serbia’s political landscape, the new parliament is meeting for the first time in Belgrade.

The vote redrew Serbia’s parliamentary map as a grassroots, student-led movement won the largest single share, removing President Aleksandar Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS).

The Student List group was backed by 2.3 million citizens, altering the previous parliamentary arithmetic and balance of power. It holds a majority with 140 parliamentary seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with the Serbian Progressive Party’s 104.

Tuesday’s session is chaired by the oldest member of parliament until a new speaker is elected, assisted by the four youngest MPs from the largest electoral lists. Hundreds of supporters cheered the new lawmakers as they entered the National Assembly. The new speaker could be announced later on Tuesday.

The formal agenda follows a clear legal framework: verifying parliamentary mandates based on a report by the Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), taking the solemn oath of office, electing the speaker and deputy speakers, appointing the secretary-general, and forming parliamentary committees and permanent delegations to international bodies.

But beyond legal formalities, the political atmosphere is complex and large sections of the public have high expectations.

A new balance of power

Political analyst Djordje Vukadinovic told Al Jazeera, “Everyone is eagerly awaiting it. I would avoid making any predictions, because with the current opposition structure, you never know what might happen or what stance they will take.”



He added, “What I do know is that this is only the beginning of establishing a new government, and I believe not everything will be wrapped up today.”

Ahead of the session, a group of students wrote to the new lawmakers, reminding them of their “serious” responsibilities.

“All of you are becoming members of parliament in the highest legislative body of the Republic of Serbia for the first time. And only that. Nothing more. The fact that the highest state offices have for decades been presented as ‘comfortable armchairs’ is a systemic flaw. The people elected you. We are the people. You are the people. Act accordingly,” warned the Student Plenum of the Higher School of Civil Engineering and Geodesy in Belgrade in an open letter.

Aleksandar Cupic, an incoming Student List MP and an assistant professor in engineering, said new lawmakers must demonstrate institutional maturity.

“We do not plan to speak about our candidate for five or 10 hours, because that is neither in the spirit of the values we will represent nor is it rational. We owe it to the citizens to proceed with electing the speaker of parliament,” Cupic told reporters ahead of the session.

He said political groups had been consulting one another in a more moderate atmosphere than reports have suggested.

But on Tuesday, tensions were seen outside parliament.

A woman threw yoghurt over Lidija Vukicevic, a well known actress who supports the SNS, outside parliament and the crowd booed Vucic as he walked in.

The Serbian actress and former MP Lidija Vukicevic, who is backing the ruling SNS party, had yoghurt poured over her as she arrived at Serbia’s National Assembly for its first session following elections won by a student-led opposition movement.

The swearing-in session marks the start of a critical political countdown – a 90-day constitutional deadline to elect a new government.

Should that expire without parliament voting in a new cabinet, Serbia’s constitution mandates the dissolution of the National Assembly and the calling of snap parliamentary elections.

The developments are being watched across the region, as well as in European and global political circles.



Observers say the new political leaders will have to govern the state and rebuild sustainable cooperation with neighbouring countries and the European Union – ties that have been strained in recent years.

Echoing that point, Student List representative Aleksandar Baucal told the international EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels that a peaceful transfer of power is only the start of a complex array of work.

“Changing power through non-violent and democratic means is only the first step,” Baucal said in Brussels. “Serbia now faces the task of rebuilding institutions that will prevent the personalisation of power and serve all citizens, regardless of who they voted for. I am convinced that from now on, the news coming out of Serbia will be largely positive.”

In a similar vein, the European Democratic Party (EDP) weighed in on the eve of the parliamentary session.

“Serbia must now heal the wounds of recent years through truth, justice and accountability … we sincerely hope a new chapter of freedom, democracy and reconciliation will begin,” the EDP said, adding that the session will test whether Serbia is ready for institutional reform.

World.title: US officially loses measles-free status after 26 years amid outbreak
World.content:
A major health organisation declares measles endemic in US for first time since 2000, reversing decades of progress.

The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, reversing a public health achievement maintained for 26 years, as the country grapples with its largest outbreak in more than three decades.

The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the Americas branch of the World Health Organization (WHO), declared measles endemic in the US, Bolivia, and Mexico on Tuesday after determining that the same strain of the virus had circulated continuously in the country for at least 12 months.

An international panel of experts that advises PAHO on the prevalence of measles and rubella “recommended that the measles elimination status be withdrawn,” said Dr Jarbas Barbosa, director of PAHO, “a recommendation which I have accepted.”

Measles was declared eliminated in the US in 2000.

PAHO’s announcement follows a review of epidemiological and laboratory evidence submitted by the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The US has recorded approximately 7,700 measles infections since the beginning of 2025, according to CDC figures.

It is the highest number of cases the country has seen in more than 30 years. The climbing numbers come as vaccine hesitancy has grown under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has repeatedly cast doubt on the safety of vaccines despite scientific evidence to the contrary.

Before taking office, Kennedy claimed that no vaccine was “safe and effective” and promoted the discredited theory that vaccines cause autism.

To protect against illness, children are commonly given the measles vaccine in a combined shot with mumps and rubella vaccines, known by the acronym MMR.



But the vaccination rate among preschoolers in the US has fallen to about 92 percent, below the level experts say is needed to prevent major outbreaks.

As health secretary under US President Donald Trump, Kennedy has questioned the MMR vaccine’s ability to protect children.

He has suggested that the MMR’s effectiveness wanes by about 4.5 percent a year and said it contains “aborted fetus debris”, a claim experts have rejected as false.

The CDC has confirmed six measles-related deaths this year, but state health officials in Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York have reported 10 deaths combined, a discrepancy that has fuelled tensions between federal and state health authorities over how measles fatalities are classified and counted.

Measles is considered highly infectious, and the WHO credits the virus with 95,000 deaths worldwide in 2024, mostly among children.

A reversal of decades of progress

Matt Ferrari, a biology professor and director of Pennsylvania State University’s Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics, believes the loss of the US’s measles elimination status can serve as a wake-up call for public health officials.

“This should be a humbling statement for the United States,” Ferrari told Al Jazeera.

For much of his career, Ferrari has studied strategies to control measles in countries around the world. The US was previously seen as a model.

“It was a motivating achievement that we use to drive support for measles elimination programmes all around the world,” said Ferrari. “Now we need to be looking for expertise elsewhere because we haven’t been pulling our weight.”

Edwin Asturias, a professor of paediatrics, infectious disease and epidemiology at the University of Colorado, described the loss of status as a “stain” on the country’s public health programme.

“Measles cases are a signal that your immunisation programme and other systems within your public health services are having problems,” he told Al Jazeera.

Asturias said the US had the resources and experience to prevent the resurgence of the virus, pointing to its success in eliminating local measles transmission for more than a quarter of a century.

About 40 percent of current US measles cases are among adults older than 20, he said, highlighting the need to expand vaccination efforts.

Reaching these populations will require making vaccines available in workplaces, places of worship and other community settings, rather than relying solely on paediatricians and family doctors, Asturias explained.



The loss of elimination status also has implications beyond US borders, as measles can spread through international travel and migration.

“The United States is not, anymore, a place where you’re safe from measles,” Asturias told Al Jazeera. “If you’re a common person walking around with your children, you need to know now that measles has come to the country to stay unless something else is done.”

The risk is particularly concerning for unvaccinated people and those who cannot receive the vaccine, including those with weakened immune systems or undergoing cancer treatment.

What happens next?

Public health experts say the announcement should serve as a catalyst for a more extensive vaccination response.

While they do not expect PAHO’s announcement to prompt a significant change in federal policy, some hope it will spur action among state and local health departments.

Ferrari argued that the US should look to countries with experience containing measles outbreaks, including India, where community health workers visit households to identify children who may have missed vaccinations or whose families may be reluctant to vaccinate.

He also suggested that states may need to reconsider vaccination strategies, including whether to offer an earlier first or second dose to protect young children in areas where measles is circulating.

In the US, children are routinely given two doses of the MMR vaccine. The first dose is typically administered to children at 12 to 15 months of age and the second at four to six years, before they start school. Two doses are about 97 percent effective at preventing measles.

In countries where measles transmission is more widespread, the second MMR dose is often given between the ages of 18 and 24 months.

In June, Pennsylvania began recommending an additional early dose, called a “dose zero”, for infants aged six months and older in areas with sustained measles transmission. Ferrari said this is a perfect example of how states could adapt their approaches locally.

But the prospect of a broader shift in the federal response remains unlikely.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz said last week the agency would continue “doing the same exact thing” in terms of its measles response, if the US lost its elimination status.

For Asturias, the federal response so far raises concerns about whether the country has the public health leadership needed to reverse the outbreak.

“This is hard to see happen,” he said. “But at the same time it is predictable when you don’t have experts running a public healthcare system.”

World.title: Trump’s Whirlwind Asia Trip Begins in the Philippines
World.content:
A painting by the Russian artist Alexey Sergienko depicted the leaders of the United States, Russia and China. It was unveiled in St. Petersburg, Russia, on Thursday.

President Trump sets off this week for meetings in Asia that will culminate in a summit with two strongmen he has often praised: President Xi Jinping of China and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia.

It will be the first time the three men, who command the world’s largest nuclear arsenals, will have sat down together. Mr. Trump plans to discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world and the war against Iran, according to a White House spokeswoman. He is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.

Mr. Trump will travel first to Manila, then to southern China, and will meet with regional leaders confronting an array of uncertainties. Those include the course of the war between the United States and Iran, high energy prices and mounting concern over the risks of artificial intelligence.

For Mr. Trump, the trip will be a pivot to foreign policy and relationships after American voters delivered a swift rebuke to his party in the midterm elections. His trip also comes as his administration faces scrutiny over a scandal involving the former chief executive of Nvidia, the tech giant, which has raised questions about Chinese espionage and American tech exports.

Echoes of Yalta

The highlight of Mr. Trump’s trip is expected to be his meeting with Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin on Thursday in China.

The prospect of their summit has drawn comparisons to the 1945 conference in the Crimean city of Yalta, where the leaders of the United States, the Soviet Union and Britain met to decide the shape of postwar Europe.

The White House has said that Mr. Trump wants to discuss the threat of nuclear proliferation. U.S. officials have expressed concerns about China’s accelerating nuclear buildup, expected to reach 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030.

The last nuclear arms control treaty between the United States and Russia expired in February. Trump administration officials have said that any new agreement on nuclear arms control must include China, but Beijing has shown no interest in the topic. China has an estimated 620 nuclear warheads, compared with the more than 5,000 that Russia and the United States have each, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Image DF-61 nuclear missiles were displayed at a military parade in Beijing last year. China, which has the world’s fastest-growing nuclear arsenal, has made clear it that is not interested in arms control talks. Credit... Tingshu Wang/Reuters

U.S. administration officials said they did not expect a deal out of the meeting, which they characterized as a starting point for discussions.

The gathering has prompted concern in Ukraine that Mr. Putin might push for a deal, deciding Ukraine’s fate without Kyiv’s involvement. A U.S. administration official said Ukraine was not expected to be part of the discussion between the three leaders.

U.S. Partners Look for Reassurance

Mr. Trump will start his trip in the Philippines, the oldest American treaty ally in the Asia-Pacific region, as the United States faces questions about its support for its partners in a region where China’s military and economic might continues to grow.

In Manila, President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. plans to discuss with Mr. Trump the South China Sea, where the Philippines and China have competing claims. Philippine officials have said that they hope Mr. Trump’s visit might result in more American military assistance.

Image President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. of the Philippines spoke at a meeting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila on Sunday. Philippine officials hope Mr. Trump’s visit might result in more U.S. military aid. Credit... Pool photo by Lisa Marie David

Mr. Trump is also expected to meet with leaders of ASEAN, a Southeast Asian grouping of 11 nations, as well as a gathering of the so-called Quad grouping of the United States, India, Australia and Japan.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of Australia said on Sunday that he expected “lots of engagement” with Mr. Trump during the meetings.

“Obviously, that’s our most important ally,” he said. “But we want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts that are around the world.”

Chinese analysts described the meeting of the Quad group, formed in part to counter China, as an effort by Mr. Trump to project power after his party’s defeat in the midterms. “Its symbolic value outweighs its practical value,” Xu Liping, a senior scholar at Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, told Shanghai Observer, a state-run outlet.

The Spy Scandal

After Manila, Mr. Trump will travel to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, where he will meet Mr. Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation.

Jensen Huang, a key adviser who accompanied Mr. Trump on his last trip to China, will not be by his side. Mr. Huang helped shape the president’s views about technological competition with China and persuaded him to loosen restrictions on selling advanced chips to China.

Mr. Huang stepped down from his role at Nvidia after revelations that he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was collecting intelligence on Mr. Huang for Beijing. China has rejected the allegations, calling them “smears.” Ms. Huang has not responded to requests for comment.

So far, the president has not raised the issue with Mr. Xi and is not expected to during their meeting on Thursday. But the saga is likely to cause unease in China about whether Washington will impose tighter controls on the export of technology to the country.

As a result, U.S.-based analysts speculated that Mr. Xi might try to use his personal relationship with Mr. Trump to forestall such restrictions.

Image In September, Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, sat at the same table as Mr. Trump during a White House state dinner for Mr. Xi. Mr. Huang had traveled with Mr. Trump to China before, but will not this time. Credit... Doug Mills/The New York Times

Yun Sun, director of the China program at the Stimson Center in Washington, said Mr. Huang’s downfall would likely mean “there is going to be more anxiety on the Chinese side about their access to American chips.” She expects Mr. Xi to emphasize the importance of easing U.S. controls on chip exports to China during their meeting.

Cooperation between China and the United States on artificial intelligence may be more difficult after the Nvidia scandal.

Still, there may be progress on the creation of a notification system that would allow the countries to alert each other about national security issues related to artificial intelligence, which the two sides agreed to in September.

“There’s some shared concern on both sides that U.S. or Chinese models might be misused by bad actors and cause damage to the U.S., China, or other countries,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution focusing on China’s technology development.

Xi May Have a New Calculus

When Mr. Xi sits down with Mr. Trump in Shenzhen, he will be dealing with a president who will soon face a new constraint at home: a Democrat-controlled Congress.

Lawmakers may pressure Mr. Trump to tighten export controls against China or accelerate weapons sales to Taiwan, according to Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser focusing on U.S.-China relations at the International Crisis Group. That means that “Xi will have to work much harder to keep Trump on side,” Mr. Wyne said.

Mr. Trump will be the first American president to visit China twice in one calendar year.

Analysts say the leaders’ summits, which have included state visits in Beijing and then in Washington, have been the only thing holding together a fragile détente between the two countries as they clash over A.I., export controls, Taiwan and other issues.

The two sides declared a trade truce last year when they met in Busan, South Korea. That deal, which was to expire this month, has been extended until January.

Image Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi after their meeting in Busan, South Korea, last year. Analysts say their summits have been the only thing holding together a fragile détente between the countries. Credit... Haiyun Jiang/The New York Times

China’s restrictions on the export of crucial rare-earth metals and rare-earth magnets, which are needed to manufacture most modern technology, remain one of the most difficult unresolved issues.

Mr. Trump is likely to raise this with Mr. Xi, according to a senior U.S. administration official who said that China’s continued restrictions is one reason Washington only agreed to a two-month extension of the trade truce.

Ana Swanson contributed reporting from Washington, Aie Balagtas See from Manila, and Laura Chung from Sydney, Australia.

World.title: Ecuadorean Fishermen Who Survived U.S. Boat Strike Sue Trump Administration
World.content:
Ecuadorean fishermen sued the United States in U.S. federal court this week, claiming American military drones bombed their vessel in the Pacific Ocean earlier this year. It is the first lawsuit by survivors of a boat strike who are seeking accountability for a Trump administration campaign that has been cloaked in secrecy.

Since September 2025, U.S. forces have carried out 72 strikes against alleged drug-trafficking boats, killing at least 244 people, a tally by The New York Times shows.

Filed Monday in Pittsburgh, the suit seeks financial damages for 17 fisherman from the port city of Manta, Ecuador, and an order halting U.S. strikes on small boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific.
