Expected outcomes include harmonised judgment templates and drafting standards, a quality-assurance framework, improved legal research support and stronger institutional collaboration.

The retreat is also expected to produce an agreed 2027 judicial calendar, guidelines for external and virtual court sessions, recommendations on procedural instruments and measures to improve the utilisation of the electronic case management system.

The 2026 Judicial Retreat is aligned with the ECOWAS Court’s Strategic Plan 2026–2030, which seeks to strengthen judicial efficiency, expand access to justice, promote regional integration and reinforce the rule of law and protection of human rights across West Africa.

World.title: Troops arrest seven suspects, recover 38 phones in Jos
World.content:
By Golok Nanmwa

JOS – Troops of Sector One, Operation Enduring Peace (OPEP), have arrested seven suspected criminals and recovered 38 mobile phones and other suspected stolen items during separate operations in Jos North Local Government Area of Plateau State.

The operations, involving troops deployed in Jos and Naraguta, also led to the recovery of a suspected stolen motorcycle, a toy pistol and a Mercedes-Benz E350 car.

Parading the suspects before journalists, the Media and Information Officer of OPEP, Captain Polycarp Oteh, said the first operation followed a report of phone-snatching at gunpoint on November 6, 2026.

He said the report led troops to Prime House Hotel along Ring Road, Jos, where five suspects were arrested.

Oteh identified them as Tahir Suleiman, 25; Muhammed Ahmed, 25; Muhammed Labaran Haruna, 27; Yahya Yunusa, 20; and Aisha Mohammad, 22.

Items recovered during the operation included 38 mobile phones, 27 phone pouches, three MP3 devices, two earpods, an HP laptop, four smartwatches, a dagger, four power banks and a Mercedes-Benz E350 with registration number Plateau BBK-01NB.

He said the operation was in line with the mandate of the Commander, Operation Enduring Peace, Maj. Gen. W.M. Dangana, to sustain peace and security across Plateau State, particularly during the yuletide season.

The OPEP spokesman further disclosed that troops deployed at Naraguta, working with members of the Vigilante Group of Nigeria (VGN), arrested two additional suspects during a routine patrol.

He identified them as Mudasiru Ishaq, 27, and Hasiya Sani, 22, adding that they were allegedly found in possession of a suspected stolen Boxer motorcycle and a toy pistol.

Oteh said all seven suspects, alongside the recovered items, would be handed over to the Plateau State Police Command for further investigation and possible prosecution.

“These operational successes underscore the commitment of the Commander of Operation Enduring Peace, Maj. Gen. W.M. Dangana, to combating criminal activities while ensuring the safety of lives and property within its Joint Operations Area,” he said.

He reiterated the commander’s directive for sustained intelligence-driven operations and effective collaboration with other security agencies and local vigilante groups to deny criminal elements freedom of action.

Oteh urged members of the public to remain vigilant and provide credible and timely information to security agencies to support ongoing efforts to restore and sustain peace in Plateau State.

World.title: ADC to INEC: Don’t tamper with our leadership, candidates
World.content:
…files 17 grounds of appeal against Lifu’s judgment

By Luminous Jannamike

ABUJA – The African Democratic Congress (ADC) has asked the Court of Appeal to restrain the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) from altering its leadership records and the nomination particulars of its presidential and governorship candidates pending the determination of its challenge to a judgment by Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court, Abuja.

The party is seeking to stop INEC from implementing a judgment it considers legally defective, arguing that any changes to its leadership records or candidates’ particulars before the appeal is decided could undermine the outcome of the proceedings and jeopardise its preparations for the 2027 elections.

In a statement by the Director of Strategic Communication of the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Phrank Shaibu, the party said its 17-ground Notice of Appeal challenged the trial court’s jurisdiction to entertain what it described as an internal party leadership dispute.

It also questioned the treatment of an earlier Federal High Court judgment delivered on July 2, 2026, concerning its leadership transition, which it maintained remained valid and had not been set aside.

“The 17 grounds challenge the foundation, findings and orders of Justice Lifu’s judgment. The ADC has asked the Court of Appeal to examine whether the trial court had jurisdiction, whether the claimant had standing, whether disputed evidence was properly assessed, and whether the sweeping orders made against the party can stand in law,” Shaibu said.

Beyond the substantive appeal, the ADC is separately challenging a July 24, 2026, ruling which granted Hon. Nafiu Bala Gombe leave to amend his originating summons despite the party’s pending preliminary objection to the trial court’s jurisdiction.

In its appellant’s brief, the party argued that the court ought to have determined the jurisdictional objection before considering Gombe’s application to amend the suit.

It further contended that the proposed amendment altered the description of parties and the capacity in which a defendant was sued without prior leave of court.

The brief, settled by Chief J.S. Okutepa, SAN, the ADC’s lead counsel in the appeal against the amendment ruling, seeks to set aside the order and have the outstanding jurisdictional objection considered.

The ADC also argued that Justice Lifu proceeded to judgment on the basis of an amended court process that was already the subject of an appeal, before the appellate court had determined whether the amendment was properly granted.

The party warned that allowing INEC to act on the November 5 judgment before the appeal is resolved could create changes that would be difficult to reverse, even if the ADC eventually succeeds.

“These are serious questions before the Court of Appeal. INEC must not make changes that could preempt the court’s decision or put the party’s candidates in jeopardy while our applications are pending. We are asking the court to protect the subject of the appeal so that its eventual decision has practical effect,” Shaibu said.

The ADC said it was making the legal challenge public to clarify the issues before the appellate court, insisting that it would defend its leadership and the decisions of its members through lawful means.

World.title: APC accuses ADC, NDC of sponsoring violence at rallies
World.content:
Minister of solid minerals development, Dele Alake.

The All Progressives Congress (APC) Presidential Campaign Council has accused opposition parties, the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), of allegedly sponsoring violence and orchestrating protests at its campaign rallies ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The council also alleged that the opposition parties were using artificial intelligence-generated images, deepfakes, fake news and other propaganda techniques to manipulate public opinion against President Bola Tinubu and the APC.

The allegations were contained in a statement issued on Tuesday by the council’s spokesperson, Dele Alake.

The council recalled that ahead of the flag-off of its presidential campaign rally in Kaduna on October 24, it had warned Nigerians about what it described as plans by opposition elements to create tension, promote disharmony and introduce violence into political campaigns.

It alleged that the ADC and NDC had devised strategies involving sponsored protests and misinformation to portray widespread public discontent against the Tinubu administration.

The APC campaign council further alleged that opposition elements were mobilising young Nigerians to disrupt its rallies by chanting ‘Bamaiyi’ and carrying banners.

It cited an incident at a mosque in Abuja last Friday, alleging that some protesters threw stones at the presidential motorcade.

The council commended security personnel attached to the presidential convoy for exercising restraint during the incident.

It also praised Tinubu for directing the Abuja Police Command to release those detained in connection with the incident.

The statement further expressed concern over alleged attacks and threats against some APC members and supporters in the South-East, claiming that they were being labelled saboteurs for not supporting the NDC presidential candidate, Peter Obi.

It also alleged that APC campaign billboards were being destroyed by individuals sponsored by opposition elements.

The council described the alleged incidents as unacceptable, insisting that the country’s democratic space should remain open to all political parties and candidates.

Reaffirming its position on peaceful political campaigns, the APC campaign council said it supported credible, free and fair elections across the country.

It urged leaders of the ADC and NDC to desist from allegedly mobilising young Nigerians for activities that could expose them to danger.

The council also called on political parties to conduct their campaigns peacefully and allow Nigerians to freely support candidates of their choice.

World.title: NRS seeks media partnership to tackle illicit financial flows
World.content:
By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief

The Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) has called for stronger collaboration with the Nigerian media to combat illicit financial flows (IFFs), which it said continue to deprive the country of substantial revenue needed for economic growth and national development.

The Service made the call on Tuesday at a media workshop in Abuja, where it urged journalists to deepen their understanding of illicit financial flows and strengthen investigative reporting to expose financial leakages and revenue losses.

An NRS official, Idris Abdullahi, said illicit financial flows were denying the government resources that could otherwise be channelled into critical infrastructure, healthcare, education and other socio-economic development programmes.

He emphasised the importance of media engagement in raising public awareness, exposing vulnerabilities and promoting accountability in the management of the nation’s financial resources.

Speaking at the workshop, an expert in illicit financial flows investigations, Adebayo Kayode, said Nigerian journalists required specialised training to enable them to play a more effective role in identifying and exposing suspicious financial activities.

Kayode said there was a fundamental difference between reporting that money had disappeared and investigating how, why, through whose arrangements and under what institutional circumstances it disappeared.

He said journalists needed the capacity to examine customs declarations, corporate ownership structures, extractive-sector export records, government budgets, procurement processes and tax policies to identify inconsistencies and potential revenue losses.

According to him, journalists must also understand the implications of financial statistics and regulatory decisions to ensure accurate reporting without exaggerating or downplaying their significance.

He described the fight against illicit financial flows as a national development imperative rather than a political contest, stressing that the scale of the challenge required collective action by government agencies, regulators, development partners, civil society organisations, the private sector and the media.

However, Kayode cautioned that collaboration must not compromise press independence, insisting that journalists should remain free to question government policies, investigate wrongdoing and hold public institutions accountable.

He said responsible governments should welcome an informed media that demands evidence, insists on transparency and helps citizens understand how public resources are managed.

On the way forward, Kayode identified the National Action Plan for 2027–2030 as an important framework for strengthening Nigeria’s response to illicit financial flows.

He said the plan’s success would depend not only on the institutions responsible for its implementation but also on effective public scrutiny and media engagement.

He urged journalists to pay closer attention to emerging areas of financial vulnerability, including virtual assets and cryptocurrency transactions, blockchain monitoring, extractive-sector activities, beneficial ownership, customs and trade integrity, public procurement and public asset transparency.

Other areas he identified included the licensing and taxation of virtual asset service providers, suspicious financial transactions, trade misinvoicing, corporate ownership disclosures, procurement-related financial risks and evidence-based investigations into unexplained wealth.

He also stressed the need to monitor production, valuation, exports and proceeds in the extractive sector to ensure that Nigeria receives the full value of its natural resources.

Kayode maintained that journalists had an important role in moving the country from fragmented financial information to integrated intelligence, from detection to prevention, and from policy declarations to measurable results.

Although journalists might not conduct forensic audits, issue regulatory licences or prosecute financial crimes, he said their investigations could expose institutional weaknesses, uncover financial irregularities and stimulate public demand for accountability.

He urged participants to ensure that the training translated into more rigorous investigative reporting, better-informed citizens and stronger institutions.

“The fight against illicit financial flows is ultimately a fight for the future of Nigeria. It is about protecting the integrity of our economy, safeguarding public revenue, strengthening our institutions and ensuring that the nation’s resources serve the people,” he said.

He called on journalists and relevant institutions to work together to trace financial movements, interrogate evidence, expose vulnerabilities and promote accountability, warning that funds whose movements were not properly traced could remain beyond public scrutiny.

World.title: Makinde Campaign faults Tinubu over federal recruitment embargo
World.content:
The Makinde-Daura Presidential Campaign Organisation (MDPCO) has criticised President Bola Tinubu over the Federal Government’s decision to impose an embargo on federal employment, describing the policy as insensitive to the plight of Nigerians, particularly youths seeking jobs.

The organisation said the decision contradicted the All Progressives Congress (APC)’s promises on job creation and raised concerns about the government’s commitment to addressing unemployment.

In a press statement dated November 17, 2026, and signed by its Director of Strategic Communications, Richard Nnanna Ihediwa, the campaign organisation described the recruitment freeze as an indication of what it called the shortcomings of the Tinubu administration’s economic policies.

It also expressed concern that the embargo could precede possible mass retrenchment in the public service under the guise of fiscal discipline, particularly if Tinubu secured re-election in 2027.

The organisation cited World Bank estimates that approximately 3.5 million Nigerians enter the labour market annually, arguing that restricting federal recruitment would further limit employment opportunities for young people.

The MDPCO also rejected the Presidency’s explanation that the embargo was intended to consolidate public service reforms and enable the government to properly determine personnel requirements for the 2027 budget.

It argued that the government should instead focus on expanding the economy, harnessing the country’s human and natural resources, and creating employment opportunities.

The campaign organisation further faulted comments attributed to the Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, describing Nigerians complaining about hunger and hardship as lazy.

According to the statement, the 2027 general election would provide Nigerians an opportunity to assess the economic direction of the country and decide on the leadership they want.

It contrasted the Federal Government’s recruitment policy with what it described as employment-generating initiatives under Oyo State Governor, Seyi Makinde.

The organisation said Makinde’s administration had expanded economic opportunities in Oyo State through public and private sector initiatives, particularly in agriculture, infrastructure, education, transportation and other critical sectors.

It specifically highlighted the establishment of the Oyo State Agribusiness Development Agency (OYSADA), which it said had transformed traditional farm settlements into modern agro-industrial hubs.

Other initiatives cited included investments in power generation, aviation, road infrastructure, water resources, revenue reforms and improvements in the public workforce.

The campaign organisation said Makinde’s proposed RESET Nigeria Agenda was anchored on expanding economic opportunities, reducing waste without weakening public institutions, maintaining fiscal discipline without restricting employment, and pursuing economic stability without undermining citizens’ livelihoods.

It said the agenda offered an alternative economic direction ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

The organisation urged Nigerians to consider Makinde, who is the presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), for the 2027 election, arguing that his administration’s development approach in Oyo State could be replicated at the national level.

World.title: INEC urges stakeholders to collaborate for peaceful, credible elections
World.content:
The Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) in Kwara has called on stakeholders to collaborate with the commission to ensure credible, peaceful and successful elections in 2027.

The state Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC), Mr Ahmed Yushau, made the call during a stakeholders’ meeting held on Tuesday at the INEC office, Ilorin.

Yushau urged Nigerians to recognise that the responsibility for ensuring credible elections rests on all citizens, not on INEC alone.

According to him, every stakeholder has a role to play in the electoral process.

He stressed the need for stakeholders to respect the rights of others while fulfilling their obligations to the state.

He also urged citizens to support security agencies in maintaining a safe and peaceful environment.

The REC noted that the police and other security agencies need public cooperation to discharge their responsibilities effectively.

He emphasised the importance of public knowledge of electoral laws and guidelines, urging stakeholders to study INEC regulations, manuals and procedures rather than relying solely on the commission for information.

According to him, adequate knowledge of the legal framework will prevent misinformation, misunderstanding and possible manipulation during elections.

He urged stakeholders, particularly media practitioners and political actors, to keep and study copies of relevant electoral documents to understand their rights and responsibilities.

The REC, recalling his time as a pension officer in the Office of the Head of Service, said the knowledge of regulations and circulars was essential to avoid misleading the public.

He stressed that stakeholders with informed understanding of the electoral laws would be better positioned to engage constructively with INEC and hold the process accountable.

He reiterated that credible elections required collective responsibility, mutual respect and compliance with the law, urging all stakeholders to work together towards peaceful elections in the state.

A stakeholder, Mr Olatunji Gabriel, representing the African Democratic Congress (ADC) in Kwara, commended INEC for organising the forum.

Gabriel described the meeting as successful, saying it enabled political parties, NGOs and other stakeholders to exchange views with INEC on its level of preparedness for the elections.

The Kwara chairman of the National Democratic Party (NDP), Mr David Ifabiyi, urged political parties to adhere to electoral rules and promote peaceful conduct ahead of the forthcoming general elections.

Ifabiyi called on state chairmen of political parties to caution their members against acts that could disrupt public peace and advised them to remain law-abiding throughout the electoral process.

The NDP chairman urged security agencies and other social actors to support efforts towards ensuring a peaceful election.

He said Kwara was known for its peaceful disposition, urging stakeholders to sustain the reputation by promoting unity, tolerance and peaceful coexistence.

World.title: World Bank: MSMEs in Developing Countries Face $4trn Finance Gap
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

* Insists addressing financing constraints stifling MSMES’ ability to create jobs critical

Ndubuisi Francis in Abuja

Micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) across developing countries face a $4 trillion finance gap that limits their ability to grow, trade, compete, and create jobs at scale, a new World Bank Group report has said.

The Finance and Prosperity 2026 report, which was released on Tuesday, revealed that MSMEs account for 90 per cent of businesses and employ 75 per cent of workers, yet encounter significant barriers to accessing credit and equity financing.

Between 2019 and 2023, the MSME finance gap reached $4 trillion.

The report tracked country-level finance gaps over time showing where shortfalls are concentrated, while also identifying constraints that limit providers’ ability to assess and serve MSMEs, especially in International Development Association (IDA) countries as well as fragile and conflict-affected settings.

According to the MSME Finance Gap report also released on Tuesday, with 1.2 billion young people in developing countries reaching working age over the next 10–15 years, closing these gaps will be critical to accelerating job creation and opportunities for a rapidly growing workforce.

Financial systems in EMDEs have largely proved resilient to a broad range of global challenges, including trade and investment policy uncertainty, geopolitical tensions, elevated interest rates and conflict and fragility.

The World Bank noted that despite growing concerns over sovereign and corporate debt burdens around the world, financial systems had remained relatively stable to date.

However, it stated that this resilience was uneven across countries, and at risk of fraying in some parts of the world.

According to the report, this was notably in the Middle East and North Africa, Afghanistan, Pakistan and sub-Saharan Africa regions—where the youth employment crisis is most acute, and weak financial institutions are especially vulnerable.

“In this context, policymakers and regulators in developing countries would do well to carefully monitor their financial systems and build resilience to shocks.

Digital money, payment innovations and artificial intelligence (AI) applications in financial services and supervision are rapidly expanding across EMDEs.

They can be drivers of financial sector efficiency and inclusion promoting inclusive growth and jobs. At the same time, policy makers need to manage new risks such as rising digital fraud, illicit activity and cyber vulnerabilities.

“Deeper domestic capital markets can mobilize private capital for investment, growth, and jobs in EMDEs, but many markets remain shallow, with limited liquidity and narrow investor bases.

“To unlock this potential, policy makers should promote strong policy, legal, regulatory, and institutional frameworks; stronger domestic institutional investors; and a broader range of financing instruments to crowd in private capital.

“Over the next 10 to 15 years, around 1.2 billion young people in developing countries will reach working age, yet current trends suggest a major shortfall in the availability of jobs. Micro, small- and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) will be critical to meeting this jobs challenge.

“Globally, MSMEs account for approximately 70% of all jobs; in low-income and lower-middle-income economies, the share is even higher, reaching 80% to 90%,” the report said.

It stated that developing countries must address the financing constraints that stifle the ability of MSMEs to grow and create more and better-paid jobs.

“It is estimated that formal MSMEs in EMDEs need $4 trillion worth of credit to reach their full productive potential, equivalent to 11% of GDP. Meanwhile, there is an estimated shortfall of $1.4 trillion in equity investment – equivalent to 3.3% of GDP – for early-stage and growth financing of formal MSMEs.

“Narrowing these gaps is possible, but it requires deliberate action: implementing the reforms that allow countries to harness the transformative potential of financial technology and data-driven finance, while also addressing the distinct challenges of longer term and equity financing, which are critical for firms seeking to grow and scale,” the report added.

World Bank Group Vice-President for Prosperity, Pablo Saavedra, said: “MSMEs face four major constraints to growth: they are invisible to financial systems because they lack a digital footprint of their transactions, disconnected from markets and services, burdened by regulatory complexity, and chronically underfinanced.

“The World Bank Group’s new MSME strategy will put our own financing to work, alongside private lenders and investors, to expand credit to the businesses with the highest potential to grow.”

The World Bank Group’s new MSME strategy, launched in October 2026, will use data and digital tools to make these enterprises visible, connected, enabled, and funded.

Through the strategy, the Bank Group will support banks, fintechs and governments by sharing risk, investing equity and cutting red tape, with a particular focus on fragile and conflict-affected countries.

The Finance and Prosperity Report also examined overall financial sector performance in EMDEs.

The conflict in the Middle East has contributed to rising commodity prices, tightening financial conditions, and increased volatility, all of which pose risks to vulnerable EMDEs.

Financial markets’ resilience was uneven across countries, and the outlook remains subject to much uncertainty, with significant risks ahead.

Banks’ large holdings of fragile sovereign debt can be a major risk in some countries. Most countries facing high financial sector risks lack sufficient capacity to deal with financial stability challenges and should urgently shore up prudential supervision and financial sector safety nets.

The World Bank Group’s Finance and Prosperity 2026 report also highlighted the growing insurance protection gap in EMDEs when facing natural disasters. Over the last decade, financial losses that were not covered by insurance exceeded 80% in parts of Africa, Asia, and Latin America.

Key policy recommendations include reducing risk and enhancing the availability and affordability of natural disaster insurance.

World.title: Speaking Truth is Best Reputation Strategy for Any Organisation, Says United Nigeria Airlines boss
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

The Executive Chairman of United Nigeria Airlines (UNA), Prof. Obiora Okonkwo, has said that speaking the truth is the best reputation management strategy for any organisation.

Speaking during a dialogue on Responsible Business Communication: Building Trust and Financing Investments for Sustainable Human Development at the 2026 World Public Relations Forum (WPRF) in Abuja on Tuesday, the UNA boss maintained that organisations must not confuse reputation protection with withholding or manipulating facts, warning that attempts to conceal the truth could eventually cause greater damage than the original crisis.

He added that telling verified truths demonstrates respect for stakeholders and helps build confidence in an organisation, irrespective of how uncomfortable the information might be.

Recounting an incident in which UNA diverted to Asaba instead of Abuja, Okonkwo explained that the aircraft was scheduled to fly from Lagos to Abuja but landed in Asaba following an error by the dispatcher, who mistakenly entered Asaba as the destination in the flight documentation.

He said the pilots followed the destination indicated in the documents and landed accordingly, while the cabin crew, believing they had arrived in Abuja, welcomed passengers to the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

According to him, the incident itself was not necessarily a major crisis until the airline’s communication team issued an inaccurate explanation.

Okonkwo said the airline’s communication team, in an attempt to protect the company’s reputation, attributed the incident to bad weather in Abuja, despite the fact that the aircraft had landed in Asaba because of an error in its flight documentation.

Okonkwo cited another experience involving a passenger who threatened never to fly United Nigeria Airlines again, not because of a delayed flight but because the airline departed earlier than its advertised time.

He said the passenger complained that the airline had advertised an 11:30 a.m. departure but took off at 11:20 a.m.

He said: “A typical Nigerian traveller has his mind set on the timely departure of the airline, and if anything happens, you have to communicate the truth. You may have an AOG, technical issues, and sometimes that message doesn’t really sink.

“I had a passenger last week who sent me a message saying they will never fly United Nigeria Airlines anymore and I said, why? He said, because they left on time. He said United Nigeria Airlines advertised departure for 11:30am but departed at 11:20am, and as the chairman, I was actually worried about how to respond.

“I wanted to get angry, I wanted to shout back at him. But again, my experience being a member of this forum came into play, and I simply sent him a message saying, ‘I apologise for United Nigeria Airline leaving on time.’ That was my answer. He never got back.”

He continued: “The best word of public relations is to tell the truth and challenge responsibly. Whenever the truth is told, it builds trust, it builds confidence, and it also shows respect for stakeholders.”

Professor Okonkwo further emphasised that crisis communication should not be regarded as the exclusive responsibility of corporate affairs or public relations departments, insisting that organisational leadership must take collective responsibility for communicating with stakeholders during difficult situations.

“Communication is not only the responsibility of the corporate affairs department. When there is a crisis and there is a need for proper communication, leadership quality is also called into question. It becomes a collective responsibility of leadership,” he stated.

He urged airlines and other service providers to deploy all available communication channels, including airport information displays, information technology platforms and social media, to keep customers informed about operational developments.

He also advocated prompt disclosure of issues affecting flight operations, including industrial actions and safety concerns.

“Do you have a strike? Announce that you have a strike. That’s why we are disrupting our services. Do you have a safety issue? Announce!” he said.

While speaking, the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, said building public trust sometimes required organisations and government institutions to adhere strictly to communicated timelines, whether they were delivering earlier or later than expected.

He said the passenger’s complaint was a reminder that organisations must explain deviations from what they had communicated, even when such deviations appeared to be positive.

“Sometimes building trust requires that you be on time, not earlier and not later. And if you go earlier than you communicated previously, you must explain,” Oyedele said.

Drawing a parallel with government revenue performance, the minister said some departments under the Ministry of Finance occasionally exceeded their revenue targets without providing explanations.

He said where an agency projected revenue of 10 but generated 12, it was important to establish whether the original target was too conservative or whether the additional revenue was a one-off occurrence.

“I need to know whether your 10 was too conservative. Maybe it should have been 15. I also need to know whether this extra 2 is sustainable or whether it’s one-off,” he said.

The session also featured Edith Jibunoh, Director of External Affairs at the World Bank Group, and Sharon Ezzeldin, founder of Honor Public Relations in the United Kingdom.

It was moderated by Kyembe Kyalusanza, Head of Corporate Communications at Zambia National Commercial Bank (Zanaco).

World.title: NDC: Tinubu’s N11.2trn Pipeline Security Bill Exceeds Twice Defence Budget
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

* Party demands forensic audit of NNPCL’s energy security expenditure

* Seeks disclosure of N11.2tr payments to private contractors

Sunday Aborisade in Abuja

The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has questioned the transparency of the Federal Government’s management of pipeline security expenditure, alleging that the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL) has an opaque N11.2 trillion balance linked to energy security costs and other deductions from oil revenues.

The opposition party, which expressed concern over what it described as questionable financial disclosures in NNPCL’s audited accounts, said the amount was more than twice the N4.91 trillion allocated to all defence and security agencies in the 2025 budget.

It also claimed that the disputed sum was more than three times the N3.10 trillion allocated to the Ministry of Defence for the Army, Navy and Air Force combined.

The NDC, therefore, demanded an immediate forensic audit of the N11.2 trillion balance, insisting that the government must account for every naira spent on protecting the country’s oil infrastructure, while the Armed Forces continue to grapple with inadequate funding for military equipment.

In a statement issued Tuesday by the spokesperson of its National Campaign Council, Dr. Chiogo Constance Ikokwu, the party said the financial disclosures raised serious questions about the government’s spending priorities, particularly against the backdrop of escalating insecurity across the country.

The statement, titled, ‘How Tinubu’s Administration Presides Over an Opaque N11.2 Trillion Pipeline Security Bill That Doubles the Entire Military Budget While Starving Our Armed Forces and Insecurity Continues to Escalate’, alleged that the amount recorded as ‘other receivables from the Federation’ was tied to energy security costs and unverified off-budget deductions.

According to the NDC, the disparity between the alleged pipeline security expenditure and allocations to the country’s military establishment demands urgent public scrutiny.

“While insecurity continues to escalate across Nigeria, with citizens abducted, slaughtered on farmlands and forced to pay crippling ransoms, this administration presides over books showing trillions tied to protecting oil conduits, even as our Armed Forces remain starved of modern weaponry,” the party said.

It added: “Strip away the accounting jargon, and this N11.2 trillion expenditure looks like nothing more than a massive political patronage slush fund disguised as ‘energy security’.

“Are patronage payouts to political allies now worth more than Nigerian lives?”

The opposition party, however, acknowledged that protecting the country’s oil pipelines and other critical petroleum infrastructure was essential to national economic security.

It argued that the government should adopt modern surveillance technologies and transparent expenditure mechanisms rather than allow huge sums to accumulate under what it described as poorly explained financial arrangements.

The NDC cited fibre-optic sensors, surveillance drones, satellite radar and transparent Host Community Development Trusts as some of the technologies and institutional mechanisms that could strengthen pipeline protection while reducing security costs.

It maintained that the government should prioritise investments in modern equipment for the Armed Forces instead of allowing substantial oil-related security expenditures to remain outside transparent public scrutiny.

The party also questioned the structure of military spending, citing figures which it said showed that 75.9 per cent of the 2026 core defence budget of N3.15 trillion was devoted to personnel costs, while only 14.7 per cent, representing N464 billion, was allocated to capital expenditure on military equipment.

It further alleged that only seven per cent of the 2025 Defence Capital Budget had been released, describing the situation as evidence of the funding challenges confronting the country’s security establishment.

The NDC argued that the alleged funding imbalance could undermine the operational capacity of the military at a time when troops were confronting multiple security threats across different parts of the country.

It said: “Instead of 21st-century technology and empowering our Armed Forces, where 75.9 per cent of the 2026 core N3.15 trillion budget goes to personnel and only 14.7 per cent (N464 billion) to capital weapons, after just seven per cent of the 2025 Defence Capital Budget was released, this government chose opaque patronage.”

The party outlined three demands which it said were necessary to restore public confidence in the management of the country’s petroleum revenues and security expenditure.

First, it demanded an immediate forensic audit of the N11.2 trillion NNPCL energy security balance, with full disclosure of payments made to private contractors and a clear breakdown of legacy deductions.

Second, it called for comprehensive disclosure of funds released for military capital equipment and troop welfare in 2025 and 2026.

Third, it demanded an end to what it described as off-budget deductions, insisting that all oil revenues should be paid into the Federation Account and subjected to appropriation by the National Assembly.

The NDC maintained that Nigerians were entitled to know how much the government spent on protecting oil infrastructure, the identities of contractors involved, the services rendered and the extent to which the expenditure had improved security in oil-producing communities.

It also argued that transparency in the management of petroleum revenues was particularly important because of the country’s persistent security challenges and the competing demands on scarce public resources.

“A government that prioritises opaque political patronage over human life while insecurity continues to escalate has lost its moral legitimacy,” the party declared.

The opposition party subsequently urged Nigerians to support its presidential ticket of Peter Obi and Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, saying the candidates were committed to changing the country’s political and economic governance structure.

“The Obi/Kwankwaso ticket believes that Nigeria must work for all, and not a few,” it said.

The statement did not, however, provide a breakdown of the individual transactions making up the N11.2 trillion balance or identify the private contractors allegedly involved in the expenditure.

World.title: Foundation to Support Diabetic Patients with Locally Sourced Foods
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Oghenevwede Ohwovoriole in Abuja

The Florence Ayodele Ajao Foundation (FAAF) has announced plans to support people living with diabetes by providing them with locally sourced foods to help manage their blood sugar levels.

The founder of the foundation, Olayinka Deborah Ajao, made this known during the official launch of FAAF and a public awareness campaign on the dangers of diabetes and how it can be managed, held in Abuja over the weekend to mark World Diabetes Day 2026.

Ajao called on well-meaning Nigerians to support the initiative, which she said would provide affordable food options for diabetic patients, alongside glucometers to enable them to monitor their blood sugar levels.

She said, “We are trying to tell people, we are bringing our support to diabetes patients to tell them that there are some locally sourced food that are cheaper, that you can buy in the market. Or we are giving you the locally sourced food to help you curb your sugar.

“By the time you take this food in portion control, in moderation, we would expect that you get a good result when you combine it with the medications your doctors are giving you.

“In FAAF, we are not giving anybody medication because so many other foundations are already doing that. I guess my foundation will be the first to start to give out food to diabetes patients.

“And I think that will help a long way because we are also giving them glucometer to help them check and monitor their sugar levels every day and also record it for empowerment.”

Explaining the motivation behind the foundation, Ajao said she was inspired by her desire to contribute to humanity and honour her late mother, who lived with diabetes.

“I wanted to do something for humanity. And I didn’t know which niche to pick from. I just wanted to do something and then I said, why not diabetes? Because my mum was a diabetic before she passed.

“And I decided to honour her with the name, of the foundation,” she said.

She also said the foundation had brought in a medical team to educate members of the public on basic emergency response procedures, including cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), to equip them to respond when people collapse or choke in public places.

“People don’t even know what to do when they see people collapsed on the floor or are choking to death; that is why we actually brought CPR to teach people. Because we want to curb the ignorance and the stigmatisation people attach to people living with some illness,” she emphasised.

She called on well-meaning Nigerians to support the foundation’s efforts to provide succour to people living with diabetes.

Speaking at the event, Dr Chinasa Tony said diabetes was not a death sentence, stressing that the condition could be prevented, controlled and managed.

“Diabetes is not a death sentence. It can be prevented. It can be controlled and it can also be managed,” she said.

She advised people living with diabetes to pay attention to portion control and adhere to their prescribed medication, noting that avoiding starchy foods alone did not necessarily prevent the condition.

“Because even if you say you’re not eating those starchy food,: Even with you eating all those meals that are not starchy food, you can still have diabetes. Portion control is very, very important. And also take your drugs too,” she said.

Tony also urged medical personnel to closely monitor patients using insulin to prevent their blood sugar levels from dropping dangerously low.

“In using insulin, it must be monitored. If not monitored well, the sugar level can go so down that the person can enter into coma,” she warned.

She further called on Nigerians to regularly check their blood sugar levels and avoid late-night eating.

Also speaking, a counselling psychologist, Chibuzor Stella, urged families and medical personnel to show people living with diabetes love, care and encouragement.

“When a patient is down with diabetes, you have to show them love, because even the Bible said that love conquers all things, if somebody have diabetes, doesn’t mean that that person is going to die immediately,” she said.

She encouraged patients to remain committed to their treatment plans, adding, “You have to encourage the person to always stick to the medicationl already prescribed to he or she, and that is the way out.”

World.title: Alleged Cyberbullying: INEC Lawyer Alleges Harassment by Sowore’s Supporters
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

*Commission files motion to set aside subpoena on chairman

Lead counsel to the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). Alex Iziyon, SAN, on Tuesday told a Federal High Court in Abuja that supporters of African Action Congress (AAC) presidential candidate, Omoyeye Sowore, have been harassing him since he took the brief of the electoral commission.

Sowore, who is standing trial for allegedly cyberbullying President Bola Tinubu, recently opened his defence. Among the politician’s application was to serve a subpoena compelling the appearance in court of INEC chairman, Prof. Josh Amupitan.

However, Iziyon expressed concern over those who have been inundating him and his legal team with calls and text messages, pleading, “Please, let the courts do this job. Leave the lawyers. Leave their jobs.”

He told the court that his client had filed an application seeking to set aside the subpoena issued on the INEC chairman at Sowore’s instance.

Izinyon said his client wants the subpoena set aside on grounds of alleged irregularities. He added that the application was ripe for hearing since Sowore had been served and was expected to respond.

He also faulted the claim by Sowore’s lawyer, Reuben Adakole, that his client filed an application to amend the subpoena.

The senior lawyer argued that Sowore’s lawyer could not introduce another application seeking to amend the subpoena without properly addressing the existing challenge.

He further argued that the applicant should first clarify whether Sowore intended to withdraw the original subpoena or proceed with the application to amend it.

Izinyon contended that the subpoena could not simply be altered by Sowore without an appropriate order by the court.

Earlier, the trial judge, Justice Mohammed Umar faulted the ex-parte motion filed by Sowore to amend what he said was a defect in the subpoena issued on the Chairman of INEC.

Adakole had told the court that the motion was seeking the court’s permission to amend the subpoena issued by the court and regularise its service on the INEC chairman, adding that he was ready to move it.

Justice Umar however, questioned the propriety of filing an ex parte application when parties were already before the court.

The judge said since the subpoena had already been served and challenged, any application seeking to alter or regularise it should involve the affected parties.

He ordered Sowore’s lawyer to make his application on notice and serve the other parties. The judge adjourned till November 23.

Shortly before the case was adjourned, Izinyon told the judge that since he served Sowore with INEC’s application to set aside the subpoena, his office had received numerous text messages, some of which expressed respect for him, some questioned why he got involved in the case, while others suggested that he was attempting to humiliate or rubbish an individual.

Izinyon expressed concern about the nature of the messages and appealed to those behind the messages to allow the court to hear and determine the case.

Izinyon said: “Please, let the courts do this job. Leave the lawyers. Leave their jobs.”

He further suggested that the messages could have come from supporters of individuals involved in the matter, even though he did not establish who were responsible.

Justice Umar also expressed displeasure that the issue about his ill-health, which informed why the court did not sit on the last day, was made a media item.

He said: “I was not feeling fine. Since I came, I have never been sick. I am a human being. I don’t know why it should be a subject of announcements all over the world that I was sick.”

World.title: All Nigerian Teachers Must Be Registered, Licensed by 2027, Says TRCN Registrar
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

* As Adamawa deputy gov sits for professional qualifying exam

Kuni Tyessi in Abuja

The Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) has declared that all teachers in the country must obtain professional certification and licences to practise, saying the end of 2027 is the deadline for full compliance.

The Registrar/Chief Executive of TRCN, Dr. (Mrs.) Ronke Soyombo, said the council was intensifying efforts to professionalise teaching through compulsory registration, licensing and professional qualifying examinations, warning that teaching without the required certification would no longer be tolerated.

Soyombo, who disclosed this during an interaction with journalists in Abuja, said the council had made significant progress in enforcing professional standards, adding that even senior public office holders were not exempted from its qualifying examination.

She revealed that the Deputy Governor of Adamawa State recently sat for the TRCN professional qualifying examination, demonstrating that the council’s certification requirements applied to everyone, irrespective of status.

“In Adamawa State, for the first time, we actually saw the deputy governor of Adamawa State coming to sit for our exam,” she said.

“She sat for the exam on Friday. And that’s to tell you that everybody that owns schools or those that are putting in effort into education are coming to sit for the exam,” she said.

The registrar, however, disclosed that the council recorded a disturbing case of examination impersonation in Taraba State during its latest professional qualifying examination, where an invigilator reportedly identified more than 47 individuals attempting to write the examination on behalf of registered candidates.

“One of my girls actually went to lead in Taraba to be the invigilator. She actually said she got over 47 impersonators,” Soyombo disclosed.

She explained that the council had strengthened its examination security through the introduction of candidates’ photographs, surveillance cameras and other technological measures to identify examination offenders.

According to her, the use of candidates’ photographs in the examination process has helped the council identify individuals attempting to sit for examinations on behalf of other people.

The registrar said the council had also introduced a more sophisticated examination platform capable of accommodating 5,000 candidates at a time, compared with its initial capacity of 120 candidates.

She, however, acknowledged that the recent examination experienced connectivity challenges in two states, despite being conducted across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

Soyombo said the council was working with its technology developers to address the challenges and improve the efficiency of subsequent examinations.

On the broader professionalisation drive, she explained that TRCN registration and certification were compulsory for teachers, while professional licences must be renewed every three years through evidence of participation in Mandatory Continuous Professional Development (MCPD).

“Every teacher must be certified, every teacher must be licensed before they can actually teach in our schools,” she declared.

She explained that certification would be obtained once in a lifetime, while practising licences would require renewal every three years to ensure teachers continually update their knowledge and professional competencies.

World.title: Enugu Assembly Passes Bill To Curb Arbitrary Rent Increases
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Gideon Arinze in Enugu

The Enugu State House of Assembly has passed an amendment to the Landlord and Tenant Law aimed at protecting tenants from arbitrary rent increases, excessive agency charges and unfair eviction.

The passage followed the adoption of a report presented by the Chairman of the Joint Committee on Housing and Foreign Investment, Judiciary, Public Petitions, Ethics and Privileges, Mr Anthony Mbah, during plenary Tuesday in Enugu.

Presenting the report, Mbah said the amendments were informed by widespread complaints from residents over exploitation and extortion in the process of securing rented accommodation across the state.

He said the amended law provides for a four-year period before landlords can increase rent, with subsequent increases restricted to two per cent of the annual rent.

According to him, where rent adjustments are necessitated by modifications or renovations carried out on a property, the increase must not exceed 10 per cent of the annual rent.

“The law introduces a bond account to be managed by the Office of the Attorney-General, into which tenants would deposit 10 per cent of their annual rent,” he said, adding that the deposit would be refunded to tenants without interest after they vacate the property.

On tenants’ protection against arbitrary eviction and legal proceedings, Mbah said landlords must properly serve tenants before initiating court action.

“A tenant must be properly served before being charged to court. Without proper service, no case should be established or treated in the first instance,” he said.

He expressed confidence that the amended law would address more than 60 per cent of the challenges residents face when securing rented accommodation in Enugu State.

World.title: ‘90% fake’: MaMkhize’s ‘designer’ fashion up for auction [video]
World.content:
MaMkhize's personal items have gone on auction again. Images via X

Hundreds of supposedly designer fashion items from MaMkhize’s wardrobe have gone under the hammer at auction in a bid to recoup her R120 million outstanding SARS debt. However, an industry expert has claimed that up to 90% of the goods are fake

The auction includes the listing of clothes, handbags, shoes, jewellery and other accessories whose authenticity could not be confirmed

Over the years, the businesswoman, real name Shauwn Mkhize, has also been accused of tender fraud, corruption, and forgery.



MAMKHIZE: MORE PERSONAL ITEMS GO ON AUCTION

Last week, over 1000 personal items, including designer clothes, handbags, shoes and jewellery, went under the hammer at a court-ordered auction.

On Monday, another 400 items were listed.

The auction house, Bidders Choice, has stated that many of the goods in the auction could not be authenticated.

The auction forms part of SARS’s ongoing efforts to recover over R120 million in MaMkhize’s outstanding taxes – both personal and business-related. The matter dates back to November 2024, when the Durban High Court granted SARS a search and seizure warrant.

Since then, several auctions have taken place over the year, with items such as luxury cars, movable assets, and even designer alcohol going under the hammer.

Last month, the High Court ordered that five properties in Sandown, Johannesburg, linked to MaMkhize and her family, be sold.



FAKE?

Meanwhile, an industry expert has boldly claimed that nearly all the designer items currently on auction are counterfeit.

In a video posted by TimesLIVE, Sandton boutique owner David Leven – speaking from the auction at Mooikloof – stated that a friend who had previously done authentication work for SARS told him that of the items on auction, that “90% were fake”

Pointing to a green crocodile-skin Hermès Birkin bag, Levin said: “It’s not real….I’m in the industry [I know my stuff]”.

WATCH | David Leven, owner of a high-end Sandton boutique, attended the auction of Shauwn Mkhize’s items out of curiosity. Despite it being his first auction, he believes 90% of the items are fake, a view shared by some bidders at the venue.



Video: @Koena_xM pic.twitter.com/QGBq1ZK30n — Sowetan (@Sowetan1981) November 16, 2026

It’s not the first time the authenticity of MaMkhize’s personal items has been called into question.

Last year, Bidders Choice claimed that only 23 out of 200 designer handbags and luggage pieces were authenticated.

World.title: Gayton McKenzie says sorry to Tatjana Smith, launches attack on Swimming SA
World.content:
Tatjana Smith celebrates after winning a gold medal at the Paris Olympics in 2024. Image: Anton Geyser / Team SA

Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie has ordered a full investigation into Swimming South Africa (SSA) following Olympic champion Tatjana Smith’s decision to pursue her swimming career under the Dutch flag.

McKenzie also issued a public apology to Smith, accusing the national swimming federation of treating one of South Africa’s greatest sporting champions disgracefully.

READ | Roland Schoeman blasts Swimming SA after Tatjana Smith’s shock Netherlands switch



Speaking at a media briefing at Parliament on Tuesday, 17 November, Gayton McKenzie said he had lost complete faith in Swimming SA and believed the federation needed urgent intervention.

Smith shocked South African sport last week when she announced that she intended to represent the Netherlands, following growing tensions with Swimming SA over sponsorship arrangements, fines and prize money.

READ | THIRD South African Olympic swimmer to pursue career under another flag

Gayton McKenzie said he had no ill feelings towards the swimmer for her decision, arguing that the federation’s treatment of her had contributed to her departure.

“She’s been treated in the worst possible way. They should be ashamed.

“And what angered me the most is that immediately after we got the news that Tatjana is going to swim for the Netherlands, they tried to cover up and make her the scapegoat,” he said.



€46 000 penalty and withheld prize money

Gayton McKenzie highlighted Smith’s lengthy battle to receive money owed to her following her performances at the 2023 World Championships in Fukuoka, Japan.

According to the minister, Smith was invoiced €46 000 for an alleged sponsorship infringement after she failed to wear a particular sponsor’s brand.

Swimming SA subsequently withheld her prize money, resulting in a prolonged dispute over payment.

McKenzie said Smith only received the money in 2024 after instructing her lawyers to pursue legal action.

The minister also said his department had ensured that all money owed to the swimmer by the department was paid without delay.

“We paid her as fast as she swims. We want to thank her for the years that she’s given, for the medals that she’s given us, for what she’s done for this country,” he said.

Gayton McKenzie described Smith as South Africa’s greatest Olympian and said she deserved an apology for the way she had been treated.

SASCOC given 90 days to investigate Swimming SA

McKenzie has written to the South African Sports Confederation and Olympic Committee (SASCOC), requesting a full investigation into Swimming SA’s administration and financial affairs.

The investigation will examine the federation’s sponsorship agreement with Arena, including the penalties imposed on athletes and who was responsible for paying them.

McKenzie also wants investigators to establish whether other swimmers have been fined or had prize money withheld.

However, the investigation will extend beyond the sponsorship dispute.

The minister said SASCOC had also been asked to examine how money was spent on the Franschhoek High-Performance Centre and identify alleged shortcomings in Swimming SA’s constitution.

He believes Smith may have been made a scapegoat for broader administrative problems within the federation.

“I’ve asked it to establish how the Arena sponsorship agreement works, what penalties were levied and who paid them, and whether other swimmers were fined or had money held back.

“I’ve asked it to look at how money was spent on the Franschhoek High-Performance Centre and the flaws in the federation’s constitution. And that’s why our swimmers are choosing to represent other countries,” McKenzie said.

SASCOC’s acting head, Lwandile Simelane, has pledged to complete the investigation within 90 days.

McKenzie said regulations require SASCOC to deal with the matter first, making its investigation an important initial step before further action can be considered.

McKenzie says Swimming SA needs urgent intervention

The minister has also called for a task team to help stabilise the federation, describing its current condition in particularly strong terms.

“I’ve asked SASCOC to deploy a task team to stabilise the federation, because the federation is in ICU. And we should not run away from that,” he said.

McKenzie warned that Smith should be the last South African athlete to experience such treatment from a national sporting federation.

“But I want to assure South Africans that she’s the last athlete who will be treated in such a fashion by these federations. That is not how a national federation should treat the people it exists to serve,” he said.

Tatjana Smith’s departure raises questions about South African swimming

Smith won Olympic gold in the 200m breaststroke at Tokyo 2020 and silver in the same event at Paris 2024.

Her decision to pursue representation by the Netherlands has raised wider questions about athlete welfare, funding and the administration of South African sporting federations.

McKenzie’s intervention now places Swimming SA’s sponsorship arrangements, financial management and governance under scrutiny.

The outcome of the 90-day SASCOC investigation could prove significant for the federation and the future of South African swimming.

For now, McKenzie has made his position clear: he believes Smith deserved better and wants those responsible for the federation’s administration to answer questions about how it operates.

World.title: St James retirement village plans have residents up in arms
World.content:
Plans for a retirement village on PRASA land between St James tidal pool and Danger Beach have raised concerns about traffic, public access and coastal views. Image: Facebook @KalkBaycommunity

Plans for a seaside retirement village on railway land between St James tidal pool and Danger Beach have sparked opposition from residents concerned about the future of one of Cape Town’s most recognisable coastal stretches.

The proposed development would occupy approximately 1.1 hectares of Passenger Rail Agency of South Africa (PRASA)-owned land in St James, including the Danger Beach car park, historic station master’s houses, tennis courts, the railway station and an old post office.

READ | Kalk Bay tidal pool battle: Protesters vs Brass Bell



Residents of St James and neighbouring Kalk Bay fear the project could affect public access, coastal views, the area’s heritage and an already congested transport route.

The proposal forms part of a wider property development programme by Intersite Asset Investments, a subsidiary of PRASA, which has identified six railway-linked sites in the Western Cape for private investment.

R3.6 billion development programme

The six proposed projects represent a combined investment of approximately R3.6 billion.



They are expected to deliver around 790 residential apartments and more than 4 400 student accommodation beds across sites in Eerste River, Somerset West, Stellenbosch, Kalk Bay/Muizenberg and Cape Town Station.

Intersite CEO Annette Lindeque previously described the development awards as an important step in the company’s strategy to turn strategically located railway assets into mixed-use precincts.

The broader objective is to attract private investment, make better use of underutilised public assets and strengthen the role of rail infrastructure in economic development.



However, the proposed St James retirement development has raised questions about whether the coastal location is suitable for further residential construction.

Residents raise concerns about traffic, views and public access

The Kalk Bay and St James Ratepayers and Residents Association has expressed concern about the lack of information available to the community.

Rex Schilling, a key figure in the association, said residents had raised questions and received acknowledgement but had not received substantive feedback from PRASA.



He also highlighted concerns about transport access, particularly following recent wildfires that demonstrated the vulnerability of infrastructure in the area.

Traffic congestion and limited parking are already challenges along this stretch of the False Bay coastline. Residents fear additional residential development could make the situation worse.

The visual impact is another concern, with artist impressions reportedly showing buildings of up to four storeys.



Residents fear the proposed structures could obstruct ocean views and change the character of the coastal neighbourhood.

City says no land-use application has been submitted

The City of Cape Town has confirmed that it has not received a land-use application for the proposed development.

This means the municipality has not yet been able to assess the project’s potential planning and environmental impacts.



The City said any future proposal would have to go through the relevant statutory planning processes and comply with municipal regulations.

Given the site’s public significance, the City also indicated that any application would be widely advertised, allowing interested and affected parties to examine the plans and submit objections or comments.

The community is preparing to scrutinise any formal application, including through legal, environmental and heritage assessments.



Political concerns over the choice of location

GOOD Secretary-General and Western Cape MPL Brett Herron has also questioned whether the site is appropriate for residential development.

Herron argued that residential densification should be focused on urban inner cores rather than extending into peripheral locations such as the St James coastal site.

Meanwhile, the residents’ association is coordinating community feedback and has requested documents under the Promotion of Access to Information Act (PAIA) to establish how the development was selected and what decisions have been made.



For now, the proposed retirement village remains at an early stage, with no land-use application submitted to the City.

The next steps will be closely watched by residents concerned that a major private development could change the character and accessibility of one of Cape Town’s best-known seaside areas.

World.title: SA Rugby quick to react to Rassie Erasmus’s six-Test BAN
World.content:
SA Rugby has requested a full misconduct hearing for Springbok head coach Rassie Erasmus following his six-match suspension. Image: SA Rugby website

SA Rugby has requested a full misconduct hearing for Springbok head coach Rassie Erasmus following his six-match suspension imposed by an independent World Rugby panel.

The request comes after the panel found that comments made by Erasmus about match officials following South Africa’s Nations Championship clash against France amounted to serious misconduct.

A SA Rugby spokesperson confirmed that the organisation respected the disciplinary process, but wanted Erasmus to be given an opportunity to explain the context of his remarks.



The organisation also wants the coach to assure the panel that he did not intend to suggest that any match official had acted with ulterior motives.

SA Rugby said it trusted that the hearing could be expedited, given the seriousness of the charge.

The organisation added that it would not make any further comment until the hearing had been completed.

Why was Rassie Erasmus suspended?

World Rugby announced that Erasmus had been suspended for six international matches after an independent panel reviewed comments he made during a media conference in Dublin on Monday.

The panel considered his remarks about the television match official (TMO) following the Springboks’ controversial match against France.



It ruled that the comments suggested match officials had acted with bias or prejudice, or had deliberately influenced the outcome of the match.

The panel concluded that, taken as a whole, the comments represented an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the officials.

The sanction was imposed under World Rugby’s Match Official Abuse Sanction Process, introduced in July 2026 to provide a framework for dealing with public criticism of match officials.

What does the six-match suspension mean?

The suspension applies immediately and covers international match days.

Rassie Erasmus is prohibited from coaching, having direct or indirect contact with team management or players on match days, entering the stadium or technical areas, approaching match officials and participating in match-official feedback processes.

He is also barred from carrying out media duties during the suspension.

However, SA Rugby’s request for a full misconduct hearing could provide an opportunity for the circumstances surrounding his comments to be considered further.

The organisation has made clear that it wants the coach to explain his intentions and the context in which the remarks were made.

The outcome of that hearing will be an important next development in a disciplinary dispute that has placed the Springbok coach’s international match-day involvement under scrutiny.

The Springboks are due to play Ireland in Dublin on Saturday, 21 November at 18:40 (SA time).

World.title: BREAKING | Rassie Erasmus banned for six Tests
World.content:
Springbok head coach Rassie Erasmus has been suspended for six international matches by World Rugby. Image: Charmaine Visser

Springbok head coach Rassie Erasmus has been suspended for six international matches following an independent disciplinary review of his comments about officiating during South Africa’s Nations Championship clash against France.

The suspension takes immediate effect and follows a media conference earlier this week in which Erasmus made wide-ranging comments about match officials, particularly the television match official (TMO), following Friday’s encounter.

An independent panel ruled that the comments amounted to serious misconduct under World Rugby’s Match Official Abuse Sanction Process.



The process was introduced in July 2026 in collaboration with national member unions, competitions, International Rugby Match Officials and the International Rugby Players’ Association.

It operates alongside World Rugby Regulation 18 and provides a framework for dealing with public criticism of match officials, particularly comments that could undermine their integrity or expose them to online abuse.

Why has Rassie Erasmus been suspended?

The disciplinary panel considered Rassie Erasmus’s comments using the Match Official Abuse decision-making matrix.



The panel, chaired by senior Australian officer Adam Casselden SC, concluded that the threshold for serious misconduct had been reached.

It found that the comments suggested match officials had acted with bias or prejudice, or had deliberately influenced the outcome of a match.

The panel further determined that, when considered as a whole, the statements amounted to an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the match officials.



It also considered the timing and reach of Erasmus’s comments, as well as the allegations of bias or bad faith.

The panel concluded that the conduct amounted to disrespecting the authority of match officials by questioning their integrity.

A six-match automatic suspension was therefore imposed.



What does the suspension mean for Erasmus?

The sanction is particularly significant because it extends beyond simply preventing Rassie Erasmus from coaching from the sidelines.

During the suspension, he is prohibited from having any match-day involvement at international fixtures.



This includes:

Coaching the Springboks on match days

Direct or indirect contact with team management or players on match days

Entering the stadium, coaches’ box, playing enclosure or technical area

Approaching or communicating with match officials

Participating in any match-official feedback process

Carrying out media duties during the suspension

The restrictions apply to international matches and take effect immediately.

Erasmus has right to full misconduct hearing

World Rugby stressed that respect for match officials is fundamental to rugby and that officials must be able to perform their duties without abuse or intimidation.



The governing body acknowledged that robust debate about officiating is part of the game, but emphasised that teams have established channels for raising concerns before and after matches.

It drew a distinction between challenging a decision and questioning an official’s integrity in a way that could expose them to personal abuse.

Rassie Erasmus is entitled to have the matter referred to a full misconduct hearing.



The six-match suspension marks a significant development for the Springboks, with the team’s head coach facing restrictions on his involvement on international match days following the fallout from the France encounter.

WORLD RUGBY’S RAPID RESPONSE TO RASSIE’S RANT

An independent disciplinary panel ruled that his comments crossed the threshold for serious misconduct under World Rugby’s Match Official Abuse Sanction Process.



The framework was introduced in July 2026, with backing from national unions, competitions, International Rugby Match Officials and the International Rugby Players’ Association.

It operates alongside Regulation 18 and aims to provide a consistent approach to public criticism of match officials.

The panel used a decision-making matrix to assess Erasmus’ comments against a set of defined criteria.



After reviewing his remarks about the match television match official (TMO), it concluded that they suggested match officials had acted with bias or prejudice, or deliberately influenced the result.

Chaired by Australian senior officer Adam Casselden SC, the Match Official Abuse Committee ruled that the comments amounted to an unacceptable attack on the credibility and competence of the officials.

The panel also considered the timing and reach of Erasmus’ statements, alongside the allegations of bias and bad faith.



It concluded that his conduct undermined the integrity and authority of match officials, triggering an automatic six-match suspension.

The ban takes immediate effect and applies to international matches. It also prevents Erasmus from having any match-day involvement with the team, including:

Coaching or providing direct or indirect contact to players and team management.

Entering the stadium, coaches’ box, playing enclosure or technical area.

Approaching or communicating with match officials on match days.

Taking part in any match official feedback process.

Carrying out media duties during the suspension.

ERASMUS RESERVES THE RIGHT TO APPEAL

World Rugby reiterated its commitment to protecting match officials, stressing that their wellbeing and integrity must be respected throughout the game.



The governing body acknowledged that robust debate over refereeing decisions is part of rugby, but insisted that teams have established channels for raising concerns before and after matches.

It added that challenging a decision is different from questioning an official’s integrity or making comments that could expose them to personal abuse.

Erasmus retains the right to have the case referred to a full misconduct hearing.
