World.title: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
World.content:
LONDON — When European nations said they wanted greater involvement in Ukraine peace talks, this was almost certainly not what they had in mind.

Europe has long demanded more say in negotiations to end Russia’s war, fearful of being frozen out by Washington and Moscow. They dread a deal favorable to President Vladimir Putin — who will meet President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a historic three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.

The good news for them is that the United States says it is now pushing to include Europe in the next rounds of diplomacy. The bad news, say governments, officials and foreign policy analysts, is the alarming new suggestion from Trump’s team: that the entire future of European security should be up for discussion too — the same demand that Putin has pushed for years.

To the Russian leader, redrawing Europe’s security map means scaling back NATO’s presence, righting what he perceives as the injustices imposed on Moscow after the Soviet Union’s collapse. A succession of senior European officials have lambasted the idea, warning that Washington risks “walking into Moscow’s trap,” as Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, put it.

“This is all rather bizarre,” former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves said, summing up this sentiment in an interview with NBC News on Monday.

It’s not clear how or why the U.S. came to float a maximalist demand that Putin first made in 2021, one that was widely rejected by Western governments months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. But in recent days, as Washington ups its pressure for a breakthrough in peace talks, Russia and the U.S. have both revived the idea.

Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and envoy, wrote Friday that talks should tackle the “broader postwar European security arrangements.”

Earlier this month, he lamented “decades of mistrust” and “competing security concerns” between Russia and Europe, vowing to address these by building an “enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” Kushner has also stressed that NATO would remain central to European defense and that no country should have a veto over another’s alliances.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy, center, flanked by U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, following their meeting near Dublin last week. Paul Faith / AFP via Getty

Trump himself has also hinted that he seeks a final deal encompassing the entire continent. “It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” he told reporters in the Oval Office earlier this month. “I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.”

Instead, the idea has been met with unease and dismay, viewed by many in Europe as echoing Putin’s hard-line war goals.

Whereas Kushner described Europe and Russia as neighbors unable to resolve their differences, the historical record shows the aggression has chiefly been directed one way. Russia seized Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula in 2014, then launching a full-scale invasion in 2022, while waging sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation against the West.

Kushner’s suggestion also touches on a central European fear: that Washington will pursue a deal at almost any cost, even if that emboldens Putin to expand his aggression.

“Why are two real estate agents pushing this idea?” Ilves said referring to Kushner and Steve Witkoff, another Trump envoy, both of whom made their fortunes in real estate before entering diplomacy.

“These people aren’t even diplomats,” said Ilves, who led his former Soviet republic from 2006 to 2016. “I’m not sure they have much of an idea of the long history of the development of security architecture in Europe relating to Russia.”

Asked about the criticisms, assistant White House press secretary Olivia Wales said the U.S. proposal sought to “strengthen existing European security arrangements, with NATO at their core, while developing practical mechanisms to prevent future conflict.”

Security guarantees for Ukraine “cannot be designed without understanding the broader security framework in which they will operate,” she said in an email, adding that any final agreement must respect Europe and Ukraine’s sovereignty “and be agreed by the relevant parties.”

European officials are nonetheless unnerved by Kushner’s remarks.

Kallas, the E.U. foreign policy chief, described Russia’s maximalist war demands as “really absurd,” while German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pointed out that “Europe has a security architecture — we don’t need a new one.”

Elsewhere, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the rules were not the issue: “The problem is that Russia is breaking them.” And even Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was adamant that the “security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe and NATO, not by Russia.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the idea as “dangerous,” saying that European security “should not be the main agenda.”

Ukraine’s view is that Russia is in no place to make such demands, given that it’s spent more than four years failing to win the war.

“At this stage, the most Putin can negotiate is a fair ceasefire along the current line of contact,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said. And “frankly, Europe does not need a new security order; it already exists, and Russia is constantly violating it.”

Kyiv and its European backers also argue that a ceasefire must come before any peace talks, accusing Russia of stalling so it can keep bombing civilian infrastructure ahead of the frigid winter.

If Europe accepts Russia’s demands about wider continental security before there is a ceasefire, Moscow “will try to create the impression that it’s our fault that the war continues, because we don’t want to accept all their demands,” according to Sven Biscop, a director at the Egmont Institute, a Belgian think tank.

He said he believed dialogue with Russia is a good thing, a view echoed by influential Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who in an interview with the Financial Times published Tuesday said that it had been “irresponsible” to outsource talks with Putin to the U.S., which he said could be leaning toward carving up Europe into spheres of influence.

Back in Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., urged Trump’s team to refuse Putin’s demands.

The Russian leader not only wanted control of Ukraine but “he wants to redesign NATO to accommodate his revisionist ambitions,” Shaheen said, adding that any discussions about European security infrastructure should be a “nonstarter,” for the U.S. which “has benefited from the Alliance.”

Amid all of this, any substantial progress toward ending the war remains elusive.

The latest round of talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week produced no major breakthrough. Kushner said Washington was working toward what could be the largest prisoner swap of the war, while reporting that Russia had agreed to give Europe a seat at the table during the next round.

Putin met with Kushner and Witkoff at the Kremlin in Moscow last week. Vyacheslav Prokofyev / Pool / AFP via Getty

Russia hasn’t quite confirmed that, instead saying that it needs “to understand from the Europeans themselves” what they can “contribute to the peace process” before allowing them to join, as Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday.

There has been some internal wrangling among the European nations about who might represent them. Leaders have agreed on a team comprising the United Kingdom (which left the E.U. in 2020), France, Germany, Italy and Poland, alongside representatives of the European Commission and European Council. Kallas herself was left off the team.

“I don’t know who among the current leaders could be a sane dialogue partner,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the state-run news agency Tass on Monday.

He likened the chosen group of European countries to “the Quartet,” a satirical poem by Russian author Ivan Krylov. In it, a monkey, a donkey, a goat and a bear blame their failure to form a string quartet on the seating arrangement rather than their lack of musical ability.

That, at least, involved agreeing to a seating arrangement.

World.title: Highlights from Pope Leo’s historic, 12-day tour of South America
World.content:
LIMA, Peru — They turned out in the millions to greet Pope Leo as he made his way around Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on a grueling 12-day tour of the South American nations, weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.

00:00 00:00 Pope keeps energetic pace in trip to South America after surgery 01:19

For some — particularly those in Argentina, which had not received a papal visit since Pope John Paul II in 1987 — it was the first time they would get to see a pontiff in person. A record 2.5 million people flooded onto the streets of Buenos Aires last week to try and catch a glimpse of Leo.

The Vatican dubbed it a “homecoming” tour for the 71-year-old, as the Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, spent the final six days in the country where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.

NBC News takes a look at some of the highlights from his trip.

Montevideo, Uruguay

After a 17-hour flight from Rome, Leo and his entourage touched down in Uruguay’s capital, Montevideo. Praising the Lord and thanking his wonderful medical assistants, Leo said that while some had questioned whether he would be able to make the trip because of his recent surgery, he “had no doubt and was convinced that this trip had to go forward.”

World.title: Gavin Newsom sued by prosecutors and victim rights group to stop mass death row commutation
World.content:
Prosecutors and loved ones of murder victims asked California’s high court on Monday to take action against Gov. Gavin Newsom, claiming he overstepped his power in seeking to commute the death sentences of more than 500 condemned killers.

Only the state’s Supreme Court can stop Newsom’s “disregard of the law — his abuse of power,” according to a lawsuit filed by the Criminal Justice Legal Foundation (CJLF).

The victim rights group filed its action on behalf of 30 county district attorneys and more than two dozen family members of those slain by killers now sitting on California’s death row.

Newsom failed to give proper notice to “the victims of these heinous crimes,” thus denying grieving loved ones the “opportunity to be heard before a commutation decision,” according to the plaintiffs.

The mass commutations were also made without mandated “individualized consideration of the intended recipients,” plaintiffs said.

“Thousands of jurors and hundreds of judges set aside their personal views on the merits of the death penalty to render judgments based on the evidence and the law,” according to the filing by CJLF president and CEO Anne Marie Schubert, the former district attorney of Sacramento County.

“Governor Newsom decided his personal views should override all those who actually participated in the process, followed and applied the law,” Schubert wrote.

A representative for Newsom did not immediately respond to an NBC News request for comment on Tuesday.

Earlier this month, Newsom announced that he intends to commute all California death sentences, declaring that “state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with” values in America’s most populous state.

The governor, in an open letter to constituents, said that this move was “among the most difficult of my career.”

Newsom moved to grant clemency to 548 people, 529 men and 19 women, who are currently sentenced to death in California. The state constitution mandates that California’s high court must approve gubernatorial clemency to anyone convicted of more that one felony, meaning it’d have to sign off on 382 of those proposed commutations, according to Newsom.

Whether Newsom can issue a blanket order on the fate of those condemned inmates is uncharted territory.

“This is all new and we don’t really have answers,” said Michael Vitiello, a professor at the University of the Pacific’s McGeorge School of Law. “There’s no record (of a previous mass commutation). This is not something that we have a great deal of precedent.”

The Golden State hasn’t put a prisoner to death since Jan. 17, 2006, when Clarence Ray Allen was executed via lethal injection.

While the plaintiffs appear to have the general backing of California law enforcement, at least a handful of district attorneys support Newsom’s action.

“As a prosecutor, I believe that we will remain safer from crime and injustice as long as we believe that we can and should change outdated and ineffective practices like the death penalty,” five-term Santa Clara County DA Jeff Rosen said in a statement released by Smart Justice California, a criminal justice reform advocacy group.

“We must always work toward a better criminal justice system. We will be a safer community if we never lose faith in human dignity, including our own,” Rosen said.

World.title: NSA's classified internal network goes down, sources say
World.content:
The National Security Agency's internal network used to store and share classified information went offline Tuesday, according to multiple U.S. officials familiar with the situation, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for some personnel at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland.

The network, dubbed "NSA Net," is used for classified communications and information sharing within the nation's largest intelligence agency.

Two U.S. officials told CBS News that, at this point, there is no evidence the disruption was caused by a cyberattack. Two sources familiar with the situation said the outage resulted from routine system patching, though the precise circumstances surrounding the disruption remain unclear.

The NSA has also implemented staggered arrival times for non-emergency personnel at Fort Meade, according to two sources familiar with the measure.

The news was first reported by CNN.

Multiple sources told CBS News that the agency was seeking to avoid having large numbers of employees log on to their computers simultaneously while the network was experiencing problems, which is why they decided to stagger arrivals. Sources referred to this as "Code Gray," part of a modified reporting schedule.

In the meantime, some activities are being redirected to other NSA facilities around the country, according to sources familiar with the situation.

It was not immediately clear how long the network had been offline or when full service might be restored.

The NSA, home to one of the largest workforces in the U.S. intelligence community, is responsible for collecting and analyzing foreign signals intelligence, identifying and countering cyber threats, and protecting U.S. government communications

CBS News has reached out to the NSA, the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, the White House, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and Fort Meade for comment.

World.title: U.S. identifies remains of 6 soldiers killed in Korean War, including teens
World.content:
Six soldiers who died in the Korean War, including two teenagers, have been accounted for decades after their deaths, the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency announced Monday.

The identifications are part of an ongoing effort to locate and identify the remains of those killed in the Korean War. When a soldier is marked as accounted for, they receive a burial with full military honors.

U.S. Army Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman was a member of Battery B, 99th Field Artillery Battalion, 1st Cavalry Division. Thurman, 18, was a forward observer near Waegwan, South Korea, when his post came under heavy attack, according to the agency, and was last seen trying to evacuate a shell-shocked officer from the area while under heavy enemy fire.

Afterward, Thurman was reported missing in action. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953. His remains were declared unrecoverable two years later, in January 1956.

The agency said that a set of remains, designated X-5814 Tanggok, was recovered by the Quartermaster Graves Registration Company near Kumhwa-dong, South Korea, in October 1952. The remains were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu, Hawaii. In November 2022, the agency disinterred the remains. Analysis allowed the agency's scientists to identify the remains as Thurman's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 18, 2026.

U.S. Army Cpl. Jackie Lee Thurman. Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency

U.S. Army 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert was a member of B Battery, 503rd Field Artillery Battalion, 2nd Infantry Division, who was reported missing during the battle of the Ch'ongch'on River in North Korea, according to the agency. Witness statements allowed the Army to determine that Gilbert, 23, had been taken as a prisoner of war by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army and died from battlefield wounds in a POW camp on Jan. 31, 1951.

After the war, a recovered set of remains was returned to U.S. custody as part of a 1954 exchange known as Operation Glory, the agency said. The remains could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. They were disinterred on July 1, 2024, and sent to the agency's laboratory. Analysis, circumstantial and historical evidence allowed the agency to identify the remains as Gilbert's. His remains were marked as accounted for on June 4, 2026.

U.S. Army 1st Lt. Raymond Banker Gilbert. Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency

U.S. Army Cpl. William R. Laughlin Jr. was a member of Company D, 1st Battalion, 32nd Infantry Regiment, 7th Infantry Division, attached to the 31st Regimental Combat Team, according to the agency. Laughlin, 21, was among the U.S. soldiers ambushed by the Chinese People's Volunteer Army at the Chosin Reservoir in North Korea.

The ambush sparked a 17-day battle in frigid weather. Each side took thousands of casualties. U.S. and United Nations forces eventually retreated south toward the supply base of Hagaru-ri. Laughlin could not be located after the battle and was reported missing in action on Dec. 2, 1950. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953.

A pair of remains returned during Operation Glory were connected to an isolated burial east of the Chosin Reservoir. They could not be identified and were interred as unknowns at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The agency disinterred the remains in July 2022 and used modern forensic techniques at its laboratory to identify them as Laughlin's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on Sept. 28, 2026.

U.S. Army Cpl. William R. Laughlin Jr. Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency

U.S. Army Sgt. Joseph A. Platzkoester, a member of Company H, 2nd Battalion, 38th Infantry Regiment, 2nd Infantry Division, was last seen during an ambush near Inje in South Korea. Platzkoester, 28, was part of a convoy doing counteroffensive clearing operations at the time, the agency said. The convoy encountered an enemy roadblock. While his battalion pushed through, Platzkoester could not be found after the fight and was reported missing in action.

The area was searched, but Platzkoester's remains were not found. A presumptive finding of death was issued on Dec. 31, 1953, and his remains were declared nonrecoverable in January 1956.

In 1951, the 148th Quartermaster Graves Registration Company found a set of remains that could not be identified. They were interred as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. In November 2023, the set of remains was disinterred and sent to the agency's laboratory, where analysis identified them as Platzkoester's. He was marked as accounted for by the agency on May 29, 2026. A photo of Platzkoester was not available.

U.S. Army Cpl. Andrew R. Tischler, 21, was assigned to Company F, 2nd Battalion, 15th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, and was reported missing in action during a road march near Taewol Village in South Korea, according to the agency. The agency said it was able to account for him on May 5, 2026. Information about how his remains were found and identified was not available. A photo was not shared by the agency.

The other teen soldier, U.S. Army Cpl. Richard N. Lennox, 18, was accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025, the agency said. He was a member of Company C, 1st Battalion, 7th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division reported missing in action after his unit was attacked by enemy forces near Sachang-ni, North Korea, on Nov. 28, 1950. He was captured and marched to a prisoner-of-war camp in Changsong, where he died in October 1951.

Lennox's remains were among those handed over during Operation Glory, the agency said. They could not be identified at the time and were buried as an unknown at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. The remains were disinterred on June 13, 2016. The agency analyzed the remains and said that Lennox had been accounted for on Aug. 7, 2025. A photo of Lennox was not available.

The National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific on July 5, 2025, in Honolulu, Hawaii. AaronP/Bauer-Griffin/GC Images

Each missing soldier's name was engraved on the Walls of the Missing at the National Memorial Cemetery of the Pacific. Now that they have been accounted for, rosettes will be placed alongside their names.

More information about each soldier, including how they were identified, may be shared after their families are briefed by the agency. The agency told CBS News in 2024 that history, diplomacy and science all come into each investigation. First, researchers start with archival records. Investigators then search for surviving witnesses and clues. Once the potential location of a set of remains is identified, a recovery mission is sent to bring those remains to the agency's laboratory.

At the lab, scientists use dental evidence and other records to study the remains. For soldiers who disappeared during the Korean War, experts can use tuberculosis skin test results taken before someone shipped out. The remains also undergo X-rays, DNA analysis and isotope analysis. Finally, a reference sample of DNA from a family member is compared to the remains. The process can take decades, the agency told CBS News.

About 7,500 Americans are still unaccounted for from the Korean War, the agency says. Efforts to bring home fallen soldiers from the conflict are complicated by relations with North Korea: While the agency operates in 46 countries, North Korea is an outlier. Sometimes, war dead are recovered during exchanges like Operation Glory.

World.title: U.S. officially loses measles elimination status: "What a tragedy"
World.content:
The United States has officially lost its measles elimination status, global health officials announced Tuesday.

The decision from the Pan American Health Organization came after the U.S. recorded over 5,400 measles cases so far this year — more than double last year's total. The Pan American Health Organization is a regional office for the World Health Organization, covering North and South America. Researchers with knowledge of the decision had previously confirmed it to CBS News partner KFF Health News on Saturday.

A country is considered as having eliminated the measles if there are "no locally transmitted measles infections or outbreaks lasting 12 months or longer," according to the World Health Organization.

The United States did not meet that standard for the first time since 2000. According to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about a third of this year's measles cases are linked to outbreaks that began in 2025 and continued to spread.

After a 30-year record of 2,242 cases last year, the CDC has tallied 5,412 cases to date in 2026, resulting in more than 590 hospitalizations and at least six measles-related deaths, with some states reporting additional fatalities.

"It's profoundly sad and disappointing," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center, told CBS News. "What a tragedy. We have had children die of measles this past year. That should never have happened. Those deaths and all those cases, 5,000-plus, were completely preventable."

The biggest outbreak has been in Pennsylvania, where state health officials have reported more than 1,500 cases and seven deaths associated with the disease this year. Wisconsin reports two children have died and New York had its first measles death in more than 30 years.

Measles cases have been confirmed so far this year in 45 states and Washington, D.C.

"The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does," CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said in a statement. "We know where transmission is occurring and we've invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach those communities." She said the CDC remains focused on stopping outbreaks.

Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Republican from Louisiana who is also a doctor, said health officials, including Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., should be doing more to promote the importance of vaccination to protect against measles.

"Speaking as a physician, you may decide not to be vaccinated because it's your free will, but the child who's too young to be vaccinated is vulnerable if you come into that child's presence, and we're seeing children die from measles who are too young to be vaccinated," Cassidy said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

"So if you've not been vaccinated, you could be the person that brings death to another. That's something to remember."

What does it mean to lose measles elimination status?

A country or region loses its measles elimination status once its population immunity lowers enough that there is sustained spread of the disease, CBS News medical correspondent Dr. Céline Gounder explained. When a country has measles elimination status and a high rate of vaccination, a case of measles or small outbreak will soon fizzle out. But when there are this many gaps in the population's immunity, there can be "ongoing chains of transmission," Gounder said.

"It means that we're at risk of being exposed to measles and getting measles if we're not vaccinated," Gounder said. "It means ERs and pediatricians need to consider measles in anyone with a fever and rash, whether they've traveled overseas or not. And we may now become an exporter of measles to other countries."

Dr. Omer Awan, a trained epidemiologist and senior public health contributor for Forbes, said that the loss of measles elimination status is a setback to the nation's public health infrastructure.

"It's frustrating and heartbreaking ... because we have the tools to fight this. The tool is the MMR vaccine, which we know is 97% effective at preventing the onset of measles," Awan said. "It'd be one thing if we didn't have the tools to fight this, but the tools are at our disposal, we just aren't using the tools that can help us mitigate the spread and beat measles."

How can the U.S. regain measles elimination status?

A country earns measles elimination status by ensuring there is no local spread of the disease or outbreaks that last for more than a year.

PAHO says that the best way to maintain the elimination of measles is maintaining a vaccination rate of 95% or higher. Countries should also have sensitive surveillance systems to detect cases quickly, laboratory capacity and a guaranteed rapid response to outbreaks. Data about these trends must be submitted to and verified by the organization.

For the U.S. to curb outbreaks and regain measles elimination status, it needs to return to higher rates of vaccination, Awan said. He said battling misinformation and ramping up vaccination campaigns would be key to that effort.

Data shows childhood vaccination rates have declined in many communities around the U.S. in recent years, often below the threshold needed to help ward off measles outbreaks.

Gounder also noted that lawmakers can create policies that lead to increased vaccination rates.

"States set the school vaccine rules. Nine states made opting out of vaccination easier in 2025. States ending nonmedical exemptions saw kindergarten vaccination rise 2 to 4 points," Gounder said. "Most legislatures reconvene in January. Your state lawmakers will write next year's exemption rules."

Measles in the U.S.

The United States started collecting national data on measles in 1912, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About 6,000 measles-related deaths were reported each year in the first decade of that data collection.

In the decade between 1953 and 1963, nearly all children in the U.S. caught measles before they turned 15, with an estimated 3 to 4 million people infected each year and tens of thousands hospitalized, according to the CDC. In those years, 400 to 500 people, mostly children, died of measles annually.

Then in 1963, the measles vaccine first became widely available. The numbers began a sharp decline and several generations of Americans grew up without ever encountering measles.

By 1981, reported measles cases had dropped by 80% compared to the previous year, the CDC said. The country was officially declared as having eliminated measles in 2000.

The U.S. maintained its elimination status for over 25 years. That didn't mean there were no cases at all — in 2015, an outbreak that spread among unvaccinated people was traced back to overseas visitors at Disneyland in Southern California, and a 2018-19 outbreak in New York was eventually contained by public health measures including curtailing vaccine exemptions. But those spikes were just a fraction of the spread now being seen in the U.S.

The nation recorded 2,242 measles cases in 2025, according to CDC data, linked to 48 separate outbreaks. The CDC reported 245 hospitalizations, mostly in children, and three measles deaths last year. Infections were confirmed in at least 44 states. It was the most cases the country had seen in over three decades.

That record was shattered in 2026, when the U.S. recorded more than double that number of cases by October — a total that topped 5,000 earlier this month.

Almost all of the cases have been in people who were not vaccinated. Measles-related deaths have been reported in Pennsylvania, New York and Wisconsin.

The CDC said 43 new outbreaks — defined as three or more related cases — have been reported so far in 2026, while about a third of the cases reported this year are tied to outbreaks that have been ongoing since 2025.

Who is at risk from measles?

Measles is one of the most contagious infectious diseases. Those who are unvaccinated for the disease are most at risk of getting it. CDC data shows that 96% of people infected with measles in 2026 had not been vaccinated for measles or were unsure of their vaccination status; only 2% of cases were in people who'd been fully vaccinated.

Medical research has shown that two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is extremely safe and effective at protecting against measles.

But some people — including babies, pregnant women or people with weakened immune systems — cannot get vaccinated and must rely on population immunity to keep the disease from spreading.

"They will be the ones that are most vulnerable to getting infected and experiencing the complications," such as pneumonia or encephalitis, Awan said.

Many of the recent cases have been occurring in tight-knit and largely unvaccinated Amish or Mennonite communities.

"It really shows you who's vulnerable because these are totally unvaccinated communities," said Dr. Deborah Birx, a longtime public health official who was a leader of the White House Coronavirus Task Force during the pandemic. "You can see it in who's hospitalized. The largest percentage are children under 4 and adults over 50."

"I hope this is a wake-up call to every parent," Birx told CBS News. "If you had decided to not vaccinate your children, you've been relatively protected by all of us and all of our grandchildren and other children who got vaccinated. But that protection and that shield is going away" as vaccination rates slip. "And so your child is now vulnerable at a level they never were vulnerable before."

Measles is known for causing a rash, but Schaffner said that's the least of it. "What's bothersome is children, even with uncomplicated measles, are miserable for a week or a week and a half with red eyes, runny nose, cough, and just debilitating fever and diarrhea. And then you have the complications of dehydration, pneumonia, and on occasion, encephalitis."

There can be other lingering health consequences, Birx warned. Measles patients "can end up with what we call immune suppression, so that they're more susceptible to all other diseases after they've had measles."

While many people recover, measles can cause severe infections in the lungs and brain that can lead to cognitive issues, deafness or death.

"Measles is a nasty, nasty virus," Schaffner said. "In contrast, the vaccine is wonderfully effective."

World.title: Ukraine says underground gas pipeline used to mount sneak attack
World.content:
Ukrainian soldiers spent weeks navigating a decommissioned, underground Soviet-era gas pipeline to sneak behind enemy lines and launch a surprise attack on Russian troops this autumn as part of an operation to prevent the invading forces from reaching the eastern city of Kupiansk, according to the Ukrainian unit involved.

The operation forced the soldiers to get past barricades laid by Russian forces — including the bodies of fallen troops — and involved close-quarters combat inside the roughly three-foot-wide pipeline, Ukraine's military said.

"Operation Veles" was carried out by members of the Ukrainian National Guard's Khartiia Corps in the Kharkiv region within the last couple of months, according to a series of posts by the unit on social media. The unit said troops crawled and were pulled on wheeled carts some nine miles through the underground pipeline before emerging behind Russian positions.

An image from video shared on social media by the Ukrainian National Guard's Khartiia Corps shows a soldier with the unit wincing as he moves through a decommissioned underground gas pipeline north of the front-line city of Kupiansk, as part of "Operation Veles," in the autumn of 2026. Khartiia Corps/Ukrainian National Guard/Telegram

The operation was part of a broader Ukrainian effort, more than four and a half years into Russia's full-scale invasion, to prevent the invading forces from advancing toward the front-line city of Kupiansk.

The unit's social media posts quoted soldiers saying they engaged in close combat with grenades and small arms inside the pipe, where the cramped space came with pooled freezing water and traces of natural gas lingering years after the pipeline was decommissioned. Some Ukrainian forces spent as long as a month underground during the operation, the Khartiia Corps said.

"They used electric winches to move through the pipe, and transported ammunition and equipment on small wheelbarrows," the unit said in one post. It called the conditions "extremely harsh," and noted that the troops "constantly moving on their knees caused injuries, and dirt clogged the mechanisms of their weapons and caused malfunctions."

Russian troops had laid obstacles in some sections of the pipeline, with Ukrainian soldiers saying that some of those barricades included the bodies of other Russian soldiers. The claims by the Ukrainian forces about the battle have not been independently verified by CBS News.

An image from video shared on social media by the Ukrainian National Guard's Khartiia Corps shows a soldier with the unit inspecting dirt-caked ammunition inside a decommissioned underground gas pipeline north of the front-line city of Kupiansk, during "Operation Veles," in the autumn of 2026. Khartiia Corps/Ukrainian National Guard/Telegram

Russian authorities have acknowledged the operation, referring to a Ukrainian raid.

The Khartiia Corps has not confirmed any Ukrainian casualties, but at least one report on the battle, by Britain's Telegraph newspaper, mentioned Ukrainian forces recovering the body of a fallen comrade from inside an underground gas pipeline.

The pipeline offered a way for Ukrainian forces to conceal their movements in one of the most heavily monitored sectors of the nearly 1,000-mile front line that stretches from the far north to the far south of eastern Ukraine.

Both sides have sought to exploit underground infrastructure to evade increasingly sophisticated aerial surveillance in a conflict shaped by drone warfare. In September 2025, Russian forces similarly attempted to use sections of underground pipeline to move troops closer to Ukrainian positions around the northern outskirts of Kupiansk without being detected by drones.

Military analysts say operations like the underground pipeline assault highlight how the widespread use of drones in Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion, and Ukraine's defense, have transformed modern warfare. Both sides rely heavily on surveillance and attack drones to find and strike troops and hardware moving in the open.

As a result, even short movements above ground can expose soldiers to near real-time observation and attack.

While underground operations present their own dangers, including limited ventilation, restricted movement, navigational challenges and the risk of entrapment, soldiers involved in the Ukrainian mission suggested the hazards were outweighed by the dangers posed above ground, where they could have been spotted by Russian drones.

"It's damp, it's dark, it reeks. There are corpses lying around, but I felt safer there," one Khartiia Corps member, using the callsign "Sgt. Santa," was quoted as saying in a post by the unit.

The operation came ahead of what could prove a critical juncture in the war. President Trump, who campaigned on ending the war quickly, has pushed hard for Ukraine and Russia to agree to a peace deal. Kyiv and its European allies fear, however, that the White House appears to be offering Vladimir Putin and Russia too much — including the prospect of major energy deals, with no significant concessions in return, while putting pressure on Ukraine to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.

Ukraine says the operation in the gas pipeline helped stop Russian forces from gaining more ground near Kupiansk, a city that Ukrainian forces recaptured from Russia's invading troops in 2022.

World.title: Groups raise concerns over DOJ's new Civil Rights Division chief
World.content:
Washington — Eighteen civil rights organizations asked President Trump on Tuesday to withdraw his appointment of Craig Trainor as the new acting assistant attorney general for the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division, saying he has a track record of undermining the laws he is tasked with enforcing.

Trainor was appointed last week to replace Harmeet Dhillon, who resigned from her post shortly after the midterm elections.

Trainor most recently served as assistant secretary for fair housing and equal opportunity at the Department of Housing and Urban Development. Prior to that, he held several senior roles at the Department of Education.

He also previously served as a senior special counsel to GOP Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio on the House Judiciary Committee as well as the Select Subcommittee on the Weaponization of the Federal Government.

Tuesday's statement opposing his appointment was signed by a variety of organizations, including the National Center for Youth Law, the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, National Council of Jewish Women, Human Rights Campaign, the Sikh Coalition and Stop Sexual Assault in Schools, among others.

"In the midterm elections, the American people rejected an agenda to divide, discriminate against, and diminish our communities," the groups said.

"Instead of rebuilding a Civil Rights Division decimated under Harmeet Dhillon, the Administration has chosen to elevate the official behind a court-blocked classroom censorship agenda who seeks to undermine the rights of survivors and equal opportunity in our schools and communities," they added.

CBS News has reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

The civil rights groups said that Trainor took action in his prior roles at the Department of Education and HUD that scaled back civil liberties.

After a court struck down a Department of Education rule that broadened the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment under Title IX of the Civil Rights Act, Trainor issued a directive to schools in February 2025 that ordered them to revert to less-stringent standards that were adopted in 2020.

Many civil rights groups have long criticized the 2020 standards and referred to them as "anti-survivor" rules because the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment is narrower.

The 2020 rules also only require schools to investigate allegations of sexual assault or harassment under Title IX that occur on school grounds, excluding conduct that may occur abroad or off campus.

The groups also pointed to threats that Trainor directed toward schools in a Feb. 14, 2025, letter, in which he threatened to withhold federal funding if they had diversity, equity and inclusion programs.

Several federal courts later enjoined the Department of Education from following through on its threats to withhold the funds.

After he left and went to HUD, Trainor also shuttered many discrimination investigations under the Fair Housing Act, the groups said.

In announcing his appointment, Attorney General Todd Blanche praised his actions at HUD, saying he helped to "cut the Biden-era Fair Housing case backlog in half."

Trainor is taking over the helm of a Civil Rights Division that was largely gutted under Dhillon's leadership, as more than 75% of its staff left since January 2025.

Although Dhillon later hired more attorneys, the staffing level is still not what it once was.

Dhillon reoriented the division away from its historical mission of protecting some of society's most vulnerable and marginalized groups. She shifted its focus to other priorities that included protecting gun owners' rights, curbing the use of equity, diversity and inclusion policies at universities, and adopting legal positions that oppose civil rights protections for transgender people.

World.title: Jensen Huang says he "would be honored" to return as Nvidia CEO
World.content:
Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang broke his silence after resigning from the company following revelations of multiple affairs, saying he'd be willing to return as its CEO.

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," Huang said in a statement Tuesday morning. "I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the board's independent investigation."

He added, "If the board of directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO."

Huang may face significant hurdles in returning to his former role, however. Nvidia board members are not interested in reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO or in any other role at the chipmaker, a source directly familiar with their thinking told CBS News.

But Huang has gained support from the more than 190,000 people, including several thousand Nvidia employees, who have signed a petition to reinstate him. On Monday, President Trump suggested to reporters that he would support Huang returning to Nvidia.

"I would not mind seeing that," Mr. Trump said. Later, the president said he recommended former Apple CEO Tim Cook as Nvidia's next leader.

In his Tuesday statement, Huang thanked his allies for their support since his departure last week, saying that in addition to the public calls for him to return to the company, many "continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive and geopolitical dynamics."

Nvidia's board said on Tuesday that it has formed a committee to oversee its national security policies and ensure compliance with U.S. export controls. The former CEO has also agreed to appear before House lawmakers on Dec. 1 to address questions about a potential breach of national security amid an investigation into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The former CEO's return to Nvidia is unlikely, said Yorkville Ives & Co. technology analyst Dan Ives.

"In our view the sequencing is the tell: Jensen has conditioned his return on a board decision, and the board's first public act this week was to build a compliance structure around the issue that forced him out, which is not what a board preparing to reverse itself does," he said in a Tuesday research note.

Shares of Nvidia declined $2.63, or 1.7%, to $153.51. The stock has lost 16% of its value since Huang's extramarital relationships became public.

World.title: Trump reacts to Iran's "dirty bomb" threat: "We take it very seriously"
World.content: Trump on Iran's "dirty bomb" threat President Trump says the U.S. is taking a potential Iranian threat against Washington, D.C., "very seriously." This comes ahead of his planned summit with China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin. CBS News' Aaron Navarro reports. More

World.title: Trump in Asia for Putin, Xi summit; possible Kim meeting
World.content:
President Trump arrived Tuesday in the Philippines to start a multiday swing in Asia, where he's scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping for a highly anticipated summit later this week.

After landing in Manila, Mr. Trump met with the leaders of the Quad nations that have sought to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific region, a relationship Mr. Trump described as "very special." Those nations are Australia, India and Japan, as well as the United States.

Mr. Trump announced an $85 million investment in artificial intelligence software, describing it as the "greatest opportunity for economic growth since the Industrial Revolution."

There were protests in Manila ahead of Mr. Trump's trip, with demonstrators holding signs reading "Trump Out," drawings of him as a clown or devil, and signs calling on the public to reject an AI hub named Pax Silica.

Mr. Trump acknowledged that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have "two lines of thought" on how to handle China, adding that "they handled that very well."

Ahead of his departure from Washington Monday, Mr. Trump called it a "big trip" and said he may also meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China. After arriving, he said Kim "would like to" come, but "we'll see what happens."

President Trump waves American and Philippine flags after he arrived at Ninoy Aquino International Airport on Nov. 17, 2026, to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila. Eloisa Lopez/POOL/AFP via Getty Images

The meeting between Mr. Trump, Xi and Putin, which marks the first among the three leaders, is expected to center on decreasing the proliferation of nuclear weapons, the White House said, and comes as the wars in Iran and Ukraine remain in focus.

Mr. Trump said Monday they would discuss denuclearization, which he called a "tough subject," as well as Iran and Ukraine, although an official said over the weekend that Ukraine was not expected to be discussed.

In Manila, the president will attend the annual Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. He will meet with leaders of Japan, India and Australia on security in the Indo-Pacific on Tuesday. He's also scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand and attend a dinner with leaders of the Southeast Asian nations and other regional leaders, the White House said.

On Wednesday, the president is set to hold a state visit and lunch banquet with Philippine President Bongbong Marcos at the presidential palace, before departing for Shenzhen, China. There, he'll meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit with APEC leaders, and on Thursday, hold the meeting with Putin and Xi. Mr. Trump said Tuesday that he would be open to a one-on-one meeting with Putin, but he didn't know if it had been scheduled.

Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk is expected to join the president on the trip, according to a senior White House official, but will not be part of the meeting with Putin and Xi.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia comes after he visited China in May for a summit with Xi, where he touted making "fantastic trade deals" and acknowledged a shared desire to end the U.S.-Iran conflict. Xi also visited the U.S. in September, marking his first visit to the White House in over a decade, as the two countries extended a tariff truce.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

It will be Mr. Trump's third face-to-face meeting with Xi this year.

As for Putin, Mr. Trump and the Russian president last met in Alaska in August 2025 for a high-stakes summit on ending the war in Ukraine. But the talks failed to yield a ceasefire that the U.S. was seeking.

Mr. Trump's trip to Asia also coincides with issues back at home, including the recent revelations regarding an affair between Jensen Huang, the former CEO of chipmaker Nvidia, and a suspected Chinese spy. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Huang, who has a relationship with Mr. Trump, traveled on Air Force One during his May trip to China, and he and his wife were at the head table when Mr. Trump hosted Xi in Washington for a state dinner in September. White House officials said they do not think the Nvidia situation will loom over the trip.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," an official said.

When asked Monday if Secretary of State Marco Rubio had told him that the woman with whom Huang was having an affair, Alice Huang, was suspected of being a spy, Mr. Trump said he didn't know if she was, saying, "I haven't heard that." Mr. Trump also said it "isn't a bad idea" for Jensen Huang to be reinstated at Nvidia, but he also added that he recommended Apple's Tim Cook for the job.

Both Bessent and Lutnick are traveling with the president. Bessent last week accused Lutnick of failing to prevent China from getting some of Nvidia's most advanced chips.

Mr. Trump told reporters before he left that he was not considering replacing Lutnick.

The Nvidia Board of Directors announced Tuesday morning that it would be creating a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee. Mr. Trump said on Tuesday that he believed that is a "good idea."

World.title: Huang says he'd be "honored" to return to Nvidia as he agrees to testify to Congress
World.content:
Huang says he'd be "honored" to return to Nvidia as he agrees to testify to Congress

toggle caption i Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Tuesday he would return to lead the company he cofounded if Nvidia's board of directors allowed him to. Huang also agreed to appear before Congress to answer questions about the national security scandals swirling around the company.

"I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret," wrote Huang in a statement posted on social media. "I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."

Sponsor Message

Huang stepped down from the company last week after acknowledging that he had been unfaithful to his wife. News reports have tied him to a woman who U.S. intelligence officials say was recruited by China's spy agency, as well as with another woman who is an executive at Nvidia. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.

Huang said he would be "honored" to return to the company if Nvidia's board agreed. His comments come as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."

"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday.

Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors from the House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence Committees and the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party on Dec. 1st and 2nd.

Sponsor Message

Lawmakers say they want answers about Nvidia's role in alleged chip smuggling and efforts to evade export controls meant to block China from accessing the most advanced U.S. AI chips. They will also ask Huang about his involvement with Alice Huang, who was an executive with Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that was a major customer for Nvidia's chips. In a statement emailed to NPR, Megaspeed said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business," and that Alice Huang left the company in 2025, but that it is conducting an internal investigation.

Nvidia's board said on Tuesday it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies, compliance with U.S. export controls, and risk management of global trade.

On Monday, the U.S. Commerce Department announced new rules to prevent remote access to advanced artificial intelligence chips and servers, closing a loophole that may have let Chinese companies remotely access advanced Nvidia chips through overseas data centers. The Commerce Department and Justice Department also announced Monday that the DOJ is conducting a criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

Later Tuesday, investors will hear directly for the first time from Nvidia's new acting CEO, Colette Kress, when the company announces its quarterly earnings after markets close for the day.

World.title: Trump is in Asia ahead of Xi, Putin summit. And, tech leaders want Huang back at Nvidia
World.content:
Trump is in Asia ahead of Xi, Putin summit. And, tech leaders want Huang back at Nvidia

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

A technology issue with United Airlines delayed departing flights yesterday evening, just as air travel was returning to normal after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop on Friday. President Trump said yesterday that he hopes this incident will prompt Congress to allocate more funds to upgrade the outdated air traffic control system.

toggle caption i Adam Gray/Getty Images North America

🎧 Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the FAA will reevaluate future maintenance procedures, NPR's Joe Hernandez tells Up First. Mike McCormick, a former FAA senior executive and air traffic manager, told Hernandez that he thinks another nationwide ground stop is unlikely. McCormick says that in cases like this, the FAA sometimes imposes a maintenance moratorium, temporarily halting such work. The ground stop happened while L3Harris workers converted copper wires to a fiber optic system and installed a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas.

President Trump is in Manila today to meet with allies at the ASEAN summit. Tomorrow, he travels to Shenzhen, China, for a joint summit with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. It's the first time those three have had a joint summit. The meeting will happen on the sidelines of the APEC summit that Xi is hosting in Shenzhen.



Sponsor Message

🎧 When leaving the White House yesterday, Trump said they would discuss his "favorite subject": Ukraine, NPR's Deepa Shivaram says. The White House had previously announced that Ukraine would not be on the agenda for the trilateral meeting. Shivaram says that Europe and Ukraine are concerned about how Ukraine may be discussed at the meeting, and what might come out of it, because President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will not be at APEC and Trump has recently been more lenient toward Putin and Russia.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation has shaken Silicon Valley, prompting calls from some tech leaders for the board to reinstate him. Trump said he agreed with them. Meanwhile, the U.S. government introduced a rule to block remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, closing a loophole that could allow adversarial governments to access American AI technology through overseas data centers. Nvidia is the world's dominant producer of AI chips.



🎧 Many prominent AI and venture capital figures have recognized Huang as a visionary whose company played a significant role in the AI boom, NPR's Shannon Bond says. An online petition supporting his reinstatement has garnered more than 160,000 signatures, but Bond says some of them may not be real. Elon Musk says he signed it. Brad Gerstner from Altimeter Capital, a key Nvidia investor, has urged the board to thoroughly investigate and keep all options open. Bond says the interim CEO and CFO will address the public for the first time following today's earnings report.

Sponsor Message

Prosecutors are moving to retry Lindsay Clancy for the deaths of her three children. The new trial is set for March 29, 2027. Although there was speculation about potentially reducing the charges to manslaughter or second-degree murder after her previous trial ended in a mistrial, no changes were made during Monday's court hearing. Judge William Sullivan, who presided over the first trial, will oversee the new proceedings. He denied Clancy's defense team's request to dismiss the charges based on double jeopardy. Clancy's defense argues that she shouldn't be held criminally responsible for killing her children because she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis.

Deep dive

toggle caption i Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR

One year ago, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to all families regardless of income, as long as adults are working, seeking work, in school, or unable to work. Many parents have found this initiative life-changing, but capacity was limited. Only 50% of the some 67,000 children ages 5 and under are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other programs, such as PreK and Head Start. New Mexico officials say the program must expand to meet demand. The issues observed in New Mexico are mirrored across the nation, prompting policymakers and childcare advocates to closely monitor the state's initiative.



👶 Almost half of U.S. children aged 5 and under live in licensed childcare deserts, where demand exceeds availability, according to the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank.

👶 New Mexico's program has an operating budget of nearly $600 million, but some lawmakers are concerned it could be $50 million over budget this year.

👶 New Mexico state Sen. Steve Lanier tells NPR that the steep cost of the program is why he only supports universal childcare for some people, since someone earning around $450,000 or $600,000 might not need assistance. Lanier has previously sued to end the initiative, but the lawsuit was unsuccessful.

👶 Since the enactment of free, universal childcare in New Mexico, lower-income mothers have experienced significant gains. Their full-time employment has risen by 23%, according to a new paper from Arizona State University.

Sponsor Message

Picture show

toggle caption i Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR

Millions of shorebirds embark on epic migrations to Alaska each year to breed. They often travel thousands of miles from places like New Zealand, Asia and South America. But researchers have found a concerning trend: Nearly half of the 41 shorebird species that breed in Alaska are in decline. These birds time their journeys to coincide with peak insect availability, and climate change is throwing off their schedules. Warmer springs lead to earlier insect emergence, creating a mismatch that could leave shorebirds without enough food supply. Scientists are now racing to understand if these migratory birds can adapt to the changing Arctic landscape.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Gareth Cattermole/Getty Images Europe

British actor Robert Pattinson will be the seventh James Bond, taking his place among an iconic lineup of stars that started with Sean Connery and most recently featured Daniel Craig. The 69th annual Grammy Awards nominations were announced yesterday. British singer-songwriter RAYE leads with 11 nominations, followed by Spanish artist Rosalía with nine nods. Civil rights champion Dolores Huerta made history yesterday as the first non-elected individual and the first woman to lie in honor at the California State Capitol. She died of cancer last month at age 96. (via KQED)

World.title: Sen. Jack Reed says FAA needs a real plan, not just more money
World.content:
Sen. Jack Reed says FAA needs a real plan, not just more money

toggle caption i Graeme Sloan/Getty Images

After last week's nationwide ground stop, Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., raised concerns Tuesday about the Federal Aviation Administration's oversight of contractors.

"Was the contractor properly supervised? I have questions too about whether FAA, after DOGE, is capable of supervising these types of activities," Reed told NPR's Michel Martin on Morning Edition.

Reed said the administration's explanation of an apparent contractor error made sense, but called for a closer examination of its cause.

Friday's four-hour ground stop occurred as a federal contractor was replacing copper wiring with fiber optic cables at an FAA facility in Arkansas. The exact cause remains under investigation, and federal officials say there is no indication of a cyberattack.

Sponsor Message

The disruption has renewed debate in Congress over funding for the aging system.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy initially requested $30 billion in additional funding before increasing the figure to $50 billion. Congress has already provided $14.5 billion for FAA modernization. Roughly $9 billion is still unspent.

Reed, who sits on the Senate Appropriations Committee, criticized the administration for seeking more money without presenting a detailed plan.

"They're just trying to throw money at a problem," he said.

Reed also agreed with Texas Republican Sen. Ted Cruz, who has questioned whether some of the proposed funding would go toward airport improvements rather than safety.

"The top priority in my book is getting this system back up to speed," Reed said.

Listen to the full interview using the blue button above. This story was adapted for digital by Majd Al-Waheidi and edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow?
World.content:
Can Google win the AI race without killing its cash cow?

toggle caption i Dave Rowland/Getty Images/Getty Images AsiaPac

Google became one of the most valuable companies in the world by revolutionizing how humanity finds information. Now, a new generation of AI rivals is challenging its dominance and pushing Google to spend a fortune to secure its future. Can Google embrace this disruptive technology without breaking the business that made it rich?

Former Google executive Marissa Mayer remembers when the company was just a scrappy startup, working out of a small office above a bike shop in Palo Alto, Calif. She joined the company back in 1999, fresh out of nearby Stanford with a master's in computer science.

Sponsor Message

" It's pretty wild. When I interviewed at Google, there were just seven people there," Mayer tells Planet Money. By the time she got hired, a month or two later, she became its 20th employee.

toggle caption i ROBYN BECK/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

That year, Google brought in just over $200,000 in annual revenue. By 2022, the eve of the AI boom, the company — by then reorganized under a parent company called Alphabet — was generating more than $280 billion . That's more than a millionfold increase.

Google made its fortune selling ads next to its search results. It monopolized internet searches so thoroughly that its name became a verb. And its search business became like an unstoppable money machine.

In 2012, Mayer left and became the CEO of Yahoo, trying to revive a competitor that Google had blown out of the water. But neither Yahoo nor any other rival managed to dethrone King Google. The company's dominion just kept expanding. Its share of the U.S. search-engine market grew from 80% in 2009 to nearly 90% in 2020.

For a time, it seemed like the only forces that could cut this juggernaut down to size were politicians or antitrust lawyers.

But the craziest part? The biggest threat to Google was maybe coming from inside the house! From what it was developing in its own labs — and the industrial race it would unleash.

Sponsor Message

Google plowed the profits from its search business into research and development of AI. And, in 2017, a team of eight Google employees developed the transformer , a breakthrough technology that made today's AI chatbots possible.

Mayer, who is now CEO of the AI startup Dazzle and remains a Google shareholder, sees Google's pioneering AI work as a reason for optimism about the company's future. "This is not a technology that's happening to Google," she says. "They helped invent this new technology."

Yet, today, Google is spending enormous amounts to build its AI capabilities and fend off rivals. And it's overhauling its search business, using AI to answer questions directly instead of just providing links.

Wall Street is getting nervous. In late October, Alphabet released its most recent earnings report. The company's stock price plummeted more than 12% the next day — the biggest single-day percentage decline since the company went public in 2004.

If this whole AI transition goes sideways for the company, it's a bit like a mother giving birth to a baby and then that baby slapping her in the face and stealing money from her wallet.

Which brings us to… a classic business theory we've been thinking about recently: the innovator's dilemma.

The late Harvard Business School professor Clayton Christensen developed the theory in his 1997 book, The Innovator's Dilemma: When New Technologies Cause Great Firms to Fail.

Christensen theorized that the very thing that makes a business wildly successful can lead to its downfall in the face of a "disruptive" technology. He helped put disruption in Silicon Valley's vocabulary, long before it became a cliché.

The core innovator's dilemma is basically this: embrace a disruptive technology, and risk the profits you're making today. But if you fail to embrace it and let others run with it, you may end up risking your company's health tomorrow.

Sponsor Message

Today in the Planet Money newsletter we ask: has Google been caught in the innovator's dilemma? And can it pivot to a new technological era without sacrificing its enormous profits?

Did Google squander its AI head start?

Google didn't just invent the transformer. Over the decades, its researchers made computers translate languages , recognize speech and images, drive cars autonomously, and even beat one of the world's best players at the game Go .

The company even developed an internal chatbot called Meena that employees played with years before AI chatbots became a sensation.

But they didn't release it.

Then, on Nov. 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT and offered a completely new way to find information and a glimpse of a future where people didn't need to go to Google to find answers anymore.

Google scrambled to respond, reportedly declaring a "code red" as ChatGPT captivated the masses.

So, first question, why wasn't Google the first out of the gate with something like ChatGPT?

Christensen's theory offers one possible explanation: When you're making tons of money from your existing business in search, why rush to release something that could undermine it? Why disrupt yourself?

His theory wasn't just that companies seek to protect their cash cow. It was that a company can get too focused on the best way to nurture and milk that cash cow. Like, dang, I love this cow. Then when a disruptive technology comes along, they might be like, wait, this won't help me milk my beautiful cow. No thanks.

In other words, a company's focus on its core business can lead it to not see a disruptive technology's market potential. It can create a kind of myopia.

Last year, Google's chief scientist, Jeff Dean, offered an explanation for why Google hadn't released something like ChatGPT sooner— and it suggested the company had fallen victim to the kind of myopia Christensen warned about. Dean told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel that they looked at their existing chatbots through the lens of their search business. You know, their cow.

Sponsor Message

"From a search perspective, you want to get the right answer 100% of the time," Dean said. "These models were not near that bar." They were prone to hallucinating and also saying offensive things.

Those were problems ChatGPT had as well. It made tons of mistakes and said racist , sexist , and other incendiary things that made headlines. Yet it took off like a rocket ship when they released it.

And it turned out that people didn't just use ChatGPT as a way to find information or get answers. Dean acknowledged that Google had underestimated how useful chatbots could be for things people wouldn't necessarily turn to a search engine for, like drafting a note or summarizing text.

Christensen warned about this very trap in The Innovator's Dilemma. Companies that keep disruptive technologies "bottled up in their labs," he wrote, risk losing out to rivals willing to run with them, however imperfect they may be.

Mayer, however, questions whether releasing a chatbot first would have gone as well for Google as it did for OpenAI. "The standards for an established company like Google in terms of what users expect, in terms of quality, how good the search is, how great the product is fundamentally different than for an upstart or a newcomer," Mayer says.

We don't know what would have happened if Google had released a chatbot first. Would a Google chatbot have taken off in the same way, giving Google a first-mover advantage? Or would its flaws have created big headaches for a company with an established reputation to protect?

Whatever explains Google's initial hesitation, it's now going all in. It's fought back with its own chatbot, now called Gemini, and by putting AI-generated answers directly onto its search page, even at the risk of undermining the advertising business that made it rich.

Sponsor Message

The question now is whether all this will leave Google as dominant — and as profitable — in the AI age as it was in the age of old-school web search.

Goodbye, Monopoly?

Benedict Evans is a widely read technology analyst who was previously a partner at the Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz.

He says that every 10 or 15 years or so, a revolutionary "platform shift" shakes up the tech industry, giving newcomers a chance to challenge dominant companies. It happened with the rise of personal computers, then the internet, then smartphones. Now, he says, it's happening with AI.

"The whole table gets reset and the things that meant that they had won and you couldn't take them on suddenly don't matter anymore," Evans says.

toggle caption i John Phillips/Getty Images/Getty Images Europe

For Google, the consumer pivot to AI could mean it loses some of the competitive advantages that helped it monopolize search.

The process toward monopolization began with Google building a better search engine than rivals. Then, Evans says, its success became self-reinforcing: more users gave Google more data to improve its results, helping it attract still more users. Economists call this a "network effect," a kind of positive feedback loop that helped Google cement its dominance.

Of course, Google also actively worked to catch and keep customers as well. It, for instance, paid to make its search engine the default in browsers and on devices — deals that a federal judge ruled in 2024 had illegally helped maintain its search monopoly.

Google also cemented its dominance by weaving itself into our lives. It runs the operating system on many of our phones. We use free Google services to send emails, write documents, find directions, and watch a stranger explain how to fix our washing machine. Many of us keep going back to Google search out of sheer habit or because, when we're navigating the Google digital complex, we keep getting nudged to go there.

Sponsor Message

But a platform shift could loosen Google's grip on us. Why go to Google dotcom to search for information if you're using an AI system made by a rival that can answer your question well enough? And, maybe, those rival AI systems will borrow from Google's playbook and work to intertwine themselves into our lives.

It's still early days in this rapidly transforming market. One big question, Evans says, is whether AI models will develop winner-take-all dynamics like those that helped Google dominate search. So far, it seems like the frontier labs keep catching up with each other. One possibility, he says, is that AI could become increasingly capable of improving itself — what those in the biz call "recursive self-improvement" — allowing whichever company gets there first to build a lead that rivals struggle to overcome. But whether the AI race will end with a dominant leader — and whether Google will be the one that emerges victorious — is still a huge question.

Mayer doesn't expect a single winner. Yes, the mammoth cost of the computing power and energy needed to develop and run frontier models creates a barrier to entry, making it hard for smaller companies to compete. But she believes there's room for several giants. "There will be multiple big players," she says. "I don't think there will be just one."

Google has a really good shot at remaining one of the big players, but it could lose the dominance it has enjoyed in search. As Evans puts it, "Google's share of search has really got only one way to go."

But losing market share doesn't necessarily mean making less money, Mayer argues. She expects AI to attract more people looking for answers and draw more advertising dollars into the market. Sure, she says, Google's share could get smaller, but the pie could get bigger.

Sponsor Message

Evans points to Microsoft as an example of how a company can lose dominance after a technological disruption but still keep growing. When high-speed internet took the world by storm, it opened up new ways for rivals to compete with Microsoft in software. Companies like, yes, Google developed products like Docs and Sheets that people could use in a web browser, whether or not they were running Windows. Controlling the dominant operating system no longer gave Microsoft the same advantages in the internet era.

But the internet also gave more people a reason to buy computers — and many bought PCs that ran Windows. Microsoft sold more copies of Windows and Office, and its business kept growing because of this and other reasons.

"Well, go look at Microsoft," he says. "Microsoft lost, but at the same time, the market became so much bigger" that "the shareholders got a lot more money."

That said, Microsoft shareholders needed some patience. Its stock price didn't surpass its dotcom-era peak until nearly 17 years later .

Can AI pay Google's mounting bills?

Beyond just the threat to Google's monopoly in search, AI is also challenging the advertising model that made search so lucrative.

Google's historic stock plunge in late October suggested that investors are concerned about this.

On the company's earnings call, executives acknowledged that the growing use of "AI Mode," its chatbot-style search feature, was contributing to slower growth of search advertising revenue because it earned less per query than traditional search. Meanwhile, Alphabet said it expects to spend a whopping $200 billion this year alone on infrastructure, including data centers, largely to support its AI push.

Watching Google's stock price plummet that day, it felt like seeing Google struggle with the innovator's dilemma in real time. Like it was willing to risk cannibalizing its core business to feed its ambitions in the AI age, accepting short-term pain in the hope of long-term gain.

Sponsor Message

Sundar Pichai, the CEO of Google and its parent company Alphabet, has made clear he believes embracing innovation is the only way forward. He was actually asked about the innovator's dilemma on the All-In podcast last year. "I think the dilemma only exists if you treat it as a dilemma," Pichai said. "All along in technology you have these massive periods of innovation and you lean into it as hard as you can. It's the only way to do it."

toggle caption i Ramin Talaie/Getty Images/Getty Images North America

Mayer is optimistic about Pichai's aggressive approach and Google's position in this new technological era. Google helped pioneer this technology, she says, and using it to answer people's questions draws on what has been its core expertise. She even questions whether there is really any dilemma for Google when it comes to using AI to give consumers better answers.

"They actually aren't doing something new by deploying it," Mayer says. "They're just answering questions differently and arguably better."

She does, however, acknowledge there is a dilemma when it comes to advertisers, who pay most of the company's bills. Google may need to fundamentally revamp its system of clickable ads it has spent decades showing alongside search results.

" So I think that piece of it is hard," Mayer says. "How do I take that advertising spend and move it to a new format that keeps my customers, my advertising customers, as happy?"

But advertisers will follow users, she argues, and AI could provide the basis for an even more lucrative business.

"I don't see why it can't be as profitable," she says. "In fact, I think it probably, in the end, will be more lucrative than it has been in the past."

Who knows what advertising will look like as the AI era advances. Maybe we'll see familiar-looking banner ads or clickable links on chatbot screens. Or maybe we'll be confiding in an AI assistant with a disembodied voice, like Scarlett Johansson in Her, sharing our most intimate thoughts, only to hear a word from our sponsor. Awkward.

Sponsor Message
