Mayer sees other possibilities. Her startup, Dazzle, uses AI to analyze people's photographs. Those photos can help the system learn about you — which brands you like, what products you own, and what you might want to buy next. You can also snap a photo of something you like and ask where to buy it.

"If we can identify the product and send you there," she says, "there's an opportunity for s or lead generation."

The more people share with AI systems, the more those systems learn about them, creating valuable personalized data that could be used to microtarget ads or nudge people to buy things.

For Google, the question is whether AI's new ways of connecting people to products can replace — or exceed — the profits of its existing advertising business.

In a statement to Planet Money, Google said its AI features are already leading to more searches on its platform. "This past quarter, Search queries grew at their fastest year-over-year rate in five years," the company said. It says they're taking a "deliberate approach" to developing ad revenue in this new technological era: "building the best user experience first and then scaling monetization."

Beyond Search

But the AI race is about much more than just building systems that can help people find information and make money from ads along the way. Investors are dreaming of AI models that can do things that once sounded like science fiction, including automating vast amounts of knowledge work. They're betting revolutionary applications will give rise to incredibly profitable businesses.

Evans believes the most exciting market opportunities will be found in entirely new uses for AI — some we haven't even dreamed up yet.

What will those applications be? How profitable will they become? Will they justify the mind-blowing investments Google and other companies are making in this technological revolution?

Sponsor Message

Evans says the uncertainty around fundamental questions like these helps explain stock market volatility. Investors don't know how much money these companies will ultimately earn — or how long they'll have to wait. And even if AI creates enormous wealth, he says, it's far from clear who will capture it.

One risk Evans sees is that competing AI models become so similar in their capabilities that their developers struggle to charge much for them. The most lucrative businesses could be the products and services other companies build using those models.

He points to cellphone service providers as a cautionary tale. They spent billions to build out the network infrastructure for the mobile internet, allowing people to watch videos, order taxis, and much more on their cellphones.

"All the stuff that they were talking about happened," Evans says, "but it happened 10 years later."

And when that future finally arrived, the service providers weren't the big winners from all that spending. Ouch! Yes, they owned the infrastructure, but it was the companies making smartphones and building apps and services on top of that infrastructure that captured the biggest rewards of the mobile revolution.

Evans suggests that the same risk hangs over the companies building today's AI models. "The point is just because it's amazing and cool and exciting and it's going to change the world doesn't mean that you have value capture or pricing power." In other words, AI could change the world without sending these companies' profits — or stock prices — soaring.

Of course, the fate that befell the cellphone service providers is just one possible scenario. Evans says the AI industry could develop like advanced chip manufacturing, where the rising cost and complexity of making chips left fewer and fewer companies able to compete. Or, he says, it could look like cloud computing, where several big companies make good money supplying the infrastructure that other businesses run on.

Google has a good shot at thriving under more than one of those scenarios. Its empire spans search, AI chatbots and assistants, YouTube, cloud computing, and even driverless cars through Waymo.

Google can make money both from supplying AI infrastructure and building products and services with AI, Evans says. On one side, Google already sells access to its own AI models and supplies computing power to other companies, including Anthropic. Google is also a major investor in Anthropic, and has a stake that could become even more valuable when that company goes public.

But if the business of building and running frontier AI models turns out to be less profitable than so many investors hope, Google could still make money using the technology in its own products. It also has the money and in-house expertise to compete for entirely new AI businesses.

The question is whether it can make enough money from all this to make its huge investments worthwhile — and make up for whatever it might lose in search.

Google helped invent the technology behind this revolution. Now it's betting a fortune that AI can deliver a whole new herd of cash cows — without killing the one that made it rich.

World.title: I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker
World.content:
I'm a human doctor with human intelligence. But I sure do like my AI notetaker

Sunny Rebecca Choi for NPR

Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., answers reader health questions monthly. Send in your question to: thrive@npr.org.

Question: My doctor has started recording our office visits with an artificial intelligence scribe. She says it helps write notes in my medical record. I said yes when she asked if I was comfortable with it, but in hindsight I feel a little freaked out. Should I be worried about AI listening in on my private medical conversations?

Answer: AI scribes are all the rage in medicine right now. Doctors are using them to take notes everywhere from the gynecologist's office to the emergency room.

Sponsor Message

I admit I've been an eager adopter in my own primary care practice. I use an app on my phone that records my conversation with a patient and then uses AI to write a preliminary summary for the medical record.

Sunny Rebecca Choi for NPR

It saves me time . But more importantly, I like using it because it helps me focus more fully on my patient. When I use the AI scribe, I don't have to talk and take notes at the same time – I can actually make eye contact with my patient rather than staring at the computer screen.

But I totally get why people feel uncomfortable with the technology. I share my patients' concerns about privacy and how AI scribes might impact the doctor-patient relationship.

I also worry that corporate health systems will put pressure on doctors to use any time we save with an AI scribe to squeeze in even more patients.

And like many people, I worry that artificial intelligence might one day put me out of a job!

Here's what you need to know.

How AI scribes work

When I use an AI scribe during a primary care visit, I first ask the patient if they're comfortable using the service. If the patient says yes, I start recording using an app on my smartphone. I usually set it down on the desk in the exam room.

Sponsor Message

The scribe uses a technology called "automatic speech recognition" which records our conversation and automatically distinguishes between the doctor's and patient's voices. (Sometimes, when the patient has a family member accompanying him, the app needs to distinguish between three – or more! – voices.)

When the visit ends, the recording is then transcribed. A large language model – the kind of AI technology that powers ChatGPT, but specifically geared toward medicine – converts the raw transcript into a medical note. These notes follow a standard format that is specific to the speciality and the type of visit. They reflect what the patient told the doctor, physical exam findings, and the doctor's medical decision-making.

What is the software like?

Sunny Rebecca Choi for NPR

There are lots of AI scribes on the market, ranging from products embedded within the electronic medical record to free apps a doctor can download on her phone. Most scribes use a smartphone's recording capabilities to "listen in" on the conversation, although there are some that use a desktop computer or a separate recording device.

I use my personal smartphone for this purpose, as do many physicians I know. I downloaded the AI scribe software as an app on my phone. This causes occasional hiccups. For example, I've gotten notification pings from my book club's group chat while recording a patient visit – which made me make sure to put the phone in "do not disturb" mode whenever I'm using it for patient care.

What about privacy?

Even though I use my personal phone for scribing patient visits, our conversations aren't stored on my device. They're uploaded directly to a HIPAA-compliant cloud , where the data is then transcribed into the AI-generated clinical note. Most scribe systems then delete the recording and the note after a set period of time.

HIPAA-compliance is an important feature of all AI scribe services. It means that the computer program was designed in accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, a federal law designed to protect patients' privacy.

Sponsor Message

The software company is responsible for safeguarding the data at every step of the process, from recording to generating notes. AI scribe companies encrypt the data, control who has access to it, and have systems to protect against "data breaches." It also means these companies are liable if the data is leaked.

AI scribes can make mistakes

Recently, I saw a patient who had metastatic cancer. Despite multiple conversations about his diagnosis with me, his oncologist, and his surgeon, he did not believe he had cancer. I had even – with his permission – called his spouse to tell her what was going on. He still did not accept it.

This kind of tricky clinical situation comes up on occasion, and the AI scribe did not get it right. Rather than reflecting the nuances of our conversation, the note that the scribe produced simply said that the patient had been misdiagnosed.

I often catch other errors that the software makes, like mistaking a patient's gender or age. Alarmingly, these scribes are also known for mistaking "I do" statements with "I do not." In medicine, this can be critical: The difference between "I do have chest pain" and "I do not have chest pain" can be a matter of life and death.

To better understand how AI scribes can contribute to errors in the medical record, I talked to Dr. Eileen Kim , an assistant professor of internal medicine at the University of California San Diego. Kim specializes in clinical informatics and thinks a lot about how AI might shape the future of medicine.

"You have a doctor who's overburdened, seeing way too many patients," she said. "They have this AI tool that's offered to them that seems like a great solution, but they don't have time to adequately review everything. It goes into the chart. Then you have another AI tool that's reading through all these notes. But they're wrong. And then it just propagates errors throughout the chart."

Sponsor Message

In my work caring for patients, I come across erroneous information in the electronic health record all the time. It's hard to know how much is related to AI and how much is caused by human error. But I think Dr. Kim is right to worry that AI scribes might make the problem worse.

Sunny Rebecca Choi for NPR

Who is liable for errors?

As the doctor caring for my patient, I'm ultimately the one responsible for the content of the AI-generated note, so I always read them carefully before clicking "sign" and adding them to the medical record. Most AI scribe software makes doctors sign a user agreement stating doctors are liable for everything they write in the medical record, even if a scribe helps them with it.

When the AI-generated notes are factually accurate, I almost always end up editing them to make my clinical decision-making more clear. I'm happy to have robots help me with my administrative tasks, but I still take pride in being a human doctor with human intelligence!

Health equity concerns

Many AI scribes can only be used with English-speaking patients. Health equity advocates say they fear this means unequal access to the technology, which could further widen health disparities.

For example, the scribe allows me to look more at my patient and less at my computer, which might make a patient feel more comfortable disclosing a stigmatizing health concern. Or the opposite might be true, too: A patient fearful that an AI company is "listening in" to our conversation might be afraid to share sensitive information, which in turn could affect the quality of their medical care.

Are the recordings ever used for anything other than scribing?

As a security feature, most AI scribe companies delete the recorded conversations within a set period of time. This is to protect patient privacy and also protect doctors from lawsuits. There is widespread concern in health care that the transcriptions could be used in medical malpractice lawsuits.

Sponsor Message

But some researchers call the recordings "digital gold" that could be used to assess the quality of AI-generated medical notes or even to study broader questions about physician-patient communication.

For example, I'd love to know how other doctors handle tricky conversations with patients who are fearful of vaccines. There are theoretical best practices, but analyzing hundreds of thousands of office-visit transcripts could help doctors learn what actually works best in real life.

For now, recordings of regular doctors' appointments — unless you've been enrolled in a research study — are not used for research purposes.

Can I opt-out?

Most of my patients readily agree when I ask if it's OK to use the AI scribe software, but occasionally my patients have concerns. They worry that the data isn't really secure or that it could be used to identify them in the future.

If a patient doesn't want to use the AI scribe, it's no problem. I just take notes on the computer while they talk — it's what I've done for years before the AI scribes became available.

Opting out of AI in medicine more broadly may prove to be tricky.

"It's just everywhere," said Kim, the clinical information specialist. "It would be impossible to separate. We use it throughout the healthcare system."

Software that relies on machine learning is used for billing, for clinical decision-making, and for communication between the doctor's office and patients.

AI is often used in risk calculators, like clinical tools that estimate a patient's risk of, say, heart disease based on variables like cholesterol levels and blood pressure. AI is also common in "early warning" systems that notify clinicians their patients might be vulnerable to high-risk conditions like sepsis, based on vital signs and lab values.

Kim says it's basically impossible for patients to opt out entirely from having AI involved in their medical care, "unless you're so healthy that no risk calculators ever come near you," she said.

Sponsor Message

Will AI replace my doctor?

I asked Kim — a primary care doctor like me — if she thought AI would replace us in the coming years. If the AI scribe could learn to ask the same questions I do, could it generate a treatment plan as good — or better — as the one I recommend?

Kim thought AI might change how patients experience primary care. (Possibly for the better, she said, if AI scribes allow doctors to focus more on their patients and less on the computer!)

But ultimately, she thinks human intelligence is critical in medicine.

"It looks really good because it's really good at sounding like us, and it's really good at pretending to be us," she said. "But it's still just pretending in a way. There's no real brain."

I agree. I think the AI scribe technology has the potential to do both good and harm for health care. But the core of medicine is the relationship I have with my patients. No robot can replace that.

World.title: Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip
World.content:
Trump arrives in Philippines to kick off Asia trip

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

MANILA, Philippines — President Donald Trump arrived in the Philippines on Tuesday, where he was scheduled to meet regional partners, talk trade, and seek a break from a series of setbacks at home, ranging from a major disruption to the U.S. aviation industry to a scandal that has shaken the global AI industry.

Manila, the Philippine capital, is Trump's first stop on a three-day trip that will later take him to China for historic three-way nuclear talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and, according to Trump, potentially for a meeting with North Korea's leader Kim Jong Un.

The visit marks Trump's first travel abroad since his party suffered deep losses in midterm elections. The White House and stock market alike have been rattled by the departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia last week after admitting to an affair with an alleged Chinese government agent. Beijing has said it was not involved.

Sponsor Message

As he descended the stairs from Air Force One, Trump pumped his fist. A child handed him small American and Philippine flags, which Trump waved and then swooped in big circular motions as he smiled. The U.S. president was greeted by a marching band playing "YMCA" while he walked to a waiting helicopter.

Trump to be feted at the annual ASEAN summit

Trump's first hours in the Philippines will include all the reassuring optics from Washington's oldest treaty ally in Asia, including a cocktail reception and dinner with other world leaders, an intermission from some of the thorniest issues at home. He's being feted Tuesday night at a gala as the "guest of honor" at the annual summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

The ASEAN leaders have been working on a non-aggression pact with China in the contested waters of the South China Sea, a key global trade route. Confrontations have escalated in recent years, particularly between Chinese and Philippine coast guard and naval forces in disputed shoals.

First on Trump's agenda Tuesday is a meeting with the leaders of the Quad nations, comprising the U.S., Australia, India, and Japan that have aimed to counter China's influence in the Asia Pacific. It will be their first meeting since Trump returned to the White House last year.

Sponsor Message

Trump is then scheduled to sign a trade deal with Thailand, the type of agreement he has relished striking since launching a trade war last year buttressed by steep tariff threats.

The U.S. had announced a trade framework last October in which Thailand would remove tariffs on most American goods, as well as barriers for importing U.S. autos, food products and pharmaceutical drugs, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. At the time, the Trump administration said Thailand would also spend more than $18 billion on U.S. aircraft and buy U.S. farm goods and liquefied natural gas.

The U.S. Supreme Court overturned in February the 19% tariff that Trump placed on goods from Thailand. The administration sought replacement tariffs in July by levying a 12.5% tax on imports from Thailand for not taking steps to oppose the use of forced labor.

Before the gala dinner Tuesday night, Trump will participate in what's billed as a "special summit" with the ASEAN leaders, where they are expected to discuss efforts to deepen trade and security ties as well as the region's longstanding conflicts, including yearslong violence in Myanmar and escalating disputes in the South China Sea, which Beijing claims virtually in its entirety.

Washington rejects China's expansive claim in the waterway, and has repeatedly stated that it's obligated to defend the Philippines if Filipino forces come under an armed attack.

toggle caption i Firdia Linsawati/AP

Anti-Trump protesters are gathered in Manila

About 1,500 left-wing protesters held a noisy rally in a downtown Manila square ahead of Trump's arrival, calling on Philippine leaders not to take their foreign policy cues from the U.S.

They waved red flags and held up a large streamer that read, "Resist U.S. war and plunder!" They planned to burn an effigy of Trump. Riot police with shields and wooden truncheons stood nearby.

Sponsor Message

"The Philippine government should not deal with such a loser so our call to the Marcos administration is to stop being a puppet of Donald Trump and to uphold an independent foreign policy for the Philippines," protest leader Teddy Casiño told The Associated Press at the Liwasang Bonifacio square, referring to President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

Planned meetings with the Philippine president — and possibly an old friend

On Wednesday, Trump is set to receive a red-carpet welcome and full military honors from Marcos Jr., followed by a state banquet as part of his visit to the Malacanang presidential palace. Trump and Marcos are expected to affirm their commitment to their countries' longstanding treaty alliance.

Officials are arranging a possible brief reunion in Malacanang with an old acquaintance — Imelda Marcos — if she's well enough and gets her doctors' nod.

Now 97 and using a wheelchair, the former jet set Philippine first lady and mother of the incumbent president partied in New York decades ago in her heyday as the controversial wife of a strongman leader, who was to be ousted in a pro-democracy 1986 "People Power" public uprising.

But the friendship with Trump endured, with Trump often asking Marcos Jr. and other Philippine officials: "How's Imelda?" Philippine Ambassador to Washington Jose Manuel Romualdez told The Associated Press.

"Personal connections are very important to him," Romualdez said.

When the Philippine leader met Trump in the White House last year, he carried a note from his mother that thanked the U.S. president for his strong backing of the Philippines. "President Trump was very happy and told Marcos, 'please say hello to your mother,'" according to Romualdez.

Trump is also expected to announce a series of commercial deals and investments in the aviation, defense, energy, and technology sectors, before heading to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

World.title: She went to college to become a social worker. Now she's joined the skilled trades
World.content:
She went to college to become a social worker. Now she's joined the skilled trades

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR



COLUMBUS, Ohio — A few miles south of The Ohio State University, Ashley Baukman is wrestling with a piece of steel tubing, using only a manual tool called a foot pedal and her sheer strength to bend it 90 degrees.

This class in conduit bending at The Electrical Trades Center of Central Ohio is part of an apprenticeship program Baukman began in the spring. She's here in class one day out of every two weeks. Other days, she's out on construction sites, working under the supervision of journeymen electricians.

Sponsor Message

For the 36-year-old college graduate and social worker, it's a new chapter — one she hopes will be the foundation of a long-term career.

College didn't deliver

Being the first in her family to graduate from college had been a point of pride for Baukman.

"I was like, 'Oh, I'm going to do this. I'm going to do it the right way,'" she says. "But it didn't really work out that way, and that's okay. You live and you learn."

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR

Now, as an apprentice, she's getting paid just over $25 an hour for time on the job and a stipend for days she's in class. Already, she's earning more than she was as a social worker and is set to nearly double her wage in just over three years. So far, she's finding the work engaging and rewarding.

"You can see a project to completion, and you can — 'Hey, I did that,'" she says. "It's been pretty fun."

A high point for apprenticeships

With AI throwing into question the future of work and the cost of college higher than ever, apprenticeships in the skilled trades are having a moment.

Once pushed primarily to the non-college bound, apprenticeships are increasingly being seen as a compelling alternative to higher education for anyone curious about the trades. The earn-as-you-learn model, which combines coursework with on-the-job training, requires no prerequisites or prior work experience. Acceptance is generally based on contractor need.

Right now demand for skilled tradespeople — especially electricians — is up.

Sponsor Message

The construction boom fueled by data centers has contributed to the rapid expansion of The Electrical Trades Center. Enrollment has grown from 500 apprentices in 2022 to more than 800 today. Once a night school, they now hold daytime classes to accommodate the growth.

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR

Baukman may be the only social worker among the apprentices, but as a college graduate, she has plenty of company. Trent Parker, the center's director and an electrician himself, says several dozen currently enrolled have four-year degrees, and roughly 300 applicants have at least some college on their resumes.

While Parker hasn't tracked the share of college graduates in the apprenticeship over the years, he's confident it's rising as sentiment toward the trades has shifted.

Parker recalls a recruiting visit he made to a technical high school 16 years ago. The school's vice principal told him they were grateful for the visit because they needed more opportunities for students who were "flunking out."

Parker was taken aback at the comment. He had just started as the apprenticeship's instruction coordinator and was realizing how deep the misconceptions run, how little this vice principal knew about the rigors of the work. That's now changing.

"You know, we're looking for high performers," Parker says. "The same people that are going to be successful in college are the same people that are going to be successful here."

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR

He notes that the apprenticeship's curriculum is equivalent to college-level coursework. Conduit bending is based on trigonometry. Apprentices have to be able to manipulate decimals and fractions.

Parker was thrilled when in 2023, Ohio's governor signed into law a requirement that licensed school counselors visit a training center like this one to learn about apprenticeships and the careers they lead to, a major step in changing the "college or bust" mentality and recruiting more broadly into the field.

When his own two daughters were deciding about college, he encouraged them to consider following in his path.

Sponsor Message

"I asked them several times, 'Are you sure you don't want to be an electrician?'" he says. "Now I get to log into their Sallie Mae loan accounts and — you know — ugh. I agreed to pay what?"

Rethinking earlier choices

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR

Gather together some of the college graduates at The Electrical Trades Center, and you hear similar themes. A common one: Careers they pursued after college just didn't pay enough.

After finishing her degree in social work, Baukman found jobs in local government agencies working with children and seniors but never earned enough to support her blended family. Her last job was as a prevention specialist in schools, but what she really wanted to do was to become a school social worker, a role that requires a master's degree. With five children at home, plus an estimated $80,000 in student loans, she couldn't figure out how to make it work.

"It just wasn't in the cards," she says. "So I was looking for a change."

Mike Hansen entered the apprenticeship after completing college, ten years in the Army, and some graduate school. He was originally on track to do a doctoral degree in sport and performance psychology, but had seen how others who had gone into academia had struggled.

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR

"They were doing 40 hours of teaching and zero hours of research for $40,000 a year," he says. He left school after finishing his master's degree.

Now, at 39, he wishes he could go back and tell his 17-year-old self to consider a career in the trades from the start. The opportunity was there. His father was an airline mechanic and a member of the Teamsters union. His high school had a vocational school attached to it, but going there was highly stigmatized.

"I distinctly remember as part of our generation... it was massively looked down upon. You were considered a burnout," he says. "Guidance counselors, teachers, my parents, everyone was like, 'Go to college, get an engineering degree. You'll make six figures.'"

Sponsor Message

For Michael Hughes, the message was slightly different. "The expectation was to get a four-year degree in some field whatsoever, and you'll be fine," he says.

He wasn't sure what he wanted to do, so he majored in English.

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR

"I had a pipe dream of, you know, writing for TV and movies," he says. After college, he did work for a time for the Geek Squad, mounting televisions and installing home theater systems, among other jobs.

Now, as an apprentice, he's been pulling wire, adding pipe, and replacing panels and fuses in a variety of settings including a police station, a paper mill, a sheet metal plant and an auto plant. He's appreciating the breadth of what he's learning and the chance to apply it immediately.

"It's almost like learning a foreign language by just going to that country and communicating, and then also taking classes and someone teaching you the proper conjugations of verbs," he says.

A future of six-figure earnings

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR

Between new construction, commercial renovations and the data center buildout, electricians in Ohio are flush with work. With data center projects in particular, contractors are offering big incentives to get the jobs done quickly.

Parker has heard of projects paying $5 or $10 over the union-negotiated hourly wage. On other projects, all overtime is double time. Apprentices have even heard rumors about triple time.

"There's some crazy money to be made out there," he says.

The apprentices are guaranteed a minimum hourly wage that starts at $23 an hour. There are built-in raises that come as they reach milestones for hours worked, topping out at $46 an hour. With overtime, many journeyworker electricians earn well over $100,000 a year, something the apprentices are looking forward to.

For now, these apprentices don't get to choose where they work. The program assigns them, based on contractor need. Harry Cekovich has been happy with his assignment at a solar field, where he's primarily running cables through rows of solar panels. There too, he's been picking up overtime while also collecting a $100 per diem. It's money he puts towards gas, although the site is less than an hour from his home.

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR

Cekovich is the only one in the group who knows what it's like to earn six figures. For a time, the 34-year-old Ohio State graduate was making pretty good money as a massage therapist and a bartender.

Sponsor Message

"Granted, I was working 60, 70 hour weeks," he says. "Crazy, nonstop hours, so nothing too great, honestly."

None of those jobs came with benefits. Now, through the union contract, he has both retirement benefits and health insurance with no premiums.

"It's nice to be able to go to doctors and get checked up now," he says.

Mixed feelings about data centers and AI

toggle caption i Andrew Spear for NPR

With all the data center construction around Columbus, it's a given that the apprentices will work on a data center at some point. Some are more excited about it than others.

"If it's true about them making double or triple time… I want to work at data centers exclusively," jokes Cekovich.

Hansen is not so enthusiastic.

"There's enough concern and discussion going on right now about the harms that data centers cause," he says, citing their heavy energy and water use and the noise they generate. "Once I become a journeyman, and I'm allowed to pick my calls, I probably won't pick a job call for a data center, personally."

Ohio Gov.-elect Amy Acton has called for a "conditional moratorium" on new data center construction to ensure that developers cover their own utility costs, adhere to environmental standards and use union labor, among other things.

Whatever happens, Hansen expects there will be plenty of work at area hospitals, schools, commercial buildings and factories.

The apprentices are aware that the rapid buildout of data centers — especially hyperscale ones built to power AI — is a big reason the apprenticeship has been able to bring in so many recruits. At the moment, it accounts for about half the work in the school's jurisdiction.

"It kind of seems like it is, for better or worse, the way of the future," says Cekovich, adding that the proliferation of data centers influenced his decision to go into the electrical trades. "Are we contributing to the end of civilization with AI getting to be what it might become? Not totally sure."

Sponsor Message

Come what may, Hansen believes he and his classmates will be okay.

"I would like to see Chat GPT wire a three-way switch," he says. "We're still going to need electricians."

World.title: More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?
World.content:
More people are getting the flu. Should you get a flu shot before you travel?

toggle caption i Thibaut Durand/Getty Images

More people are getting the flu than usual this fall, according to the latest influenza tracking numbers from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

"Flu started a bit early this year, so it's out there and spreading," Dr. William Schaffner, a professor of infectious diseases at the Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville. "So people who are thinking of Thanksgiving travel need to get their protection as quickly as possible."

Sponsor Message

The flu shot takes about ten days to reach its full efficacy, so there's still time to get one before Thanksgiving, Schaffner says. And the sooner someone gets it, the better – especially because people will be gathering in enclosed spaces for the holidays.

AAA predicts that this year, around 82 million people will travel more than 50 miles over Thanksgiving break, including 73 million by car.

Getting the vaccine doesn't mean someone won't get the flu – but it does mean they'll be less likely to wind up in the hospital from influenza-related complications. Those include pneumonia and secondary bacterial infections.

"It can strike a healthy person at any age and put them in the emergency room. Flu is like that," Schaffner says.

People at the highest risk are seniors, young children and people with underlying health conditions.

Schaffner also says not enough people are getting their COVID boosters.

"Somehow they think that COVID has disappeared," he says. "But the people who are admitted to my hospital with COVID are invariably people who are not up to date with their vaccinations, as with flu. That COVID vaccine helps keep you out of the hospital. It is still a threat. It hasn't gone away."

People should have no trouble finding available vaccines for the flu, COVID and the highly contagious respiratory syncytial virus, RSV, at their local pharmacies and health care providers' offices, says Claire Hannan, the executive director of the Association of Immunization Managers, adding that vaccination season is in "full swing."

Sponsor Message

"Now is definitely the time to get vaccinated," says Hannan. "Influenza is circulating, people are traveling, people are getting ready for Thanksgiving, the holidays. And the best protection you can get is from the vaccine."

World.title: Carney government amends controversial bill to fast-track pipelines and mines
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Liberal MPs have agreed to make some changes to a controversial piece of government legislation that's supposed to speed up the approval of major projects.

A special House of Commons committee is studying Bill C-39, the Building Canada Strong Act. MPs began going through the massive piece of legislation line-by-line Monday, with committee sitting until midnight. They will resume work on Tuesday morning.

Tucked inside the bill are a dizzying array of more than 300 clauses that amend more than a dozen separate pieces of federal legislation, including laws to protect species at risk, water quality and fisheries. Also inside are proposed changes to the Labour Code , which have upset unions.

Liberals call the legislation one of the most important economic bills in a generation that will enable the federal government to deliver decisions on mines, pipelines and power lines in Ottawa's jurisdiction within one year.

Environmentalists, on the other hand, say the bill guts Canada's environmental safeguards.

Conservatives strengthening guardrails in the bill

Liberals are keeping parts of the the bill largely intact, resisting any major changes the opposition parties are suggesting.

But Conservatives secured an early amendment Monday evening, adding some safeguards and protections around new legislated powers that would allow shovels to hit the ground before an impact assessment takes place.

Typically construction cannot begin on projects like railways and ports, until the environment and climate change minister signs off on an impact assessment review — a thorough evaluation of a proposed project's potential environmental, social, economic and health effects.

Referring to the proposed Alto High speed rail project, Ontario Conservative MP Phil Lawrence said he has heard from constituents concerned about the preliminary work Alto would need to do in his riding.

"There are actions that are being taken with respect to the Alto that may not be reversible at the early stage," he said.

Conservative MPs added language to the bill that would require the review agency to post a copy of any early project work online. In theory, such a notice could enable opponents of a project to challenge in federal court early activities before they begin.

In the eyes of the bill's critics, the proposed amendments may improve transparency and accountability, but they do little to strengthen environmental protections.

"Any amendments being passed right now are small attempts at harm reduction that won't change the balance of harms that the bill proposes," Isabel McMurray, a lawyer with Ecojustice, said Monday night outside the committee hearing.

Ottawa removes blank cheque to approve pipelines

CBC News obtained a copy of the amendments that parties are proposing. The 228 pages of amendments are nearly as long as the bill itself.

WATCH | Protests on Bill C-39: National day of action prompts rally in Thunder Bay, Ont., against Bill C-39 | Duration 1:37 More than 60 communities across Canada held a national day of action on Thursday against Bill C-39. Labour unions, Indigenous rights groups and environmental organizations are calling for the proposed legislation, known as the Building Canada Strong Act, to be scrapped. Here are some of the concerns raised during Thursday’s rally in Thunder Bay, Ont.

Conservatives, the Bloc Québecois, New Democrats and the Green Party are all pushing for changes to the bill that would place more guardrails under the government's ability to designate regions of national interest.

The act gives cabinet powers to designate entire zones as regions of national interest, giving Ottawa broad authority to approve future activities. One example of such an area that could be a candidate is the Ring of Fire, a mineral-rich and ecologically sensitive area of northern Ontario.

Environmentalists have referred to these areas as "sacrifice zones where projects could get rubber stamped."

The Conservatives have submitted amendments that would require more certainty on what kinds of areas could receive the new designation. According to the amendment, the region must contain "existing or reasonably foreseeable development" and contribute to international trade, energy security, critical mineral or national defence.

The Greens want language added to the bill that prevents the government from including existing or future national parks and other protected areas from these zones.

Notably, Liberal MPs are proposing new curbs on the Canada Energy Regulators's powers to approve pipelines without cabinet approval.

When the bill was first tabled in September, Liberals said the bill regulator could approve pipelines on its own that are under 300 kilometres.

But as it stands there is also a clause buried in the bill that gives the pipeline regulator a blank cheque to approve a pipeline of any length without a cabinet approval.

Some Liberals uncomfortable with C-39

The Carney government's willingness to make amendments follow concerns that were raised within the ranks of the Liberal caucus. Two MPs shared their discomfort with the lack of safeguards in the legislation.

WATCH | Liberal MP express concerns about Bill C-39: Liberal MP speaks out over party's major project fast-tracking legislation C-39 | Duration closed caption 7:11 B.C.-based Liberal MP Will Greaves says he supports his party's Bill C-39, which proposes to expand government's powers to fast-track major projects — but tells CBC's Rosemary Barton he wants 'appropriate safeguards' in place as the legislation moves forward.

NDP MP Leah Gazan proposed several changes to protect the constitutional rights of Indigenous peoples and to strengthen the language around and free prior and informed consent.

Liberals supported one of those amendments, but rejected most of Gazan's other proposals.

Debate on the C-39 comes as a new report shows federal permitting is rarely a "bottleneck" in getting clean energy projects built. The report cites other factors including "delayed engagement with Indigenous nations, lack of meaningful community involvement."

"We want to see renewable energy projects built from coast to coast at the scale this moment demands," Katie Gibbs, the national policy manager for Climate Action Network Canada, said in a statement.

"But speed doesn’t mean sacrificing environmental safeguards. The sweeping deregulation being pushed through with Bill C-39 will not get projects built faster."

World.title: How China is positioning itself as a global leader as it hosts Trump, Putin
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As China welcomes world leaders to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum this week in Shenzhen, it presents a very different nation than the one that last hosted the event in 2014.

Amid global conflicts, tariff disputes and economic instability, Beijing is using the summit to cast itself as a reliable global power capable of uniting leaders and brokering international economic co-operation.

Trump, Xi, Putin

Beijing's current standing is perhaps best captured by a proposed tripartite meeting hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping with U.S. President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the world's three largest nuclear powers.

Choosing Shenzhen places the talks in the heart of China's drive for technological self-reliance. Once a small fishing village, it has transformed into a sprawling metropolis of skyscrapers and factories, and home to companies like electric vehicle maker BYD and telecom giant Huawei.

Some observers compare the gathering to the 1945 Yalta Conference, where the U.S., U.K., and Soviet Union formalized their post-war spheres of influence.

"Who else could broker this three-way right now?" said Greg Chin, associate professor of political economy and director of the Global China Research Lab at York University in Toronto.

"It's really only China and President Xi."

Russian President Vladimir Putin attends a summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on Sept. 1. (Sputnik/Petr Kovalev/Reuters)

Trump arrives in a weakened domestic position following a devastating midterm election defeat, with voter anxiety over the cost of living and the U.S.-Israel war with Iran taking centre stage. That conflict is expected to come up, given that both China and Russia maintain strategic partnerships with Iran.

Another likely agenda point is the war in Ukraine — where Russia has made only slow, incremental gains — notably with neither Ukraine nor other European states seated at the table.

A Russian drone hits a car in the frontline town of Kramatorsk, Ukraine, on July 15. Russia has recently made only incremental progress in its invasion. (Iryna Rybakova/Press Service of the Ukrainian Armed Forces/Reuters)

"Both the U.S. and Russia are at war with someone," said Henry Huiyao Wang, the founder and president of the Center for China and Globalization, a think-tank in Beijing.

"China is the only one without a war."

Wang says both Washington and Moscow are growing fatigued, leaving an opening for China to step in as a mediator.

As he departed the White House for his Asia trip, Trump even suggested a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un was possible.

WATCH | Tariff relief for Canada: Carney, Xi strike trade deal offering $400M in tariff relief | Duration closed caption 2:48 Prime Minister Mark Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping have struck a trade deal that will see China reduce tariffs on roughly $400 million worth of Canadian exports, including frozen pork and shrimp, until 2028. In return, Canada will extend tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminum products.

"He may come. I don't know. That's up to President Xi," he said.

And although China appears to be wary of the discussion, Trump says he is planning on bringing up nuclear disarmament.

"[It's a] tough subject because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes," Trump said Monday.

Thorny issues

Economic and trade talks will run parallel to high-profile diplomacy.

Considering the shakeup at Nvidia — with Jensen Huang resigning as CEO of the microchip giant following revelations he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy — it could be harder for China to access advanced chips even though the U.S. loosened restrictions last year at Huang's lobbying.

As a result, AI competition between Washington and Beijing could be high on the agenda, considering Huang's ousting has prompted Congress to close the loophole that allowed China to access the chips.

Despite some thorny issues, some deals have been announced, including loosened restrictions on Canadian pork, seafood imports into China, in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum, a sign of Ottawa's continuing strategic pivot away from the U.S.

A robot serves ice cream in the press centre ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Tuesday. (Anupam Nath/The Associated Press)

From the Philippines earlier this week, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade talks with the U.S. don't result in preserving the North American auto industry, in the wake of Stellantis announcing it's selling its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to armoured vehicle manufacturer Roshel.

Carney's comments on autos already drew ire from the White House, and the announcement on steel, especially, is likely to irk Trump. Whether it comes up during the talks remains to be seen.

With geopolitical caveats to the trade relationships with North America and Europe, China may also focus on maintaining and expanding its relationships with the other of the 21 APEC member economies, especially those that are emerging.

"Latin American and southeast Asian countries are becoming increasingly important," said Ning Leng, assistant professor at the McCourt School of Public Policy at Georgetown University in Washington, D.C.

With the issue of its overcapacity looming, she said Beijing will try to "reassure these countries" by promising industrial upgrades and building up their AI capacity and digital infrastructure.

With China's own economic woes, however, "it is even more important for the Chinese government to show to the world that it is doing great," she said.

And despite the sluggish economy, stability is relative, said Chin, with York University.

"Relative to everyone else, China is still doing pretty well."

World.title: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang signals willingness to return as CEO
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned from the chipmaker last week under a cloud of scandal, said on Tuesday he "would be honoured" ‌to come back as CEO if the board decided his return would be in the best interest of shareholders and employees.

"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia’s employees, investors, business partners and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in his first public statement since he resigned on Nov. 12 over revelations of extramarital affairs that intensified scrutiny of the chip firm's China business.

"I created problems for the board that I deeply regret. ​I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to co-operating with the board’s independent investigation," he ​said.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Huang's statement.

His comments come on the same day that Nvidia announced it has created a board-level national security ‌and export-control committee as fallout from Huang's resignation, and as Huang agreed to appear for transcribed interviews before U.S. lawmakers next month.

The interviews will take place on Dec. 1 before the House committees for foreign affairs and intelligence, and the select committee on the Chinese Communist Party, according to a statement.

Nvidia's general counsel ‌Tim Teter will appear before the same committees on Dec. 2.

"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim ​Teter on their roles in a potential breach of ⁠our national security," the Republican chairmen of the committees, ⁠Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford, said.

"The ​American people need answers on Mr. Huang and ​Nvidia's role in ⁠allowing dangerous [People's Republic of China] actors to access our most advanced chips, as well as the role of a potential Chinese intelligence asset in this scandal."

WATCH | What's Trump saying about Huang?: Trump says he 'would not mind' if Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia CEO | Duration closed caption 2:45 U.S. President Donald Trump says he 'would not mind' if Jensen Huang returned to his position as Nvidia CEO and backed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who is facing increased scrutiny about his potential role in the alleged spy scandal.

As for the committee on national security, Nvidia said the group will be chaired by director Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former Goldman ​Sachs vice-chair and veteran U.S. corporate director, and will include directors Stephen Neal, former CEO ⁠of law firm Cooley ⁠LLP, and John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical ‌engineering at Caltech.

U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed Nvidia's move on Tuesday, saying it was a good idea for the company to launch a national security initiative.

Huang's relationships have sharpened scrutiny of Nvidia's governance and whether its oversight kept pace with its explosive growth ​and growing importance to U.S. national security.

The crisis had wiped ​more than $400 billion US off Nvidia's market value by the close of markets on Monday.

The Trump administration said Monday it would further restrict China's access to advanced AI chips from companies ⁠including Nvidia, tightening controls as Trump headed to China for talks with President Xi Jinping.

Washington has sought for years to curb Beijing's access to Nvidia's most sophisticated processors, putting the company's China business at the centre of an increasingly contentious debate ‌over national security, trade and U.S. technological leadership.

However, Chinese companies have repeatedly found ways around the curbs. Huang had long advocated allowing more chip exports to China.

LISTEN | Huang's fall is an AI game-changer: Day 6 10:48 How Jensen Huang’s implosion at Nvidia reshapes the global battle for AI supremacy

The new committee will oversee Nvidia's national security and global trade compliance programs and work with independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.

Nvidia's existing ​national security team and global trade compliance team will report to the committee, while interim CEO Colette Kress will oversee day-to-day operations. The committee plans ⁠to meet at least quarterly, including with management and in executive session.

The company did not have a chief ⁠compliance officer, according to its 2026 proxy statement.

It was not immediately clear whether the committee was created in ⁠response ⁠to revelations about Huang's affairs. Nvidia did not ​immediately respond to a Reuters request for further comment.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to ​help establish and advance a ⁠robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones said.

Nvidia is due to report third-quarter earnings after the market closes on Tuesday.

By some estimates, the company has more than $500 billion US in commitments, including supply and capacity backstops for chip purchases, data-centre leases and equity investments, though that remains ⁠a fraction of its market capitalization.

World.title: Fear, outrage grow as Quebec moves to ban religious symbols for elementary students
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Mehwaish Raja’s 11-year-old daughter surprised her during a conversation this past summer on the way to day camp.

“She shared with me during the car ride: ‘Mama, I will wear my hijab at the end of the summer,’” Raja said.

Up until that point, her daughter only wore the hijab for special occasions, and Raja had never insisted she wear it regularly.

“I just said, ‘OK.’ And by the end of the summer, it actually happened,” Raja said.

Her daughter now wears the hijab every day in her Grade 5 class in a public school in Montreal’s West Island.

Now, the new Parti Québécois government is proposing a law that would make that practice illegal as part of a series of measures announced on the campaign trail to strengthen secularism.

Raja is struggling to understand why.

“Honestly, I'm out of words. I'm out of words when I hear things like this,” she said.

She doesn’t think the government should be able to decide what her daughter wears to school.

“When we step out of our house, we leave as who we are. What part of us do we leave at home?” she said.

WATCH | Experts raise concerns about Quebec's religious symbols ban for school children: Parents, experts raise concerns over Quebec’s proposed ban on school kids wearing religious symbols | Duration closed caption 4:55 Over the years, Quebec has gradually tightened restrictions on wearing religious symbols in schools for teachers, staff members and parent volunteers. The Parti Québécois has stood firm on its plans to extend that law to school kids, but experts and researchers raise concerns, saying it could lead to marginalization and even dehumanization.

Religious symbols gradually squeezed out of schools

The previous CAQ government already introduced several laws restricting religious symbols in schools, preventing at first teachers , and then all school staff – even parent volunteers – from wearing them.

Generally, religious symbols bans in Quebec have targeted employees of the state considered to be in positions of authority, but the CAQ opened the door to targeting students by introducing a ban on full face coverings at school.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is opening that door wider, proposing a blanket ban preventing elementary school students from wearing "conspicuous" religious symbols while at school.

“Separating children through what they wear and through religious beliefs at such a young age is not helping cohesion and integration,” St-Pierre Plamondon said in September when announcing the measure, without providing any specific examples.

“We think it's a good policy in terms of letting children just be children, with no connection whatsoever to what their parents believe about religion,” he'd said.

When proposing the religious ban for elementary schools during the election campaign, PQ Leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said the symbols 'interfere with cohesion and integration.' (Ivanoh Demers/CBC/Radio-Canada)

Winning a minority government in the general election did not soften the PQ's resolve, with new Education Minister Joël Arseneau saying the measure was a "non-negotiable."

"It’s on this basis that we were elected, and it’s on this basis that we’re working,” Arseneau told reporters at the National Assembly in late October.

Mother says proposed law based on misconceptions

Asma Qureshi says the PQ's proposal comes from a place of ignorance.

Qureshi, who lives on Montreal’s South Shore, has four children. Her oldest daughter, now in high school, started wearing a hijab to school when she was in Grade 4. Her youngest daughter, currently in kindergarten, wore one to school a couple of times this year just to try it.

Qureshi – who wears a hijab herself – says in both cases, she didn’t ask or order her daughters to wear one.

"I told myself that I would never impose it on my kids," she said.

"There’s this narrative that goes around – and it's been there since I was a young kid – that children and women are being forced to wear the scarf."

Qureshi thinks that misconception is what’s feeding the gradual tightening of restrictions on wearing religious symbols in Quebec, particularly in schools.

She says she hasn’t yet discussed the proposed ban with her daughters.

“How do you tell a child it’s against the law for you to wear something that your mother wears?” she said.

Raja says her daughter's decision to start wearing the hijab regularly this fall convinced her to do the same. (CBC News)

For Raja, who up until now had been reluctant to wear a hijab in Quebec for fear of standing out, says her daughter's decision to wear one at school this fall convinced her to do the same.

“I'm really proud of her because at 11 years old, she decided to wear it, whereas I’m 40 and I hadn't been able to,” she said.

“My daughter truly inspired me."

Ban would cause harm, experts say

Experts in secularism and child development told CBC there is no justification for banning students from wearing religious symbols — and that the measure would be harmful.

Thomas Dee, an economist at Stanford University who specializes in how education policy affects student outcomes, disagreed with the notion of asking children to leave their parents' religious baggage behind.

“Parents are children's first and most impactful teachers, and to sideline their guidance and insights just seems misguided to me and disrespectful,” he said.

Dee testified as an expert witness in the court challenge to Bill 21, Quebec’s first secularism law.

Thomas Dee, an economics professor at Stanford University who studies the effects of education policy on student outcomes, says a policy that marginalizes parents' values in school is misguided and disrespectful. (CBC News)

Sivane Hirsch, a professor in the faculty of education at Université Laval who specializes in cultural and religious diversity in schools, believes the ban is a horrible idea.

“We don’t want children to feel they’re being taught in school against their parents, against their family,” Hirsch said.

Dee said such a conflict would also hurt students’ performance.

“Anything that makes students feel less welcome or less at ease will imply they're not able to bring their full attention and motivation to the realization of their academic potential,” Dee said.

Zeinab Diab, a religious studies researcher at Université de Montréal and author of Au nom de la laïcité, a book about Islamophobia in Quebec, said a secularism law that targets young children is inhumane.

“They are dehumanizing them and limiting their access to school. What kind of society allows that?” she said.

Author and religious studies researcher Zeinab Diab says targeting children for a religious symbols ban is inhumane. (CBC News)

Dee said the presence of religious symbols in the classroom could actually help.

“If you engage with people across difference, you no longer use simple rules of thumb to judge them, but rather you judge them as people,” he said.

Qureshi said that was her daughter’s experience.

She said no other students made negative comments or gave her daughter a hard time when she started wearing the hijab.

“It was just like she was any other regular person,” she said. “That's the beautiful thing – when people can recognize you for who you are rather than what you wear."

PQ needs support of at least 1 other party

In order to adopt the ban, the PQ will need support from at least one other party in the National Assembly.

Charles Milliard, leader of the Quebec Liberals and the Official Opposition, said last week his party wouldn’t support the measure.

“We're talking about children. I'm not going to do politics on the backs of children,” Milliard said.

Québec Solidaire also doesn’t support the measure.

That leaves the Conservative Party of Quebec.

On Monday, leader Éric Duhaime said his party generally supports secularism, but wanted to see more details before deciding whether to support the proposed law.

"I mean, what are we going to do with those kids if they don't respect the rules?" Duhaime told reporters.

"That's the kind of thing that I want to know before we move forward."

Education Minister Joël Arseneau says he's negotiating with other parties about the idea of banning religious symbols for elementary school students, and that their positions may evolve. (CBC News)

Last week, Arseneau said he was in negotiations with other parties about the bill, and that their positions may evolve. He declined CBC’s request for an interview.

Raja says if the ban does become law, her daughter would likely leave her current school.

“If the public system is really asking us not to practise certain values that we strongly believe in, I would choose another way of educating my children,” she said.

For her that would likely be private school, but she said some other parents might choose homeschooling.

Diab said not all families have either the money or the time for those options.

“Maybe they’re going to adapt, but no one should be always in fight and survival mode,” she said.

“This is exhausting.”

World.title: Hooked by design: How gambling apps keep 'losers' spending more cash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.

After three years of compulsive online betting, Robin Koczerginski tried to quit in 2025.

He stopped using his favourite sports gambling apps: Bet365, DraftKings and BetMGM.

He says that after installing special software on his devices to prevent him from accessing the apps, almost immediately his phone lit up with email notifications and special offers luring him back.

"Bonuses, free bets, all this stuff. I honestly felt like it escalated even more after I stopped playing," the Toronto father, writer and communications strategist told CBC News.

It was all to "entice [me] to come back in," he said.

It worked. He relapsed and started gambling again.

A CBC News investigation has found Koczerginski's relapse is indicative of a larger problem fuelled by a sophisticated, multibillion-dollar online gambling industry that routinely uses automated inducements and design features to try to keep users hooked.

This despite rules in most jurisdictions, including Ontario and Alberta, that require online casinos to monitor player behaviour and intervene when players show signs of addiction or high-risk play.

WATCH | One man's battle to save himself, his family from online gambling: Addicted: one man’s battle to save himself, his family from online gambling | Duration closed caption 5:03 Robin Koczerginski’s online gambling began as an escape, but spiralled into a years-long addiction. He shares his story of recovery and how he and his partner, Rachel Lefebvre, overcame his addiction in hopes of helping other families.

'Dark patterns' make cashing out difficult

Casino and sports betting apps welcome users into an online experience purposely built to keep people playing and losing money, experts told CBC News.

Beyond attractive colours, flashing animations and a rapid pace of play, experts say companies employ design features known as "dark patterns" crafted to trick users into playing for longer or not notice their losses.

CBC spoke to a former designer from Bally's Corporation in the U.K., a mid-sized global casino, sports betting and online company, who said they installed features to discourage users from setting up spending limits and added colourful pop-ups to distract them from the feeling of losing.

"Everything on the screen is playing with your psychological feelings," the former Baily's designer said, noting this is true of the designs of many popular social media apps and consumer websites.

CBC agreed not to identify the designer, as they fear repercussions for speaking about trade practices.

They also said the company used dark patterns to delay the process of closing an account to allow time for users to change their minds.

Bally's declined to answer questions about its design features but instead offered a statement that reads in part: "We take our responsibility to our players seriously and work closely with our regulatory partners to ensure responsible gaming principles and safeguards are reflected throughout our products and offerings."

Experts who study online gambling apps say these features are common.

"On any gambling site that you go to there will be a large deposit button at the top of the screen, but the withdrawal button will be more than likely hidden," said Jack McGarrigle, a PhD candidate in psychology at Swansea University in Wales who is studying the phenomenon .

Jack McGarrigle, a PhD candidate in psychology at Swansea University in Wales, says gambling apps often make it difficult to withdraw money, cancel accounts or access safer gambling tools in a bid to keep gamblers hooked. (Mat Heywood/CBC)

It works to discourage withdrawals, according to Koczerginski.

"Deposit, it takes 10 seconds. You just click a couple of buttons and your money's in your account," he said. "When you withdraw, it is different. There's a period of time that you have to wait, and it's super easy to cancel that withdrawal, which I've done before, too."

McGarrigle says apps also often obscure the "responsible gambling" features that allow players to set daily or weekly spending limits.

He likens these features that keep gamblers playing to ones used by social media and online shopping platforms that keep users scrolling as long as possible.

But the stakes are different.

"If you spend too much time on TikTok, you're not going to go bankrupt or lose your house," McGarrigle said.

LISTEN | New bill tries to rein in online gambling: The Current 19:44 New bill tries to rein in online gambling The federal government is considering a bill to regulate online sports gaming. CBC senior reporter, Dave Seglins, describes what he and his team have revealed in their series on the negative impacts, and Matthew Young explains why Canada needs a lot more data to really understand the scope of the problem.

CBC looked into these features by setting up accounts on multiple popular gambling apps and found that cashing out took several extra steps and required waiting eight to 10 days to receive a physical cheque in the mail.

It's also common for gambling apps to de-emphasize the loss of cash.

T.S., a 22-year-old recent university graduate from Ontario, quit gambling in 2025 after losing $14,000 in one night on blackjack.

"When you played blackjack on FanDuel, for example, they wouldn't even say that you'd lost money," he recounted.

"But if you won, you get a big pop-up on your screen that says you won … It's obvious that they're trying to make it fun to win and easy to ignore when you lose."

CBC has agreed not to name him as he fears being stigmatized by prospective employers.

T.S., 22, says the design of gambling apps makes it easier to ignore losses and celebrate wins. (YanJun Li/CBC)

In a statement to CBC News , FanDuel said the company "is committed to providing customers with a clear and transparent entertainment experience."

"Responsible gaming tools are built directly into our apps and are easily accessible to every customer. These include reality checks, deposit and time limits, and the My FanDuel Spend dashboard, which gives customers visibility into their spending and activity so they can make informed decisions about their play."

'Targeting losers'

A former data analyst at DraftKings has been speaking out about his time at the company, which is one of North America's biggest online gambling companies.

Jayden Butts told CBC and The New York Times that his work between 2022 and 2024 involved identifying and targeting potentially vulnerable gamblers.

Butts says he was tasked with studying DraftKings player data to identify the most profitable customers to target with bonuses.

Jayden Butts, a former data analyst at Draftkings, says the company was using player data to send promotions to potentially high-risk gamblers. (Submitted by Jayden Butts)

"What I was asked to do is, given all the immense amounts of data that we had on customers — where they're from, how they play, what they like to play, you name it — with all of these features, can we create something that tells us who we should be sending our promotional offers to?"

But he became uncomfortable as he concluded the most profitable customers might also be high-risk problem gamblers.

DraftKings told CBC in a statement, "We do not market to customers based on indicators of potential problem gaming."

Butts, however, felt he was exploiting vulnerable players.

"I'm making their lives harder and their financial situations worse, the better I do at my job," he said.

"It's targeting losers. I don't want it to sound like, ‘Oh, they're targeting the suckers.' It's literally like they are targeting people who are most likely to lose money."

Butts says he was dismissed in late 2024 for performance issues. He says he'd become disillusioned.

DraftKings told CBC News in an email that it uses "basic marketing practices" such as data science and analytics — and not AI — to customize its promotional targeting toward "customer groups, not individual customers."

"Statements by Mr. Butts only reflect his views, as a single junior-level business analyst at DraftKings who was employed at the company for less than two years."

"The premise that a problem gambler would be 'the best investment' is patently false. Our long-term success depends on customers who engage responsibly."

DraftKings also rejected the characterization that withdrawals are more difficult to make than deposits.

“Withdrawals and deposits involve different processing requirements. DraftKings approves and sends 97 per cent of withdrawal requests within five minutes,” a spokesperson wrote in an email Monday.

Calls for stricter regulation

After Butts's initial allegations were published by The New York Times in September, politicians and gaming regulators in the U.S. launched inquiries into whether DraftKings and other companies are misusing data and AI to target problem gamblers.

Ontario's regulator, the Alcohol and Gaming Commission, did not respond to CBC's questions about whether it is investigating DraftKings.

The AGCO issued a detailed statement citing Ontario's regulatory standards , which set requirements for game design, player information, advertising, inducements and player protections.

CBC looked into design features of gambling apps by setting up accounts on popular apps, and found that cashing out took several extra steps and required waiting 8-10 days to receive a physical cheque in the mail. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

"Operators must monitor for indicators of gambling-related harm and intervene appropriately …. Player data or analytical tools cannot be used to target high-risk players with marketing or inducements," the AGCO wrote.

T.S. and Robin Koczerginski have both quit gambling, sought addictions treatment and are now in recovery. Koczerginski has enrolled in a program called BetGuard , which excludes him from all regulated gambling sites in Ontario, making a relapse near impossible.

They both say that when they were gambling, erratically and at all hours, they felt highly targeted despite showing classic signs of problem gambling.

"They're really trying to pinpoint exactly who you are, what you like, what is, like, your particular flavour of bets that you like to place, and trying to use that to keep you going, especially as you are fighting really hard [to stop] when you're addicted," Koczerginski said.

T.S. believes governments need to step in with stricter controls on gambling companies.

"[The companies are] not going to do it on their own," he said.

"They're never gonna stop targeting problem gamblers. That's where their money comes from."

World.title: Stolen 120-year-old church bell found discarded in rural Manitoba ditch
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A heavy church bell stolen from the top of a belfry in rural Manitoba has been found abandoned in a ditch.

RCMP recovered it around 5:30 a.m. Tuesday near the small community of Malonton after receiving a tip from a passerby.

It was dumped about 10 kilometres southwest of the S acred Heart of Jesus Ukrainian Catholic Church, which is 80 kilometres north of Winnipeg near Fraserwood.

It was stolen from the church during the week leading up to Nov. 14, when the theft was discovered, police said.

" That was a really unique piece of history, and we're just really relieved that it's been recovered and it's in good condition. It appears to be mostly undamaged," said RCMP Const. Merry Ploeg .

"Now we can kind of shift our focus over to figuring out who took it and how they took it. Even just recovering it took a few people, so it's quite a heavy piece of history."

Damage can be seen at the top of the wooden belfry. (Tyler Searle/CBC)

The bell, estimated to weigh about 135 kilograms (300 pounds), was somehow removed from a 1½-storey belfry that stands at the back of the Sacred Heart of Jesus churchyard in Manitoba's Interlake region.

Some boards were broken and removed from the top of the belfry, but how it was lowered is a mystery.

"That one … I haven't quite figured it out," said Ploeg.

There’s nothing on the ground to indicate where it might have landed if it was pushed out, and there are no tracks from any vehicles.

"I went over there and I was going over it pretty thoroughly just because, personally, I like to see if there's any cigarette butts left behind or anything that we could use as evidence. And I really wasn't finding anything," Ploeg said.

It was spotted in a ditch along Road 12 East by someone heading out to their hunting spot, she said.

The original church was built in Fraserwood in 1906. The current building was erected in 1942, two years after the original one was destroyed by a fire. (Tyler Searle/CBC)

Ploeg and the church parishioners were worried the ornate brass bell, which dates back to 1906, had been stolen to be sold to a scrapyard or melted down.

All the media attention the theft garnered likely scared the thieves off, said Ploeg, who believes they left it in a place where it could be found "so that they could get the heat off of them."

"Typically when we recover stolen property it'll be quite well hidden in the bushes or on properties, like rural areas, where people will stash them and wait until they can either use them or dispose of them another way or sell them or whatever," she said.

"The way that the bell was abandoned just in the ditch on the side of the road in plain view makes me feel very much that it was, like, purposeful. It wasn't stashed. It was left there to be found because now it's a hot item and it's all over the news."

The Interlake has large swaths of bushland and uninhabited areas where the thieves could have hidden the bell, Ploeg said.

"Even if you had a drone, what are the odds of you spotting it? It's the exact same colour as the grass [right now in fall]," she said.

The bell is now with the RCMP's forensics unit, which will be looking for fingerprints or other evidence that can be gathered from it.

Ploeg has spoken with representatives of the church to let them know it's been found.

The church isn't ready to take it back, anyway, because they need to do some repairs to the top of the belfry, where some of the wood was damaged during the theft, she said.

"So we'll give them some time to kind of figure that out and we'll make a plan of how it's going to be returned."

Gimli RCMP ask anyone with information about the theft or who may have seen anything suspicious in the area to contact the detachment at 204-642-5106.

World.title: 5 European countries want to start deporting migrants to Rwanda, despite concerns from human rights groups
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In one of his first acts as Britain's prime minister, Keir Starmer in 2024 quashed the U.K. government's controversial plan to deport asylum seekers to Rwanda, saying it was "dead and buried before it started."

Now, five European countries are trying to resurrect a similar scheme.

Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Austria and Greece announced Monday that they are working with Rwanda to set up a "return hub" for migrants who do not have the legal right to remain in the European Union.

"We need to take back control of our borders," said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen during a joint news conference in Vienna. "What we are pushing for is a more sustainable and, I will also say, a more orderly asylum and migration system."

Those sent to Rwanda will be given the chance to integrate and settle there or another nation that grants them the legal right to stay — or return to their home country.
