World.title: Being Deposed as a Governor in Cuba with No Details Made Public
World.content:
The deposed governor of Camaguey, Cuba, Jorge Enrique Sutil Sarabia

By Amado Viera

HAVANA TIMES – On Saturday, November 14, during the debut of a radio program he will appear on every two weeks to “establish direct communication with the people,” Walter Simon Noris, the Communist Party’s first secretary in Camagüey, was so intent on focusing on his achievements at the helm of the province that he ended up with almost 20 minutes of airtime to spare.

He could have used precisely that time to reveal the “errors incompatible with his responsibilities” that had cost Governor Jorge Enrique Sutil Sarabia his position four days earlier. The accusations against the latter were so serious that the official announcement of his dismissal described it merely as a “resignation at his own request,” rather than softening it with terms such as “release from duties” or “assignment to other responsibilities,” which Cuban bureaucratic language typically uses in cases involving disgraced officials who have not been implicated in corruption or other similarly serious offenses.

Sutil had been “elected” governor of Camagüey in May 2023. At the time, the position of first secretary of the Communist Party was held by Federico Hernandez a party official from Granma province who would be dismissed two years later so that his involvement in a beef-trafficking network extending all the way to Havana could be investigated. The last information about him, several months later, was that he was in the capital awaiting legal proceedings in which several farm owners, private business owners, and a sizable group of Agriculture Ministry officials would also stand trial.

To get an idea of the magnitude of Sutil’s blunder, it is enough to note that, even under those circumstances, Hernandez’s removal had been described in official statements as a “release from duties as part of a renewal process.” That was far more lenient language than the wording used now.

“And What Do You Expect Me to Do?”

Sutil had arrived at Quinta San Zenon—the seat of the Camagüey provincial government—to replace Yoseily Gongora Lopez, a young politician who had taken advantage of her position to undergo a marathon series of cosmetic surgeries in Havana between 2021 and 2022. Thanks to those procedures, she managed to lose nearly 50 kilograms (110 pounds) and overcome her obesity. The problem was that she did so at the most critical point of the pandemic, when the province was on the verge of collapse. Gongora not only neglected the crisis but also clung to her office, aware that the preferential treatment she was receiving was due to her status as governor.

“If you ask me, it wasn’t an improvised decision but one based on pure calculation. Faced with a choice between improving her health and sacrificing herself to fulfill the responsibilities for which she had been elected, she chose the former. She must have known it would cost her career as a government official. That’s why, when she returned to lead the province, she didn’t make the slightest effort. You could see her at meetings and during official visits and realize she was there simply to go through the motions,” explained an official with the Camagüey provincial government.

Despite the controversies surrounding her, when Gongora was removed from office, she received “recognition for the effort, work, and dedication devoted to government service.” She was also appointed to a comfortable administrative position at Artex, a state-owned company that markets cultural performances and products.

Sutil’s final weeks as governor are reminiscent of that period under his predecessor. In fact, the only photograph published by the state press of the meeting at which he was dismissed shows him sitting in the second row of the officials presiding over the meeting, staring blankly into space and almost leaning against the wall. It was much the same way Gongora could sometimes be seen during her final official appearances.

There has been considerable speculation on social media about the reasons behind Sutil’s dismissal. More than one online content creator has claimed credit for bringing it about through alleged revelations concerning fuel trafficking, influence peddling, and other economic crimes. But the truth is that no one has been able to provide evidence beyond the testimony of sources who requested anonymity. Not a single incriminating document has come to light.

What is beyond dispute is that during the weeks preceding the former official’s “resignation”—when he had already been effectively excluded from major decision-making—some changes did occur in the way the province was run.

For example, the previous weekend, a massive cleanup campaign was launched in the city of Camagüey. The fuel needed to carry it out, which had been unavailable for weeks, suddenly appeared. State-operated minibuses also resumed service, transporting thousands of people daily at fares far lower than those charged by private operators. And several people connected to the Ministry of Public Health confirmed that the fleet of electric vehicles delivered to the province just a few months earlier to support healthcare services had been reorganized. These were the same vehicles that could often be found just about anywhere except at hospitals.

“It would be unfair to accuse Sutil of being directly responsible for so many things going wrong, but it’s equally true that he allowed them to happen. Even when problems were reported directly to him or were so obvious that there was no way to ignore them. I remember that about a year ago, a highly respected doctor approached him to denounce the shady dealings surrounding fuel sales in dollars. One specific example was the Sputnik gas station, where people who controlled places in line charged customers for their turns, and the regulations limiting the number of liters each customer could purchase were blatantly violated. ‘And what do you expect me to do?’ was Sutil’s response. That’s no way to run a province,” the official interviewed pointed out.

The former governor was not even capable of making simple decisions that would have been widely applauded by his fellow citizens, such as restoring order to Agramonte Park and Republica Street, the two busiest public spaces in the provincial capital, now overrun by skateboarders, beggars, and vehicles moving about as they please.

By the time rumors of his possible dismissal began to spread, Sutil had virtually no supporters left. In three years, he had exhausted the political capital he brought to office. Faced with that obvious reality, the government’s efforts have focused on preventing the details of his downfall from becoming public. There is little more they can hope to accomplish.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Nicaragua and The Fear of Dignity
World.content:
Carlos Brenes and Salvadora Martínez have now spent 15 months in detention, with the authorities providing no information regarding their whereabouts.

How terrified the Nicaraguan dictatorship is of the dignity of a 71-year-old man and his 69-year-old wife.

By Thelma Brenes Muñoz (Confidencial)

HAVANA TIMES – My father, Carlos Brenes Sanchez, was arrested on August 14, 2025, along with Salvadora Martinez. As of November 15th of this year, it has been 15 months without any news of them. Both suffer from high blood pressure. My father is insulin-dependent. Salvadora was scheduled to undergo gallbladder surgery the week after her disappearance, 15 months ago. Every day without medication and adequate medical care puts their lives at risk. That is why the Nicaraguan state is responsible for whatever happens to them.

I have called the prison system from abroad to ask whether they are being held there. I do not make these calls expecting an answer. I make them to demonstrate that I am still searching for them, to document my efforts, and to expose the silence of the Nicaraguan state.

My father had already been unjustly detained in August 2018. He was prosecuted and put on trial despite being innocent. He was released from prison in June 2019 under a general amnesty that the government was forced to grant political prisoners because of international pressure. The state itself issued a judicial order under the Amnesty Law, ordering his “immediate release,” directing that his “criminal records be expunged,” and expressly ruling that “the conditions associated with the precautionary measures are hereby rendered null and void.” However, the regime lied. They never left him in peace.

Since his release in 2019, police officers in Carazo regularly visited his home to monitor him. They also imposed the arbitrary requirement that he send daily photographs via WhatsApp to report to the police. Despite the illegality of these measures, he complied with the rules imposed by the dictatorship and demonstrated his integrity. The government failed to honor the provisions of the amnesty it had granted.

Why, if my father was a free citizen, did he have to keep reporting to the police and remain under surveillance through visits by police patrols? My father was not arrested and forcibly disappeared for committing a crime. They are holding him captive and isolated out of revenge: for thinking differently, for remaining true to his ideals, and for maintaining a dignity that the regime cannot break.

We will not stop searching for him and Salvadora. We will not stop demanding their unconditional release, and we will not allow them to be erased in the darkness of the cells of La Modelo and La Esperanza prisons.

First published in Spanish by Confidencial and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Nicaragua here on Havana Times.

World.title: What I’ve Learned in My Home Barbershop
World.content:
My first customers were my friends.

By Erick Hernandez

HAVANA TIMES – I come from a journalism background, as I’ve already mentioned in this space. I wasn’t an early reader, but from the age of fourteen, when someone sent me a folder full of ebooks, I read every night until my phone fell out of my hands.

The next morning, the device would be completely drained after spending the night displaying a page that no one would read. Back then, before buying my first books, I read exclusively on my phone, but I did so with a voracious appetite that I hope to recover.

That didn’t prevent me from socializing with other kids my age or having friends, both boys and girls, at school. Nevertheless, the barbershop gave me a crash course in practical knowledge and pragmatism. Suddenly, I found myself talking to strangers who had all kinds of stories to tell.

Once, I even cut the hair of a drunk man who said his father had died two days earlier and that he had gotten a tattoo in his honor. When he showed it to me, the tattoo turned out to be nothing more than the Real Madrid emblem, which looked more like a melted piece of candy.

I learned to communicate and to understand, above all, to understand. Not to understand the big problems, which I may already have explored through journalism, but to understand why a man gets a haircut before leaving for a week of work, and why a mother brings her child in, and sometimes it’s the grandmother who comes instead.

I learned a great deal about fatherhood and watched different kinds of fathers deal with their children’s restlessness. I didn’t learn about failures of the National Electric Power System, water shortages, or the lack of medicines. My customers faced all those problems, but I was already familiar with them myself. The lessons all those men taught me went much deeper and lay in the small details of their lives, in their motivations. They were there in the young man who wanted to raise fighting roosters and went to Uruguay, only to return because he couldn’t bear the loneliness.

I also learned a great deal about myself. On those mornings when no one came in, when I had grown tired of reading and listening to music, there was nothing left for me to do but think. And little by little, a quiet kind of understanding began to settle in. I thought about my work projects and household matters, but those subjects barely filled a day. If the following morning found me idle again, I had no choice but to venture into more uncertain territory.

My thoughts ranged from imagining the lives of people walking by, to fictional scenarios I invented for amusement, to observing the grass and plants in the garden. Every morning, I checked on the condition of those green stems that kept me company.

Sometimes I was in that introspective state when a customer arrived, and then I found it difficult to snap out of it. It was easier if the person was a regular, but if he was a stranger, with no previous conversation to pick up, sometimes we wouldn’t speak at all, and I would simply continue thinking about whatever was on my mind.

I didn’t realize it then, but now, looking back, I understand that I was discovering myself during that period. I reflected on many things and resolved questions that had lingered in my mind. I was able to think so deeply about subjects that interested me that I eventually felt confident enough to take a position on them. Out of that process came several professional decisions that I’m glad I made.

Those periods of reflection and conversations with customers made me, if not a more mature person, at least a more humane one, someone more directly connected to other human beings. And whenever I have to make a difficult decision, I remember that young man, the one who came back to be with his family.

Read more from the diary of Erick Hernandez here on Havana Times.

World.title: Dignity Still Survives in Guamuta, Cuba
World.content:
Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano. FREEDOM

By Francisco Acevedo

HAVANA TIMES – In contemporary Cuba, protesting is not merely a public expression of discontent: it is also an act of personal exposure. Those who raise their voices against those in power face not only the possibility of arrest but also a system of surveillance, discrediting, isolation, and punishment that can turn a social demand into a personal tragedy.

It is in this context that the name Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano emerges. He is a resident of Guamuta, a community in Cuba’s Santiago de Cuba province, marked—like all the others—by the economic and political tensions that permeate everyday life on the island.

This young man became well known in late 2025 for confronting President Miguel Diaz-Canel during one of those carefully planned visits that the “handpicked president” makes to mingle with the crowds, although those gatherings are generally thoroughly screened to prevent uncomfortable situations.

In this case, however, Hurricane Melissa had just swept through eastern Cuba, and apparently the screening apparatus had not been fully activated. Somehow, Yoel Alejandro managed to reach the president and tell him some hard truths about how badly his fellow citizens in the eastern region were suffering. As usual, the responses were evasive, and everything seemed to end there—until the young man decided to take matters into his own hands.

First, he decided to write a book so that silence would not be the final outcome of his concerns, although he never made its title or publication date public, to avoid reprisals.

With the support of prominent dissident Jose Daniel Ferrer, the young man took small steps to improve his neighbors’ quality of life. But he committed the sin of saying that none of it had been accomplished with government assistance.

As though that were a grave offense rather than an undeniable truth, the regime’s henchmen arrested him and sent him to jail at the Versailles Police Operations Unit in Santiago de Cuba.

When someone is imprisoned after participating in a protest, the essential question is not simply which legal provision is invoked, but whether that provision is applied in a manner consistent with freedom of expression and assembly. Laws can become instruments of justice or mechanisms of intimidation. It all depends on whether they protect citizens from abuse or end up protecting those in power from the citizenry.

Protest in Guamuta, Cuba over Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano’s arrest.

Perez Serrano’s case is not an exception

As with other protesters against the regime whom we have discussed in recent months, Perez Serrano’s case should not be viewed merely as an individual case, but as a window into the broader problem of the criminalization of protest.

In Guamuta, as in so many Cuban communities outside the major urban centers, scarcity is felt more personally, and support networks are limited. Complaints circulate by word of mouth, through private messages, in family backyards, and in discreet conversations. When a protest erupts, it does not come out of nowhere: it represents months or years of accumulated frustration.

In this setting, the figure of the political prisoner—or the citizen detained for participating in a protest—takes on symbolic significance. Their body becomes the battleground between two opposing interpretations. For the authorities, the person may be a violator of public order, someone accused of contempt, disobedience, assaulting authorities, or public disorder.

For their relatives and supporters, however, that person is being punished for demanding rights or expressing legitimate grievances. In Perez Serrano’s case, he also tried to do something about the problems he denounced, contributing what little he could to alleviate the difficult circumstances facing his fellow citizens.

Unlike on other occasions, this time the person who stood up against tyranny was not met with indifference. Several videos are circulating on social media showing Guamuta residents demanding his release.

In Cuba, protests in recent years have revealed a profound transformation in social discontent. It is no longer simply a matter of organized opposition groups or voices from exile. Demonstrations have involved neighbors, workers, young people, mothers, and individuals who may never have considered themselves political.

Many take to the streets not with a fully developed ideological platform, but with immediate demands: “food,” “freedom,” “electricity,” and “medicine.” That spontaneity makes any power structure uncomfortable because it reveals that discontent can emerge outside official channels.

The state’s response to these expressions of discontent has included arrests, interrogations, prison sentences, and subsequent restrictions intended to silence certain individuals temporarily. Yet these measures simultaneously deepen social resentment.

A community may learn to remain silent, but that does not necessarily mean it stops thinking. Imposed silence is not the same as consensus, and sometimes it is merely a pause filled with fear.

The fundamental solution is not simply to release one person, although freedom for those unjustly imprisoned is an immediate demand. It is also necessary to review the laws that allow protests to be punished disproportionately, guarantee public and impartial trials, permit the presence of independent observers, and recognize citizens’ right to assemble peacefully.

A country does not grow stronger by punishing every dissenting voice. It grows stronger when it can listen to those voices without feeling that its very existence is constantly under threat.

Guamuta reminds us that Cuba’s political history is not written solely through official speeches or in major capitals, but also in small towns, on anonymous streets, and through the voices of those who, tired of waiting, decide to speak out.

Dignity remains in Guamuta, because a society that forgets its prisoners ends up normalizing injustice, and a society that turns protest into a crime gradually loses its ability to correct itself.

True stability does not arise from fear, but from the ability to voice grievances without facing persecution. And that distinction determines not only the fate of one man—in this case, Yoel Alejandro Perez Serrano—but also the public dignity of an entire country.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Leo XIV after his tour: “There is no need to hate each other or use such violent language”
World.content:
Leo XIV after his tour: “There is no need to hate each other or use such violent language”

17th Tuesday, November 2026 - 16:37 UTC Full article

Pope Leo XIV speaks to reporters aboard the papal plane after his tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

Pope Leo XIV criticised aggressive political debate and polarisation, “in many situations intentionally provoked”, at the press conference he gave on his flight back to Rome after an eleven-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, in which he also said his health is good and recounted that he spoke with Argentine President Javier Milei about caring for those most in need.

Pope Leo XIV criticised aggressive political debate and polarisation, “in many situations intentionally provoked”, at the press conference he gave on his flight back to Rome after an eleven-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, in which he also said his health is good and recounted that he spoke with Argentine President Javier Milei about caring for those most in need.

“There will no doubt continue to be differences of opinion. But there is no need to hate each other, to use such violent language and to create, even within families, an inability to dialogue and rediscover unity,” the pontiff said. He blamed part of the problem on algorithms and “a polarisation that is not accidental”, citing his visit to Argentina as an example: “How is it possible that people of the right and the left were together in the streets, celebrating and rejoicing over something much more important than a political debate?” The media, he added, have a “very great” role in reducing polarisation.

On his meeting with Milei, the Pope said his message “is not political”. “Although in some countries there are those who try to push me to the right or the left, asking me to criticise or not, I speak of the encyclical Magnifica humanitas. And that is precisely what I spoke about with President Milei: respect for human beings and the need for greater consideration, especially for the neediest in Argentine society,” he explained. “He was willing to listen to this message. It was very positive.” The Pope also argued for a fairer redistribution of wealth and for “strengthening the working class, individuals and social movements”.

On his health, after the removal of a lung tumour on October 13, he said: “I cannot say I am at 100%, but I am quite well.” He reiterated that he will need no further treatment and said he has not signed any letter of resignation: “For now, I see no need, thank God.”

On clergy abuse, he called on bishops to take “responsibility for accompanying the victims”. He ruled out doctrinal changes for now, and said why Francis never returned to Argentina would remain “a mystery”. He promised Mexican faithful a visit: “I will come, I will come!”

The plane landed in Rome at 8.48 a.m. local time on Tuesday. According to El País, more than 13 million people attended his events in the three countries.

World.title: Venezuela uses US$12 billion in US-supervised oil revenue to prop up the bolívar
World.content:
Venezuela uses US$12 billion in US-supervised oil revenue to prop up the bolívar

17th Tuesday, November 2026 - 16:30 UTC Full article

An oil pump jack in Venezuela, where crude sales under US oversight have funded dollar sales to prop up the bolívar.

Venezuela has spent most of the more than US$12 billion earned from oil sales under US supervision on propping up the bolívar, with modest results: inflation has slowed but remains the world's highest, and consumption has yet to recover.

Venezuela has spent most of the more than US$12 billion earned from oil sales under US supervision on propping up the bolívar, with modest results: inflation has slowed but remains the world's highest, and consumption has yet to recover.

According to a US State Department report cited by El País, the account through which Washington has supervised Venezuelan revenue since the January 3 military operation received US$12.263 billion by September 30, almost all from crude sales. Some 98.7% has already been disbursed at the request of Venezuela's Central Bank, which used it mainly to sell dollars to commercial banks to prevent shortages and keep the currency's price from soaring. Venezuela now sells its oil without discounts, at just over US$90 a barrel, and has raised output to 1.22 million barrels a day.

The intervention has had some effect. According to the Central Bank, October inflation was 6.2%, the lowest of the year and the third consecutive month below 10%. The bolívar lost 67% of its value against the dollar in the first ten months of the year, but over the past two months the decline has been around 6%, and the gap between the official and parallel dollar has narrowed from 50% in January to about 15%. Even so, prices rose 245% between January and October, and annual inflation stands at 376.9%. The minimum wage has been frozen at 130 bolívares since March 2022.

Economists blame the limited results on the design of exchange rate policy. “There are too many restrictions on access to the official market,” said Leonardo Vera, president of the National Academy of Economic Sciences, which pushes buyers to the parallel dollar and fuels prices. “The slowdown in inflation is very slow, too slow for the effort that has been made,” said José Guerra, a former opposition lawmaker and professor at the Central University of Venezuela. “The market does not trust the government's word.” Jesús Palacios, of the Andrés Bello Catholic University, called for a single exchange rate and fiscal reforms, with a deficit of 7.2% of GDP, according to that university's economic research institute.

The government of acting President Delcy Rodríguez last week signed a memorandum with ExxonMobil for the US oil company's return to the country.

World.title: Falklands close November with cricket, archery and hockey after opening Sports Complex
World.content:
Falklands close November with cricket, archery and hockey after opening Sports Complex

17th Tuesday, November 2026 - 13:40 UTC Full article

Cricket against Costa Rica, the archery competition, and Princess Anne alongside the lawn bowls team during the opening of the Complex.

The Falklands are going through a month of intense international sporting activity, a week after the official opening of the new National Sports Complex in Stanley.

A series of T20 cricket matches against the visiting Costa Rica side was played in the archipelago in recent days. Running alongside it is an archery competition with international teams, under the name North South Archery Tournament.

Also in recent weeks, hockey teams across different age groups competed in Iquique, Chile, in the Drakons Cup.

The local calendar closes at the end of the month with the Falklands Games, scheduled for November 27, 28 and 29.

The National Sports Complex, opened on November 10 by Princess Anne during her visit to the archipelago, required an investment estimated at around £5 million, funded by the Falklands government with contributions from private sector companies. It is the first major investment in the Islands’ sporting facilities since the construction of the Stanley Leisure Centre and Swimming Pool some thirty years ago.

The facilities include a floodlit all-weather football and rugby pitch; an indoor centre for archery, lawn bowls and cricket nets, known as the Gold Centre; and a 50 by 52 metre sports hall for synthetic ice hockey, indoor football, basketball, netball, volleyball, tennis, table tennis, weightlifting and climbing. Exercise studios also allow for yoga, Pilates, dance exercise, ballet and spin classes. The complex complements the existing Stanley Leisure Centre, which houses the swimming pool.

The opening was attended by officials from international sporting bodies in whose competitions Falklands teams take part: Katie Sadleir, Chief Executive of Commonwealth Sport, and Andrew Inkster, of the International Island Games Association.

The Falklands competed in July 2025 at the Island Games held in the Scottish archipelago of Orkney, where 24 island groups took part, and expect to attend the next edition, to be held in the Faroe Islands from July 3 to 9, 2027, with 27 island teams anticipated. The archipelago also took part in the Commonwealth Games held in Glasgow, Scotland, between July 23 and August 2 this year.

Mike Summers, of the Falkland Islands National Sports Council, said work would continue towards delivering the Sports Strategy agreed by the Legislative Assembly, encouraging every sector of the community to get involved in sport, both competitively and recreationally, in an environment that promotes inclusion and the values of sportsmanship.

World.title: FAO Food Price Index remained relatively stable during October
World.content:
FAO Food Price Index remained relatively stable during October

17th Tuesday, November 2026 - 13:23 UTC Full article

World wheat prices declined following four consecutive monthly increases, largely reflecting subdued international demand and improved production in Argentina

The benchmark measure of world food commodity prices edged lower in October, as weaker import demand contributed to month-on-month declines in the price indices for cereals, dairy products and meat, according to new data released by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO).

The FAO Food Price Index (FFPI), which tracks monthly changes in the international prices of a basket of globally traded food commodities, averaged 133.9 points in October 2026, down 1.6 points (1.2%) from its revised September level, as lower price indices across most commodity groups more than offset a sharp rise in sugar and a marginal increase in vegetable oils. Despite the monthly decline, the index stood 5.9% above its level a year earlier but remained 16.4 percent below its March 2022 peak.

The FAO Cereal Price Index fell 4.5 percent from September. World wheat prices declined following four consecutive monthly increases, largely reflecting subdued international demand and an improving production outlook, particularly in Argentina. Expectations of easing constraints on Black Sea export flows added to the downward pressure on prices, although continued disruptions to Black Sea logistics limited the decline.

International maize quotations also eased after reaching a three-year high in September, weighed down by harvest-related pressure in the United States of America, expectations of ample supplies in major exporting countries in South America, and renewed prospects for an easing of tensions in the Black Sea region. By contrast, the FAO All Rice Price Index increased by 1.6 percent in October 2026, as harvest delays in some rice exporting countries added to the upward price pressure exerted by adverse weather conditions and rising costs.

The FAO Vegetable Oil Price Index increased marginally, by 0.3 percent from September, as higher soybean and sunflower oil quotations more than offset lower rapeseed oil prices. Soybean oil quotations rose to their highest levels since late 2022, driven by continued firm demand from the biofuel sector and seasonally declining supplies from South America. Meanwhile, sunflower oil quotations rebounded from multi-month lows amid persistently tight export availabilities from the Black Sea region.

The FAO Meat Price Index fell 1.2 percent from September, while remaining slightly above its year-earlier level. Quotations declined for pig, ovine and bovine meats, while poultry meat prices remained broadly stable.

The FAO Dairy Price Index was down 1.1 percent from September, with the October decrease reflecting declines in international butter and cheese quotations amid ample supplies and subdued buying interest. The declines more than offset further increases in milk powder prices.

The FAO Sugar Price Index marked its fourth consecutive monthly increase to reach its highest level since December 2024 after rising 6.6 percent from September and 28.8 percent from a year ago. The rise was mainly driven by rainfall-related disruptions to sugarcane harvesting and crushing operations in Brazil's key Centre-South producing region as well as concerns over production prospects in India, the European Union and Thailand in the 2026/27 season.

World.title: S.S. ‘United States’ Is Now the World’s Largest Artificial Reef
World.content:
S.S. ‘United States’ Is Now the World’s Largest Artificial Reef

17th Tuesday, November 2026 - 13:19 UTC Full article

An aerial view of the S.S. United States making 35 knots across the Atlantic in 1952

The World’s Fastest Ocean Liner finally hits the ocean floor. The 53,330-Ton S.S. ‘United States’ is now the world’s largest artificial reef. Longer than the “Titanic,” once carried celebrities and politicians across the Atlantic in midcentury style. Now, after decades of uncertainty and rust, it’s taking on a second life as an underwater refuge for marine creatures and curious divers, according to a piece from the Smithsonian Magazine.

Finally at 8:59 p.m. central time, the S.S. United States slipped below the waves, starting a new chapter as a home for marine life and a destination for divers from across the world, which is quite some time from June 29, 1952, when a state-of-the-art ocean liner, nearly 1,000 feet long, opened up to the public. Some 70,000 people flooded to its berth in New York City to catch a glimpse of the S.S. United States before it hit the Atlantic for its maiden voyage.

Almost immediately, the liner proved worthy of the intense interest. On July 3, 1952, the S.S. United States reached England in a record-breaking three days, ten hours and 40 minutes, a speed that has yet to be surpassed to this day by any passenger liner. In its 17-year run, the ship would go on to host numerous notables, including Marilyn Monroe, Walt Disney, Salvador Dali, and even the Mona Lisa, after the painting’s one and only trip to the US.

However last week more than 70 years after its record-setting maiden voyage, crowds once again came out in droves to see the legendary liner depart on one last journey. This time, the S.S. United States was heading to the bottom of the sea for a new life as an artificial reef in the Gulf of Gulf of Mexico.

Designed by the prolific 20th century naval architect William Francis Gibbs, the ocean liner represented the peak of post-World War II maritime technology. Over 100 feet longer than the Titanic, the United States contained no wood except the ship’s grand pianos, built with fire-resistant mahogany. “She will have more aluminum in her than Mr. Gibbs cares to say, a design feature that will contribute to the dual goal of strength and relative lightness,” George Horne reported for the NY Times in 1951.

Throughout the 1950s and ‘60s, the liner completed more than 800 journeys across the Atlantic, carrying more than 1 million passengers, including many celebrities and politicians.

Throughout its 17-year tenure, the S.S. United States carried four presidents: Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower, John F. Kennedy and a young Bill Clinton, who took it to study at Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar in 1968.

With its intricately designed interior featuring patriotic art, amenities including a movie theater and its unparalleled speed, the S.S. United States provided many passengers with lasting memories.

But as airline travel became more accessible, the age of luxury ocean liners soon drew to a close. In 1969, the S.S. United States was abruptly decommissioned. Even crew members were shocked by its sudden withdrawal from service. Several left personal belongings on board, assuming they would go back to work the next day, only to show up to locked gangway doors.

For the next nine years, it languished as a reserve ship for the U.S. Navy, ready to for action if the need arose. But there was no need, and in 1978, the ship was put up for sale.

In the following decades, the ship passed from port to port, from owner to owner, each with different plans for the ship: floating condominiums, hazardous waste removal in Ukraine, a revived cruise liner. But no idea garnered enough money or momentum to last. By 2024, the ship had foundered on a Philadelphia pier for decades.

When the pier’s landlord raised the daily dockage fee to US$1,700—US$ 620,500 per year—the S.S. United States was evicted and faced the possibility of getting scrapped. Instead, Florida’s Okaloosa County purchased the ship for US$1 million, with plans to turn it into the world’s largesgt artificial reef. The county already has a fleet of sunken ships off its coast, but the S.S. United States is its crowning jewel.

Officials expect the liner-turned-reef will become home to a variety of marine species, including red snapper, grouper, amberjack, mackerel and tuna. The ship will also be open to divers.

“She’s being reefed and will remain intact and will become a vibrant and dynamic marine habitat,” Susan Gibbs, the conservancy’s president and granddaughter of the ship’s designer, tells the Guardian’s Richard Luscombe.

The conservancy plans to run a museum adjacent to the pier where diving expeditions will set out, featuring the ship’s iconic smokestacks, alongside other parts of the ship’s interior and a collection of artifacts and memorabilia.

Unlike the liner’s legendary maiden voyage, the trip from Philadelphia to the ocean floor was far from speedy. After a handful of false starts and a last-ditch lawsuit, it took months of preparation at a port in Alabama to ready the vessel for its voyage to the bottom of the sea, the New York Times’ Jesse Pesta reports.

Workers removed the ship’s wiring, ductwork, glass and anything that could potentially pose a danger to divers or marine life. They also cut strategic passages through the ship’s interior to create open pathways that would reduce stagnant water and enable divers to easily pass in and out. Finally, they removed off the ship’s two iconic, six-story smokestacks, earmarked for the future museum. The S.S. United States was finally ready for sinking.

The ship then set out from Destin, Florida. A crew cut holes in the ship and removed more than 400 portholes. Water flooded in, but as night descended, it still hadn’t sunk.

“She was designed to be unsinkable, and that fact has definitely given our crews some challenges today,” Nick Tomecek, a spokesperson for Okaloosa County, told ABC 6. Or, as William Francis Gibbs once bragged, “You can’t set her on fire, you can’t sink her and you can’t catch her.”

World.title: Orsi praises “excellent” ties with Milei and Lula’s re-election ahead of the Mercosur summit
World.content:
Orsi praises “excellent” ties with Milei and Lula’s re-election ahead of the Mercosur summit

16th Monday, November 2026 - 20:47 UTC Full article

Orsi also praised Lula’s regional role and described his October 25 re-election as “fundamental”

Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi described his government’s relationship with Javier Milei’s administration in Argentina as “excellent” and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s re-election in Brazil as “fundamental”, in a Mercosur assessment given in Madrid less than three weeks before the bloc’s summit of heads of state in Montevideo on December 4.

“The relationship is excellent,” Orsi said of Argentina at a breakfast forum organised by Nueva Economía Fórum, according to Europa Press. “Things we had never achieved, we did achieve with this government.” The Uruguayan president, of the left-wing Broad Front, attributed the good ties with Milei’s government to fluid contact even from “different philosophies and positions”, citing as examples progress on dredging the access channel to the port of Montevideo and the resolution of tensions over HIF Global’s green hydrogen plant project in Paysandú. Both countries also agree on the need to make Mercosur more flexible and modern.

Orsi also praised Lula’s regional role and described his October 25 re-election as “fundamental”. “It is good news because of the positions both candidates took on integration,” he said.

The remarks come at a time of strong tensions within the bloc. Relations between Argentina and Brazil are at their lowest point following Milei’s repeated attacks on Lula and the departure of defeated candidate Flávio Bolsonaro from Brazil via Argentine territory. Paraguay is also going through an institutional crisis after the removal and arrest of President Santiago Peña over the collapse of Ueno Bank, with his successor, Pedro Alliana, sworn in ten days ago.

The Montevideo summit, which will close Uruguay’s pro tempore presidency, is expected to address the debate on making the bloc more flexible and ongoing trade negotiations with Canada, the United Arab Emirates, Vietnam and Japan. The trade agreement with the European Union has applied provisionally since May 1.

World.title: Venezuela accuses Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi of “interference” over call for free elections
World.content:
Venezuela accuses Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi of “interference” over call for free elections

16th Monday, November 2026 - 20:42 UTC Full article

Uruguay and Venezuela broke off diplomatic relations in 2024, after the Uruguayan government refused to recognise Nicolás Maduro’s proclamation as winner of the presidential election

Venezuela’s government on Monday rejected as “interference” remarks by Uruguayan President Yamandú Orsi, who had said hours earlier in Madrid that he cannot recognise a democratic government in Venezuela until free elections are held. Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco replied that the country’s future “belongs to the sovereign will of Venezuelans”.

Orsi, of the left-wing Broad Front and Uruguay’s president since March 2025, was speaking at a breakfast forum organised by Nueva Economía Fórum in the Spanish capital, during a visit in which he also met Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. “Let’s call things by their name. Since my election campaign and before, Venezuela did not function as a democracy. What needs to happen in Venezuela is a roadmap that culminates in free and transparent elections,” he said. He added that “until there are free elections” he cannot “recognise a democratic republican regime”, but that this does not prevent restoring relations. “Uruguay does not only have relations with democratic countries or with our style of democracy. Countries relate as countries, not as friends,” he said.

Blanco replied on X that a president’s agenda “should be marked by attention to the affairs of his population and the development of his country”. “Mutual respect, sovereign equality and cooperation between our countries are the basis for a constructive dialogue that contributes to peace, stability and Latin American integration,” he wrote. Blanco, a former opposition aide, was appointed foreign minister in late October by acting President Delcy Rodríguez.

Uruguay and Venezuela broke off diplomatic relations in 2024, after the Uruguayan government refused to recognise Nicolás Maduro’s proclamation as winner of the presidential election, which the opposition says was won by Edmundo González Urrutia. In June 2025, the two countries reactivated consular services in Montevideo and Caracas, although Uruguay maintained its political position. Rodríguez has governed as acting president since January, after Maduro’s removal from power in a US military operation, and on October 29 promised elections organised by a “renewed” electoral authority, though without setting a date.

World.title: How Online Postgraduate Education Can Support South American Professionals in England
World.content:
How Online Postgraduate Education Can Support South American Professionals in England

16th Monday, November 2026 - 19:50 UTC Full article

Photo: Magnific

For South American professionals living in England, career development can involve adapting existing qualifications and experience to a different labour market. Someone who previously worked in finance, hospitality or management may encounter unfamiliar workplace expectations and recruitment requirements. Online postgraduate education offers an opportunity to develop advanced knowledge while continuing to work and build a professional future in England.

Why Advanced Skills Matter in the British Workplace

Employers in the UK may expect professionals to combine specialist knowledge with leadership, analytical thinking and effective communication. A Brazilian finance professional might explore postgraduate courses to strengthen strategic reporting skills, while a Colombian hospitality manager could focus on advanced service operations.

Such programmes allow professionals to gain specialised knowledge without putting employment on hold. Choosing a relevant course can help them connect their previous experience with the demands of their current industry. However, applicants should check whether their existing qualifications meet the programme's entry requirements. Recognition by employers or professional bodies may also depend on the occupation and the qualification involved.

Connect Postgraduate Learning to Career Goals

Before enrolling, identify the responsibilities you want to take on in England. An experienced administrator might aim for a management position, while a marketing specialist could focus on strategic decision-making and data analysis. A clear development plan helps connect postgraduate study with realistic career objectives. Consider these five steps before choosing a programme:

- Review your responsibilities. Identify existing strengths and areas requiring more advanced knowledge.

- Compare job requirements. Examine vacancies and professional expectations in your chosen UK sector.

- Define a career goal. Decide which responsibilities or positions you want to pursue.

- Assess postgraduate options. Check course content, entry criteria, fees and qualification recognition.

- Apply new knowledge. Use relevant techniques in workplace projects and evaluate the results.

Recording your progress can help you explain how further education contributes to your professional development. Practical examples may also strengthen future job applications.

Make Online Study Work Around Employment

For South American expatriates balancing work and family responsibilities in England, attending regular campus-based classes may be difficult. Online postgraduate programmes can offer greater flexibility, although students still need to consider their weekly workload and assessment deadlines.

Look for courses that combine academic concepts with practical assignments and feedback. For example, IHCL uses its ACEL pedagogical model and a custom-made learning management system to support structured online study. Its postgraduate options include master's degrees and preparatory pre-master's pathways, which serve different academic purposes. Prospective students should understand these distinctions before selecting a programme.

Turn Further Education into Career Progress

Postgraduate learning becomes more useful when professionals can apply new knowledge at work. A project coordinator might introduce improved reporting methods, while a hospitality supervisor could use management concepts to develop team procedures.

These practical outcomes can provide evidence of professional growth during performance reviews or job interviews. They may also help South American professionals demonstrate how their international experience contributes to organisations in England.

For those building long-term careers in the country, continued education can support professional ambitions without requiring another relocation. IHCL offers flexible postgraduate learning opportunities that allow working adults to develop advanced knowledge while planning their next career step.

World.title: Sheinbaum phones in from Shenzhen after meeting with Chinese president: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:

Sheinbaum said she spoke about Plan México at the APEC CEO Summit on Tuesday and met with Chinese President Xi Jinping. She has met Trump before at the World Cup draw and the World Cup Final, but has not held a formal in-person discussion with him.
