The announcement came five days after she said she wouldn’t hold a bilateral meeting with Trump in China. She has met Trump before at the World Cup draw and the World Cup Final, but has not held a formal in-person discussion with him. Trade is likely to feature, with Mexico seeking lower U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and vehicles. 🚶 Migrant caravan in Chiapas down to 781 people: Rodríguez said some members have returned to their countries. The caravan, now in Mapastepec, is just over half the 1,500 migrants reported to have left Tapachula last Tuesday. The National Migration Institute (INM) is encouraging migrants to return home, and Rodríguez said some can stay in Mexico as long as they comply with “legal conditions.”

Why today’s mañanera matters

Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez took the reins of the morning press conference for a second consecutive day as President Sheinbaum is in Shenzhen, China, for this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting.

Sheinbaum joined the mañanera via video link from her hotel in Shenzhen, a city described by the BBC as China’s “AI wonderland.”

The president spoke about her address on Tuesday at the APEC CEO Summit and her bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Sheinbaum’s revelation that she will meet face-to-face on Wednesday with U.S. President Donald Trump was also noteworthy. The president has previously met with Trump at the FIFA men’s World Cup draw in Washington, D.C., last December and the World Cup Final in New Jersey in July. However, she has not held a formal, pre-arranged in-person discussion with the U.S. president.

Trade is likely to be among the issues Sheinbaum and Trump discuss on Wednesday as Mexico and the United States are currently aiming to resolve a range of trade differences. Mexico is seeking a reduction in U.S. tariffs that apply to Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles, while Trump is particularly concerned about the United States’ large trade deficit with Mexico. His administration announced in July that it had decided not to renew the USMCA for an additional 16 years, but the trilateral free trade pact remains in effect.

Sheinbaum joins mañanera from China

Early in her remarks, Sheinbaum noted that Shenzhen, in the space of around 40 years, was transformed from a small fishing village into a “city with a lot of development” and “very high buildings.”

She also noted that various technology companies, including ones involved in the development of AI, have a presence in the city. Sheinbaum described Shenzhen as “very impressive.”

#MañaneraPresidenta | 🚨 ¡SHEINBAUM INFORMA SU AGENDA DESDE CHINA! 📍 Desde Shenzhen, la presidenta destacó el Plan México y la reducción de la pobreza. 🤝 Se reunió con Xi Jinping 🇨🇳 y Mark Carney 🇨🇦. 📅 Mañana prevé encuentros con los presidentes de Vietnam 🇻🇳 y Donald Trump 🇺🇸, además de visitar un hospital inteligente y participar en actividades de la APEC. #SheinbaumLíderMundial

#APECChina2026 — Juncal Solano (@juncalssolano) November 17, 2026

She highlighted that she spoke at the APEC CEO Summit in the southern Chinese city on Tuesday.

“We spoke about Plan México,” she said, referring to the government’s ambitious economic initiative.

“… We spoke about what has happened in our country since 2018 and particularly in the two years we’ve been in government,” Sheinbaum said, noting that she had mentioned investment in highways, electricity generation and transmission, and ports.

She also noted that she spoke about poverty reduction in Mexico.

Sheinbaum subsequently referred to her bilateral meeting with President Xi.

“We greeted each other and then we had a meeting of cabinets, in which we were with President Xi’s cabinet,” she said, noting that she was accompanied by several of her ministers, including Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco, Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard and Energy Minister Luz Elena González.

“We spoke about the importance of the Mexico-China relationship and how we should strengthen this relationship in the areas of technological development, science and tourism, and in other areas that are fundamental for the development of Mexico and China,” Sheinbaum said.

She noted that she also met with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, with whom she spoke about the Mexico-Canada Action Plan.

“Trade between Mexico and Canada has increased and Canadian investment in Mexico and Mexican investment in Canada has also increased. So this action plan has had a significant impact,” Sheinbaum said.

She said she will meet with the president of Vietnam on Wednesday and visit a “smart hospital.”

“We’re very interested in collaboration with China on healthcare issues,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum to hold a ‘brief meeting’ with Trump

Sheinbaum said she will also hold a “brief meeting” with Donald Trump on Wednesday.

That revelation came five days after she told reporters that she wouldn’t hold a bilateral meeting with Trump in China.

Sheinbaum said that “activities related with the APEC Leaders’ Meeting” will take place after her meeting with the U.S. president.

She said she hoped to once again join the mañanera via video link on Wednesday, and noted she will attend the APEC Leaders’ Meeting on Thursday before returning to Mexico.

Sheinbaum said her visit to China has been “very productive” before thanking Rodríguez and other officials for running the government in Mexico in her absence.

Rodríguez: Migrant caravan in Chiapas is made up of 781 people

Rodríguez told reporters that some of the members of the migrant caravan that set off from Tapachula, Chiapas, last week “have returned to their countries.”

She said that the caravan — which arrived in the town of Mapastepec, Chiapas, on Monday — is currently made up of “781 members.”

That figure is just over half of the 1,500 migrants that were reported to have departed Tapachula last Tuesday.

Last Thursday, Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods if Mexico didn’t stop the caravan. In response, President Claudia Sheinbaum said that “no migrant caravan has reached the northern border” since Trump began his second term in January 2025. Rodríguez reiterated that message on Tuesday morning.

The interior minister noted that the caravan is in Mapastepec and said its members are being assisted by the National Migration Institute (INM). She said that INM officials are trying to persuade migrants to return to their countries of origin, among which are Honduras, Guatemala and El Salvador. Rodríguez noted that the government offers to “facilitate” migrants’ safe return to their homelands.

She said that “in some cases,” migrants can remain in Mexico as long as they “comply with the legal conditions for their stay.”

“There are cases in which [migrant] minors have a Mexican relative, which is usually a father or mother, and that allows them to regularize their status based on their family ties,” Rodríguez said.

World.title: Beans, baldness and the search for Mexico’s secret to great hair
World.content:
The male ego is a peculiar thing. It can allegedly survive any number of abasements, including discovering that your ex’s new boyfriend can assemble an IKEA wardrobe without cursing all of Sweden and fit a duvet cover with NATO only on standby.

According to clinical psychologist Dr. Roberto Olivardia, the male ego’s fragile architecture is currently built around jawlines.

Wait, what? Men are far more complex.

What about hair?

Hair. Say it aloud: “Hair.” A gentle, harmless little word, its H barely more than a polite puff of air. The sort that ought to come wearing a tiny Abercrombie cardigan with a Sally Rooney novel tucked under its arm.

Yet hair carries an absurd amount of identity. And envy. Mostly envy, at least for me.

Meanwhile, men across Mexico appear to wander beneath apocalyptically luxurious mops. Glossy. Abundant. The sort you could confidently leave your child beneath during a hurricane.

Then there is Sergio “Checo” Pérez, who has spent years cramming his noggin into a Formula One helmet and still emerges looking better than I do after 45 minutes alone with a mirror and a bagful of expensive products. I consider this a personal attack.

But perhaps the interesting question is not whether Mexican men lose less hair. It is whether they approach losing it differently.

A different approach in the barbershop

Ángel, my former landlord in Campeche, trained as a young man in his uncle’s barbershop. He recalls customers being more interested in achieving a modern, clean-cut look than in asking the barber to conceal a receding hairline or bald patch.

Nor was hair loss a regular topic among his male friends. That doesn’t mean nobody worried about it, only that in his experience, it took up less space in their heads than it does on mine.

His cousin Gael, a barber in Tucson, Ariz., encountered something different. Ángel recalls middle-aged white American customers often asking him to minimize signs of recession. Rather than attempt an elaborate cover-up, Gael worked with the retreat: short sides and texture on top. The objective was to make the recession look intentional.

This is the sort of emotional maturity I admire in other men and cannot muster myself. I simply want an honest, hardworking mop. Hair that, when asked to cover the crown, does not down tools and go for an early lunch.

Ángel, who still sports a splendid head of hair, offered another explanation for Mexico’s apparent follicular advantage: beans. Specifically, the vast quantities his compatriots consume from childhood.

Peer-reviewed? Hardly. But it was the first theory that allowed me to tackle male-pattern baldness with a shopping list.

The genetics behind thicker strands

Then an actual scientist stepped in.

According to geneticist Dr. Yana Kamberov, an associate professor at the University of Pennsylvania, a genetic variant called EDAR370A, inherited from Indigenous American ancestors, contributes to thicker, straighter hair in some Mexicans.

Human studies associate the variant with those characteristics. Kamberov also induced the mutation in mice and found it was enough to thicken their hair. Essentially, the variant arose in an ancient population and spread into the Americas through migration.

So my ridiculous observation may contain a tiny follicle of truth. But it cannot be stretched into a single Mexican hair type. Mexico’s population and migratory history are enormously diverse, and not every Mexican man possesses those characteristics, however aggressively my scalp insists otherwise.

Ancient hairstyles and warrior status

My historical theory proved equally complicated.

After doing some cursory research, I learned that Mexica warriors may have believed hair contained their courage or masculine vitality. Professor Caroline Dodds Pennock of the University of Sheffield in the U.K. corrected me.

“The ‘tonalli’ was one of three spirits the Mexica believed existed in the body. A warm life force located in the head and linked to personality and destiny, it could adhere to hair or nails after they were cut.

“When a warrior retained a captive’s warrior lock,” Dodds Pennock explained, “he took a piece of the captive’s tonalli, effectively increasing his own life force, reputation and status. Hair also signaled rank. Commoners wore theirs short; particular warriors had distinctive hairstyles; and priests never cut theirs, partly to concentrate the tonalli required by their sacred role.”

So a Mexica hairstyle was essentially an ancient LinkedIn profile, except the endorsements came in the form of a captive’s warrior lock and the skills section leaned heavily toward “ritual violence.”

Sounds cool to me, though I suspect my own hairline would’ve struggled to secure an entry-level position.

Anyway, Mexico may not have been awarded all the hair in the world. Genetics might explain those lusher strands I envy, just as culture might explain different attitudes toward balding. Still, my deep dive has yielded remarkably little beyond a habit of staring resentfully at strangers.

Ángel’s bean theory? Totally unproven. Pending further research, I’ll have mine with extra salsa.

Paolo Ferrari is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: In a sign of wetlands recovery, 2 young wood storks are spotted at Lake Texcoco
World.content:
Two young wood storks have been formally documented for the first time at Lake Texcoco in a new sign of continued environmental recovery in the area that includes the canceled airport construction site near Mexico City.

A community monitoring brigade found the juveniles Nov. 5 near a ditch on communal farmland in San Salvador Atenco, México state, according to a Facebook post by managers of the Lake Texcoco protected area.

The species was not previously listed in the reserve’s management plan.

The sighting brings to 20 the number of bird species that have returned after periods of absence or been newly recorded, reserve director Jorge Daniel Fonseca Cando said.

He suggested the wetland could provide a temporary winter stopover for the storks.

🦩✨ ¡Nuevo registro en el Lago de Texcoco! La cigüeña americana llega por primera vez a este ecosistema del #Edomex. Con ella, ya son 20 las especies de aves que regresan tras años de desecación o que llegan por primera vez. Una señal de recuperación de la vida silvestre. #ExcélsiorDigital #LagoDeTexcoco #Conservación — Excélsior (@Excelsior) November 12, 2026

The species, Mycteria americana, is known in Spanish as cigüeña americana, literally “American stork.”

The discovery does not establish that the birds are permanent residents.

But it does add to signs of improving habitat in an ecosystem damaged by drainage and construction of an international airport that was canceled in 2018 — yet won an international architectural design award in 2021. The project was championed by President Enrique Peña Nieto and canceled by his successor, Andrés Manuel López Obrador.

Fonseca Cando attributed the wildlife gains to rehabilitation work and this year’s rainy season, which flooded more than 4,700 hectares, or 47 square kilometers. He said improved water quality and recovering bodies of water have encouraged greater species diversity.

The Lake Texcoco protected area in México state not a single continuous lake. Areas flooded this year include Lake Nabor Carrillo, San Juan Marsh, Xalapango Lagoon and parts of the former airport construction site.

Recovery extends below the surface, as well, Fonseca Cando said, noting that the mexclapique, a fish native to the region, expanded its presence across more than 1,200 hectares this year. The small, freshwater fish’s common name in English is Chapultepec splitfin.

Fonseca Cando reported more than 290,000 migratory and resident birds representing 285 species in the protected area.

Recovery was also evident in November 2025, when roughly 4,300 hectares were covered with water following abundant rain.

Restoration efforts have included replanting grass, reforestation and rehabilitating lakes and wetlands.

In November 2025, Fonseca Cando reported that more than 280,000 birds had arrived to winter in the reserve, compared with 60,000 in a related survey in 2021. Parts of the abandoned airport’s infrastructure have been repurposed to create wetlands, architect Iñaki Echeverría told Uno TV.

Mexico granted protected status to more than 14,000 hectares (54 square miles) in March 2022. The designation prohibits urban development and ecosystem destruction while allowing conservation, restoration and sustainable farming.

The Lake Texcoco protected area, which includes the 2-year-old Lake Texcoco Ecological Park, also helps regulate water around the capital. Fonseca Cando said the reserve collected more than 43 million cubic meters of water in 2025.

With reports from La Jornada, El País and Excélsior

World.title: Migrant caravan continues journey northward from Chiapas
World.content:
A migrant caravan made up of around 1,200 people arrived in Mapastepec, Chiapas, on Monday, after leaving the town of Escuintla on Sunday afternoon.

The migrants walked more than 30 kilometers from Escuintla to Mapastepec, where they began arriving in the early hours of Monday morning.

Jessica López, a Salvadoran woman, told the newspaper La Jornada that she and other members of the caravan were “very tired” and sore all over, especially their feet.

“But here we are with one goal in mind: to get to the United States,” she added.

The caravan mainly consists of Hondurans, but also includes migrants from various other countries, including El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti and Cuba. It includes men, women and children, and is traveling under the name “Dios con Nosotros, el Señor nos Protege (God with Us, the Lord Protects us).

The migrants set off from the city of Tapachula last Tuesday and have since walked more than 100 kilometers. Some 1,500 migrants were initially part of the caravan, but its numbers have declined as some people have left the group for reasons including fatigue.

Last Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods if Mexico didn’t stop the caravan. In response, President Claudia Sheinbaum said that “no migrant caravan has reached the northern border” since Trump began his second term in January 2025.

What’s next for the caravan?

The migrants set up camp on a basketball court after arriving in Mapastepec on Monday. After resting there, they plan to walk to Pijijiapan, a town and municipality north of Mapastepec.

North of Pijijiapan is Arriaga, a town near Chiapas’ border with Oaxaca where a group of some 100 migrants is reportedly waiting for the migrant caravan to arrive.

Reuters reported last week that the caravan is first aiming to get to Mexico City “to seek assistance from the Mexican federal government and protection from being detained while traveling toward the U.S. border.”

The news agency also reported that the migrants “are hoping that the election ​victory by Democrats that gives the party control of Congress starting in January could open pathways for them to live and work in ​the United States.”

López, the Salvadoran migrant, told La Jornada that the migrants are seeking help from Mexico to achieve their goal of reaching the U.S., or at least the northern border.

“We ask Mexico to support us, to help us achieve our goal,” she said.

“We’re only seeking an opportunity to work. We didn’t come to cause problems; we want to work to get ahead,” López said.

Sheinbaum said last Thursday that Mexican authorities tell migrants that entering the United States is “very difficult” due to the Trump administration’s strict border policies.

“We tell the people in the caravan that it’s very difficult to get to the United States, that if their goal is to get to the United States, they won’t be able to achieve it,” she said.

“We seek a way for them to safely return to their countries. If someone wants to stay in Mexico under certain conditions in a certain place, they can. But the vast majority return to their countries of origin once they find out they won’t be able to cross Mexico’s border with the United States,” Sheinbaum said.

It is likely that some of the members of the migrant caravan currently in Chiapas will seek to work in Mexico, at least temporarily.

Sheinbaum said that the government wouldn’t use force against migrants traveling through the country, as has occurred in the past.

With reports from Diario del Sur, La Jornada and Latinus

World.title: In China, Mexico’s environment minister takes notes on its waste-to-energy circular economy
World.content:
Mexico is aiming to convert its waste management strategy to an energy-from-waste model and it’s looking to China, a world leader in the relevant technology, for the know-how needed to take a major step toward a circular economy.

Waste utilization would not only provide a new source of clean energy but also solve waste disposal problems and reclaim public spaces that would otherwise be used for landfills.

Toward that end, Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena visited several Chinese facilities over the weekend specializing in waste utilization and water restoration to understand how they work to restore ecosystems and clean waterways, and to assess their potential use in Mexico.

Her tour came in advance of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China, where President Sheinbaum will stress deepening technological cooperation with China, including the development of solutions for the use of organic waste (including sargassum, the brown seaweed that plagues Mexico’s Caribbean shore) to produce energy and cut greenhouse gas emissions.

Bárcena traveled to the city of Zhuhai in China’s southern Guangdong province to visit the SUS Environment plant, which processes up to 3,000 tonnes of waste per day and produces up to 90 megawatts of electricity.

She also noted that China has tackled its waste problem by increasing the share of solid waste used for energy from 9.8% in 2005 to 84.6% in 2024. Meanwhile, China’s landfill disposal has decreased from 64% to 5%.

“Learning about this experience allows us to identify alternatives for waste management in Mexico,” Semarnat wrote on X on Saturday.

Many of China’s waste-to-energy plants use advanced technologies, such as artificial intelligence, to enhance operations, something that could be incorporated into any new Mexican operation.

In Shenzhen, where the APEC summit will take place, Bárcena visited the Honghu underground plant, which can process up to 100,000 tonnes of wastewater a day. Above ground, Honghu houses a public park, demonstrating the potential for providing more clean public spaces.

“Shenzhen is… an example of how to reclaim rivers, restore ecosystems and transform formerly polluted spaces into meeting places and gathering spots for communities,” Bárcena said. “The Chinese experience demonstrates that it is possible to move beyond landfills and advance toward a circular economy model.”

With reports from La Jornada and XEU Noticias Veracruz

World.title: Guadalajara Cartel co-founder and convicted murderer Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo dies at 80
World.content:
Miguel Ángel Félix Gallardo, a drug lord known as the “Boss of Bosses” who was convicted of the 1985 murder of U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena, died in a hospital in Guadalajara, Jalisco, on Sunday. He was 80.

The Jalisco Security Ministry announced Félix Gallardo’s death, which came two days after he was transferred from the Puente Grande prison near Guadalajara to a private hospital in the state capital. The ministry said that “multiple organ failure” was the cause of his death. He was also suffering from pneumonia.

Félix Gallardo, the co-founder and erstwhile leader of the now-defunct Guadalajara Cartel, had been in poor health for years. He spent the last 37 years of his life in prison after he was arrested in Guadalajara in 1989.

DEA Administrator Terry Cole acknowledged Félix Gallardo’s death in a social media post on Sunday night.

“The cartel kingpin who built an empire of violence and orchestrated the brutal murder of DEA Special Agent Enrique ‘Kiki’ Camarena has died in custody after more than 37 years behind bars,” Cole wrote.

“Kiki’s sacrifice will never be forgotten — nor will the criminals and corruption behind his death. His courage lives on in every agent carrying out our mission, and our pursuit of truth and justice will never end.”

In 2017, Félix Gallardo was sentenced to 37 years in prison for the murders of Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar, who worked with Camarena. Before the murder conviction, he had received a 40-year sentence for drug trafficking, weapons offenses and bribery.

In 2022, a federal judge took Félix Gallardo’s advanced age and poor health into account when ruling that he could complete his 40-year sentence at a residence in Zapopan, Jalisco. However, the federal Attorney General’s Office challenged the ruling, preventing the release of the then 76-year-old Guadalajara Cartel co-founder.

Rafael Caro Quintero, another Guadalajara Cartel co-founder who was transferred from a Mexican prison to a U.S. prison in early 2025, was also convicted of the murder of Camarena, a Mexicali native who joined the DEA in 1973.

The early years

Félix Gallardo was born on Jan. 8, 1946, in Culiacán, Sinaloa, a city that has been plagued by Sinaloa Cartel infighting for the past two years.

His parents were farmers and exported legumes to the United States, according to the now-deceased drug lord.

Félix Gallardo, who left school after completing the second grade of primary school, told Noticias Telemundo in a 2021 interview from prison that he had “dedicated” himself to “agriculture and ranching” since he was a boy.

Before founding the Guadalajara Cartel with Caro Quintero and Ernesto Fonseca Carrillo in the 1970s, Félix Gallardo worked as a police officer and spent a period as a bodyguard for former Sinaloa Governor Leopoldo Sánchez Celis, who was in office from 1963 to 1968.

The New York Times reported that his employment as a police officer and bodyguard for Sánchez allowed him to forge “connections that helped him and his partners transform the Mexican drug trade in the 1970s and 1980s.”

A life of crime

Félix Gallardo, Caro Quintero and Fonseca Carrillo co-founded the Guadalajara Cartel in the late 1970s. Under their leadership, the Guadalajara Cartel became a major trafficker of narcotics, including cocaine and marijuana, to the United States.

Félix Gallardo, who was also known as “The Godfather” and “The Drug Czar,” forged alliances with criminal groups in Colombia — the world’s largest producer of cocaine — that helped the Guadalajara Cartel establish itself as Mexico’s dominant drug trafficking organization in the 1980s.

The BBC reported that he “led the organization which revolutionized drug smuggling in the region by entering into partnership with the Colombian cartels, particularly [Pablo] Escobar’s Medellín Cartel, to combine production in the Andes with Mexican transportation across the border into the United States.”

“At one point an estimated 80% of all cocaine that entered the U.S. came from the Medellín Cartel. Félix Gallardo and his organization played a major role in smuggling it in,” the BBC wrote.

“At its height, the Guadalajara Cartel under Félix Gallardo exerted huge influence over Mexican politics and law enforcement, controlling entire police networks and state governorships,” reported the British broadcaster and media organization.

His nickname, “The Boss of Bosses” (El Jefe de Jefes), is a testament to the immense power he once wielded in Mexico’s criminal underworld.

CNN reported that “the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in ensuing decades.”

“… His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials and innovations like using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent.”

The Wall Street Journal reported that Pablo Escobar turned to Mexico — and Félix Gallardo — after “U.S. interdiction efforts began seizing his submarines, speedboats and freighters.”

“Through his government contacts, Félix Gallardo arranged protection for overland routes carrying cocaine from South America through Mexico to the U.S. border,” the Journal reported.

“For a fee, traffickers could move their product under the protection of the Mexican state. Rather than cash, Félix Gallardo demanded a percentage of each shipment — an innovation that made him one of the richest men in the hemisphere and altered the global narcotics business.”

In the 1980s, Félix Gallardo also worked with Joaquín “El Chapo” Guzmán, the erstwhile Sinaloa Cartel leader who is now imprisoned in the United States.

The New York Times reported that Guzmán got his start in the drug trafficking business “working as an air logistics expert for Mr. Félix Gallardo.”

The murder of Camarena and Félix Gallardo’s capture

In 2017, Félix Gallardo was found guilty of involvement in the murders of both Camarena and Zavala. He was frequently described as the autor intelectual, or mastermind, of Camarena’s murder. Félix Gallardo always denied involvement in his killing.

The slain DEA agent angered the Guadalajara Cartel leadership due to his involvement in a 1984 raid on a large marijuana plantation in Chihuahua that belonged to the criminal group.

The BBC reported that the murder of Camarena in February 1985 “sparked one of the biggest manhunts the U.S. government has ever launched in North America,” and “the net started to tighten” around the leaders of the Guadalajara Cartel. The murder strained U.S.-Mexico relations for years and led to an intensification of the U.S. government’s war on drugs.

Caro Quintero and Fonseca were both arrested in April 1985, while Félix Gallardo was detained on April 8, 1989, ending his life of crime.

At the time of his arrest, Enrique Álvarez del Castillo, then Mexico’s attorney general, described Félix Gallardo as the “No. 1 narcotics trafficker in Mexico.”

The news outlet N+ reported that the Guadalajara Cartel “fragmented” after his capture, giving rise to the Sinaloa and Tijuana cartels.

Félix Gallardo gained international notoriety after the DEA accused him of the kidnapping, torture and murder of Camarena. His infamy grew when he was portrayed as a central figure in the Netflix series Narcos: Mexico. Mexican actor Diego Luna played the role of Félix Gallardo in the hit series, whose first season began in late 2018.

Among Félix Gallardo’s surviving relatives are his children Miguel Ángel Félix and Abril Félix.

Jorge Eduardo Montiel, a spokesperson for the Jalisco Security Ministry, said on Sunday that relatives of Félix Gallardo would attend a small religious ceremony at the hospital where he died.

With reports from Animal Político, El Universal, Reforma, N+, BBC, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and CNN

World.title: Sheinbaum lands in Shenzhen on a commercial flight, then heads straight to tacos with Mexicans living in China
World.content:
Listen to this article

President Claudia Sheinbaum has arrived in Shenzhen, China, on a visit featuring a packed agenda of meetings with state leaders, diplomats and businesspeople at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

As with her previous travels to Brazil and Canada, the president elected to take a commercial flight — a symbol of government austerity, anti-elitism and a commitment to connecting with everyday citizens that started with her predecessor Andrés Manuel López Obrador, who sold the presidential plane to Tajikistan for US $92 million in 2023.

Sheinbaum arrived at the Mexico City airport at 11 p.m. Saturday for a 12:35 a.m. flight to Tijuana before boarding China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032 to Shenzhen, China.

While in Tijuana, Sheinbaum released this message:

“We’re going to a two-day event with business leaders from all the APEC countries. Afterward, we’ll have a Cabinet meeting and will participate in the APEC forum. I’ll keep you updated. Look for me during the morning press conference (in the National Palace); I’ll be connecting there.”

The Cabinet members in Sheinbaum’s entourage are Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard, Energy Minister Luz Elena González, Health Minister David Kershenobich, Environment Minister Alicia Bárcena and Science Minister Rosaura Ruiz. A contingent of Mexican business leaders is also accompanying the president.

With the time change, the president arrived in the city hosting the APEC meeting at 11:30 a.m. Monday, before hustling to the Tequila Coyotes restaurant to meet with Mexican citizens residing in China.

Afterward, she praised “the extraordinary Mexicans who have decided to live their lives [in China],” adding that “we should find ways for them to stay connected with Mexico.”

On Tuesday, Sheinbaum will speak to the APEC Business Advisory Council, where she will outline her Plan México investment strategy to more than 1,000 business leaders.

She will then meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney.

Her talk with Xi comes amid a backdrop of trade tensions after Mexico slapped tariffs of up to 50% on certain products from countries with which it does not have free trade agreements, including China. Sheinbaum said she’ll deliver a message of “cooperation for development and friendship” to Xi and will discuss projects related to smart hospitals, renewable energy, waste transformation and scientific development.

She will also meet with Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva.

Sheinbaum intends to return to Mexico by Friday morning, Nov. 20, in order to lead the commemorative activities for the 116th anniversary of the start of the Mexican Revolution.

With reports from Reforma, Latinus, SDP Noticias, Expansión and EFE

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: Water deliveries set to rise, while new initiatives aim to clean the environment and protect threatened city cats
World.content:
With social media awash in stories of Guadalajara residents who have gone without water for a month or longer, city officials shifted into high gear. Last week, the city announced expanded water truck service to more than 35 affected neighborhoods.

Meanwhile, there is some good news on the environmental front. Various state agencies are cracking down on illegal waste disposal, clean technologies are slated for installation in Guadalajara’s historic center and a new program is in the works to combat animal cruelty.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Verónica Delgadillo G (@verodelgadillog)

Let’s dive in.

Water truck deliveries are increasing to address critical shortages

With numerous city neighborhoods enduring water outages lasting much longer than the advertised rationing schedule, Guadalajara expanded its water distribution program this past week.

Commenting on the changes to local media, Mayor Verónica Delgadillo said, “Our goal is to deliver 2.1 million liters of water to the most critical areas of the city, and we have set ourselves the goal of visiting (at least) 35 neighborhoods (daily).”

The new volume equates to roughly 210 standard 10,000-liter tanker trips daily and a tenfold increase over the 200,000-liter average daily volume delivered last month, when the water distribution program began.

Pipa deliveries are focused in particular on high-elevation areas and neighborhoods where severe low pressure keeps water from reaching rooftop tanks (tinacos). These neighborhoods are primarily located on the city’s east and south sides.

In addition to mobile deliveries, the government is also increasing its network of fixed community water cisterns from 19 to 33 across the affected neighborhoods to improve access to water.

The Jalisco state government is also supplying roughly 20 additional pipas daily to city hospitals, schools and emergency facilities to alleviate the burden the water crisis is having on myriad public service providers.

Residents can request free pipas or report low water pressure on WhatsApp using the Siapabot phone number, 33-5164-4440.

Solar energy and electric charging stations are coming to Guadalajara’s historic center

With an eye to lowering pollution levels and energy costs in Guadalajara’s historic center, the Association of Business Owners of the Historic Center of Guadalajara has developed a plan to install solar panels on rooftops across the neighborhood.

According to Diego Amorós Alfaro, the organization’s president, their green initiative involves generating electricity through photovoltaic systems that would allow businesses to recoup their investment in as little as three years.

The plan also calls for expanding infrastructure to support electric vehicles. To this end, the association looks to create partnerships with hotels and parking facilities to install more charging stations, making it easier for visitors who drive these low-polluting vehicles.

Finally, the project aims to promote other unspecified measures to optimize electricity consumption and reduce the carbon footprint of downtown businesses.

Local agencies step up efforts to improve environmental protection citywide

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Unidos por Jalisco (@unjalmx)

The Jalisco State Environmental Protection Agency (Proepa) recently shared several accomplishments that highlight the agency’s stepped-up commitment to environmental protection this year.

In a public statement, Proepa announced its staff has conducted 596 inspection visits, addressed 253 citizen complaints and imposed 233 temporary closures to remedy industrial pollution associated with manufacturing businesses and waste management and prevent further environmental damage.

Among the most significant actions is a new agreement with waste management operator Caabsa Eagle Guadalajara to comprehensively remediate environmental damage caused by the Los Laureles and Coyula-Matatlán landfills in Tonalá. The deal reportedly includes a bond posted by the company for 341 million pesos (US $18.37 million).

In another high-profile case, Proepa has temporarily closed a property near Technology Park Guadalajara and the University Center of Biological and Agricultural Sciences (CUCBA) in Zapopan due to improper hazardous waste disposal. In conjunction with the State Attorney General’s Office and Zapopan’s city government, Proepa also arrested several individuals responsible for the illegal dumping at this facility.

Separately, Proepa has been expanding its work focused on pollution prevention, with new training aimed at businesses involved in livestock farming, industrial activities and tequila production. In cooperation with the state Secretariat of Environment and Territorial Development (Semadet), it is also training city workers in methods to improve their inspection and oversight capabilities.

A new plan is announced to protect the cats of Alcalde Park

The shocking dog-poisoning incident in Parque España in Mexico City’s Condesa neighborhood last month received significant media coverage. Meanwhile, far less attention has gone to a similar incident affecting the feral cats living in Alcalde Park.

Alcalde Park, located immediately north of Guadalajara’s historic center, has long been known as a place where irresponsible pet owners dump their unwanted cats. Cleanup efforts have come and gone, but the cat abandonments have continued in recent years, albeit on a smaller scale than in decades past.

Tended by compassionate neighbors, the park’s feral cat colony rose to around 40 cats.

Late last month, caregivers discovered as many as 16 deceased cats due to suspected poisoning. Toxin-laced food packets were reportedly found scattered about the park grounds, prompting a public outcry.

Formal criminal complaints and public petitions followed. In response, city and state authorities launched an investigation, with analysis of both the dead specimens and laced food packets.

In recent days, the Metropolitan Agency for Urban Forests (AMBU) announced a formal plan to improve the well-being of the cats living in Alcalde Park and prevent more felines from being abandoned there.

Jesús Alexandro Félix Gastélum, director of AMBU, said the plan calls for a roughly 800-square-meter space to house the cats, with day and night surveillance to ensure their safety. The agency also plans a new adoption program for younger cats with the potential to be socialized, along with training for citizen volunteers assisting in the cats’ care.

MND writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Drone Attacks Outpace Colombia’s Defences
World.content:
Security: Colombia

Armed groups carried out 318 explosive-drone attacks in Colombia in 2026 up to 1 October, about one every 20 hours, the Fundación Ideas para la Paz (FIP), a Bogotá security think tank, said on 8 October 2026. The state still has no large anti-drone shield, and Defence Minister Jorge Mora has said the one promised was neither structured nor financed.

The weapon is cheap, commercial and spreading, which matters to US readers who follow Colombia as travellers, investors or policy watchers. Our recent reports on strikes in Cesar, Norte de Santander and Huila are linked below.

Key Facts What. Armed groups launched 318 explosive-drone attacks in Colombia in 2026 to 1 October, about one every 20 hours.

Toll. Since 2024, drones have killed 25 uniformed personnel and six civilians and injured 456 people, to 1 October.

Shield. The promised anti-drone shield, over 6 trillion pesos (about US$1.8 billion), is not yet structured or financed.

Power Index. Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.1 points (November 2026 edition).

As of. As of 17 November 2026, 17:35 GMT

Colombia’s armed groups have found a cheap way to attack soldiers and police from the air. The government says the promised shield against them was never built.

How the Drone War Grew

The FIP counted 318 attacks in 2026 to 1 October, with a peak of 56 in August. It also tracks them by group and region, and its figures are the most complete public record.

The EMC, the Estado Mayor Central, is a dissident faction of the demobilised FARC guerrillas, and the ELN is the National Liberation Army, a guerrilla group. A kamikaze drone is one that crashes into its target and explodes.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.1 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The EMC accounts for 72% of attacks and the ELN, the National Liberation Army, a leftist guerrilla group, for 23%, the FIP said on 8 October 2026. The ELN rose from 36 attacks in 2025 to 132 in 2026.

Four departments, Cauca, Chocó, Valle del Cauca and Norte de Santander, hold 71% of the attacks, the FIP said. The groups use drones to watch troops and civilians, check their own camps, attack rivals and tighten control of mining and coca areas, according to the FIP.

Training a drone operator is quicker than training a fighter, it noted.

The Casa de Nariño in Bogotá, the presidential palace, where the government’s response to the drone threat is decided. (File photo: Juanjo70000, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, 2015)

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Colombia 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What Happened This Month

On Thursday 12 November 2026 President Abelardo de la Espriella condemned a drone attack in Tibú, Norte de Santander, that killed four soldiers, the presidency said. He ordered the security forces to use all their intelligence and operational capacity to find those responsible.

Colombia’s Defence Ministry said the anti-drone shield announced by the previous government, valued at more than 6 trillion pesos (about US$1.8 billion), was neither structured nor financed. A Colombian trillion, written “billones”, is a million million; the rate used is about 3,310 pesos per dollar (market rate, 17 November).

Minister Mora said only 800 billion pesos (about US$240 million) were announced for a first phase, and that its funding for 2026 was never guaranteed. He also said no awarded contract and no system in the process of being bought were handed over to his team.

The Shield and Its Critics

The FIP said on 8 October 2026 that the Defence Ministry reports about 9,000 attempted attacks detected in 2025, with roughly 96% jammed. The remaining 4% is enough to cause damage, the FIP said, and fibre-optic drones, which send signals down a cable, cannot be detected or jammed.

The FIP called current state measures necessary but insufficient and urged anti-drone equipment for the smallest and most remote units first. Three kamikaze drones also hit the 3D air-traffic radar at Candelaria, Valle del Cauca, a key air-defence asset in Valle del Cauca, it said.

Colombia’s Congress is also working on drone rules. No date for a full vote in the Chamber of Representatives, the lower house, is confirmed.

What It Means for You

Counts differ by source and period, so any single headline number needs care. Readers tracking Colombian risk should note that most attacks sit in four departments, Cauca, Chocó, Valle del Cauca and Norte de Santander, the FIP said.

The US State Department publishes a Colombia travel advisory, but we could not open it on 17 November, so we do not quote it. We also found no official confirmation of US counter-drone aid.

What Is Not Known

We could not confirm other tallies circulating this month, including figures of 351 attacks or 43 uniformed dead, and we use only numbers from the FIP and the presidency. No official 2026 total for deaths after 1 October is public in the sources we opened.

The content and budget of the ministry’s “shock plan” are not yet published, and the date of a full vote in the Chamber on drone rules is not confirmed. We also have no verified comparison with other Latin American countries.

In Plain English

EMC. Estado Mayor Central, a dissident faction of the former FARC guerrillas. ELN. National Liberation Army, a leftist guerrilla group. FIP. Fundación Ideas para la Paz, a Bogotá think tank on conflict and security. Fibre-optic drone. A drone steered through a thin cable, so radio jammers cannot stop it. Billones. In Colombia, a million million pesos, or one trillion in US usage.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many drone attacks has Colombia had in 2026?

The FIP counted 318 attacks from January to 1 October 2026, about one every 20 hours. Counts from other sources differ, and no official total for the full year exists yet.

Who carries out the drone attacks in Colombia?

The FIP attributes 95% to two groups, the EMC (72%) and the ELN (23%). The presidency does not yet name those behind the Tibú attack of 12 November.

Does Colombia have an anti-drone shield?

Not at scale. Defence Minister Jorge Mora said the announced shield, over 6 trillion pesos, was neither structured nor financed.

Are drone attacks a risk for foreign visitors?

Most recorded attacks hit security forces, though the FIP counts six civilian deaths since 2024. We could not open the US State Department advisory, so check it directly.

Sources: Fundación Ideas para la Paz, 8 October 2026; Colombia’s Defence Ministry, statement by Minister Jorge Mora, November 2026; Presidency of Colombia, 12 November 2026; Chamber of Representatives, 23 October 2026.

World.title: Mexico and Canada Deepen Security Ties
World.content:
Politics: Mexico

Mexico and Canada agreed on Tuesday 17 November 2026 to speed up a joint plan that includes closer security cooperation. President Claudia Sheinbaum of Mexico and Prime Minister Mark Carney of Canada met on the sidelines of a Pacific Rim leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China.

The meeting matters to US readers because both neighbours trade heavily with the United States, and their shared trade pact with Washington is unsettled. The United States has not renewed the USMCA (the US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement), so Ottawa and Mexico City are strengthening their own link.

Key Facts What. Leaders met in Shenzhen on 17 November 2026 and agreed to speed up an action plan.

Trade. Goods trade rose 19% in nine months; Canadian investment in Mexico tops C$3.7 billion (about US$2.6 billion).

Prediction markets. Polymarket, a betting market, prices 5% that the USMCA is extended in 2026 (12:28 p.m. ET, 17 November).

Power Index. Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 70.8 points (November 2026 edition).

As of. As of 17 November 2026, 17:35 GMT

Canada and Mexico say they will push their joint plan harder in its second year. The public record shows closer security ties, but no new critical minerals deal.

Why Canada and Mexico Are Moving Closer

The partnership began on 18 September 2025, when Carney visited Mexico City and the two leaders announced a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and a Canada-Mexico Action Plan, Canada’s Prime Minister’s Office said. Their joint priorities then included border security and fighting transnational organised crime.

Washington is on a different track. On 1 July 2026 the US Trade Representative, the White House’s trade negotiator, said the United States “did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form”, while the pact “remains in force”.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 70.8 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Under the pact’s rules the three countries now review it every year, the same office said in an October 2026 notice. That continues until all three confirm a new 16-year term or the agreement expires.

Canada and Mexico want the opposite outcome. On 20 August 2026 Carney and Sheinbaum spoke by phone and stressed renewing the pact “as soon as possible”, Canada’s Prime Minister’s Office said, and on 17 November they again reaffirmed that aim.

File photo: the flags of Canada, the United States and Mexico at the opening ceremony of a FIFA World Cup match. (Photo: Omar David Sandoval Sida, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Mexico 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What Was Announced in Shenzhen

Canada’s Prime Minister’s Office said the leaders met on the margins of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, a Pacific Rim forum. Mexico’s Presidency confirmed the meeting and said the pair discussed rising trade and investment under the 2025-2028 action plan.

The Canadian readout put merchandise trade up 19% in the first nine months of 2026 against the same period of 2025. It cited nearly $1 billion in Mexican investment in Canadian mining and food production (about US$700 million) and over $3.7 billion in Canadian investment in Mexico (about US$2.6 billion).

Those dollar figures appear without a currency label, and we read them as Canadian dollars at about US$0.70 per Canadian dollar (market rate, 17 November 2026). The readout also reports more than 3,700 business meetings and over 100 commercial agreements from trade missions.

On security, the readout cites a new Strategic Security Dialogue, close to 30 stakeholder engagements and training exercises, and over $10 million (about US$7 million) for security projects. It does not say what the dialogue covers.

The leaders agreed to speed up the action plan in its second year, with a focus on supply chains, trade and investment, and security. They also expressed “a desire to identify further areas of cooperation, including in critical minerals, defence”, which is an intention, not a signed deal.

What It Means for You

This meeting changed no tariff or trade rule, and the USMCA stays in force. For anyone with supply chains across North America, the annual reviews mean the rules can still shift, and Canada and Mexico are building a second line of cooperation in case they do.

What To Watch

First, the USTR deadline of 12 January 2027 for public comments on the 2027 annual joint review, set in its October 2026 notice. The date of the 2027 review meeting and of the public hearing is not confirmed.

Second, the Polymarket market on a 2026 extension closes on 31 December 2026. Its 5% price shows traders see little chance of an extension this year.

What Is Not Known

No text of a security or critical minerals agreement has been published, and the readout does not say what the Strategic Security Dialogue discusses. Mexico’s Presidency summary, as published on 17 November, gives no detail on security or critical minerals.

The time of the meeting and the exact currency of the readout figures are not stated. We have not seen a Mexican figure for trade or investment to compare with Canada’s.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction market where users place real-money bets, priced 5% for “USMCA extended in 2026?” on 17 November 2026 at 12:28 p.m. ET (17:28 GMT). About US$12,461 had been traded, and the market ends on 31 December 2026.

These prices are bets, not polls. Thin volume of US$12,461 limits what the price tells us.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

In Plain English

Sheinbaum. Claudia Sheinbaum, Mexico’s president since October 2024. Carney. Mark Carney, Canada’s prime minister. USMCA. The US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement, called CUSMA in Canada and T-MEC in Mexico. Action Plan. The 2025-2028 Canada-Mexico plan covering trade, security and other areas, launched in September 2025. APEC. Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, a forum of Pacific Rim economies whose leaders met in Shenzhen. USTR. The US Trade Representative, the White House’s trade negotiator. Critical minerals. Metals such as lithium and copper used in batteries and electronics.

Frequently Asked Questions

Where and when did Sheinbaum and Carney meet?

They met on Tuesday 17 November 2026 in Shenzhen, China. It was a bilateral meeting on the margins of the APEC leaders’ summit, not a phone call.

Did Canada and Mexico sign a critical minerals deal?

No signed deal has been published. The Canadian readout says the leaders want to identify further cooperation areas, including critical minerals and defence.

Is the USMCA still in force?

Yes. On 1 July 2026 the US Trade Representative said the pact “remains in force” although the United States did not renew it, and the three countries now review it annually.

How much did trade between Canada and Mexico grow?

Canada’s readout says goods trade rose 19% in the first nine months of 2026 against a year earlier. It gives no total.

Sources: Prime Minister of Canada readout, 17 November 2026; Prime Minister of Canada readout, 20 August 2026; Prime Minister of Canada readout, 18 September 2025; Presidency of Mexico, 17 November 2026; US Trade Representative, 1 July 2026; US Trade Representative notice, October 2026; Polymarket, 17 November 2026.

World.title: Angola Central Bank Cuts Rate to 14%
World.content:
Rio Times Markets · Angola

Published Tuesday, 17 November 2026 · Source: Banco Nacional de Angola (central bank), INE Angola (national statistics institute)

Angola’s central bank lowered its main interest rate to 14.00% from 14.75% on Tuesday 17 November 2026, another step in a series of cuts this year. Governor Manuel Tiago Dias of the Banco Nacional de Angola (BNA) said the bank’s Monetary Policy Committee, its rate-setting panel, acted because inflation keeps slowing and the short- and medium-term outlook is favourable.

Annual inflation was 8.16% in October, Angola’s National Statistics Institute (INE) reported on 6 November, which is 9.27 points lower than a year earlier. For US investors and companies with exposure to Angola, a lower rate is meant to make local credit cheaper and may lower returns on savings and bonds in the kwanza, Angola’s currency, though the gap over inflation is still wide.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Key Facts What Angola’s central bank cut its main rate to 14.00% from 14.75%, a 0.75-point cut.

When Tuesday 17 November 2026, after the rate committee met on 16 and 17 November.

Why Annual inflation fell to 8.16% in October from 8.43% in September.

The run The rate was 17.5% before the May cut, so it is down 3.5 points since.

Next The date of the next committee meeting has not been confirmed.

Angola is borrowing more cheaply because prices are rising far more slowly than a year ago. The rate is still 5.84 points above inflation, by our arithmetic.

How Angola Got to 14%

In May 2026 the committee cut by half a point, from 17.5% to 17.0%. It then took 1.25 points to 15.75% and, on 15 September, a full point to 14.75%.

Tuesday’s 0.75-point move brings the total since the May meeting to 3.5 points. In September the committee also lowered the share of deposits that banks must hold in reserve, in national currency, to 16.5% from 17.5%.

Each step followed slower prices. INE has put annual inflation at 8.78% in August, 8.43% in September and 8.16% in October.

The October figure is 9.27 points below that of October 2025.

File photo: the bayfront promenade in Luanda, Angola’s capital.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on angola central bank Email address Follow

What the Central Bank Wants

The committee’s stated reason is the progress inflation has made, and the governor repeated on Tuesday that the outlook for prices and the economy is favourable. In September it kept its end-2026 inflation projection at 8.6%, give or take one point, a level October’s 8.16% already sits below.

We have not seen a statement on how many more cuts the committee has in mind. A rate of 14.00% against inflation of 8.16% still leaves a gap of 5.84 points by our arithmetic, so borrowing remains costly in real terms.

In Plain English

Main interest rate: the BNA’s benchmark rate, which sets the tone for borrowing costs across the economy.

the BNA’s benchmark rate, which sets the tone for borrowing costs across the economy. Monetary Policy Committee: the BNA panel that sets that rate several times a year.

the BNA panel that sets that rate several times a year. Kwanza: Angola’s currency.

Angola’s currency. Real return: the interest rate minus inflation, a rough measure of what savers earn after prices rise.

What It Means for You

Lower policy rates feed through to what Angolan banks charge companies and pay savers. Cheaper kwanza loans can help firms that borrow locally, while holders of kwanza treasury bills, short-term government debt, may see yields drift down.

For the oil side of Angola’s economy, see our report on how the global oil price, Brent, affects Angola. Households feel the cut mostly through prices: the October inflation figure is covered in our inflation report.

What Is Not Known

The full text of the committee’s written communiqué has not been confirmed. We therefore cannot say whether it changed reserve requirements or its inflation forecast.

The date of the next committee meeting is also unconfirmed. INE’s November inflation release is the next hard price data; October’s came out on 6 November, but the November date has not been confirmed.

Background: Angola Slashes Benchmark Interest Rate by 125 Basis Points and Who Runs Angola’s Economy.

More: Angola news, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Angola’s central bank decide?

It cut its main interest rate by 0.75 points to 14.00% from 14.75% on Tuesday 17 November 2026. It is the latest in a run of cuts this year.

Why did the central bank cut the rate?

The governor, Manuel Tiago Dias, pointed to the slowing of inflation and favourable short- and medium-term prospects. INE puts annual inflation at 8.16% in October.

How far has Angola’s inflation fallen?

Annual inflation was 8.16% in October 2026, against 8.43% in September, and 9.27 points below October 2025. INE, the national statistics institute, published the figure on 6 November.

What happens next?

The date of the next committee meeting has not been confirmed. INE’s November inflation figure will show whether prices keep slowing.

Sources: Banco Nacional de Angola, Monetary Policy Committee decision, 17 November 2026 (https://www.bna.ao); INE Angola, Índice de Preços no Consumidor Nacional (national consumer price index), October 2026 (https://www.ine.gov.ao/publicacoes/detalhes/NTg1MjA%3D). World.title: Puerto Rico Alert Test Is Not a Power Test
World.content:
Society: Puerto Rico

A US-wide emergency alert test runs today, Tuesday 17 November 2026, at 2:20 p.m. Eastern Time, including in Puerto Rico. The test is real, but it only briefly interrupts radio and television programmes.

Puerto Rico is a US territory whose residents are US citizens, so the test reaches Americans there too. The official notices say nothing about electricity.

Key Facts What. A US-wide emergency alert test runs at 2:20 p.m. ET today (3:20 p.m. in Puerto Rico).

Power. The FCC notices mention neither electricity nor Puerto Rico; the test uses broadcast channels.

The test. Radio and television only, with the message “This is only a test.” Not sent to phones.

Next. If the test is postponed, the backup date is Thursday 3 December 2026.

As of. As of 17 November 2026, 17:45 GMT

Today’s national alert test is a broadcast exercise. It is run through radio and television, not through the power grid.

What the Alert Test Is

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the US broadcast regulator, announced on Wednesday 16 September 2026 that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the US disaster agency, would run a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System (EAS). It is set for 2:20 p.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday 17 November, with Thursday 3 December 2026 as the backup date.

The test travels through the Integrated Public Alert and Warning System (IPAWS), FEMA’s national alert network, and the FCC says it is sent in English and Spanish. The alert text says the exercise is only a test and that the public need take no action.

FEMA said ahead of the test that it would air on radio and television only and would not be sent to mobile phones. It says the broadcast lasts about one minute.

The FCC’s public notices mention neither electricity nor Puerto Rico. Nothing in them links the test to the power supply.

File photo, April 2018: a transmission tower and power lines in the hills near Caguas, Puerto Rico, during repairs after Hurricane Maria. (Photo: US Army Corps of Engineers, South Atlantic Division, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

The test is due at 3:20 p.m. local time on the island, the same moment as 2:20 p.m. Eastern Time. It will pause radio and television programming briefly.

What It Means for You

If you have family, a business or a trip in Puerto Rico, expect a short alert on television and radio around 3:20 p.m. local time, with no instruction attached. Phones are not expected to ring.

A power cut on any day would come from the grid, not from this test. Official guidance for the test is the broadcast message itself, which carries no instruction.

What To Watch

First, the test itself at 2:20 p.m. ET on Tuesday 17 November, with Thursday 3 December 2026 as the FCC’s backup date. Second, the FCC deadline of 2:20 p.m. ET on Thursday 19 November for broadcasters to file their day-of-test reports.

What Is Not Known

We could not confirm whether any outage occurs on the island on 17 November. We found no statement from the island’s power companies or its emergency management bureau about the test.

In Plain English

FEMA. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, the US disaster agency. FCC. The Federal Communications Commission, the US broadcast regulator. EAS and IPAWS. The Emergency Alert System and the national network that sends its messages.

Frequently Asked Questions

Will the FEMA test cause a blackout in Puerto Rico?

The FCC’s public notices on the test mention neither electricity nor Puerto Rico. The test interrupts radio and television briefly and is not a grid operation.

When is the nationwide emergency alert test?

The test is set for 2:20 p.m. Eastern Time on Tuesday 17 November 2026, which is 3:20 p.m. in Puerto Rico. The backup date is Thursday 3 December 2026.

Will my phone receive the alert?

FEMA said the test will air on radio and television only and will not be sent to mobile phones. The message says no action is required.

Why does the US run this test?

The FCC and FEMA, the US disaster agency, run nationwide tests to check that the alert system works. The date and time are set in the FCC’s public notice of 16 September 2026.

Sources: FCC public notice DA 26-989, 16 September 2026; FCC public notice DA 26-1190, 4 November 2026; FEMA, 2026 Nationwide Emergency Alert System Test.

World.title: US and Mexico Lose Measles-Free Status
World.content:
Health: Americas

The United States and Mexico have lost the official label that says measles no longer spreads at home. On Tuesday 17 November 2026 the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), the regional arm of the World Health Organization, withdrew the status from both countries and from Bolivia.

The US had held the status since 2000, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the national health agency, says. Measles is now treated as endemic there, meaning it spreads on its own, with 5,412 confirmed US cases in 2026 as of 12 November.

Key Facts What. PAHO withdrew measles-elimination status from the United States, Mexico and Bolivia on 17 November.

Why. The same measles strain kept spreading in each country for 12 months or more.

US count. The US has 5,412 confirmed measles cases in 2026, as of 12 November.

Next. Each country must show 12 months without home-grown spread to be re-verified.

As of. As of 17 November 2026, 17:30 GMT

A regional health body says measles now spreads on its own in the US, Mexico and Bolivia. Canada lost its status a year earlier and is working to win it back.

The Big Picture

Canada lost its status in November 2025, PAHO said in its release of 17 November 2026. The three new losses bring the national total in the Americas to four.

PAHO reported on 17 November that the region had 58,213 confirmed cases as of 13 November 2026, against 12,806 a year earlier. That is about 4.5 times as many.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Bolivia ranks 13th of 14 with 27.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: economic weight (11). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (CCC+); economy contracting (-1.6%); inflation of 20%. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Canada declared its outbreak over on 19 October 2026, PAHO’s question-and-answer page says. That does not restore the status automatically, because Canada must show 12 consecutive months without transmission.

File photo. A terminal hall at Cancún International Airport, Mexico, 2024. PAHO says travellers to areas with active measles should be fully vaccinated.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Measles Email address Follow

What Happened on 17 November

PAHO’s Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission, an expert panel, met from 10 to 13 November 2026. PAHO’s director, Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, accepted its recommendation, PAHO said on Tuesday 17 November.

The panel found that endemic transmission was re-established in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States. PAHO’s test is the same virus lineage circulating for 12 months or more.

PAHO counted the year from the start of each outbreak: 20 January 2025 in the United States and 1 February 2025 in Mexico. The 12-month mark was passed on 20 January and 1 February 2026.

The CDC said on 17 November, in a joint statement with public-health partner groups, that it will work to regain the status. Its director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, said: “The measles elimination designation is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does.”

The CDC said it has invested about US$100 million in state and local health departments. Epi-Aid, its team that helps states investigate outbreaks, remains available on request.

What We Know About the US Count

The CDC’s data page, updated on 13 November 2026, lists 5,412 confirmed US cases in 2026 as of 12 November. Of these, 5,394 were reported by 47 jurisdictions and 18 were among international visitors.

The CDC counts 43 new outbreaks in 2026, and 96% of cases (5,216) are linked to outbreaks. Kindergarten coverage with the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) shot fell from 95.2% in 2019–2020 to 92.4% in 2025–2026, according to the CDC’s published data.

PAHO ties elimination to at least 95% coverage with two doses in every community, its release says. National averages can hide low-coverage pockets.

What It Means for You

For a US traveller or parent, the label itself changes no rule we could find, and PAHO’s release makes no travel statement. PAHO’s question-and-answer page says people going to areas with active measles should be fully vaccinated before departure.

It adds that infants aged 6 to 11 months can get an early zero dose, which does not count towards the routine schedule. It says anyone with fever and rash should call a health provider before visiting in person.

What To Watch

First, the evidence the US, Mexico and Bolivia must submit to the commission, which then recommends a decision to PAHO’s director. The date is not confirmed.

Second, Canada’s 12-month clock after declaring its outbreak over on 19 October 2026. The date when it could be re-verified is not confirmed.

What Is Not Known

The number of US measles deaths in 2026 is not confirmed here, because the CDC page we checked does not separate 2026 from earlier years. Nor is the date of any US plan or re-verification.

Whether Argentina or other South American countries are affected is not confirmed by the official sources we checked. PAHO’s release gave no country-level counts for the United States, Mexico, Bolivia or Canada.

In Plain English

Elimination status. A label that measles no longer spreads continuously inside a country. Endemic. A disease that keeps spreading on its own, year after year. PAHO. The Pan American Health Organization, the WHO’s regional office for the Americas. The commission. PAHO’s expert panel that reviews measles status each year. Epi-Aid. A CDC team deployment to help states investigate an outbreak. MMR. The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, given in two doses.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does losing measles elimination status mean?

It means one measles strain has spread continuously for 12 months or more, PAHO says. It does not mean every area has outbreaks, or that the country cannot control measles.

Which countries in the Americas have lost the status?

Canada, the United States, Mexico and Bolivia, PAHO said on 17 November 2026. Canada lost it in November 2025, and the other three on 17 November 2026.

How can the United States get the status back?

The CDC said on 17 November that it will work to regain it. PAHO says a country must show 12 consecutive months without transmission before the commission can recommend re-verification.

What does PAHO say about travel and measles?

PAHO says people going to areas with active measles should be fully vaccinated before departure. Its 17 November release made no separate travel statement about the United States or Mexico.

More: Latin America news · Mexico’s measles outbreak passes 20,000 cases · Costa Rica confirms measles cases amid Americas outbreak · Bolivia faces a measles crisis

Sources: PAHO/WHO release, 17 November 2026; PAHO/WHO questions and answers, 17 November 2026; CDC joint statement, 17 November 2026; CDC measles cases and outbreaks, 13 November 2026; CDC measles history.

World.title: Dominican Drug Sweep in East Arrests 91
World.content:
Crime: Dominican Republic

Dominican agents arrested 91 people and seized 20,946.4 grams of drugs, about 20.9 kilograms or 46 pounds, in the east of the country. The east includes Punta Cana, the beach resort area that many American holidaymakers visit.

The Dominican National Drug Control Directorate (DNCD), the national anti-narcotics agency, said prosecutors and the National Police, the national police force, helped run 946 operations and seven raids. It published the results on Tuesday 17 November 2026, covering the previous week.

Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Key Facts What. 91 people arrested and 20,946.4 grams of drugs seized in the Dominican east in one week.

Drugs. Presumed cocaine was 17,849.9 grams, ahead of marijuana at 2,409.3 and crack-like rock at 687.2.

Where. La Altagracia 37 arrests, La Romana 26, Verón (Punta Cana area) 16 and El Seibo 12.

Status. Those arrested are suspects, and no names or nationalities were published.

As of. As of 17 November 2026, 17:31 GMT

A week of raids across four eastern areas led to 91 arrests. The agency says the pressure on street-level dealing will continue.

The Bigger Picture

Street-level dealing, called microtráfico in Spanish, means small drug sales in neighbourhoods rather than large smuggling shipments. On 10 July 2023 the National Police said about 69,000 people had been arrested and more than 9.4 million grams of drugs seized by that date.

The DNCD and prosecutors have worked the Punta Cana area before, including raids in Verón with ten arrests and about 1.4 kilograms seized. This week’s sweep is larger and spans four areas of the east.

The published figures do not say whether the week was unusually large, and they give no total for 2026. The DNCD says only that operations will continue across the eastern provinces.

The entrance of Punta Cana International Airport in the Dominican east, in an undated file photo. (Photo: Hans Buch, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Punta Cana (the Dominican Republic) Email address Follow

What the Raids Found

The DNCD said it ran 946 operations and seven simultaneous raids, backed by prosecutors and the National Police. Six of the raids were in La Altagracia province and one was in La Romana.

Presumed cocaine made up 17,849.9 grams, about 85% of the haul and roughly 39 pounds. Presumed marijuana came to 2,409.3 grams and crack-like rock to 687.2 grams.

La Altagracia, where Higüey and Bayahíbe were among the areas covered, had 37 arrests and 10,313.8 grams seized. La Romana had 26 arrests and 8,294.3 grams, including 650.6 grams of crack-like rock.

Verón, in the Punta Cana area, had 16 arrests and 1,898.7 grams seized, and El Seibo had 12 arrests and 439.6 grams. Agents also listed four motorcycles, 10 scales, 14 mobile phones, US$10 and RD$50,655 in cash (about US$840 at about 60 pesos per dollar).

What This Means for Travellers

Visitors from the United States made up 44% of the Dominican Republic’s tourists in August 2026, when 856,858 visitors arrived, Tourism Minister David Collado said at a briefing the ministry published on 13 September. Punta Cana airport took 49% of that month’s flights, the same briefing said.

So the arrests touch the area that US holidaymakers use most, but the published figures link none of the cases to tourists, hotels or resorts. The sign for travellers is more police activity in neighbourhoods near the resorts, not a newly announced danger.

What Is Not Known

The exact dates of the raids are not stated, only the previous week. Whether prosecutors will bring charges, and in which courts, is not stated either.

The published figures do not say whether any drugs were bound for the United States or whether US agencies helped. No dated next step has been announced, only that operations will continue in the eastern provinces.

In Plain English

DNCD. The Dominican National Drug Control Directorate, the country’s anti-narcotics agency. Ministerio Público. The public prosecutors’ office, which brings criminal cases to court. Microtráfico. Street-level drug selling in neighbourhoods, as opposed to large smuggling shipments. Verón. The district of the Punta Cana tourist area where 16 arrests were made. Presumed. The agency’s word for drugs not yet confirmed by laboratory tests.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people were arrested in the Dominican east drug sweep?

The DNCD said 91 people were arrested in the week before 17 November 2026. They are suspects, and the published figures give no names or charges.

How much was seized in the Dominican east drug sweep?

The agency reported 20,946.4 grams, about 20.9 kilograms or 46 pounds. Presumed cocaine was 17,849.9 grams of that total.

Does the sweep affect visitors to Punta Cana?

The published figures link none of the cases to tourists or resorts. Verón, in the Punta Cana area, had 16 arrests and 1,898.7 grams seized.

Were US agencies involved in the Dominican drug sweep?

The published figures do not mention US agencies or say where the drugs were headed. The DNCD said prosecutors and the National Police supported its agents.

World.title: Colombia Third Quarter Economy Shrinks 0.8%
World.content:
Rio Times Markets · Colombia

Colombia’s economy went backwards in the third quarter of 2026, when the consensus forecast in the RT economic calendar pointed to growth. Seasonally adjusted output fell 0.8% from the second quarter, according to DANE, Colombia’s national statistics agency.
