World.title: Gunmen Kill Costa Rican Journalist Camilo Rodríguez on Route 32 in Heredia
World.content:
Journalist and writer Camilo Rodríguez Chaverri was shot dead Monday afternoon while driving his red pickup on Route 32 near San Miguel de Santo Domingo in Heredia. The Costa Rican Red Cross said it received the alert at 3:21 p.m. and that rescuers found him without any vital signs inside the vehicle.

According to preliminary reports, men riding a motorcycle pulled alongside the pickup, fired repeatedly and fled. Fuerza Pública officers secured the scene until agents from the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) arrived. The attack took place less than 50 meters (about 165 feet) from where radio journalist Parmenio Medina was shot dead on July 7, 2001. In recent years, Rodríguez had used his social media channels to denounce drug trafficking, corruption and alleged links between judges, lawyers and criminal organizations.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said Rodríguez had reported threats against his life but declined to join the Public Ministry’s victim and witness protection program. Díaz said one line of inquiry will be the complaints Rodríguez made publicly, including a review of the people he named in his posts.

Díaz described the killing as a strong signal that Costa Rica lacks real freedom of expression. He noted that Rodríguez is the third journalist murdered here, after Medina in 2001 and Ivannia Mora in 2003. The attorney general said prosecutors and the OIJ will carry out an exhaustive investigation to identify both the gunmen and anyone who may have ordered the attack. Deputy prosecutor Tatiana Chaves, who covers the area, is handling the scene. Lawmakers also urged judicial authorities to ensure the crime does not go unpunished.

No arrests had been announced as of early this evening. Authorities had not said how many shots were fired or released a description of the motorcycle or its riders, and investigators have not confirmed a motive.

World.title: US Airline Seats to Costa Rica Fall 14% as Fares Climb
World.content:
Travelers flying from the United States to Costa Rica this winter will find fewer seats and higher fares, with scheduled US airline capacity projected to fall 14% between August 2026 and March 2027.

The steepest cut is at Juan Santamaría International Airport outside San José, where seats from the United States are projected to drop 20%, according to projections from two international consultancies that were shared with tourism sector representatives. Capacity into Daniel Oduber Quirós International Airport in Liberia, Guanacaste, is expected to dip only 3%.

Fares have already moved. A study built on Altura and Cirium data, shared by former Tourism Minister William Rodríguez, found that base fares from the United States to Costa Rica rose 22% between January and July, before taxes and airport fees. In June and July alone, the increase reached 36% nationally and 45% on routes into San José.

The same data show US passenger numbers still grew 4% from January through July, with Liberia up 9% and San José up 1%. The trend turned in midyear, however, when US passengers fell 2% nationally in June and July and 9% at San José, while Guanacaste kept growing. The gap between the country’s two main airports widened in October. In the third week of the month, weekly flights fell from 450 a year earlier to 390, a 13.3% drop. Juan Santamaría lost 70 weekly flights, going from 407 to 337, while Liberia rose from 43 to 53.

Four airlines account for 59 of the 60 weekly flights lost. Volaris cut 23 after suspending its routes linking Costa Rica with Central America and Miami in April, amid Pratt & Whitney engine inspections. Avianca cut 17. Spirit, which ceased operations on May 2 following its bankruptcy, accounted for 12, ending its Orlando and Fort Lauderdale service to San José. JetBlue cut seven after suspending its Orlando route on July 8.

Frontier paused its San José flights from August through October, and American Airlines dropped its seasonal Chicago route. Southwest, which announced a San José-Las Vegas route in January for an October start, suspended it before launch because of weak advance ticket sales, the Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) confirmed.

The ICT said the cuts reflect individual airlines’ decisions on route profitability and capacity rather than a general decline in the Costa Rican market. Through 2027, the institute plans to expand marketing and public relations in priority markets, working with travel agencies, booking platforms and US airlines to fill more seats and attract visitors who stay longer.

Víctor Umaña, executive director of the Center for Tourism Studies (CET), described a structural shift in which arrivals have stagnated and Liberia has gained ground on San José. He linked the change to a visitor profile centered on luxury, sun and beach travel, with shorter stays and fewer destinations visited.

Umaña said high costs, the strong colón and gaps in infrastructure and security are making the country less accessible and squeezing the sector’s margins. Weaker demand, he said, leads airlines to cut frequencies and seats. The CET estimates that if the gap of 60 weekly flights persists from October through December, Costa Rica could receive between 35,000 and 70,000 fewer tourists, a loss of roughly $65 million to $129 million in foreign exchange.

Martí Jiménez, president of the National Chamber of Tourism (Canatur), said fewer seats do not automatically mean fewer visitors if planes fly fuller. He noted, however, that Costa Rica’s drop in air capacity exceeds the averages for Latin America, at 4%, and Central America, at 9%, which he attributed to a loss of competitiveness specific to the country.

Jiménez added that Juan Santamaría has not grown in passengers in seven years, while Liberia keeps growing where luxury tourism is concentrated. A record number of Costa Ricans traveling abroad is filling some of the remaining seats, he said, which shows foreign arrivals are not growing.

Other markets are moving in the opposite direction. Seats from Canada rose 19.6% from January through July, led by a 28.9% increase into Liberia, while capacity from Europe grew 17%, mostly into San José, helped by new service such as nonstop flights from London Heathrow. Latin American routes shrank, with about 112,400 seats lost over the same period. Some new US service has also arrived, including the first Tampa nonstop in 25 years.

Tourism still brought in a record $5,543.7 million in foreign exchange in 2025, up 2% from 2024, according to Central Bank figures compiled by the ICT. Average spending per tourist rose from $1,601.8 in 2024 to $1,848 in 2025, though the CET cautioned that exchange rate effects may explain much of that increase, with the dollar hitting a record low against the colón last week.

The average stay for foreign tourists has fallen from 12.6 nights in 2019 to 10.3 in 2025. Tourism employment dropped from about 188,000 jobs in the second quarter of 2024 to about 167,000 in the second quarter of 2026, according to the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC).

The squeeze on seats comes just days after a US ground stop disrupted flights to and from Costa Rica. With fewer nonstop options into San José, fares into the capital have risen fastest, while Liberia has continued adding service heading into the busiest months of the year.

World.title: ‘Grampa’ says he checked cameras for a missing phone and saw his grandson take $175 from his room
World.content:
‘Grampa’ says he checked cameras for a missing phone and saw his grandson take $175 from his room

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 75-year-old man near Crooked Tree Junction says he did not know $175 had been taken from his bedroom until he watched security footage months later while looking into a separate matter involving his grandson. The grandson, 28-year-old Deallin Andre Jones, now faces two theft charges.

The man told police he reviewed the footage on November 6 and saw Jones enter his bedroom and remove the cash. The man said the footage dated to about 6:50 a.m. on June 5, when he was away from home.

He also told police that Jones borrowed a blue ZTE cellphone belonging to Budd’s late wife on September 28. The phone was valued at $400. Budd said he repeatedly asked for it back, but Jones did not return it or give him a satisfactory explanation for where it was. Neither the phone nor the cash had been recovered when Budd filed his report.

Police say they reviewed the footage and detained Jones on November 13. According to the report, Jones admitted taking the cash and phone in a recorded statement on November 15 at the Ladyville Police Station in the presence of a justice of the peace. Police formally charged him that day with two counts of theft. When offered a phone call after being charged, police say Jones called his grandfather.

World.title: Burrell Boom man says he was hit with metal bat after stepping in to help nephew
World.content:
Burrell Boom man says he was hit with metal bat after stepping in to help nephew

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Burrell Boom man told police he saw his nephew get hit twice with what appeared to be a metal bat and stepped in to tell him to leave. He said the man holding the bat then turned on him, striking him above the eye and on the wrist.

The man said he was riding to a friend’s home on October 28 when he saw two men run out of the yard and cross the street on Arnold Avenue. He told police one of them struck his nephew twice. He said he put down his bicycle, asked what the fight was about and told his nephew to leave with the others.

The man said he stayed behind to talk with his friend. He told police the man approached with the bat, warned him that he did not belong there and pretended to swing. The man said he raised the stout bottle he was holding but backed away without striking the man. As he reached for his bicycle, he said, he was hit above the left eyebrow. He said a second swing caught him on the left wrist.

Officers responding to the fight found the man bleeding above his eye and told him to file a formal report. While an officer was issuing him a medical form at the station, another man walked in and the complainant pointed him out as the person who had struck him, according to the report.

Police obtained the medical form on November 13 after a doctor classified his injuries as wounding. Investigators say a man they contacted agreed to report to police on Monday, November 16. The report does not confirm whether he appeared or whether anyone was charged.

World.title: Belize’s businessmen told to slow down before their hearts do it for them
World.content:
Belize’s businessmen told to slow down before their hearts do it for them

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): They run companies. They carry families. And too often, they ignore their own health.

That was the message at the second edition of The Gentleman’s Exchange, hosted by the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry (BCCI) on Friday, November 13, at the Wyndham Garden Belize City Grand Resort.

Held to mark International Men’s Day, the event ran under the theme “The Provider’s Pause: Leading with a Healthy Heart and Mind.”

Business leaders, doctors and wellness practitioners spent the morning talking about what many men avoid: check ups, stress and warning signs.

Dr. Joshua Canul of the Ministry of Health and Wellness addressed national health priorities. Minister Francis Fonseca and cardiothoracic surgeon Dr. Adrian Coye led a session called “Cardiovascular Health and Recovery: Listening to the Warning Signs.” Dr. Andre Castillo of the Matron Roberts Health Center spoke on preventive care.

A keynote discussion featured Finance Belize CEO Hero Balani on corporate wellness and fitness trainer Clayton Greenidge on active living.

BCCI President Giacomo Sanchez said taking care of yourself is just as important as taking care of those who depend on you.

“Good leadership takes more than drive and good judgment. It also takes balance and self awareness. It takes the wisdom to know when to slow down,” Sanchez said.

The Chamber says it plans to expand the initiative to reach more men across Belize.

World.title: A phone call, an argument, a shove: Orange Walk man charged with assault
World.content:
A phone call, an argument, a shove: Orange Walk man charged with assault

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): It started with a phone call. It ended with a criminal charge.

Giovanni Reyes, 34, a self employed resident of San Lorenzo Housing Site in Orange Walk Town, has been charged with common assault after his partner reported that he pushed her to the ground inside their home.

The 36 year old woman told police she was woken around 7:00am on Thursday, November 12, by her 12 year old daughter, who said Reyes was talking about them on the phone.

She found him in a hammock with the phone to his ear and asked who he was speaking to. He denied talking to anyone and hung up.

Reyes then accused the girl of lying. The woman told him to leave the house.

As he collected his things for work, she said, he insisted she speak to her daughter and began pushing her toward the child’s bedroom. She told him to stop and braced her hands against the doorway.

He pushed harder, she said, and she fell.

She called the police and made a formal report. Reyes was detained, and police obtained a warrant and charged him the same day.

He remained silent when cautioned.

World.title: International News: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he would return if board asks
World.content:
International News: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he would return if board asks

By Zoila Palma: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he would be willing to return to lead the company he co-founded, following his resignation last week amid revelations of multiple alleged affairs, including one involving a suspected Chinese spy.

In a statement released today, Huang thanked friends, colleagues and members of the public for their support, while acknowledging that he had made serious mistakes. “I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life,” he said. “I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation.”

Huang also said he had received calls from employees, investors, business partners and customers urging him to return, describing Nvidia as a “once-in-a-generation company.” “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he stated.

However, a person familiar with the matter told Yahoo Finance that Nvidia’s board is not looking to reinstate him.

The controversy has raised questions about Nvidia’s future leadership and its continued investments across the artificial intelligence industry, while the company has reportedly lost hundreds of billions of dollars in market value since the allegations emerged.

World.title: The man who gave Belize the 19th: Dangriga honours T. V. Ramos
World.content:
The man who gave Belize the 19th: Dangriga honours T. V. Ramos

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Before the drums, the dancing and the re enactments on Thursday, Dangriga paused to remember the man who made it all possible.

On Friday, November 13, the community gathered for the 71st Annual Tribute to Thomas Vincent Ramos, the Garifuna activist recognized as the Father of Garifuna Settlement Day. The date marks the anniversary of his passing in 1955.

The tribute honoured Ramos and the courageous activists who stood beside him in the fight to preserve Garifuna culture and win recognition for the arrival of the Garinagu in Belize.

“Their determination, dedication, and unwavering commitment ensured that our cultural identity would not be forgotten,” organizers said.

This year’s tribute came with something new. Ramos’ granddaughter, Adele Ramos, launched a website dedicated to his life and work: thomasvincentramos.info.

The site features historical records, biographical accounts and details of his civil rights and social justice activism in the 1940s. She says it will be updated over time with multimedia content so his contributions stay accessible to future generations.

“We remember! We honour! We celebrate!” the tribute declared.

Garifuna Settlement Day is this Thursday, November 19.

World.title: International News: COP31 draft declaration calls for greater electrification as 1.5°C climate goal slips out of reach
World.content:
International News: COP31 draft declaration calls for greater electrification as 1.5°C climate goal slips out of reach

By Zoila Palma: A draft declaration emerging from the United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) on Monday is calling for increased global electrification to help combat climate change while acknowledging that the Paris Agreement’s goal of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels is expected to be exceeded. The draft comes as negotiations enter their final phase, with countries still divided over key commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and finance climate action.

The proposed declaration includes a target put forward by co-host Turkey to increase electricity’s share of global final energy consumption from 23 percent to 35 percent by 2035. Greater electrification across households, industries, transportation and agriculture is being promoted as a way to improve energy efficiency and reduce reliance on more polluting energy sources.

While Germany and the European Union support the target, several African countries want concrete financial commitments to help them implement climate measures, Yahoo reports.

The draft also recognizes that the world is likely to exceed the 1.5-degree warming threshold established under the Paris Climate Agreement, but calls for efforts to limit the overshoot and bring global temperatures back down to that level as early as possible within this century.

Australia’s chief negotiator and co-host Chris Bowen cautioned that some elements of the draft may not receive unanimous support. Climate conference decisions require agreement among participating parties, making negotiations over the final wording particularly challenging.

Disagreements over fossil fuels and climate financing are also expected to complicate the negotiations, with major oil-producing countries facing criticism over efforts to resist stronger climate commitments.

World.title: 10 charged after specialized police units carry out weeklong drug crackdown
World.content:
10 charged after specialized police units carry out weeklong drug crackdown

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Ten people were arrested and charged in seven drug cases following police operations in San Ignacio, Orange Walk, Belmopan and San Pedro Town between November 9 and 15. Police reported seizing cocaine, crack cocaine and cannabis, as well as five live rounds of ammunition in one of the searches.

Police Staff Officer ASP Stacy Smith outlined the cases at Monday’s press briefing. She said several specialized units took part, including GI3, the Mobile Interdiction Unit, the Special Patrol Unit, the San Ignacio Violence Response Team and Special Branch.

November 9 — Rayan Andrews, 42, of Camalote was charged with possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply. Smith said officers saw Andrews pull two grams of cocaine from his underwear and toss it away.

November 10 — Luis Castellanos, 49, was charged with possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply after police reportedly found 12 grams of crack cocaine in his pants pocket. In a separate case that day, Sheldeen Evans and Gilda Guardado, both of Santa Elena Town, were jointly charged with the same offence after officers reportedly found 1.9 grams of crack cocaine at a residence they were occupying.

November 11 — Nigel Alexander Novelo, 32, a cybersecurity engineer from Orange Walk Town, was charged with possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply. Smith said officers found approximately 6.8 grams of cocaine in the vehicle he was driving. In Belmopan, Jaron Mejia was charged with the same drug offence and two counts of keeping ammunition without a gun licence. Police say a search of his home turned up three grams of cocaine, four live 9mm rounds and one live .223 round.

November 12 — Carmita Gonzalez, 54, of San Pedro Town was charged with possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply after police reportedly found 1.7 grams of cocaine at her home. That same day, Johnny Heibert, 43, Margaretha Heibert, 38, and John Heibert, 19, all of Indian Church Village, Orange Walk District, were jointly charged with drug offences. Smith said officers found 38 grams of cannabis, 1.9 grams of crack cocaine and 15 grams of cocaine during a search of their residence.

In a separate update, Smith said the Rural Violence Response Teams had also seized two firearms in recent weeks. She did not link either firearm to the seven drug cases.

World.title: WATCH: ATL Vikings’ title bid delayed as Sagicor cut series deficit
World.content:
The ATL Vikings will have to wait a little longer to secure a historic Business House basketball title after suffering defeat to Sagicor B in game three of the League Division Two best-of-five finals, leaving them with a 2-1 series lead and their championship celebrations on hold.

The Vikings, who are chasing a historic title, will now look to regroup and close out the series in their next encounter on Wednesday, while Sagicor have breathed new life into their challenge with the win.

(Video: Llewellyn Wynter)

World.title: Haitian trafficking network
World.content:
This file photo shows a group of Haitians who landed at Boston Beach, Portland, in 2023.

HEAD of the Portland police Superintendent Ainsley McCarthy has charged that the frequent arrival of Haitians on the shores of the parish is part of a broader trafficking network across Jamaica.

“We have a Haitian population here in Jamaica. For example, in Montpelier, St James, we have Haitians there. So these Haitians who come in from time to time, some of them are trafficked. They pay to get here, and then there are persons who pick them up to take them to other locations, most times outside of the parish,” McCarthy said during the latest episode of the Jamaica Constabulary’s

Force4good podcast.

McCarthy was supported by head of Police Area Two Assistant Commissioner McArthur Sutherland, who told the podcast that many of the Haitians are being employed by Jamaicans to conduct farming in the hills of Portland.

He said police have done numerous operations targeting that practice and, “We believe some level of coordination is outside of the Portland parish.”

According to Sutherland, last year the police had to intervene after a dispute between two of the immigrants during a party held on one of the farms left one of them dead.

“The matter is still before the court and that [Haitian] is still in custody. From an organised approach, we have sufficient reason to suspect — or I would say believe — that it is organised, to an extent. One of the evidence of that organisation is the fact that we see returnees — persons who were removed [and] returned. The last trip we had one such case, and we are dealing with it,” Sutherland added.

Last month, police apprehended 22 Haitians across Area 2 — which covers Portland, St Mary, and St Ann — within a one-week period, raising concerns about a possible human-smuggling operation along Jamaica’s north-eastern coastline.

In June, 17 Haitians arrived in the Passley Gardens area of Port Antonio. Days later an additional 11 landed on Jamaica’s shores. They were taken to Port Antonio Police Station for health and immigration processing.

According to Sutherland, Jamaica requires “infrastructural support” to successfully tackle the issue as there are multiple uncontrolled ports across the island.

“The maritime coastal domain awareness is critical, [and] Portland is no exception. We have been looking at this from several years back — from the days when we were looking at it as gun-for-drugs [trade]… where they bring down the weapon and in exchange they get the marijuana. We have not seen much of that activity. But the emergence now of, what I’d say, either people smuggling or people seeking refuge, whichever category you look at it from, we definitely need the right infrastructural support as a country to really handle that,” added Sutherland as he argued that an ongoing cross-border collaboration is needed.

That collaboration, he explained, would be “a very solid intelligence network that can identify the triggers and alert us so we can mobilise and respond to these situations as quickly as possible”.

“We know that at times they will get off the boat, out in the water, and swim towards shore in order to avoid detection. So it’s not necessarily that [the] boat [is] coming up on the shore. They have different approaches to getting here,” explained Sutherland.

He underscored that the Haitians do not arrive through a controlled port, making it difficult for law enforcers to conduct risk assessment and, in instances, health risks came to the surface and had to be treated with appropriately.

Meanwhile, McCarthy reported that through the support of the Portland Disaster Risk Management Committee and other agencies, law enforcers are better able to deal with the arrival of immigrants.

“Although it’s considered disaster risk management

— dealing with hurricane, earthquake

— we also come together to deal with the influx of illegal Haitians coming into the island. And we have the Red Cross that provides food, clothing, and meals also on a daily basis to these people while they’re here.

“We have the health department, who I just [need to] pick up my phone and I call Dr [Sharon] Lewis [medical officer of health for the Portland Health Department] and I say, ‘Doc, we have some visitors to the island and she should make special arrangement to get them medically examined.’ Then I will call PICA (Passport, Immigration and Citizenship Agency) and PICA comes in, does the interviews, and we get them out of the island as quickly as possible, in most cases. And where people apply for asylum, the matter goes through the court,” said McCarthy.

World.title: Dumb and dumber!
World.content:
CARNEY... these devices we walk around with in our hands, we become so dependent on these devices to answer questions, tell us what to do, how to think, that we’re thinking less (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

University of Technology (UTech), Jamaica chancellor, Ambassador Lloyd Carney has warned youngsters that increasing dependence on smartphones and other modern communication devices is doing more than wasting their time — it is making them dumber.

Carney issued the warning at all three of the university’s graduation ceremonies at Alfred Sangster Auditorium on the Papine, St Andrew campus over the weekend.

He urged graduates to reduce their social media use, citing studies which, he said, showed that high school students worldwide had experienced two consecutive years of declining thinking and problem-solving abilities.

According to Carney, the reported decline in thinking and problem-solving abilities marked a change from the pattern in previous years when each group of students leaving high school was expected to have stronger thinking skills than the one before.

“It’s the second year now in a row international studies have shown that students graduating high school from all over the globe, they have less cognitive skills, less logical thinking capability than students from two years ago. Two years in a row, our students are leaving high school not as smart as they used to be. Before there was always a progression every year, they’re a little bit smarter than the group before,” he said.

Carney said the findings had been linked to people’s growing reliance on devices, which, he believes, is reducing the amount of independent thought and analysis they exercise.

“These devices we walk around with in our hands, we become so dependent on these devices to answer questions, tell us what to do, how to think, that we’re thinking less. We’re not being as analytical in our way of thinking, and it is actually debilitating to us,” said Carney, who did not identify the studies he was pointing to, or provide details about the countries, number of students and methods used to reach those findings.

However, a study published in the Journal of Adolescence in 2025, which examined the academic performance of more than 1.78 million students aged 15 and 16 across 36 countries, found that results in mathematics, reading, and science had declined in many countries, particularly between 2012 and 2022.

The research, which analysed data from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Programme for International Student Assessment, also found that declines were greater in countries where young people’s access to smartphones and use of electronic devices for leisure during school hours had increased.

At Sunday’s ceremony, Carney delivered the warning in even more blunt terms.

“These smart devices we walk around with, these phones, they are sapping your intellectual capacity because they want to think for you. So it’s to their benefit that you get dumber, and that’s exactly what’s happening,” Carney said.

He pointed to China and Singapore as the only two countries which, according to the studies he referenced, had not experienced decline in young people’s thinking skills over the two-year period.

The chancellor attributed this to restrictions in those countries on young people’s access to social media.

Carney also took aim at the pressure to create an image of wealth and success on social media.

“There are people borrowing money to rent a car to look like they have money so they can show on

Facebook, or whatever, that they have money. They are going into debt to pretend they have money, so that the billionaires in Silicon Valley can make money off of your foolishness. It is time to stop doing that,” he said.

Carney also warned that artificial intelligence (AI) could make it easier for people to misrepresent themselves and urged graduates to be careful about the information they share with such tools.

He said people should also avoid becoming so dependent on AI that they use it for every decision or task, arguing that technology companies had a financial interest in encouraging people to rely heavily on their products.

Drawing on his experience in business and technology, Carney said most everyday tasks in industry and business did not require expensive large language models, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Google’s Gemini.

He estimated that about 90 per cent of the work could be done using cheaper models.

Carney also shared a story of an engineer at one of his companies who left an AI model running for a month and generated a US$200,000 bill.

The chancellor also encouraged parents to lead by example if they wanted their children to spend less time on social media.

“If you want to curtail what your children are doing on social media, when you come home from work, read with them, play a board game, talk to them; imagine that, talk to them. If they see you on social media, spending your time talking to your friends on social media, posting on social media, your children are going to imitate what you are doing,” he said.

World.title: The bet pays off for Shaggy
World.content:
Shaggy (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Ahead of the release of his seventeenth studio album Lottery in May, Shaggy scored Billboard chart entries with two of the album’s singles — Til a Mawnin (featuring Sting) and Boom Body (with Akon and Aidonia).

The project, which bears his Ranch Entertainment and the New York-based independent label VP Records, didn’t crack the major charts, but it didn’t go unnoticed by Grammy voters.

On Monday, Lottery paid off for Shaggy when it was among six albums nominated in the Best Reggae Album category of the 69th annual Grammy Awards.

When the Jamaica Observer caught up with Shaggy moments after the nominations were released, the Boombastic deejay was quite upbeat when asked how he felt about receiving the nomination.

“Amazing! I titled the album Lottery because it’s how I’ve lived my whole career. Nobody hands you a winning ticket. You bet on yourself, put in the work, and see what comes back. Thirty-plus years in, having the Recording Academy recognise this record means the bet paid off again, and I’m incredibly grateful for that,” said Shaggy.

The album contains 13 tracks and features collaborations with Sting, Robin Thicke, Anthony Hamilton, Akon, Jeremih, Beres Hammond, Dexta Daps, Aidonia, 450, Mutabaruka, Vanessa Amorosi, Noah Powa, Olaf Blackwood, and Rayvon. It combines reggae, dancehall, and pop with elements of hip hop, soul, and R&B.

Shaggy shared that Lottery was the result of a combined team effort.

“A lot of work went into this project. I’m hands-on with everything I do — from writing to production. I brought in people I trust from different corners of music, like Sting, Robin Thicke, Akon, and Jeremih, so reggae and dancehall could sit next to R&B and pop and still feel like one; cohesive record. It was a real team effort, and I’m proud of everyone who contributed,” Shaggy disclosed.

This is Shaggy’s eighth nomination in the Best Reggae Album category. He was first nominated in 1996 for his platinum selling album

Boombastic. That album, released via Virgin Records, catapulted him to international success.

Since then he has racked up nominations for 2006’s Clothes Drop, 2009’s Intoxication, 2012’s Summer in Kingston, 2015’s Out of Many, One Music, 44/876, a joint project with Sting, which won the award, and 2023’s Com’ Fly Wid Mi.

Also receiving a nomination in this year’s Best Reggae Album category were Buju Banton (Too Too Bad), Chronixx (Exile), Ziggy Marley (Brightside), Runkus (Supernova) and Protoje (The Art of Acceptance).

This is the first nod for Runkus. He commented about the nomination on his Instagram story.

“Jah is glorious. Supernova Grammy nominated.”

Brightside has given Ziggy Marley his 7th solo nomination in the Best Reggae Album category. He earned nods for Wild and Free in 2012, Rebellion Rises in 2019 and won for Love is My Religion (2007), In Concert (2014), Fly Rasta (2015) and Ziggy Marley (2017).

This is Protoje’s third attempt at winning a Grammy. He was nominated previously for A Matter of Time (2019) and Third Time’s a Charm (2023).

Buju Banton won the Grammy in 2011 for Before the Dawn. He has eight nominations to date including Inna Heights (1999), Friends for Life (2004), Too Bad (2007), Rasta Got Soul (2010), Upside Down 2021 (2020), and Born for Greatness (2024).

Chronixx’s Chronology lost out to Damian “Jr Gong” Marley’s Stony Hill in 2018. This is his second nomination.

World.title: Promoted Tru-Juice play down title aspirations despite claiming JPL summit
World.content:
Tru-Juice FC’s starting line-up against Treasure Beach FC for a Legend Jamaica Premier League football match in October 2026.

Despite Tru-Juice FC’s dream start to their debut Legend Jamaica Premier League (JPL) season, head coach Damion Gordon is refusing to entertain talk of them winning the title.

Tru-Juice extended their lead at the top of the table to four points following a 2-0 win over Racing United on Sunday at Ferdie Neita Park.

The newly promoted club took the spoils in the St Catherine derby, thanks to an own goal from Markovich Brown in the 77th minute and a stoppage time strike from Rodave Murray.

Gordon says he was pleased with the team’s execution throughout the game, despite the goals coming late.

“We have a good framework and the team does actually work along that line,” he said. “The substitutions were spot on today, I think tactically we were very involved and were able to execute what we actually asked from the players. But the starting team created a platform for the substitutes to come and finish the job and we just have to grow as a unit.”

Following their promotion from the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) Championship, known as the Tier Two competition, Tru-Juice were busy during the summer transfer window as they brought in several top talent including national players Alex Marshall, Gadail Irving and Tafari Chambers.

However, Gordon believes there’s no favouritism within the set-up as the entire squad has been proving their worth.

“It’s just the work that we have been putting in and we have to choose the players so irrespective of what the others have been doing,” he said. “If we see it fit where we need to interject a player, I don’t think it really matters the name of the player. It’s just what we want at the moment and I think sticking to that has been playing out for us and we just have to continue on that.”

“Those players have been doing well and we encourage them and I hope they continue to do well. But we as coaches, we have to know when to balance things and when to pull a player and when to make sure, you know, we keep everybody motivated.”

Tru-Juice have lost only once from their 10 games and are currently on a five game winning streak which included their 2-1 win over defending champions Portmore United earlier this month. They move to 23 points, four clear of second place Montego Bay United.

Gordon, though, says he won’t be carried away by any title talk despite their impressive start.

“We’re in the league for the first time. I know we have been doing some wonderful things but we consistently made mention of being humble and [asking] the group to stay humble,” he said.

“For us, it’s just a game at a time, what we can do a game at a time. We cannot look on ‘oh we’re going to win’, nothing like that. It’s a new team, players are learning to play together, we’re actually still in the process of working on the cohesiveness of the group, and once we can get that, we’ll be alright.”

Other winners in Sunday’s action were champions Portmore, last season’s finalists Cavalier, Montego Bay United, Arnett Gardens, and Dunbeholden.

Waterhouse’s clash with Mount Pleasant Football Academy, scheduled for Monday night, was postponed due to the number of players from the clubs called up for international duty.

World.title: BOYZ ON A MISSION
World.content:
Members of Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz squad train at Stadium East on November 13, 2026. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

INSPIRED by their famous victory over Mexico on Saturday, Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz will be looking to complete the job today and book their place in the Concacaf Nations League semi-finals.

Jamaica take on host Mexico at the BBVA Stadium in Monterrey in their second-leg quarter-final starting at 9:30 pm. The national team needs only a draw to advance following their 3-2 first-leg victory at the National Stadium.

However, the Rudolph Speid-led Boyz will be hoping the long journey to Mexico doesn’t take a toll on their performance after spending much of Sunday travelling to Monterrey on commercial flights.

The team left the island early Sunday morning but didn’t arrive in Monterrey until late Sunday evening. Players and technical staff were split in two groups, with one travelling through Miami and the other via Panama.

The team conducted their sole training session at the BBVA Stadium on Monday evening.

Speid will also be one player short after Tottenham Hotspur midfielder Tyrese Hall, who was recently named Premier League 2 Player of the Month, returned to London for personal reasons. The 21-year-old, who only has two caps including his debut last March, was left on the bench in Saturday’s win.

Mexico’s playing conditions are often a concern for visiting teams, although the Boyz will avoid the high-altitude conditions associated with the Azteca.

Speid says he isn’t concerned about the external factors as they seek to topple the hosts.

“We played in Mexico this year so some of the players are used to [the conditions]. I am not one of those coaches that worry about where we play because if you let that weigh heavily on what you do, it [causes] an adverse reaction to how the team performs,” he said.

“It is what it is. Wherever they put us to play, we’ll do the best we can. It’s the same thing when it comes to teams; whoever we get to play, we’re going to try our best. So we’re really not worried, we’re focused on Mexico. They’re a top-ranked team; they didn’t get there by fluke, but that’s where we want to be so we have to prepare for them.”

Barring any late issues, Jamaica could field a similar line-up which led the world number 10 ranked Mexicans 3-0 after 69 minutes.

They could also stick to the same approach that proved successful against Rafa Marquez’s side.

“If we sit back and just watch the Mexico team play, they’ll just take us apart eventually,” he said. “So part of the plan was not to let that happen and we picked our moments, when we press forward. So it wasn’t just a total press, it was always calculated ones; press forward when it was necessary to ensure that we kept them in their half for long periods of time.”

Jamaica have never beaten Mexico on Mexican soil in a senior men’s international match from 10 attempts. However, they did earn a 2-2 draw in their last game back in March 2023 in the Nations League group stage.

Mexico, though, have a slight advantage with the away-goals rule in effect, meaning a 1-0 or 2-1 win would be enough to send them through despite the aggregate score being level.

Head Coach Marquez is currently under immense pressure from the Mexican media having gone winless in his five games since taking over in July.

He’s expecting a strong response from his team who have made the semifinals of every Nations League tournament since its inception in 2019.

“It’s almost the same defensive line that played in the World Cup and they were extraordinary back then,” he said. “While the contexts are obviously different, I believe we must demand more of ourselves to ensure we don’t repeat these kinds of errors.”

“I think we should [also] focus on the positives, the way the team reacted, and how the substitutions really helped spark that reaction,” he said. “Now we need to take advantage of playing at home. Monterrey is a city where the atmosphere and the fan support can really give us a boost and that’s what we’re hoping for in the next match.”

Jamaica’s sole appearance in the Nations League semi-finals was in the 2023/24 season where they went on to finish third.

Defenders: Joel Latibeaudiere (captain), Miguel Freckleton, Richard King, Ronaldo Webster, Kyle Ming, Denzel Hall, Christopher Ainsworth, Damion Lowe, Jeovanni Laing

Midfielders: Courtney Clarke, Karoy Anderson, Dwight Merrick, Ramone Howell

Forwards: Kaheim Dixon, Renaldo Cephas, Javon East, Ricky Jade-Jones, Khori Bennett, Daniel Green, Warner Brown

World.content:
[ESTABLISHING SHOT]Naphtali Junior

Style and glamour took centre stage at the Harbour Lounge of the Jamaica Conference Centre on Sunday, November 15, as Style Week Jamaica Fashion Block closed in haute fashion



presenting part two of the International Mecca of Style showcase.

Presented as part of the West Indies Fashion, Art and Architecture Exchange (WIFAX), the two-part fashion show which started on Saturday, November 14, culminated on the downtown Kingston waterfront with a high-energy presentation. Bringing the best of the region and the international runway to the capital, the evening spotlighted collections from Island Bespoke’s David Newell, Glenroy March of D’Marsh Couture, Kadian Nicely, Pebbles King, and Rêve Jewellery co-principal and creative director Duane Bennett.

Tuesday Style Fashion highlights a few of the evening’s looks.

World.title: Family member in custody after body of missing 12-year-old found in St Ann
World.content:
The individual has not been charged.

Samuels, otherwise called ‘Tina’, of Hyde Park district, Alexandria, St Ann, was reported missing last Thursday.

Her body was reportedly discovered in the Halifax area of the parish on Monday.

Police are investigating the circumstances surrounding the child’s death and are appealing to anyone with information to come forward.

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Alexandria Police Station, Crime Stop at 311, or the police emergency number 119.

World.title: The 5 Labour groups that matter as Burnham shows his hand on welfare
World.content:
There’s a long way to go before MPs find out which of Milburn’s recommendations the government implements. A white paper and legislation are not due to be published until next year.

Getting Labour MPs — many of whom are long-standing anti-poverty campaigners — to back plans which ultimately aim to cut Britain’s massive welfare bill will be no mean feat.

Despite a huge majority in the House of Commons, Starmer was forced to roll back plans to reduce personal independence payments — which go to disabled people both in and out of work — after a well-organized campaign by senior Labour figures back in 2025.

POLITICO runs through the key figures from the governing party whose views on the report — and critically Burnham’s eventual proposal — are worth paying attention to.

1) The committee chairs

Treasury Committee Chair Meg Hillier and Work and Pensions Committee Chair Debbie Abrahams played a crucial role in halting some of Starmer’s welfare reforms.

Hillier wrote an amendment to Starmer’s welfare plans which would have stopped the bill at its first hurdle. More than 100 Labour MPs from across the party signaled they would back it, forcing ministers to change course and promise any changes would only be made after a review by Disabilities Minister Stephen Timms, which is due later this month.

World.title: Uganda in talks to host EU migration hub
World.content:
Bagiire said Uganda had a “discussion” with the Netherlands but “we haven’t got far.” He didn’t say which other countries Uganda had been speaking with but said the talks were not that advanced: “Let me say that the discussion is at a stage of a cup of coffee.”

In June, European diplomats said Uganda and Uzbekistan were being discussed as potential locations for EU migration centers. However, Uganda has three criteria that need to be met before it can host a hub, Bagiire said on the sidelines of a conference in Vienna hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development.

“If we are to establish a hub, it will be strictly for people of African origin; they should not have a criminal record; [and] no unaccompanied minors,” he said.

He added that the discussions involve “no more than 50” people, who would be sent to open facilities. “No detention, they’re not prisons — at all. People can integrate within the communities … they’re free to do whatever they need to do. The same way we treat our refugees,” he said.

World.title: Russia’s Lavrov says French troops in Ukraine amount to ‘direct participation’ in war
World.content:
Russia’s top diplomat accused Paris of directly taking part in the Ukraine war following a report that French troops are in the eastern European country carrying out noncombatant operations.

“We conveyed our concern through available channels, warning the relevant countries that this is no longer support for Ukraine, but direct participation in the war,” Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told reporters Tuesday at the East Asia Summit in Manila, adding that French troops were also “assisting in goal setting, providing satellite data and much more.”

Lavrov’s comments come a day after Radio France Internationale revealed Paris had kept troops in Ukraine for several months to provide training and equipment maintenance under the “Volia mission.” The troops, who are in the French military detachment in Poland, have been involved in the operation in Ukraine since at least summer 2026, RFI reported.

World.title: Brussels signals unwillingness to be Burnham’s EU sounding board
World.content:
A third EU diplomat said there could be a “gray area” in which both things are true.

While Britain can’t do “substantial negotiations” with the EU until there’s a “consensus” in the U.K., the same diplomat said it would be right for “some level of conversation with Brussels to see what’s sensible” so that realistic options can then be discussed with the British public.

But others agreed that the U.K. must provide sharper definition. A fourth EU diplomat said: “I think the next step in this process is that the EU needs a little more clarity on where the U.K. stands.”

A fifth said Burnham must first “include in his vision something that is realistic” which can then “be worked on together with the EU.”

Anand Menon, the director of the UK in a Changing Europe think tank, said a timeline where Brussels wants firmer proposals first should come as no surprise to Britain.

“The EU wants Britain to come to them and say this is the kind of relationship they want,” he said. “They want us to do that with a relationship that’s on offer rather than make up something that they are not willing to give.”

World.title: Le Pen defends retirement reform plan as opponents mock her economic credibility
World.content:
The far-right leader says her plan to lower the retirement age would be offset by savings and employer-funded pension schemes.

PARIS — Far-right French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen pushed back against the latest accusations on Tuesday that the math behind her pension reform doesn’t add up, arguing she and her team had done “a painstaking meticulous job” to create a system that is both “fair” and “economically efficient.”

“We are taking the situation seriously,” Le Pen said as she briefed reporters on the fine print of her proposal to bring down the retirement age to 62 for most workers. France’s retirement age is set to rise to 64 for most people in the coming years.

Le Pen and her lieutenants argued that while their proposal would cost more than €18 billion, that bill would be offset by more than €23 billion in savings from efficiency adjustments, thighter qualification rules for part-time workers, incentives for older people to stay in work and a host of other measures. Le Pen also floated introducing some private pension schemes, financed by employers’ contributions, in addition to France’s state pension system.

World.title: Polish far-right lawmaker Braun charged over hospital ‘citizen’s arrest’
World.content:
Grzegorz Braun faces up to five years in prison for allegedly detaining a doctor who had performed an abortion.

Polish prosecutors charged far-right European Parliament lawmaker Grzegorz Braun on Tuesday over an alleged incident in which he tried to carry out a “citizen’s arrest” of a doctor who had performed an abortion.

The Wrocław regional prosecutor’s office said it had sent an indictment to the court in the southwestern town of Oleśnica, accusing Braun of depriving the doctor of her liberty, violating her bodily integrity and insulting her. The charges carry a maximum sentence of five years in prison, prosecutors added.

Braun and several supporters entered the Oleśnica hospital in April 2025 to confront a gynecologist who had carried out a late-term abortion on a patient whose life was at risk. The doctor said Braun held her for more than an hour by blocking the exit with his body.

World.title: Crimea bridge destruction will impair Russian supply chains, says Ukraine
World.content:
The Russia-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksenov, confirmed the strike, saying the bridge was closed until further notice, but provided no details of the damage.

Russia launched a bombing campaign against Ukrainian bridges on Oct. 1, choking logistics and causing huge public transport problems. The Russian defense ministry reported hitting Kyiv’s North and South bridges across the Dnipro River, linking the two sides of the Ukrainian capital.

Ukraine said its attack against the $3.7 billion Kerch Bridge is part of its response to the Russian campaign. The road and rail bridge is a key supply line for the 2.5 million people living on the Crimean Peninsula, illegally annexed by Russia in 2014, as well as for Russian forces stationed there.

The road portion has collapsed, and the extent of damage to the parallel rail bridge is uncertain, although the Russian transport ministry said Tuesday that limited traffic will resume on a single railway track. Without the bridge, Russia will have to rely on ferries and overland transport through occupied Ukraine — both routes subject to attack by Kyiv.

"Partial destruction of the bridge affects logistics, supply chains, and the morale and psychological state of the families of Russian military personnel, intelligence officers, and officials," said Andrii Klymenko, head of the Black Sea and Baltic Strategic Research Monitoring Group.

Zelenskyy said the operation was carefully planned and gave a long list of the missiles and drones used.

World.title: Rwanda hits back at asylum-seeker return hub criticism
World.content:
Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, disagreed.

“Human rights in Rwanda are respected and granted to everyone and specifically to refugees who choose to come to our country,” Biruta said Tuesday, speaking on a panel at a conference in Vienna hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development.

He argued his country’s migration policies are among the “most progressive” as they allow refugees to work and start a business.

In a joint warning against the plan Monday, 47 organizations pointed to a 2023 court decision that slapped down the United Kingdom’s plans to process asylum seekers’ claims in Rwanda. It cited “substantial grounds” to believe that people sent to the African nation would be exposed “to a real risk of ill-treatment by reason of refoulement” — referring to a practice whereby people are forcibly moved to countries where they face real threats. Under a 2013 deal with Israel, people sent to Rwanda “were routinely moved clandestinely to Uganda,” the court added.

Biruta said he was “not surprised” by NGOs’ warnings and said the government faced “the same issue” when it was making plans with the U.K. Those plans “didn’t work but … helped to improve our asylum system,” he added.

NGOs “always … say that nothing is working, that our human rights record is bad,” Biruta said, “but I’d like them to come forward with an alternative solution.”

World.title: 19 people rescued after gas carrier 'struck' in Black Sea
World.content:
All 19 crew members were rescued after a gas carrier was "struck" in the Black Sea off Bulgaria on Tuesday, authorities and the ship's management company said.

 

Stealth Maritime, the Greek management company, confirmed in a statement that the Gas Husky had been "struck" early on Tuesday morning as it was sailing within Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.

It did not clarify what had hit the Liberian-flagged carrier.

"The vessel was carrying a cargo of LPG loaded in Alexandria, Egypt, and was heading to Midia, Romania, for discharge," it said, adding that the ship's condition was currently unknown.

According to Bulgaria's ministry of transport, the vessel was carrying 3,400 tonnes of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) before it disappeared from radar shortly after midnight. It then sent a distress signal at around 8:02 am, around 50 nautical miles east of Byala.

"Upon receiving the distress signal, assistance was requested from the air force to conduct an aerial survey of the area. During the survey, an overturned vessel was identified, believed to be the Gas Husky vessel," the ministry said in a statement. "About 300 metres away, a life raft was spotted, from which a distress flare was launched."

The crew were rescued from the life raft and flown by helicopter to the Chaika air base in Varna, it added.

It marks the latest in a string of similar incidents in the Black Sea believed to be linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

On Monday, 12 people were rescued after the Somali-flagged Betul 8 cargo ship capsized off the coast of Bulgaria following a suspected drone strike.

The Betul 8 had been travelling from Tulcea in Romania to Egypt and was carrying almost 3,000 tonnes of bulk wheat, authorities said.

The European Union has pledged €50 million for a Black Sea Maritime Security Hub hosted by Bulgaria and Romania to help combat security threats in the region.

The bloc has also committed a further €10 million in funds to help bolster Bulgaria's search and rescue operations.

World.title: Euronews Verify: What's at stake as Europe seeks to triple its data centre capacity?
World.content:
The European Union has set an ambition to triple its data centre capacity within five to seven years, as part of a push to reduce reliance on US Big Tech and develop Europe's own AI capabilities.

 

However, residents and environmental campaigners in Ireland, Poland, Denmark, Finland, Spain, the Netherlands, France and the United Kingdom took to the streets to call for a freeze on the development of these new projects.

In today's episode of Euronews Verify, Evi Kiorri gets the full picture with Owen Espley, coordinator of Stop Dirty Data Centres.eu, and Michael Winterson, secretary general at the European Data Centre Association.

"They're really concerned about the impact on land, on water, the huge energy use um that data centres demand, as well as the impact that that energy use could take away from housing," Owen Espley, coordinator of Stop Dirty Data Centres.eu, told Euronews Verify.

Europe wants to be the world's first climate-neutral continent — but will it happen?

COP31 is also in focus in today's episode.

The EU has promised to be the world's first climate-neutral continent by 2050.

EU ministers insist they are committed to the green transition despite soaring energy prices and supply concerns.

However, voters want cheaper energy now, while many of the measures designed to deliver it will take much longer to pay off.

76% of people in the Netherlands, 72% in France and 68% in Germany believe their country is unlikely to make meaningful progress towards net zero. In the Netherlands, 54% say environmental policies have left ordinary people worse off.

Euronews Verify's Inês Pereira breaks down the challenges of this awkward political balance with Sven Haremling, head of climate at CAN Europe.

"People also appreciate it if they're told the truth and what needs to change, as long as there's someone who works with them for solutions and there are changes in government regulations," Haremling said.

World.title: Beyond the green premium: Competitive advantage through decarbonization
World.content:
The opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not represent in any way the editorial position of Euronews.

For years, the business case for industrial decarbonization centred on a simple calculation: how much more would a “cleaner” technology cost, and how much would it reduce emissions? Today, that “green premium” remains important, but it is no longer the only consideration. Commercial priorities, geopolitical pressures and government policies increasingly shape investment decisions and the shift towards lower-carbon alternatives.

 

A low-carbon product can cost more but still be the smarter business choice

As a result, a low-carbon product can cost more but still be the smarter business choice. Companies investing in clean technologies must therefore weigh a broader set of factors, including volatile energy and material costs, value chain resilience, market opportunities and risks, government policies affecting industrial competitiveness, and their positioning in the low-carbon economy. In short, we are moving “beyond the green premium”.

For heavy industry, decarbonization has evolved from a narrow focus on sustainability costs to a strategic decision about the products companies will make, the markets they will serve and the supply sources on which they can rely. This shift has emerged as a clear message from the First Movers Coalition’s work with hard-to-abate industries throughout 2026.

To understand this broader calculation, it is worth revisiting the “green premium”, a term coined by Bill Gates in 2020 to describe “the difference in cost between a product that involves emitting carbon and an alternative that doesn’t”. The concept made the economics of decarbonization visible, but it never told the whole story.

The cost of cutting emissions varies widely for technologies and projects

In all sectors, the cost of cutting emissions varies widely for technologies and projects. For example, in cement production, emissions reductions of up to 50% can be achieved at negligible or low cost through clinker substitution and other supplementary routes, but further reductions often command a significant premium. By contrast, sustainable aviation fuels can cost at least twice their fossil fuel equivalent, with an even higher premium for more advanced technologies. Treating these different situations as one common economic problem obscures more than it clarifies.

As companies look beyond the immediate price difference, three factors are reshaping how businesses assess the value of decarbonization: commercial realities, geopolitics and policy.

In terms of commercial priorities, the cost of decarbonization is being assessed alongside competitiveness and growth rather than as a standalone sustainability cost. The green economy is already valued at more than $5 trillion _(Editor's note: around €4.54 trillion)_a year, and is expected to grow another $2 trillion (Editor's note: around €1.82 trillion) by 2030. For companies, this points to growing demand, new markets and the possibility of gaining an advantage by moving early.

In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaper

This does not mean that every low-carbon product will immediately compete on price. But focusing only on the green premium fails to ask who will be positioned to supply the market when demand grows, and who will have the capabilities and partnerships needed to respond.

Geopolitics, conflict, supply-chain disruption and energy price shocks have exposed the risks of relying on a small number of energy sources and materials. In stable conditions, fossil-based inputs may look cheaper, but, depending on the sector, that advantage is quickly lost when supply is disrupted or prices spike.

Jet fuel price spikes linked to conflict in the Middle East – topping $220/barrel in March (Editor's note: around 199 €) and $200/barrel (Editor's note: around 181 €) once more in September 2026 – illustrate how quickly the economics of sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) can change.

SAF remains more expensive, but the ongoing crisis has exposed what a simple price comparison leaves out: investment in SAF can reduce exposure to future energy shocks via diversified production. Early partnerships with producers can shorten and onshore supply chains, strengthening supply security and potentially lowering price volatility. For airlines, the question is not just what SAF costs, but what more resilient and diversified fuel supplies are worth.

Government policy is reshaping the industrial landscape

Finally, government policy is reshaping the industrial landscape. Regulations, standards, subsidies, permitting rules and trade measures influence investment decisions, determining which products qualify for public support, which projects can be developed quickly, and which supply chains retain access to major markets.

The EU’s proposed Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) – which is currently being debated – illustrates this shift. Alongside industrial decarbonization, it explicitly seeks to reduce Europe’s reliance on external suppliers and increase the share of strategic manufacturing from 14.3% in 2024 to 20% by 2035. Meanwhile, the Net Zero Industry Act is already linking decarbonization strategies with streamlined permitting and faster environmental procedures.

The green premium remains a useful starting point, but investment decisions demand a broader calculation: will the savings from postponing decarbonization will survive the next energy shock, supply disruption, or policy change?

In this turbulent era, the cost of waiting – from lost market access and volatile input prices to weaker supply chains and missed investment opportunities – may ultimately be higher. As with any business case, there are risks, but the opportunities that decarbonization offers have never been greater.

Noam Boussidan is the Head of the First Movers Coalition. He has 15+ years’ experience at the crossroads of climate, energy and industry transformation, having held various positions across government, private sector and non-governmental work. The First Movers Coalition (FMC) is the World Economic Forum’s flagship industry decarbonization initiative. A global coalition of companies leveraging their purchasing power to decarbonize the world's heavy-emitting industrial sectors responsible for 25% of global emissions. The FMC has 100+ members from top global corporations who have come together to send a demand signal for emerging climate technologies.

The European Commission has upgraded its Eurozone growth forecast to 1.2% of GDP, citing economic resilience despite ongoing geopolitical turmoil.
