World.title: North Macedonia prevents 'terrorist' assassination plot targeting person in Greece
World.content:
North Macedonia's National Security Agency (ANB) announced on Tuesday that it had prevented a "terrorist" assassination plot targeting a person in Greece and that it had dismantled an Iranian-linked network.

 

The ANB said it had brought down "a wide network of proxy actors" linked to Iranian Edris Jahangiri Mavaneh, who it described as a "collaborator of the Iranian security and intelligence services".

The agency said the network "undertook preparatory logistical activities to carry out a terrorist act/assassination against a person in Greece" while "under the direct instructions of the Iranian national."

Guns and sketches marking specific locations were reportedly seized as part of the operation, which was carried out in cooperation with Greece's national intelligence agency.

An anti-terrorist force also took part, police said. Raids were carried out at four locations.

The operation began in early 2026, the security agency's head, Bojan Hristovski, said, adding that the group had held "conspiratorial meetings on the territory of third countries, including Iran."

"As for the Macedonian network, it involves individuals embedded within criminal structures in the country," Hristovski told a press conference.

Four suspects have been taken into custody, while another has been placed under house arrest, an official said.

One person was detained in Greece and transferred to authorities in North Macedonia.

A sixth suspect was still being sought.

World.title: Jensen Huang breaks silence says he would be 'honoured' to return as Nvidia's CEO
World.content:
Jensen Huang has said he is prepared to return to chip giant Nvidia as its chief executive in his first statement since resigning last Thursday over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

 

"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in a statement to US media.

"If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honoured to answer these calls and return as CEO."

A campaign to reinstate Huang, the co-founder who led Nvidia for 33 years, gained steam over the weekend, with President Donald Trump on Monday adding that he was open to Huang returning.

But Nvidia's board has since said it is considering both internal and external candidates and said on Monday that it had no intention of reinstating Huang.

Huang will sit for a closed-door transcribed interview on 1 December before the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, Intelligence and the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter will then sit for a closed-door transcribed interview a day later on 2 December.

"We look forward to hearing from Jensen Huang and Tim Teter on their roles in a potential breach of our national security," said Republican representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford, the chairs of the Foreign Affairs, China Select and Intelligence Committees, in a press release.

World.title: Hormone-disrupting chemicals pose growing health threat, UN warns
World.content:
Chemicals in many everyday items that interfere with the body's hormones are a growing threat to human health and the environment, and scientists now have a better understanding of the harm they can cause, the United Nations said on Tuesday.

 

These substances, which can interfere with the body's hormonal systems, have been detected in breast milk and umbilical cord blood. Early exposure, sometimes before babies are born, can disrupt hormone activity and have lasting effects on brain development, growth and reproductive health, the UN warned.

In a new report, two UN bodies called for urgent, coordinated international action to protect human health and the environment, warning that policies and regulations aimed at transforming the products and sectors responsible for widespread exposure remain “fragmented and insufficient”.

“What makes [endocrine-disrupting chemicals] particularly concerning is that they can disrupt hormones that regulate many essential functions in both humans and wildlife, from development and reproduction to metabolism and behaviour. These effects can be long-lasting, and in some cases, irreversible,” said Sheila Aggarwal-Khan, director of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) Industry and Economy Division.

Endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) are found in many plastic items, personal care products, pharmaceuticals, toys, household goods, electronics and pesticides.

They have been linked to problems affecting fertility and reproductive development, brain development and neurological function, thyroid and other hormone regulation, metabolism, the immune system and cardiovascular health.

“This report is an important step towards a safer world, free from exposure to EDCs,” the two UN bodies wrote.

“Solutions do exist. Some safer alternatives are available. The task for policymakers is to ensure that these solutions and alternatives are deployed – to protect human, animal and planetary health, and save trillions of dollars each year.”

While scientific evidence has advanced considerably since the previous assessment from 2012, experts warn that regulation has been slower to translate that knowledge into action.

How are endocrine-disrupting chemicals regulated in Europe?

In the European Union, endocrine disruptors are regulated through several pieces of legislation, including general chemicals legislation and sector-specific rules covering areas such as packaging, pesticides and biocidal products.

However, critics say the current legislative framework is failing to adequately protect people and the environment from exposure.

“Despite some progress in the EU, such as the introduction of new hazard classes to identify EDCs, EU citizens and wildlife continue to be exposed to a cocktail of these harmful chemicals,” said Michael Warhurst, executive director at the environmental non-profit CHEM Trust.

In the EU, 231 substances have been officially identified as EDCs, while an additional 121 substances are currently under evaluation.

The challenge extends beyond Europe. More than 350,000 chemicals and chemical mixtures have been registered for production and use globally, but the vast majority have never been evaluated for endocrine-disrupting properties, the report warned.

There have been greater efforts in recent years to develop testing programmes. However, most of that testing has not led to action to regulate these chemicals and control exposure, said Laura Vandenberg, one of the lead authors of the report.

Chemicals have been removed from products when people became aware and stopped buying products containing a certain chemical, like bisphenol A, which has been used to make plastic containers for storing food and beverages, Vandenberg said.

But this can lead to a “whack-a-mole problem”, where one chemical is replaced by another that is structurally similar or has not been sufficiently tested, she added.

What are the next steps?

The UN said regulators should aim to protect vulnerable populations from exposure, particularly during pregnancy, infancy and childhood; improve monitoring and understanding of exposure to these chemicals; advance the identification and testing of them; account for the costs of exposure; and strengthen regulations.

“This report makes clear that new regulations are needed, new testing paradigms must be adopted,” said Bethanie Carney Almroth, an ecotoxicology professor at Sweden’s University of Gothenburg and the UN Special Rapporteur on toxics and human rights.

“We need to reverse responses from reactive to proactive. We need to prevent harm from occurring, rather than merely documenting and treating it after the fact,” she added.

Olwenn Martin, a chapter author, said that scientific understanding of how these chemicals disrupt the endocrine system is growing, and that they appear to be implicated in a wider range of diseases than previously thought.

“What concerns me most is that regulation still assesses most substances one at a time. That is like tackling climate change one greenhouse gas at a time, ignoring their combined effect,” Martin said.

World.title: Saudi Arabia: Rights groups raise alarm over rising number of executions
World.content:
Amid the war in Iran, Saudi Arabia's human rights situation remains bleak, with at least 211 executions, corporal punishment and an intensifying crackdown on critics. Is the regional conflict driving domestic repression?

Saudi Arabia continues to execute people at an alarming rate. On Saturday, Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani were executed in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province. Both men were convicted of terrorist offenses, according to Saudi authorities. In 2011, al-Safwani was a prominent organizer of the peaceful protests that called for civil rights and the release of detainees. Qureiris, who was a minor at the time, participated in one of these protests in the city of Qatif.

The UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention called for Qureiris' release in November 2024, after finding that his detention was arbitrary. The opinion also covered four other men. Qureiris was the fourth of these five to be executed. The fifth, Yousef al-Manasif, remains at risk after Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court upheld his death sentence, according to human rights organizations.

The two executions brought the number of people executed in Saudi Arabia in 2026 to 211, according to an AFP tally reported on Monday. The news agency said that the tally includes 126 people convicted of drug trafficking and 17 people executed on terrorism-related charges. Of the 211 people, 100 were Saudi nationals, while the rest were foreign nationals, AFP said.

In July, Saudi authorities executed five Ethiopian migrants for nonviolent drug-related offenses, Human Rights Watch reported. In October, Saudi authorities executed two Bangladeshi nationals, according to rights organizations. Human Rights Watch separately reported the execution of another Saudi national, Hassan Zaki al-Faraj, on October 17, for alleged offenses committed when he was a minor.

"In 2025, a record high of at least 356 people were executed and executions have continued at a high rate in 2026," Ahmed Benchemsi, Human Rights Watch's MENA spokesperson, told DW. "Saudi Arabia has executed more than 2,000 people in the past decade," he confirmed.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Saudi Arabia ranks third in executions after China and Iran. However, comprehensive global data for 2026 are not yet available, and many countries treat execution numbers as state secrets. However, the ranking is consistent with earlier findings from Amnesty International, which ranked Saudi Arabia as the world's third-most prolific executioner between 2022 and 2025, behind China and Iran.

According to the NGO Together against the death penalty, or ECPM , the two main methods of execution in Saudi Arabia are stoning or beheading. However, in many cases, including those of Qureiris and al-Safwani, death sentences are issued as discretionary rulings, called ta'zir. Ta'zir means that neither the crime nor the punishment is defined in Islamic law, contrary to fixed punishments under the Saudi interpretation of Islamic law, or Sharia. As a result, little to no information about the execution or the fate of the bodies is provided.

Saudi police forces reacted to peaceful protests by opening fire at the demonstrators in Quatif in 2011 Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

Is the Iran war affecting Saudi domestic repression?

Following the US-Israeli attacks on Iran in February, Saudi Arabia has been targeted by Iran and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen. In turn, Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, is faced with a profound dilemma as the attacks have killed and injured scores of people and threaten Riyadh's efforts to diversify its economy under the Vision 2030 reform plan. Several summits and international sports events had to be canceled or postponed in light of the ongoing danger.

"The Saudi government has shown itself to be unable to defend its population from repeated Houthi attacks on its airports, exposing the vulnerability of the country despite world-record spending levels on defense equipment," Sarah Lea Whitson, human rights lawyer and former executive director of the US-based human rights watchdog DAWN, told DW. "Amid the war in Iran, the Saudi government has resumed its relentless pace of executions and corporal punishment sentences," she said.

This week, watchdogs reported on a Kenyan woman in Saudi Arabia who was sentenced to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage.

"The recent executions and the sentencing of a migrant domestic worker to 100 lashes for having a child out of wedlock are clear indications that the Saudi government continues to rely on brute repression to rule the country," Whitson told DW.

Major sports events in Saudi Arabia are either postponed or canceled due to the ongoing attacks from Yemen's Houthis and Iran Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

Saudi Arabia's repression against the Shia minority

Maryam Aldossari, acting director of the London-based human rights organization ALQST , echoes this view. "Saudi Arabian authorities have undoubtedly used the war in Iran and wider regional tensions to intensify their crackdown, most notably through their increased use of the death penalty and as a tool of political repression against the country's Shia minority," she told DW.

Saudi Arabia is predominantly Sunni. The country's oil-rich Eastern Province — from which the recently executed men Jawad Abdullah Qureiris and Fadel Hassan al-Safwani hailed — is home to most of Saudi Arabia's Shia minority. Iran, on the other hand, is predominantly Shia. Saudi authorities have long viewed some forms of Shia political activism with suspicion, partly because of concerns over Iranian influence and alleged links between domestic dissent and Tehran, accusations that rights groups say have been used to justify repression of the minority.

However, Neil Quilliam, associate fellow in the Middle East and North Africa Programme at the London-based think tank Chatham House, remains cautious about drawing a direct causal connection between the conflict involving Iran and developments in Saudi Arabia's human rights environment. "The kingdom has introduced social reforms over the past decade, including measures that have expanded opportunities for women, while retaining controls over political dissent and activism," he told DW.

"What periods of regional tension can do is heighten official concern about national security," he said, adding that this reduces tolerance for any public criticism or perceived threats to social cohesion. "Whether that amounts to a change in the human rights situation is harder to demonstrate, but there is certainly a sense among some observers that space for dissent has become even more constrained, not only in Saudi Arabia, but in other Gulf states too," he said.

What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

DW reached out to Saudi Arabia's Human Rights Commission on Monday, November, 16, 2026 but has not received an answer at the time of publication.

World.title: US and Mexico lose measles-free status
World.content:
The United States lost its measles elimination status after 26 years, the Pan American Health Organization has said. Bolivia and Mexico have also lost their measles elimination status.

The ​United States is experiencing its highest number ​of cases in more than three decades. Some 7,700 people in the country have been infected and 13 have died since 2025.

As ​of November 12, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention have confirmed 5,412 measles cases and 6 deaths. US states have reported a total of 10 deaths from the highly contagious virus this year.

Pennsylvania has been the worst-hit state, reporting seven measles-related deaths and more than 1,500 cases.

Why are measles caseloads rising despite readily available vaccines?

Tuesday's declaration by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) has few practical implications and is largely symbolic, but is the latest sign of measles' avoidable resurgence.

"Losing measles elimination status is much more than losing a public health designation. It means the virus has circulated for a prolonged period, putting families and communities at risk of preventable illness, hospitalization and death," PAHO Director Dr. Jarbas Barbosa said.

Thanks to a series of functioning vaccines, measles had been virtually eradicated throughout most of the developed world for decades.

Vaccine hesitancy and disinformation has risen in recent years in the US, seemingly fueled at least in part by the COVID pandemic.

The rising influence of renowned vaccine critic Robert F. Kennedy Jr., now the US Health Secretary — who dropped out of the 2024 presidential election campaign to form an alliance with Donald Trump — was one of the clearest indicators of this.

"This is a serious warning for our region, but it is not an irreversible setback," PAHO Director Barbosa said. "We know how to prevent measles, and we know how to stop its transmission. With sustained commitment to vaccination, strong surveillance and effective outbreak response, the Americas can eliminate measles transmission once again."

Is the US experiencing a vaccine crisis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Bolivia, Mexico, US and Canada no longer designated measles-free

As of November 13, PAHO said that the Americas region had reported 58,213 measles cases and 82 deaths, compared with 12,806 cases during the same period last year.

The organization considers endemic transmission to be re-established when the same measles virus genotype and lineage circulate uninterrupted for 12 months or more in a country.

Canada had reached this status in November 2025, with Bolivia, Mexico and the US now deemed to have joined it.

The PAHO said that Canda had "interrupted the chain of transmission" that led to its designation and was working to regain elimination status.

Meanwhile, it said the other three countries "are implementing measures to strengthen vaccination, surveillance and outbreak response."

World.title: Back to 1997: Russia wants NATO to roll back its eastern expansion
World.content:
The Kremlin is reportedly calling on NATO to withdraw from large parts of Eastern Europe. What this would mean for the security of millions of Europeans — and what lies behind Russia's plan.

During talks on ending the war in Ukraine, Russian representatives in Abu Dhabi presented a document containing far-reaching demands, The New York Times reports.

Dated November 10, the document reportedly calls not only for an end to Western arms deliveries to Ukraine but also for NATO to withdraw its troops and bases and move them back to where they were in 1997.

What does Russia mean by 1997?

The year 1997 refers to the NATO alliance before its first eastward expansion, according to the Kremlin. At the time, NATO had 16 members. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary had already been invited to join but did not formally become members of the defense alliance until two years later. In the following years, more countries in Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe joined, followed most recently by countries in Scandinavia. Today, NATO has 32 member states in Europe and North America.

According to the report, Russia is not explicitly demanding that Central and Eastern European countries leave , but rather that the NATO alliance end its military presence in those countries.

What would be the consequences of a NATO withdrawal?

A withdrawal of NATO troops and bases from member states that joined the alliance after 1997 would significantly weaken their defense capabilities. For example, since 2004, NATO allies, including Germany, have taken turns policing the airspace over Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.

Because the Baltic states do not have fighter jets of their own for independent air policing, NATO provides the capability. Since 2026, the mission has been part of a broader air defense presence. The planned deployment of the German Lithuania Brigade, which is expected to be fully operational by the end of 2027, would also have to be halted.

In Romania, meanwhile, the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near Constanța on the Black Sea is currently being expanded. Once completed, it is set to become Europe's largest NATO air base by area — even larger than Ramstein in Germany.

For more than 20 years, NATO allies have provided air policing over the Baltic states Image: Arnaud Dumontier/MAXPPP/dpa/picture alliance

"Under no circumstances will we allow anyone to establish new security rules for this part of the world over the heads of Poland and Europe," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told TVP World. His Bulgarian counterpart, Rumen Radev, called a NATO withdrawal "unthinkable and unrealistic." No country should be forced by external pressure to reverse its decision on which alliance to join.

Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal also rejected any Russian say in changes to Europe's security order: "We have nothing to discuss with Russia about Europe's security order; it is working well."

The strong rejection from the capitals of NATO's eastern members, however, masks fears along the alliance's eastern flank that a deal between Washington and Moscow could turn their security into a bargaining chip.

Why isn't the mutual-defense clause enough?

In the event of an armed attack on a NATO member, the other alliance members are obligated under Article 5 to come to its aid. Each member decides for itself what measures it considers necessary, which may include the use of military force.

For the mutual defense commitment to deter a potential aggressor, that country must believe NATO can intervene militarily quickly and effectively in a crisis. The deployment of allied troops along the eastern flank serves precisely this purpose. A withdrawal would make defense more difficult and could lead Russia to believe that an attack on NATO territory would involve fewer risks for Moscow.

Signing of the treaty establishing NATO in Washington on April 4, 1949 Image: epa/AFP/dpa/picture alliance

Who decides which alliances a country can join?

As part of their security framework, European countries have agreed that states are free to decide which alliances they wish to join. NATO points to Article 10 of its founding treaty, which enshrines its open-door policy for European countries. The 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act also explicitly stated that neither side had the right to veto the other's decisions.

Back in November 1990, the participating states of the Conference on Security and Cooperation in Europe (CSCE), including the Soviet Union, had already agreed in the Charter of Paris to respect each country's freedom to choose its own security arrangements.

Was there a promise not to expand NATO eastward?

During the negotiations surrounding German reunification, then-US Secretary of State James Baker and German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher used language that suggested putting limits on NATO's eastward expansion.

In 2022, the last Russia Council meeting was held at NATO's headquarters in Brussels Image: Olivier Hoslet/AFP

Their remarks came during discussions about unified Germany's membership in NATO and the possible deployment of NATO forces on the territory of the former East Germany. However, no written, legally binding general promise was ever agreed that NATO would never expand to include other former Warsaw Pact countries.

In the 1997 NATO-Russia Founding Act, both sides declared that they no longer considered each other adversaries. NATO stated that, under the security conditions prevailing at the time and in the foreseeable future, it intended to ensure its collective defense through reinforcement rather than the additional permanent stationing of "substantial combat forces." The agreement explicitly gave Moscow no veto over NATO decisions.

In the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom reaffirmed their commitment to respect Ukraine's independence and existing borders and to refrain from the use of force. These assurances were linked to Ukraine's decision to give up its nuclear weapons. However, the memorandum did not oblige the United States or the United Kingdom to defend Ukraine militarily in the event of an attack. NATO membership was not addressed at the time.

Why is the demand back on the table?

Just over two months before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Kremlin presented two draft treaties to the United States and NATO. In them, Russia demanded an end to further NATO enlargement. The draft agreement with NATO also proposed that Russia and NATO members that had already joined the alliance as of May 27, 1997, refrain from deploying additional troops or weapons on the territory of other European countries beyond the levels stationed there on that date.

Security guarantees for the postwar period and a future security framework for Europe were also on the agenda in Abu Dhabi. Negotiating NATO troop deployments and alliance enlargement alongside an end to the war in Ukraine would give Moscow additional leverage. Russia has long maintained that the "root causes" of the war must be addressed. The Kremlin includes NATO enlargement and the alliance's military presence in Eastern Europe among those causes.

So far, no significant Western player has expressed willingness to accept Russia's demands in Abu Dhabi. On the contrary, former Polish intelligence coordinator Stanislaw Zaryn viewed the talks as an attempt to buy time and weaken the West ahead of another confrontation.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Rights court rules Turkey must release jailed lawmaker Atalay
World.content:
The European Court of Human Rights has called for the release of imprisoned elected lawmaker Can Atalay. Atalay has been in prison for almost five years despite rulings from the Turkish Constitutional Court.

The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) ruled against Turkey over the detention of human rights lawyer and elected lawmaker Can Atalay.

The ECHR published its decision on Tuesday, saying that Turkey must release Atalay and allow him to take up his seat in the Turkish parliament.

The court ruled that his continued detention had been intended to silence him and undermine political pluralism.

It ordered Turkey to pay him €32,500 (about $35,700) in compensation.

The judges stressed that Atalay's case should not be considered separately, but rather in the wider context of the detention of political opponents, human rights activists and journalists in Turkey.

No future in Turkey? Growing exodus of young Turks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Turkey was among the original signatories of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet it has previously refused to comply with the court's decisions in the cases of rights activist Osman Kavala and prominent Kurdish politician Selahattin Demirtas.

From leading activist to a jailed member of parliament

As a lawyer, Atalay represented victims in numerous social and political cases in Turkey, as well as in freedom of speech cases involving journalists and writers.

He was also among the leading voices in the 2013 Gezi protests, which the government called an attempted coup.

Because of his involvement in the protests, Atalay, along with seven others, was sentenced to 18 years in prison in April 2022 for "aiding and abetting an attempted coup."

Continuing his struggle from the infamous Silivri prison, Atalay ran as a candidate for the Workers' Party of Turkey (TIP) in the 2023 parliamentary elections.

LGBTQ+ communities in Turkey fear intensifying clampdown To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A candidate for the earthquake-hit province of Hatay, he won his seat but was denied release despite multiple rulings by the Constitutional Court, Turkey's top court.

His parliamentary status was revoked in 2024, a decision the Constitutional Court later overturned. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's party stopped the opposition from formally reading the decision in parliament.

Although a year later an opposition lawmaker read the decision in parliament, Atalay remains in jail.

After the ECHR's ruling was published, TIP leader Erkan Bas took to social media to call for Atalay's release and the restoration of his parliamentary mandate.

World.title: Fresh clashes at the Eritrean border — is Ethiopia sliding into a regional war?
World.content:
As Ethiopian troops push Tigrayan forces toward the Eritrean border, fears of a new regional war are growing. With tensions rising between Ethiopia, Eritrea and Sudan, the Horn of Africa faces uncertain times ahead.

After a few weeks of relative stability, fresh clashes in the contested Ethiopia-Eritrea border areahave raised fears of a full-fledged war. Meanwhile, diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and Sudanhave hit new lows.

Fighters allied with the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) launched their offensive on September 23. It was aimed at overthrowing the Ethiopian government as part of a larger rebel coalition. But the Ethiopian National Defense Forces (ENDF), backed by pro-government militia, have steadily pushed the TPLF out of Tigray, a region in northern Ethiopia.

According to the conflict tracker of the monitoring organization ACLED, the ENDF have pushed further into Tigray, effectively driving the Tigrayan Defense Forces (TDF) towards the border with Eritrea. Skirmishes have been reported from several locations, while the ENDF have fired heavy artillery towards dwellings close to the Eritrean border town of Badme.

While no census data is publicly available, Badme appears to be a small rural town on satellite images. However, the locality is historically significant for both sides because it was the ground zero of the Eritrean-Ethiopian War from 1998 to 2000, sometimes dubbed the Badme War.

The war ended with theAlgiers Agreement , in which both countries agreed to honor the rulings of a newly formed Eritrea-Ethiopia Boundary Commission. The commission awarded Badme to Eritrea, a decision that Ethiopia challenged at times. Abdurahman Sayed, director of the London-based Horn of Africa Center for Regional Integration, told DW that Ethiopia might see an advantage in reclaiming Badme to resolve its current internal struggles.

"It seems now if the Eritreans withdrew and the Ethiopians came back, it could be to calm down the Tigrayans, especially those who are now supporting the party in power in Ethiopia", Sayed said.

Ethiopia: Who is fighting whom — and why? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

He suggested that people like Getachew Reda, a former spokesman for the TPLF and current advisor to Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, might be able to win the Tigrayan people over to side with the federal government through territorial gains for the Tigray region.

The ever-looming threat of a full-fledged war with Eritrea

"The coming of the forces to the Eritrean-Ethiopian border clearly indicates that the conflict can be triggered any time", Abdurahman Sayed said.

Eritrean and Ethiopian government troops allied against the Tigrayan forcesduring the 2020-22 Tigray conflict. Since then, Eritrea's allegiances have shifted towards the TPLF and away from Abiy Ahmed's central government. In October, the two neighbors cut diplomatic ties. At one point, Eritrean troops reportedly crossed the border into Tigray.

Ethiopia's broken Tigray peace deal opens old wounds To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Magnus Taylor, a regional analyst with the International Crisis Group (ICG), believes that Addis Ababa's prime objective for the moment might rather be securing its northern border and destroying supply lines between Eritrea and Tigrayan forces.

"So what we might actually be seeing is a kind of a function of the attempts by the Ethiopian military to consolidate its control of Tigray, which includes pushing Tigray's borders with Eritrea", Taylor told DW.

However, securing control over Tigray could also involve direct conflict with Eritrea at one point, Taylor said: "If this happens, then it's quite likely that the Ethiopians would attempt to carry out all their objectives in Eritrea at one time."

Since Eritrea seceded from Ethiopia in 1993, Ethiopia has been the world's largest landlocked country by population. Prime Minister Abiy has repeatedly described the country's lack of sea access as an existential threat. While stating a preference for peaceful means to gain access, he said this could also mean capturing Eritrea's easternmost port, Assab, by force.

The ongoing clashes have displaced many local residents like this Amhara woman to other parts of Ethiopia Image: Marco Simoncelli/AFP

Ethiopia-Sudan relations at crossroads

At the same time, the diplomatic relations between Ethiopia and its northwestern neighbor, Sudan, have deteriorated even further.

Sudan and Egypt, both downstream the river Nile, have been on edge for years because of Ethiopia's Grand Renaissance Dam (GERD). The massive GERD, built on the Blue Nile just kilometers from Ethiopia's border with Sudan, gives Addis Ababa significant leverage over the timing and regulation of water flows downstream, raising concerns in Sudan and Egypt over water security and dam operations. The Ethiopian government has rejected claims that the dam could be used as a means to pressure Sudan and Egypt.

The RSF militants reportedly receive support from Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates. However, both countries deny the allegations Image: Rapid Support Forces/AFP

Since 2023, Sudan has been embroiled in a civil war between two rival military forces: the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF), led by General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti. In mid-November, both sides accused the other of direct participation in each other's internal conflicts.

Two countries with severe internal conflicts and mirroring alliances: Could the situation deteriorate further into potential direct fights between the two armies? ICG's Magnus Taylor believes there is a risk, but at least not for now.

"The most likely scenario is we just get a continuation of this kind of proxy style of involvement with each other's opposition groups rather than formal direct involvement on the ground in the conflict," Taylor said.

Sayed also believes that, at the moment, there is no need for direct confrontation.

"The RSF can do the job that Ethiopia and any other country backing them wants them to do," Sayed said. "But if there is a need and the RSF are failing, the Ethiopian army could be pushed to get involved."

World.title: Nvidia forms national security committee after Huang affair
World.content:
Nvidia has created a board-level committee for national security and export control. This follows the resignation of CEO Jensen Huang over extramarital affairs, allegedly including one with a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia on Tuesday said it had created a board-level national security and export-control committee.

This follows the scandal surrounding former CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned last week over extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China and working to help ensure higher quality chips crucial to AI development made it to the Chinese market.

The events have heightened oversight of the US tech giant and its importance to national security, as well as wiping several hundred billion dollars off the stock market valuation of what investors treat as the world's most valuable company in the space of a month.

Nvidia's celebrity CEO Jensen Huang, who liked to flaunt his relationship with Donald Trump, was forced to step down abruptly last week Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

What are Nvidia's plans for the new oversight committee?

Nvidia is calling the new group its National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

Suzanne Nora Johnson, a former vice chair at Goldman Sachs, will chair the committee, joined by fellow directors Stephen Neal, a former CEO of a law firm, John Dabiri, a professor of aeronautics and mechanical engineering at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech).

The committee will meet at least once every quarter. It will also incorporate independent legal, national security and trade compliance experts.

Nvidia already has a lower-level National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team; these groups will report to the board-level committee.

"We are committed to working constructively with government and industry partners to help establish and advance a robust framework that uses every tool at our disposal to safeguard national security while supporting continued technological innovation," Board Chair Harvey Jones said in a statement.

The company did not explicitly link the decision to November's developments and Huang's rapid fall from grace, but the timing seemed conspicuous.

The decision was announced hours ahead of Nvidia publishing its third-quarter results, with its still-stratospheric share price having fallen roughly 28% in the past month.



Trump's ASEAN Play: The new front in the US-China chip war To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How has the scandal highlighted the question of US-China chip trade?

US President Donald Trump, whom Huang was influential in persuading to allow the export of better-quality Nvidia chips to China than other US companies and officials deemed prudent, welcomed Nvidia's move on arrival in the Philippines on Tuesday.

"Yes, that's a good idea. It's a great company," he said during a photo opportunity at a Manila meeting with the other "Quad" leaders from Australia, India and Japan. "It's a great idea."

Trump reportedly owned Nvidia stock worth tens of millions of dollars before the share price fell. He also owns shares in other big tech companies.

Huang resigned last week after admitting to extramarital affairs in a message to Nvidia employees. This followed widespread reports, seemingly based on US and other intelligence, that one of the affairs was with a woman who used to lead a Singapore-based cloud computing company.

That company, Megaspseed International, is a major Nvidia client and is suspected of diverting advanced chips to China in violation of US export controls. Intelligence officials also suspect Huang's partner of being an asset of Chinese intelligence services.

The reporting on the case also seems to show these suspicions had been known to US officials and other countries, including Singapore, for roughly a year.

World.title: Iran dismisses report of alleged 'dirty bomb' attack on Washington
World.content:
Iran has said CNN's claim that Tehran would attack Washington with a "dirty bomb" was an attempt to manufacture further legitimacy to continue the war. Trump has said his administration takes the claim "very seriously."

Iran on Tuesday dismissed a CNN report that Tehran was preparing a so-called "dirty bomb plot."

US President Donald Trump said his administration was taking the report "very seriously."

What did reports say about an Iranian attack on Washington?

Tehran's dismissal came after CNN reported on Tuesday that "Iran is developing plans to target senior Trump administration officials by detonating a so-called dirty bomb or a chemical weapon in Washington, DC," citing multiple US intelligence sources.

The article also reported that "US intelligence has picked up Iranian chatter claiming that it has stashed bomb-making materials inside the country" and that "many national security officials assume that pre-positioned nuclear materials have already been in the US for years," citing, again, multiple US intelligence sources.

Iran's regime: Inside the system protecting its rulers To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

When asked about the story during his visit to the Philippines, Trump said that if there was such a threat, Iran would "pay a price the likes of which no other country has ever paid before."

"I hope it's not, but we take it very seriously because they happen to be crazy," he added.

Iran decries 'fabrication'

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei slammed the report, calling it "a malicious campaign to manufacture propaganda."

"Those who initiated the aggression against Iran are now seeking to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs by manufacturing and disseminating baseless allegations," he said on X.

"Step by step, they are attempting to manufacture a veneer of legitimacy for further aggression and atrocities," he said, naming CNN's reporting on the alleged "dirty bomb plot" and The New York Times without specifying any of its reporting.

Baghaei also said the US and Israel hit water storage reservoirs "during the recent acts of aggression."

Where does the Iran war stand?

The Iran war, started by the US and Israeli strikes on February 28, continues as negotiations to bring an end to the fighting stall.

Both US and Israel have been holding off from major attacks as they held elections over the last weeks.

Tehran has said it is in control the Strait of Hormuz, a key transit point for global oil and natural gas supplies, while continuing to attack ships it considers unauthorized users of the waterway. There are near-daily reports of ships hitting mines in parts of the strait Tehran says are unauthorized for transit.

The US Navy, which is enforcing its own blockade of Iranian vessels, has recently escorted tankers through the strait.

Republicans rebuke Trump on Iran war, economy after midterm wipeout To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Before the midterm elections, Trump said, "We may do another little Epic Fury," referring to US-Israeli strikes that started the war, though he did not provide any timeframe.

Trump is expected to meet Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of an APEC leaders' summit in China on Thursday and discuss ending the ​war in Iran.

Pakistan-mediated peace talks between the US and Iran on April failed to reach a conclusion.

Qatar, another mediator in the war, on Tuesday called for restraint "to avoid any escalation that could undermine negotiation efforts."

World.title: APEC summit: What Trump, Xi and Putin want
World.content:
Trump, Xi and Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of APEC. With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?

The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.

Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.

Several experts interviewed by DW do not expect any breakthroughs on US-China trade, technology or other issues. Maintaining the existing trade truce and preventing bilateral relations from deteriorating further may be the more realistic shared objectives.

Patricia M. Kim, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, believes neither leader is looking to significantly expand the bilateral agenda, as both have an incentive in maintaining the existing trade truce.

Over the next two years, Kim expects to see "neither uncontrolled escalation in tensions between the US and China nor a dramatic improvement in ties, but rather the continuation of the transactional détente we see today."

A historic trilateral between Xi, Trump and Putin is scheduled for Thursday during the APEC summit Image: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

Zhang Lun, a professor at CY Cergy Paris University, believes Trump is under pressure both at home and abroad.

"Domestically, Trump faces the prospect of becoming a lame-duck president following the Republicans' heavy losses in the midterm elections," Zhang told DW.

"Internationally, damage to relations with allies, the weakening of the US-led international order, indifference toward democratic values and freedoms, and the difficulties encountered in the Iran war have all reduced America's leverage, resources and influence."

Zhang believes strained ties with US allies and the war in Iran have weakened Trump's hand with Beijing, making him more eager to secure diplomatic wins and Xi's cooperation on key policy priorities.

Contentious issues may be left for later

Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, expects Trump and Xi to focus on stabilizing their fragile trade relationship.

She says the two leaders could make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion (€27.3 billion) on each side. "While the list of products has been announced, the timeline has not been set and an indicative implementation timeline would be an easy win" for both governments.

Washington wants Beijing to accelerate purchases of US agricultural products and increase exports of rare earths and other critical minerals. But Tee believes that "China would likely be cautious with delivering on its commitments especially when Trump is weaker at home after the midterms with Democrats pushing back on his tariffs."

She also points out that neither side would want to cede their bargaining chips easily, including rare earth exports and technology export controls.

With another meeting between the two leaders is expected in December at the G20 summit in Miami, "there is room to push more contentious issues to a later date and further extend the trade truce in the next meeting," Jia told DW.

China, the US and Russia: three leaders, three agendas

Russia hopes that talks with the leaders of the US and China will enhance its diplomatic standing and help secure a settlement to the war in Ukraine on terms favorable to Moscow.

What new alliances will reshape the world? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center, told DW that Moscow wants to create the impression that Washington is willing to sit down with Russia and negotiate. This, in turn, could undermine confidence in Europe and Ukraine.

"Trump wants trilateral nuclear talks," she said, while Beijing "wants the optics of China hosting the unprecedented historical meeting among the three."

Alicja Bachulska, a policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, believes Beijing wants to use the meeting to demonstrate its ability to bring major powers together and facilitate international dialogue.

"Russia wants recognition, the US wants arms control, and China wants status without strings attached," she said. "I expect each leader to restate their own positions rather than produce real solutions."

Ukraine: why Beijing is reluctant to mediate

Michael Kimmage, director of the Kennan Institute in the United States, told DW last month that China may be more concerned with the survival of Russian President Vladimir Putin's regime than with actively bringing the war in Ukraine to an end.

Russia remains an important source of energy and a key diplomatic partner for Beijing, Kimmage noted.

An outright Russian victory may not necessarily be Beijing's objective, he said. "More important to China is the political survival of Vladimir Putin." For that reason, Kimmage does not expect China to pressure the Russian president into ending the war if Putin is unwilling to do so.

Zhang Lun believes the current situation is "most in line with Beijing's interests."

Trump said on Tuesday he would take a separate bilateral meeting with Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen 'if it's available' Image: Dmitry Azarov/Kommersant Photo/Sipa USA/picture alliance

The Trump administration's pro-Putin stance has made it harder for Ukraine to resist Russia, Zhang said, while Europe has been forced to bear greater costs and has been weakened.

He argued that the United States has also "lost moral authority" and "the postwar international order and the alliances built around Washington have been further eroded," making China's "position and influence more prominent."

He believes Beijing wants to keep Russia from collapsing, but not support it so openly or extensively that it alienates Europe and other Western countries.

"At the same time, China does not want Ukraine to be defeated, because that would reduce Russia's dependence on Beijing," he told DW.

"For now, China is unlikely to intervene directly. Instead, it will wait for a more favorable moment and then potentially step in as a neutral mediator in order to maximize its gains."

Iran: little sign of substantive cooperation

W.A. Figueroa, an assistant professor of history and international relations at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, told DW that there is little indication of any real cooperation between China and the US on Iran.

The two countries do share some interests, "including opposition to a toll system in the Strait of Hormuz and opposition to nuclear proliferation," Figueroa noted, but "China has consistently called for negotiations and denounced both sanctions and military force as a way to achieve these or any other objectives."

Figueroa says China does not want further escalation or prolonged instability in the Middle East. However, Beijing has been able to manage the current situation without too much difficulty, leaving it with little pressure to change its position.

"China continues to provide Iran with crucial financial support through its purchases of Iranian oil," Figueroa noted, adding that Beijing's diplomatic support has so far brought no substantial change, largely because China has little leverage over either Iran or the US in the region.

World.title: La coalición compite por los votos de la izquierda en directo en La Moncloa: “El decreto está listo, portavoz”
World.content:
A solo 12 días de las elecciones, el Consejo de Ministros no puede ser otra cosa más que un escaparate electoral. Este martes, el Gobierno venía con artillería pesada para seducir a más de cinco millones de votantes: subida fuerte del salario mínimo (5,3%) y del sueldo de los funcionarios (4,5%). La semana pasada dio el primer paso para subir las pensiones a otros casi 10 millones de posibles votantes. En total, 15 millones de personas afectadas en dos consejos. Pese a las críticas de electoralismo, ha sido algo habitual en todos los gobiernos. Sin embargo, la novedad es que ahora los dos grupos que lo componen, PSOE y Frente Amplio, compiten electoralmente de forma descarnada —los socialistas se están llevando buena parte del voto que fue de Sumar, según todos los sondeos— y el pez pequeño de la coalición necesita imperiosamente frenar esa sangría y recordar que buena parte de las medidas del Ejecutivo, en especial algunas de las más valoradas, llevan su impronta.

Por eso este martes la rueda de prensa se ha convertido en una batalla amable, con sonrisas y bromas, pero con mucha carga de fondo entre la vicepresidenta Yolanda Díaz, de Sumar, y los tres ministros socialistas con los que compartía mesa: Arcadi España (Hacienda), Óscar López (Transformación Digital) y Elma Saiz (Seguridad Social y portavoz). Díaz no ha parado en ningún momento de lanzar pullas, gesticular, sonreír y bromear pero con mucho cálculo político para dejar claro quién tiene la paternidad de medidas como el registro horario o la prestación universal por crianza, que acaba de incluir el PSOE en su programa electoral. “Esto es la hegemonía”, decía Díaz con una sonrisa mientras los ministros socialistas se reían pero con cierta incomodidad. “Copiar no está mal si se copia bien”, insistía ella.

La estrategia del Frente Amplio, ya desplegada por el ministro Pablo Bustinduy, es clara: presionar al PSOE para que apruebe en estas dos semanas el registro horario y la prestación universal por crianza. “Nos han dado una campaña muy bonita hecha”, señalaba un dirigente de Frente Amplio. Y Díaz se puso a ello en el lugar más eficaz desde el punto de vista comunicativo: la rueda de prensa en La Moncloa con los ministros socialistas alrededor y todas las cámaras enfocando.

“Hemos estado hablando de esto con Arcadi [España] esta mañana”, revelaba Díaz. Ella no cortó en trasladar la presión y el reto mientras miraba a sus compañeros de Gobierno. “El reglamento [para el registro horario] está listo. Solo hay que firmarlo. No tiene que pasar ni por la diputación permanente. Además el ministro Bustinduy me dice que todos los partidos están dispuestos a votar la prestación universal por crianza”, presionaba. Elma Saiz, visiblemente incómoda, trataba de ganar tiempo.

—Contaremos las cuestiones que van al Consejo de Ministros cuando se alcance un acuerdo y se traigan, de momento seguimos trabajando”, intentaba cerrar. Y ahí Díaz, sonriendo, en voz más baja pero claramente audible, cortó a Saiz:

—El reglamento está listo, portavoz.

Después, España también esquivó la pregunta, aunque fuentes del Gobierno aclararon más tarde que no se van a llevar estas medidas que pide Sumar a los próximos consejos de ministros, que se dejan para después de las elecciones porque son una promesa electoral del PSOE, no algo que se pueda hacer en esta semana.

Díaz seguía protagonizando la escena y aprovechando así para mostrar las diferencias entre los dos partidos y hacer campaña por el Frente Amplio. Ella insistió en que en cuanto acabe la legislatura dejará la política definitivamente, pero sigue siendo un activo electoral muy evidente y en el Frente Amplio están tratando de convencerla de que haga más campaña e incluso en sectores del PSOE lo ven como buena idea, porque creen que ella activa el voto de la izquierda, como se vio en 2023. Ahí ella aprovechó para tirar contra el vicepresidente Carlos Cuerpo, con el que está teniendo tensiones internas similares a las que tuvo con su antecesora, Nadia Calviño. “No es el ministro Arcadi el que tiene un problema con el registro horario, ojo, es otro departamento”, decía de nuevo con una sonrisa en clara referencia al ministro de Economía.

Pero aun así, cuando se le preguntó por cómo llega la coalición a estas elecciones, ahora que arrecia la competencia electoral entre sus dos partes, Díaz quiso hacer un balance muy positivo. “El Gobierno de coalición es un ejemplo de gestión política al más alto nivel en este país. Ustedes lo están viendo. Tenemos debates legítimos, como este del registro horario, que yo les digo que si lo llevan en el programa electoral lo podemos aprobar ya y dar una buena noticia. Pero la coalición es un ejemplo de gestión de las diferencias políticas para aportar soluciones a nuestro país. La coalición es un ejemplo que da absoluta serenidad. España es plural y ha entendido bien que la portavoz, Elma Saiz, ha hecho una regularización extraordinaria de inmigrantes, nosotros una reforma laboral, y que caminamos juntas. Este es el mensaje y esto es lo importante para seguir cambiando España. Esto es lo bonito de este Gobierno”, remataba mientras la portavoz le correspondía con una sonrisa amable. La coalición mantiene las formas, y evita la ruptura por si los números dieran para poder reeditarla, pero también está en campaña y el PSOE y Frente Amplio ahora sí pelean por un voto fronterizo dentro de la izquierda.

World.title: Bruselas alerta de que la falta de vivienda es “el riesgo principal” para la economía española
World.content:
España lleva años creciendo a un ritmo mucho más alto que casi todos sus socios de la UE y parece que así será este año, el que viene e, incluso, en 2028. Esta es la tónica desde que se superó el desplome económico que provocó la pandemia en 2020, con crecimientos, año tras año, que multiplican por dos, por tres y hasta por seis, como pasó en 2023, los de la zona euro. Pero esta dinámica no está exenta de riesgos. Y “el principal” es la falta de oferta en el mercado de vivienda, según el informe de previsiones económicas divulgado por la Comisión Europea este martes.

“Un déficit continuado de la oferta en relación con la formación de hogares mantendría elevadas las presiones sobre los precios y podría limitar cada vez más la movilidad laboral y la llegada de trabajadores”, escriben los economistas de la Comisión en el capítulo del informe dedicado a España. Esto, señalan fuentes del Ejecutivo de la UE, también afecta a los jóvenes en sus desplazamientos hacia las grandes ciudades, puesto que es en estos núcleos en los que se concentra la mayor parte de la actividad económica. Dentro del colectivo joven, son los que tienen menos recursos los que se ven más perjudicados junto a otros grupos sociales vulnerables.

De ahí que la lógica dicte que la solución requiere construir nuevas casas. Pero aquí aparece un obstáculo: “Al mismo tiempo, el aumento de los costes de construcción podría lastrar aún más la inversión residencial”. Es decir, que el encarecimiento de los materiales y la mano de obra, provocado entre otras cosas por la crisis energética que ha causado el conflicto en Oriente Próximo, dificulta las inversiones necesarias para incrementar el ritmo de edificación.

Además, hay otros cuellos de botella a los que hace referencia habitualmente el sector en España aunque no están en el informe de previsiones europeo. Por ejemplo, la falta de mano de obra cualificada o los largos tiempos de transformación del suelo (como se llama el proceso por el que un terreno pasa de ser considerado no edificable a estar listo para acometer una obra) o la tramitación de los permisos de construcción. Y, sobre estos, ahora se sobrepone otro: el encarecimiento del crédito a raíz de la subida de tipos que ha puesto en marcha el BCE para contener la subida de la inflación, lo que nuevamente dificulta la financiación, junto con el hecho de que, desde la crisis de 2008, las exigencias regulatorias complican mucho la financiación a los promotores y constructores.

Entre todos estos factores, se ha creado el gran problema de acceso a la vivienda que, en último término, se encuentra detrás del adelanto electoral para el próximo 29 de noviembre y de la movilización que se vivió en la jornada de la huelga general, el pasado miércoles. Pero no es la primera vez que Bruselas pone el dedo sobre los problemas de acceso a la vivienda en España. Ya en junio, cuando presentó las recomendaciones de primavera para la elaboración de presupuestos, el Ejecutivo de la UE advirtió de que los precios de la vivienda se habían convertido en un “factor que dificulta la movilidad laboral en todo el país” y eso podía acabar por convertirse en “un reto para la competitividad” de la economía española.

No es que se trate de un problema exclusivo de España. Las dificultades de acceso a la vivienda están bastante extendidas en la UE, lo que ha hecho que en esta legislatura exista, por primera vez, un comisario con esta cartera, el socialdemócrata danés Dan Jorgensen. Pero una peculiaridad de España con respecto a otros países europeos es que tiene mucha menos vivienda pública o asequible para absorber el golpe. El Ministerio de Vivienda calcula que el parque social supone el 3,4% del total de casas, frente a una media comunitaria del 8% (y con los países más punteros por encima de ese porcentaje). Eso desplaza numerosas tensiones hacia el mercado del alquiler: en un mundo inmobiliario en que comprar no es asumible para muchos (algo a lo que contribuye de manera decisiva la escasez de casas) la única solución posible es el alquiler, que a su vez también tiene limitaciones de oferta y ha disparado todavía más, si cabe, los importes.

El último informe de previsiones macroeconómicas de la Comisión hace referencia, precisamente, a que el “continuado aumento de precios de la vivienda está aumentado la presión sobre su acceso, lo que tiene su impacto en el consumo, contrarrestando los efectos positivos sobre la riqueza”. Y se explica que ese incremento de precios “ha hecho que las cuestiones relacionadas con la cohesión social cobren mayor relevancia en algunas áreas urbanas”. Ante una situación como la actual, la vivienda se come cada vez una porción mayor de los ingresos de muchos hogares europeos, lo que detrae recursos y gasto que podrían ir a otras partes de la economía, y provoca diferencias cada vez más acusadas entre quienes son propietarios y quienes no.

Sin embargo, solo es en España donde se apunta a que la vivienda es “el principal riesgo” para la economía en estos momentos, a lo largo de las 252 páginas del informe de previsiones. Y a pesar de estas advertencias, la Comisión pronostica que el empleo seguirá creciendo con vigor. Menos que en años precedentes, pero todavía se mantendrá al alza. “Se prevé que el mercado laboral pierda impulso a lo largo del horizonte de previsión, en consonancia con la desaceleración del crecimiento económico. Se espera que el empleo crezca un 2,3% en 2026 y un 1,8% en 2027, mientras que las horas trabajadas aumentarán, en general, a un ritmo más lento”, apunta el Ejecutivo de la UE, que también avanza una senda de rebaja de la tasa de desempleo hasta el 9,4%.

Esa fortaleza del mercado laboral es clave para que la economía española sostenga el pilar del crecimiento de los próximos años, porque la Comisión apunta que este vendrá de “la demanda interna impulsada principalmente por el consumo privado y, en menor medida, por la inversión”. La cadencia que describe el documento conocido este martes es que el “crecimiento continuado del empleo, aunque moderado, en un contexto de inmigración” contribuye a mantener el gasto de los consumidores, lo que también se verá reflejado en “un nuevo descenso de la tasa de ahorro de los hogares”.

World.title: La estafa de la tienda en línea falsa
World.content:
Supuestos comercios ‘online’ lanzan ofertas agresivas para atraer a los compradores, especialmente durante el Black Friday y la Navidad, pero detrás de cada ganga se esconde un engaño

Los ciberdelincuentes crean negocios ficticios en internet desde los que lanzan ofertas para engañar a los consumidores y conseguir su dinero o sus datos personales y bancarios. El éxito de esta estafa reside en que ofertan artículos muy demandados, como dispositivos electrónicos o productos con cualidades casi milagrosas a precios muy bajos. Una vez realizada la compra, el consumidor nunca recibe el producto o le llega uno distinto o de escaso valor. Y sin posibilidad de reclamación alguna, porque los datos de contacto también son falsos.

El Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE) colaboró en el cierre de 4.600 sitios web en España (.es), en 2025, la mayoría relacionados con comercios ficticios. Meta, la empresa matriz de Facebook e Instagram, retiró 159 millones de anuncios fraudulentos, muchos de ellos ofertando productos engañosos, el año pasado.

TÉCNICAS DE MANIPULACIÓN

Urgencia Los ciberdelincuentes crean la sensación de que, si no se compra ya, se perderá la oportunidad de adquirir un producto con una gran rebaja Familiaridad Suplantan a marcas populares, como grandes multinacionales de la moda, la electrónica, además de supermercados Escasez y oportunidad Simulan que la página solo dispone de un número limitado de existencias para generar una sensación de pérdida de oportunidad si no se compra Prueba social Convencen al comprador de que todo el mundo está comprando con falsos reclamos

Ciberexperto Nombre Jordi Sánchez Cargo Experto en fraude de CaixaBank “Antes de comprar una ganga, conviene parar un instante y cerciorarse de que la página es legítima. Lo lograremos comprobando la url y buscando información en internet” 0:00 CÓMO RECONOCER UNA TIENDA FRAUDULENTA 1 Desconfiar de precios muy bajos. Si un artículo se oferta a un precio muy alejado del habitual posiblemente sea una estafa 2 Comprobar las valoraciones y las opiniones. Ayudan a hacerse una idea sobre la fiabilidad del negocio. Desconfiar si todos los comentarios son muy recientes. Hacer una búsqueda si se tienen dudas 3 Acceder escribiendo la dirección web en el navegador. Evitar entrar en los comercios en línea a través de enlaces recibidos por correo electrónico, SMS o redes sociales 4 Desconfiar de comercios que ofrecen métodos de pago poco habituales o muy limitados. Los comercios legítimos suelen ofreces las opciones de pago más populares 5 No dejarse presionar por ofertas por tiempo limitado. Los ciberdelincuentes apremian a la víctima para que se decida a comprar sin reflexionar

No todas las tiendas falsas funcionan igual. Las más comunes son las tiendas que anuncian productos que no existen; también existen tiendas de falsificaciones, que envían un producto de peor calidad que el comprado. Jordi Sánchez, experto en fraude de CaixaBank, señala que este fraude también se extiende a páginas de alquileres vacacionales, donde no solo se intenta robar el dinero de la víctima sino sus datos personales. “Los delincuentes piden la numeración de la tarjeta, pagos mediante Bizum, una copia del DNI...”, explica.

En caso de tener indicios de que se ha comprado en una tienda falsa. Se debe contactar con el banco. Si se han facilitado datos de la tarjeta, habrá que contactar con el banco para que se tomen las medidas pertinentes. Conviene guardar todas las pruebas y acudir a la Policía Nacional o a la Guardia Civil.

Estafas en las plataformas de venta legítimas. No solo las tiendas pueden ser falsas, con frecuencia, los ciberdelincuentes lanzan sus estafas a través de plataformas de compraventa legítimas. Se aprovechan de que el consumidor confía en ellas y buscan maneras de sortear las medidas de seguridad que establecen para proteger a los usuarios. Se pueden dar dos casos: que el vendedor publica un anuncio de un artículo que no posee o de un artículo que se anuncia como original y es una falsificación. El falso vendedor suele pedir al comprador que se cierre la operación fuera de la plataforma, a través de un programa de mensajería instantánea y que se haga el pago mediante canales alternativos a los ofrecidos por la plataforma, de manera que evita los mecanismos de protección que ofrece la plataforma para pagar.
