No changes for OTP customers

The bank has stressed that its own cardholders will not be affected by the changes. The amount they can withdraw in a single transaction will continue to depend on the ATM’s available cash and its capacity to dispense a maximum of 40 banknotes at a time.

The new conditions therefore mainly affect customers who use cards issued by other banks or financial service providers. While withdrawals in forints have become cheaper for Hungarian-issued cards, those using non-OTP cards at euro ATMs will now face a fee regardless of whether their card was issued in Hungary or abroad.

World.title: BREAKING: Russian drone hits Ukrainian city near Hungarian border, more UAVs reported in Zakarpattia – UPDATE
World.content:
A Russian drone has struck the Ukrainian city of Mukachevo (Munkács) in Zakarpattia, close to Hungary, while several more unmanned aircraft have reportedly been detected heading towards the region. No casualties have been reported so far.

A Russian drone crashed into the courtyard of an industrial site in Mukachevo on Tuesday morning, local authorities and Zakarpattia regional officials confirmed, according to Telex. The incident was reported at around 8.50 am, when residents also heard sounds resembling explosions.

The Mukachevo City Council confirmed that the city had come under attack and urged residents to take the air raid alert seriously and remain in shelters until they received official notice that the danger had passed.

Watch the video shared on Telegram HERE.

More Russian drones detected over Zakarpattia

According to Kárpátalja.ma, at least two hostile drones were initially detected in Zakarpattia’s airspace. The Ukrainian Air Force said one had approached from the direction of Lviv region and was heading towards Svaliava.

Journalist Vitaliy Glagola later reported that the drone had struck near Mukachevo’s bypass road, close to former vehicle registration offices beyond the Berehove bridge. According to his preliminary information, nobody was killed or injured.

The situation remained dangerous as the morning progressed. By 10.20 am, two more drones had reportedly been detected, heading towards the areas of Svaliava and Szarvasháza. Subsequent reports indicated drones moving towards Svaliava and Zarichchia, followed by another heading towards Mukachevo. At around 10.42 am, further drones were reported in the direction of Uzhhorod (Ungvár).

Air raid alerts remained in force around Mukachevo and Uzhhorod, while alerts in other parts of Zakarpattia had been lifted. Regional Governor Myroslav Biletsky urged people not to share information about the drones while the air threat remained active.

Hungarian Prime Minister comments on the attack

A Mukachevo resident told Telex that parents had collected their children from school, while kindergarten pupils had been taken to shelters.

The city last suffered a reported direct strike in August 2025, when a Russian attack hit the US-owned Flex factory. Air raid alerts have occurred since then, although less frequently than in central and eastern Ukraine.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar also addressed the attack in Parliament on Tuesday. He said that, according to press reports, Mukachevo had been targeted overnight, but that fortunately there had been no casualties. He called on opposition MPs to reconsider their stance on the war and urged them to stand up for ethnic Hungarians in Zakarpattia.

The Hungarian Foreign Ministry was contacted about the attack, but no response had been reported by the time of publication.

UPDATE: Air raid over

Residents of the Mukachevo, Uzhhorod and Khust raions may leave the shelters, the Transcarpathian Regional Military Administration announced on Telegram shortly before 11.15 am on Tuesday, Telex reported.

Featured image is illustration. Photo: depositphotos.com

World.title: Tisza government promises new era with 2027 budget, opposition calls it austerity
World.content:
Parliament opened the general debate on the 2027 budget bill on Monday, with the governing Tisza party declaring a new era and the opposition warning of tax rises, job losses and austerity.

Tisza Party says they centered the budget around the people

The bill, the Tisza government’s first budget, was tabled by Finance Minister András Kármán late on Oct 30. It targets a general government deficit of 4.9 percent of GDP next year, down from an expected 7.5 percent in 2026, assumes economic growth of 2.4 percent and inflation of 3 percent, and projects public debt at 77.2 percent of GDP at the end of 2027.

The central sub-system of the state budget is planned to spend HUF 47,587 billion (EUR 131 billion) next year, 2.9 percent less than in 2026, and to take in HUF 42,484 billion (EUR 117 billion), 1.4 percent more than this year. The cash-based deficit is set to narrow to HUF 5,103 billion (EUR 14 billion).

„A new era has begun in Hungary’s history,” Andrea Bujdosó, Tisza’s lead speaker in the debate, said, stressing that the Hungarian person stood at the centre of the budget. „The state’s task is not to serve the enrichment of the few. The state’s task is to create for every Hungarian the opportunity of a decent and secure life,” she said.

She added that the 2027 budget was clear proof that the country had fallen into good hands after the elections and that the government put the livelihood and happiness of Hungarian families first. „We are building a country where children grow up safe, where parents can make a living from honest work, and where the elderly feel valued,” she promised.

Fidesz and Our Homeland attacked the plans

André Palóc, the opposition Fidesz lead speaker, said the 2027 budget contained 26 new taxes or tax rises which threatened Hungarian wages and jobs. He insisted that tax rises would cost jobs, with 14 percent of companies planning layoffs, and added that factory closures had already begun over the summer.

Minimum-wage earners, he said, could feel cheated by the budget, given that the prime minister had earlier promised to double the minimum wage. Its losers also included the young, he said, with 40 percent less funding for student loans, half as much for work loans and 23 percent less for the loan for expectant women.

Mothers, too, could feel cheated, he said: 110,000-120,000 mothers of two over the age of 40 had been able to count on receiving their personal income tax exemption next year. Pensioners, he added, would not receive the second weekly instalment of the 14th month’s pension. He also insisted the figures showed that Hungarians beyond the border, too, were losers of the budget, with HUF 26 billion (EUR 71 million) less in the Bethlen Gabor Fund.

Stay-up-to-date: Billions buried in forests – Astonishing cash discovery in case involving Orbán’s former minister

Christian Democrats claim the bill is too left-wing

János Hargitai, lead speaker of the opposition Christian Democrats (KDNP), said the bill marked a bad turn for the Hungarian economy and was a „very left-wing” budget. The budget represented left-wing values, a world Hungary had been through once before, and „we even hit the wall”, he said. The country was being taken in that direction again, he added, and this would have “tragic” consequences as early as 2028.

„This is not the budget of justice and development but much rather one of austerity,” László Toroczkai, the opposition Our Homeland Movement’s lead speaker, told the debate. He said the budget benefitted not Hungarian businesses but foreign global capital and imports, adding, however, that he welcomed the advertising tax.

The 2.6-percent-of-GDP deficit reduction, he said, was twice the size of the „austerity” implemented under former prime minister Ferenc Gyurcsány. He highlighted that taxes would rise in 18 categories covering 26 kinds, while only three would fall. Our Homeland’s view, he said, was that the excessive tax burden could hold back businesses and investment.

Read also: Lake Balaton to have stricter construction laws very soon, according to Tisza minister

World.title: Serbian Court Seeks Arrest of Kosovo Serb Kingpin Radoicic
World.content:
The Higher Court in Belgrade has ordered Milan Radoicic’s detention and that an arrest warrant be issued for him for violating a measure prohibiting him from leaving his place of residence, according to media reports on Tuesday.

Radoicic failed to report to Belgrade’s Savski Venac police station on November 15, when he was required to confirm that he was still at his registered place of residence, as ordered by the court.

The businessman and former vice-president of the Belgrade-backed Srpska Lista party, who is seen as a ‘kingpin’ operator among Serbs in northern Kosovo, is under investigation over an armed attack on the Kosovo village of Banjska/Banjske in September 2023.

The Higher Court in Belgrade confiscated his passport in 2023, and warned that detention may be imposed if he violated the terms imposed on his freedom of movement, which included not leaving his place of residence. He was ordered to appear at a police station twice a month.

Belgrade Higher Prosecutor’s Office questioned Radoicic in September 2023 about allegations that he had obtained large amounts of weapons and took them to northern Kosovo, where an armed Serb group was involved in the deadly shootout with Kosovo police in Banjska/Banjske on September 24 that year.

Prosecutors allege that Radoicic “procured weapons, ammunition and explosive devices” in Bosnia, “which were delivered to him in the city of Belgrade”.

They claim Radoicic “transported and stored [the weapons] in unspecified locations” in Kosovo and “hid them in abandoned buildings and forests”. In the ensuing shootout in Banjska/Banjske, a Kosovo policeman was killed. Three of the gunmen also died.

In September 2023, Radoicic said he took sole responsibility for the shootout, while he described as a “defence” operation against the Kosovo authorities, without the knowledge of his political party, Srpska Lista, or the Serbian authorities in Belgrade.

However, he also denied guilt during the investigation.

World.title: Prison Release Plea for Besieger of Sarajevo Rejected Yet Again
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp



Dragomir Milosevic in court in The Hague, December 2004 . Photo: EPA/JUAN VRIJDAG.

The UN’s International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals in The Hague announced on Tuesday that it has rejected a request for the early release of Dragomir Milosevic, the wartime commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps of the Bosnian Serb Army, who was sentenced to 29 years in prison for crimes against civilians in besieged Sarajevo.

The president of the International Residual Mechanism, Judge Graciela Gatti Santana, stated in her decision that although Milosevic meets the eligibility requirements for consideration for early release, she believes that the request should be denied.

“The high gravity of his crimes strongly militates against granting him early release and Milosevic has not demonstrated sufficient signs of rehabilitation. Further, there is no evidence before me that establishes the existence of compelling humanitarian grounds which would warrant overriding this negative assessment,” Gatti Santana explained.

The decision states that Milosevic, who is now 84, clearly suffers from several chronic health conditions. It also states that his behaviour in prison has been consistently good.

“However, I have no information that would suggest that Milosevic has engaged in any further reflection about his crimes and specific role in them, or any other positive conduct that could demonstrate a level of rehabilitation that would warrant the exceptional relief of early release,” Gatti Santana said.

Milosevic was convicted of bearing responsibility for terrorising civilians in besieged Sarajevo with a campaign of sniper and artillery attacks as commander of the Bosnian Serb Army’s Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

The Hague Tribunal also convicted the wartime Bosnian Serb political and military leaders, Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, and another former commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, Stanislav Galic, of similar offences.

During the 44-month siege of Sarajevo by Bosnian Serb forces, more than 11,000 residents of Sarajevo were killed, including around 1,600 children.

World.title: Kosovo’s Thaci Found Guilty of Trying to Obstruct Justice in War Crimes Case
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Bos/Hrv/Srp

Hashim Thaci in court during the verdict, November 17, 2026. Photo: Kosovo Specialist Chambers/Livestream.

Former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 17 months in prison at the Kosovo Specialist Chambers in the Hague on Tuesday for attempting to obstruct justice by trying to interfere with witnesses in his earlier war crimes trial, at which he was also found guilty.

“I find you guilty of attempted obstruction of public officials in the performance of official duties through joint action, and of violation of the confidentiality of proceedings, and of contempt of court,” Judge Christopher Gosnell said.

After the announcement, Thaci told the court: “This is politics, not justice.”

The prosecution claimed during the trial that Thaci sought to exert influence over two former Kosovo Liberation Army fighters who were testifying in his war-crimes case. The testimony of both men favoured Thaci’s defence.

Also on trial were former Kosovo Intelligence Agency director Bashkim Smakaj, former deputy prime minister Hajredin Kuci, former local mayor Isni Kilaj, and Fadil Fazliu.

Thaci was found guilty of contempt of court in meetings with Fazliu in July 2023, at which he allegedly instructed Fazliu about how one of the ex-KLA men should testify.

Fazliu was sentenced to 12 months in prison for attempted obstruction of public officials in the performance of official duties through joint action, and for contempt of court. However, as he has spent more than this amount of time in detention, he will be released.

Thaci was found not guilty of contempt of court over a meeting with Smakaj in September 2023, at which he also was alleged to have also sought to influence a witness. However, Smakaj was sentenced to 12 months in prison for attempted obstruction of public official in committing their duties and contempt of court.

Thaci was also found not guilty of attempted obstruction of a public official.

Kuci was found guilty of one count of contempt of court and sentenced to a one-month suspended prison term, which will be considered served after one year, provided that Kuci does not commit any further criminal offence.

Kilaj was found not guilty and will be released.

The defendants denied any wrongdoing during the trial, and the verdict can be appealed.

Considering the time he has spent in detention, Thaci has already served the 17-month prison sentence.

However, he will not be released because in September, the Specialist Chambers sentenced him to 25 years in prison for war crimes.

He was convicted of murder, arbitrary detention, torture and cruel treatment as a leader of the KLA during the Kosovo war from April 1998 to June 20, 1999.

His co-defendants, Jakup Krasniqi, Kadri Veseli, and Rexhep Selimi, were sentenced to 25, 18 and 13 years respectively.

The defence is preparing to appeal the first-instance verdict, which triggered protests in Kosovo and in Europe by Albanian diaspora members and supporters of the KLA.

Kosovo’s parliament on October 6 voted to amend the law on the Specialist Chambers to curb its powers. The law has been returned to parliament for review by the president, however. The EU and the UK have warned Kosovo MPs not to vote for the law change without consultations with the international community, as the court was established via an international agreement.

The Specialist Chambers was created specifically to try former members of the KLA; it is located in The Hague and staffed by international judges and prosecutors due to doubts about the Kosovo justice system’s own ability to try former KLA fighters, many of whom are considered heroes in Kosovo. Witness-tampering has been one of its key concerns from the outset.

World.title: Turkish Police Raids and Seizes Control of Sozcu TV
World.content:
Police raided the Istanbul offices of Sozcu TV and sozcu.com.tr early on Tuesday, while a court placed the company that operates them under the control of Turkey’s Savings Deposit Insurance Fund, TMSF.

“A new one was added to the operations against newspaper and television channels in Turkey. Police carried out raids against Sozcu TV and Sozcu.com.tr in the morning,” Sozcu said in a statement on Tuesday.

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor’s Office said the investigation concerned allegations of membership of the Fethullahist Terrorist Organisation, FETO”, a name given to the movement of the late preacher Fethullah Gulen, which Turkey designates a terrorist organisation. It also concerns violations of anti-terror financing legislation.

Prosecutors alleged that owner Burak Akbay financed companies through overseas accounts and continued activities linked to the Gulen movement through them.

However, the Sozcu Group’s print newspapers Sozcu, Korkusuz and Tavir have not faced any police operation or court measures for now.

Four company executives and officials were detained, including board chair Funda Tuncer Sidali and former general manager Asim Akgul. Akbay, who lives in the UK, is wanted under an arrest warrant. The case against him dates back to 2017.

Sozcu rejected the basis of the operation.

“A search is being carried out at the Sozcu Group based on a case that the Court of Cassation previously overturned, finding no illegality and confirming that no crime had been committed,” the group’s lawyer, Ersan Barkin, said.

Media organisations condemned the takeover. “The appointment of a trustee to Sozcu TV is a severe blow to press freedom and the public’s right to information and is absolutely unacceptable,” DISK Basin-Is, a journalists’ union, said in a statement.

Turkey’s main opposition New Party leader, Ozgur Ozel, also criticised the move.

“After Halk TV, now there are police and a trustee at Sozcu TV’s door. They can no longer tolerate even the slightest criticism or a single truth being heard,” he said.

Turkey has seen mounting pressure on critically minded media over the past year. Tele1 was seized in 2025 and Halk TV in October 2026.

Sozcu was among the last major critical media groups outside trustee control before Tuesday’s operation.

Sozcu TV is expected to resume broadcasting under its new management, initially carrying news but excluding its regular programmes and commentary, aligning its tone to state-run new agencies.

World.title: Serbia’s New Parliament Convenes After Historic Election
World.content:
After 14 years, six parliamentary elections and an equal number of terms of parliament in which the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, and its coalition partners, held a majority of seats, a new legislature is being constituted on Tuesday.

In the new parliament, the Student List, formed by the student movement that led mass protests for almost two years against the rule of the SNS, which secured a landslide victory in the October 25 elections, will have an absolute majority.

Student List has 140 seats, the SNS has 103 seats, while minority lists won seven seats in total: the Alliance of Vojvodina Hungarians and Albanian Coalition won two each, while Rasim Ljajic – People’s Trust, Usame Zukorlic – Movement for Unification and SDA of Sandzak – Guardians of Sandzak each won one seat.

This marks a dramatic change to the previous parliament, in which the SNS had 129 seats.

In a show of support for Student List, a crowd of people gathered at 8 a.m. in Pionirski Park in front of the National Assembly. In the months before the election, this was where an SNS tent camp had been set up, but was symbolically removed when the party’s defeat became clear.

As November 17 is International Students’ Day, Student List and the student movement asked parliament’s services to allow a student delegation to observe the constitutive session from the gallery. However, their request was rejected, the student movement announced on Monday.

“But that will not stop us from gathering outside parliament,” representatives of the student movement at the Faculty of Economics in Belgrade wrote on X.

On Tuesday, the new MPs are to confirm their mandates, elect a speaker and deputy speakers, appoint a secretary general, elect members of the Assembly’s working bodies, and select members of permanent parliamentary delegations to international institutions.

Until a new speaker is elected, the session is chaired by the oldest member of parliament, in this case, Stojan Radenovic, an MP from the SNS. He is assisted by the youngest MPs from the four electoral lists with the largest number of seats, as well as by the secretary general of the National Assembly from the previous parliamentary term.

The National Assembly is deemed constituted once the mandates of at least two-thirds of its members, or 167 MPs, have been confirmed. At that point, the mandates of the MPs from the previous parliamentary term cease to be valid.

A 90-day deadline for forming a new government begins on the day the National Assembly is constituted. If a new government is not elected within that period, the President dissolves the National Assembly.

Turnout in the October 25 elections was a record high, at 68.9 per cent. Turnout at the previous elections, in December 2023 was 58.8 per cent.

The Student List won 2,35 million votes, while the SNS won 623,000 fewer – 1,73 million votes. That means the Student List won 53 per cent of the votes, and the SNS 39 per cent.

November 17 is marked as International Students’ Day. Because of this Student List and the student movement asked parliament’s services to allow a student delegation to observe the constitutive session from the gallery. However, their request was rejected, the student movement announced on Monday.

“By a decision of the Secretary General of the National Assembly, students have just been denied access to the constitutive session from the gallery of the Main Hall. But that will not stop us from gathering outside parliament,” representatives of the student movement at the Faculty of Economics in Belgrade wrote on X.

A day before the constitutive session of parliament, EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos spoke with two new Student List’s MPs, Ana Dimitrijevic and Aleksandar Baucal. Serbia is an EU membership candidate but has been accused of backsliding on democratic values under the SNS.

Baucal addressed EU Enlargement Forum in Brussels on Monday, vowing to make progress.

“For us, the European path is one of reforms: strengthening European values, building functional institutions and a genuine rule-of-law system, developing a sustainable economy integrated in the European market,” he said.

The Student List was formed by the student movement, which led almost two years of protests following the Novi Sad railway station canopy collapse in November 2024 that killed 16 people.

Its candidates’ list was mostly made up of experts, professors and public figures chosen by students.

World.title: ‘Not Good Enough’: North Macedonia Must Step Up Femicide Prevention, Judge Says
World.content:
North Macedonia's institutions often fail women reporting domestic violence right at the start, by treating risk assessments as paperwork rather than as a crucial tool for preventing further abuse, a judge experienced with domestic violence cases says.

Gabriela Gajdova, a judge at the Skopje Court of Appeal with nearly two decades of experience in domestic and gender-based violence cases, spoke to BIRN several days after protests sparked by the killing of 17-year-old Biljana Kirik in Bogdanci in southeastern North Macedonia.

The November 3 killing was the seventh suspected femicide in the country this year. Kirik's body was found in a burned car alongside that of her 21-year-old partner, who had apparently taken his own life. Initial prosecution indicators point to murder and suicide.

Kirik had reported her partner for assault. On September 30, following an argument at his family home, he allegedly attacked her, threatened to kill her if she left and damaged her mobile phone to prevent her from calling the police. She managed to escape through a window. Passers-by then called the police.

World.title: Albania Protests Challenge Traditional Party Duopoly Ahead of Elections
World.content:
The two camps of Albania’s traditional political establishment, the Socialists and the Democrats, are revving up their campaign engines ahead of the May 2027 local elections.

Meanwhile, at the Albania-Finland football match at Air Albania Stadium on the evening of November 12, fans were also making their voices on the political situation heard.

Albanian team supporters took over the post-victory celebrations with chants of “Rama, resign!” and “Rama, go!”, references to Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama.

A large banner featuring an image of a bloodshot eye was also unfurled in the stands – a tribute to 28-year-old Erjon Vishkuli, who was hit in the eye by a rubber bullet during the ongoing anti-government protests in Tirana.

World.title: ‘It Feels Wonderful’: Serbian Student Activist Savours End of Exile
World.content:
Living in exile, Antic was unsettled by the constant uncertainty and by the fact that, before the elections, developments in Serbia appeared discouraging – a constant stream of bad news. The toughest part of all was knowing that her fellow activists remained in detention back home.

“The hardest part was that our fellow activists were left in detention in Serbia, especially Lazar Dinic, who was a member of STAV and is an extremely close friend of ours,” she said.

“Everything that happened to Lazar over the past year, including the brutal attack on him during the local elections in March this year, was extremely difficult to process, especially because we couldn’t be there for him,” she added

Dinic was attacked by black-clad assailants who beat him up and forced him to say: “Aca [Aleksandar Vucic’s nickname] is the President.”

Stuck in Croatia, Antic said she tried to remain as practical as possible despite the frightening, emotionally overwhelming and exhausting circumstances.

“We found ourselves in a situation where we didn’t even have our belongings, just the things we had packed for what was supposed to be a three-day trip,” Antic recalled.

But despite the great uncertainty they faced, Antic said they felt welcome and protected in Croatia.

“After months and months of persecution, detentions and the various forms of pressure we had endured in Serbia, we were finally able to breathe a sigh of relief because we felt safer there – at least I did,” she said.

Vucic’s announcement that he had pardoned the activists was one of his last acts before he stepped down as President to fight the elections at which he unsuccessfully sought the position of prime minister. But his decision left Antic and her fellow activists frustrated rather than relieved.

“We considered our case to be fabricated and politically motivated from the very beginning. We knew we were innocent and that this would have been proven in court because there was no evidence against us,” she said. She also argued that Vucic had no right to grant the pardons.

Although a court subsequently discontinued the proceedings against them, Antic said they were disappointed at being denied the opportunity to prove their innocence at a trial.

“Unfortunately, we never got the chance to obtain an acquittal, so in the eyes of some people we are still guilty and have been placed in the same category as the criminals that Vucic pardoned as part of the same package,” she said.

Vucic pardoned a total of 49 people, including not only activists but also people accused of involvement in violent attacks against protesters during nearly two years of anti-government rallies.

The activists plan to pursue further legal action, including an appeal to the Constitutional Court, while those who were detained will seek compensation from the state. “Our ordeal is not over, but the proceedings against the 12 of us have come to an end,” Antic said.

A fight worth fighting

World.title: Second merchant ship in two days sinks off Bulgaria’s coast after being hit by drones
World.content:
A search and rescue mission was mounted on November 17 for the crew of the Gas Husky, the second merchant vessel to sink off Bulgaria’s coast in two days.

The Romanian Maritime Administration said that the ship had been hit by drones, though there was no immediate official confirmation from Bulgarian authorities.

A statement by Bulgaria’s Defence Ministry said that two Air Force Su-25 and a Cougar helicopter were involved in the operation to rescue the crew of the Gas Husky, which sank about 50 miles east of Byala.

A life raft with people had been located at the site, the Defence Ministry said.

The ministry said that the Gas Husky disappeared from radar shortly after midnight, and at 8.02am on November 17, an emergency buoy was activated, emitting a signal for a sunken ship.

The Gas Husky, a Liberian-flagged gas transport vessel, had been en route from the port of Alexandria in Egypt to the port of Navodari (Midia), Romania.

On November 16, the Betul 8 sank in the Black Sea off Cape Kaliakra and the mouth of the Kamchia River following a drone strike. All 12 crew were rescued.

The site of the sinking of the Gas Husky is not far from where the Betul 8 went down.

There have been several drone strikes against merchant vessels off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania, with loss of life and some ships sunk. The attacks are widely blamed on Russia.

The total number of such incidents in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea has now reached seven since the beginning of October, when attacks on vessels off the Bulgarian coast began. Bulgarian authorities continue to refuse to name who is behind the attacks.

(Photo: Vessel Finder)

World.title: Bulgaria’s Cabinet approves 2027 Budget package with 3.5% deficit target
World.content:
Bulgaria’s Government approved the 2027 draft Budget package on November 16 and has tabled it in Parliament, where the budget and finance committee was set to discuss it in a special sitting on November 17.

Given Prime Minister Roumen Radev Progressive Bulgaria’s majority of 131 MPs in the 240-seat National Assembly, it is expected to pass without much difficulty well before the end of the calendar year 2026.

If that is indeed the case, it would be a rather rare occurrence in Bulgaria’s most recent parliamentary history, where political instability resulted in eight elections in five years, producing short-lived parliaments that often adopted budgets very late. Of the last five Budget packages, only the 2024 Budget Act was passed before the end of the previous calendar year.

This year’s Budget set a record in terms of tardiness, being adopted in July 2026, with a deficit target of 5.7 per cent of gross domestic product, after Bulgaria was already put in the EU’s excessive deficit procedure.

At the time, Radev and Finance Minister Gulub Donev blamed the state of public finances on policies pursued by the short-lived elected and caretaker administrations of recent years (omitting the fact that he appointed some of them, including two caretaker administrations headed by Donev).

Radev said on November 16 that the 2027 Budget package was one that sought a “difficult balance” between opposing goals, namely to rein in deficits fueled by rapidly rising Budget spending, while at the same time increasing people’s incomes and the social safety net. Donev, for his part, described the Budget package as a “return to reason.”

The Finance Ministry’s Budget package targets a Budget deficit of 3.5 per cent, with Radev saying that this figure was on a cash basis. After factoring in additional defence spending (for which the EU currently makes special allowances to member states when it comes to the three per cent deficit rule), the 2027 deficit is expected to be 4.2 per cent, Radev said.

The Finance Ministry’s medium-term macroeconomic forecast envisions the Budget deficits declining further in subsequent years, to 3.1 per cent of GDP in 2028 and 2.4 per cent of GDP in 2029.

The Budget package envisions a consolidated fiscal programme with revenues of 51.07 billion euro and 55.97 billion euro in spending, with a target deficit estimated of 4.91 billion euro in real terms.

This compares to the ministry’s current forecast for this year of 49.62 billion euro in revenues and 56.81 billion euro in spending, with a projected deficit of 7.19 billion euro.

The economic growth target set in the 2027 Budget is 2.5 per cent, down from three per cent currently projected for this year, which in turn is set to exceed the 2026 Budget package target of 2.6 per cent growth.

The European Commission’s spring forecast projected 2.2 per cent growth for Bulgaria next year. Its autumn forecast is due on November 17.

The draft budget sets the debt ceiling at 44.4 billion euro (down one billion from the amount projected for 2027 in this year’s Budget package), with the government allowed to issue 8.6 billion euro in new debt in 2024.

The latter figure does not include short-term debt for the purposes of cash management of state institutions, provided such debt is repaid by the end of 2027 and does not exceed the debt ceiling.

(Bulgaria’s Cabinet building. Photo: government.bg)

World.title: Bulgaria annual inflation rises to 6.0% in October
World.content:
Bulgaria’s annual consumer price index (CPI) recorded six per cent inflation in October, rising from 5.7 per cent a month earlier, the National Statistical Institute (NSI) said on November 16.

The monthly CPI figure showed 1.2 per cent inflation in October, which was the second largest increase in the previous 12 months.

Food prices were 0.7 per cent higher in October compared to September, while non-food prices rose by 1.1 per cent and services prices were 1.9 per cent higher.

Compared to October 2025, food prices were up two per cent, while non-food prices rose by 8.1 per cent and services prices were 7.3 per cent higher.

The harmonised CPI figure, calculated by NSI for comparison with European Union data, was 0.7 per cent higher compared to September, and the annual harmonised CPI inflation rose to 5.9 per cent, up from 5.6 per cent a month earlier.

Food and beverage prices were 1.8 per cent higher in October, on an annual basis, while the price of utilities and housing rose by 5.4 per cent and transportation costs were 16.5 per cent higher compared to the same month of last year.

(Consumer price index changes since October 2025. Bars illustrate the annual CPI inflation and lines show the monthly CPI inflation. Graphic: NSI)

World.title: Cargo ship sinks off Bulgaria’s coast after being hit by two drones
World.content:
A rescue operation was mounted on November 16 as cargo ship Betul 8, which was 40 nautical miles south-east of Bulgaria’s Cape Kaliakra, issued a distress call that it was sinking, the Transport Ministry said.

Two drones hit the Betul 8, which capsized east of the mouth of the Kamchia River, Maritime.bg reports. Sailors from the crew provided the website with photos of the drones, which, it said, look like the drones used against the Contship Jet. According to the website, the 12-member crew left the ship and boarded life rafts.

The distress call was received by the Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Varna at 9.15am, the ministry said.

Four ships from the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Naval Group (MCM Black Sea) – two Bulgarian, one Romanian and one Turkish – have been dispatched to the scene of the incident, the Transport Ministry said.

The operations are coordinated by the General Directorate of Emergency and Rescue Activities at the Executive Agency of the Maritime Administration.

The operation also includes two Cougar helicopters and a Su-25 aircraft of the Air Force, which will conduct surveillance and reconnaissance of the area.

The Betul 8, sailing under the Somali flag and with a crew of 12, was travelling from Tulcea, Romania, to Egypt and was carrying nearly three tons of bulk wheat, the statement said.

Bulgarian National Television reported on November 16 that according to its information, the ship already had sunk.

There have been several drone strikes against merchant ships off Bulgaria’s and Romania’s coasts recently, attacks widely blamed on Russia.

(Photo: Transport Ministry)

World.title: EU ministers approve new sanctions to further restrict Russia’s ability to finance its war
World.content:
In response to Russia’s indiscriminate attacks against Ukraine, particularly against civilian infrastructure, the European Union foreign ministers on November 16 imposed additional restrictive measures on 12 individuals and 101 entities, a statement by the Council of the EU said.

Those listed are being sanctioned for their role in those economic sectors which provide a substantial source of revenue to Russia’s war of aggression and support its shadow fleet, the statement said.

Today’s listings include nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions. By progressively tightening and expanding sanctions on Russia’s banking sector, the EU is cutting off the financial channels that process state revenues and fund Russia’s war effort, the Council of the EU said.

Moreover, the Council is cracking down on Russia’s e-commerce. Today’s package includes the sole shareholder of Russian retail giant Wildberries, and an individual controlling the majority stake in another major Russian e-commerce company, Ozon.

The Council is also listing additional entities and businesspersons in the Russian oil and energy sector. The energy companies listed today manage Russian refineries and the St. Petersburg oil terminal and are active in the exploration and production segment.

The Council is targeting Russia’s shadow fleet, by listing various companies from the United Arab Emirates, China, Seychelles and Oman that are buyers of crude oil products of Russian origin, as well as certain businesspersons who own or manage vessels that are subject to EU restrictive measures, and illegally transport Russian oil, while engaging in high-risk shipping activities.

Today’s listings were adopted under the EU’s restrictive measures framework targeting actions undermining or threatening Ukraine’s territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. Those listed under this sanctions regime are subject to an asset freeze and it is prohibited to provide them with funds or economic resources either directly or indirectly or for their benefit. Additionally, a travel ban to the EU applies to the natural persons named in today’s listing.

The relevant legal acts have been published in the Official Journal of the European Union.

(Photo: EC Audiovisual Service)

World.title: Electricity Coordination Group: EU electricity market prepared for the winter
World.content:
The EU electricity market is suitably prepared for the winter, but it is necessary to continue monitoring the market closely, according to discussions between the European Commission (EC), national experts and key stakeholders in the Electricity Coordination Group (ECG) meeting that took place on November 12, the EC said in a statement posted on November 16.

The meeting also had a detailed presentation of the Winter Outlook by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) , which was published on November 13.

In addition, the Group took stock of the electricity system’s winter preparedness.

Even though hydro storage levels are lower than before and planned nuclear maintenance will slightly reduce plant availability, the overall situation throughout the winter is expected to remain stable.

The Commission underlined the importance of continuing to monitor the situation and remaining closely coordinated.

The situation in Ukraine and Moldova remains difficult, in particular in Ukraine, given the continuous targeted attacks on critical energy infrastructure– and the Group expressed its solidarity with the situation of electricity in both countries, confirming the importance of continued technical assistance and regional coordination, the statement said.

“For the coming winter, security of electricity supply in the two countries will depend on weather conditions, the state of critical energy infrastructure, and the availability of interconnections with the EU,” it said.

EU solidarity, technical assistance and regional coordination remain essential to supporting electricity security in Ukraine and Moldova, the statement said.

(Photo: John Mason/ freeimages.com)

World.title: Bulgaria gets two Russian banks removed from proposed EU sanctions list
World.content:
Two Russian banks with majority Bulgarian ownership have been removed from the EU sanctions list and no restrictive measures will be imposed against them when EU foreign ministers meet on November 16, it emerged from a statement to reporters in Brussels by Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova.

One of the banks is First Investment Bank (FIB) , which, however, has nothing to do with the eponymous Bulgarian FIB. The other is Investment Corporate Bank (ICB) . Both are small banks with majority Bulgarian ownership that operate on the Russian market.

Both banks are majority Bulgarian-owned. Bulgaria’s motives for removing them from the list are that if they are sanctioned, instead of causing damage to the Russian state, it will benefit from it.

“We requested their removal for a similar reason to the one with which France requested the removal of a certain entity from the sanctions package,” Petrova said.

“The two banks do not operate with financial funds of people who fall into sanctions lists. And to a large extent, the way in which they are structured in the Russian Federation does not allow them to take their investment out of there,” she said.

“If they are sanctioned, the only thing that will happen is that they will have to come into the possession of the Russian state and accordingly they will lose their asset. This will be counterproductive, because in fact, instead of there being some kind of damage and restrictions for the Russian side, it will actually be income,” Petrova said.

This is not the first time that Bulgaria’s Roumen Radev government, which took office in May, has acted to remove individuals from proposed sanctions lists. Previously, it got Russian Patriarch Kirill and a Russian oligarch removed from a proposed list.

World.title: EU ministers approve largest-ever payment of eight billion euro to Ukraine
World.content:
European Union ministers adopted on November 16 a decision that will allow Kyiv to soon receive just under eight billion euro under the Ukraine Facility, of which about five billion euro comes from resources made available from the Ukraine Support Loan in 2026, a statement by the Council of the EU said.

This is the largest-ever single payout to Ukraine made by the EU under the facility, the statement said.

This payment follows Ukraine’s fulfilment of over 20 target steps that relate to various reforms in key areas such as: the judicial system; the fight against corruption and money laundering; financial markets; the management of public assets; human capital; the business environment; decentralisation and regional policy; energy; the agri-food sector; digital transformation; and environmental protection, it said.

Funding under the Ukraine Facility is designed to bolster Ukraine’s macro-financial stability, recovery and modernisation, keep its public administration running, and support its reform efforts.

Payments are linked to the Ukraine Plan, which outlines Ukraine’s strategy for recovery, reconstruction and modernisation, along with a timetable for the implementation of reforms broadly aligned with the country’s EU accession goals.

The Ukraine Facility was established on March 1 2024 and has more than 50 billion euro available in grants and loans to support Ukraine’s recovery, reconstruction, and modernisation through 2027.

Of this total, more than 40 billion euro is earmarked for reforms and investments set out in the Ukraine Plan – Ukraine’s roadmap for recovery and EU accession – with regular disbursements tied to Ukraine meeting the Plan’s targets.

Once this ninth disbursement is made, Ukraine will have received more than 40 billion euro under the Ukraine Plan since mid-2024.

(Photo: G Schouten de Jel)

World.title: Vukovar is Preparing for the Arrival of Over 100,000 People
World.content:
November the 17th, 2026 – Vukovar is busy preparing itself for the arrival of over 100,000 people from across Croatia and indeed from elsewhere as the anniversary of the city’s fall looms.

Tomorrow marks the 35th anniversary of the fall of the defence of Vukovar, where over 100,000 people are expected to arrive once again this year. HRT reports that the entire city and its surrounding areas are ready for Wednesday and Remembrance Day. There are no more free beds, restaurants and other similar establishments are currently preparing thousands of meals, the roads and car parks are also ready to receive columns of pilgrims. The first visitors, both veterans and others, have already arrived to pay their respects to the victims of Vukovar.

students from bosnia and herzegovina arrive in vukovar

They will have travelled hundreds of kilometres to visit the sites of the city’s suffering and defence. As many as 140 students from Mostar have also arrived in Vukovar to learn about its recent history firsthand. “When we look at all these pictures and listen to firsthand stories, it really makes us think a bit about what that war meant here and everywhere in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina,” said Dolores Peša, a student at the University of Mostar.

Those who defended Croatia themselves confirm that the culture of remembrance is alive and being passed on to younger generations. “It’s important for us to come and pay our respects to those victims, and if it weren’t for those victims, we veterans wouldn’t be here either. So we come, pay tribute to all the victims, both civilian and veterans and everyone, said Željko Fekete, Association of Croatian Homeland War Veterans of the Zdenci municipality.

An unavoidable stop is also the Vukovar Water Tower, the symbol of the city’s resistance in the face of tremendous evil from the other side of the river. Increased stocks of souvenirs have been prepared due to the expected wave of visitors. Accommodation across the city and its surroundings has long been full. “We have 44 rooms, which are insufficient for that day. It’s been booked a year in advance. It’s simply a day to which all of Croatia bows down,” said Vinko Mijok, the owner of a family hotel in Vukovar.

hotels are full and restaurants are ready

“We’ve prepared around four hundred to five hundred dishes. Mostly, there will be some kind of daily menu – all Slavonian delicacies, sarma, čobanac, something simpler,” stated Mario Jakobović, the owner of a hospitality and catering establishment. Traffic preparations are also being finalised for the arrival of such a huge amount of people. The main roads in the city centre will be closed on Wednesday, meaning the inner centre will be accessible exclusively on foot.

“Parking spaces have been secured at four locations for buses and other pilgrims. What is very important is that the road towards Osijek will be temporarily opened because the vast majority of people come to Vukovar precisely from Osijek,” stated Marijan Pavliček, Mayor of Vukovar. The organisation is already well-established and everything is ready for November the 18th, the day when the entire city becomes a living monument to both the unspeakable suffering of Vukovar and to a free Croatia.

veterans and doctors from the vukovar hospital will lead the procession

To mark the 35th anniversary, an additional poster with the words “Courage, sacrifice, and freedom” was created. Mayor Marijan Pavliček has stated that everything is now ready for November the 18th.

Alongside the established slogan “Vukovar – a place of special homeland piety,” the City has also prepared a special poster this year for the 35th anniversary. The words courage, sacrifice, and freedom, Pavliček explained, highlight the courage of Croatian veterans and their sacrifice for the freedom of Croatia. What is most important to us is that this Column of Remembrance also passes peacefully, with dignity, and without politicking, said Pavliček. He added that everyone who wants to sincerely pay their respects to the sacrifice of Vukovar is welcome, regardless of political affiliation or worldview. We have enough of the other 364 days of the year for reasoned political bickering, he said. He called the Column of Remembrance “the only living monument in all of Croatia” in which all participants are equal.

a tribute to selfless wartime healthcare workers

Alongside Croatian veterans, about seventy doctors and other healthcare workers of the wartime Vukovar hospital will be at the head of the Column. Pavliček said that in this way the City wants to pay tribute to them for caring for the wounded during the defence of Vukovar. While the veterans were on the front line, it was the doctors who, in almost impossible conditions, operated on dozens of seriously wounded Croatian veterans on a daily basis, he said. He pointed out that the doctors also provided moral support to the wounded.

parking at four locations

Parking spaces have been secured for visitors at four locations, especially for buses. The road towards Osijek will be temporarily opened, so it will be possible to reach Vukovar from both the direction of Osijek and the direction of Vinkovci.

World.title: Vukovar Families: Who Will Look for The Missing When We’re Gone?
World.content:
November the 17th, 2026 – There are many Vukovar families still searching for their missing loved ones, and they’re asking who will continue looking when they too are gone.

Katica Pavlović has been searching for the remains of her father Damjan Samardžić, commander of the defence of Vukovar’s Sajmište, for 35 years. Index reports that after the fall of Vukovar he was taken to Ovčara, where he was killed, but his body has still not been found.

“He defended Vukovar, gave everything he could, made sure the city would not go hungry. His last task was to guard the Serbian soldiers in the hospital. He protected them, and when the Chetniks came, they were handed over. We thought they’d protect Dad because he had protected them, but he ended up… we still don’t know where,” Katica Pavlović told N1.

She last saw her father in May 1991, and last spoke to him when she called him to inquire about her husband, a Croatian policeman who was in Borovo. Last year the remains of her half-brother Zorislav Gašpar were identified. They were found together with the remains of Jean-Michel Nicolier.

In the meantime information appeared in the media that the remains of Damjan Samardžić had also been found, but it turned out that this was not true. His daughter still hopes that she will find her father and after 35 years of uncertainty finally learn where he is buried.

“I hope they will find him. Who will look for my father when I am no longer here?” she asked at the end.

World.title: Croatia Introduces Permanent Price Transparency Rules in Shops
World.content:
November the 17th, 2026 – Croatia has now officially introduced permanent price transparency in shops, allowing customers to have a far better insight into price comparison.

As of yesterday (the 16th of November), customers in Croatia will face new rules on the display of prices in stores and when providing services. Poslovni reports that the previous measures with which the government sought to increase price transparency cease to apply and are being replaced by a new system that should enable consumers to compare prices more easily and gain better insight into their movements.

At today’s session the Government adopted decisions on the cessation of validity of three previous measures of direct price control. These concern the obligations to publish price lists, to display an additional price, and to publish price lists of products and services. However, this does not mean that traders will no longer have to display prices transparently. On the contrary, from Monday the application of new ordinances begins by which this obligation is regulated in a more permanent manner. Economy Minister Ante Šušnjar spoke about the changes and explained why the previous measures are being replaced by new rules.

two prices will have to be permanently displayed

One of the most important novelties concerns the obligation to display a base price alongside the current selling price of a product or service. As of the 16th of November, retailers and service providers will have to display, in addition to the current price, an additional, i.e. base price. This is the price that applied to the same product or service back on the 10th of September 2026. For products and services that were included in the offer after that date, a special rule will apply. The amount that applied on the day the product or service was first introduced into the offer will be taken as the base price. Traders will also have to clearly indicate that date. This way of displaying prices should enable customers to more easily assess whether the prices of individual products have increased or decreased in the meantime.

The new rules don’t apply only to physical stores. Traders and service providers who have their own websites will have to publish the valid price lists of their products and services on them. It is particularly important that price lists will not be able to be published once and then left unchanged. Every change in price will also require a corresponding update of the published price list. This is intended to enable consumers to check how much something costs even before coming to the store or using a particular service.

why is the government scrapping previous measures?

Economy Minister Ante Šušnjar recalled that the earlier, on the basis of the Act on Exceptional Measures of Price Control, the government initially adopted three decisions by which measures were introduced to increase transparency and better inform consumers. Their intention was to help curb inflationary pressures, increase the transparency of prices on the market and enable the general public to make more informed decisions when shopping.

However, those measures were from the beginning conceived as temporary, i.e. as a response to special circumstances on the market: “It’s important to emphasise that the exceptional measures of price control were by their legal nature temporary and intended for action in special market circumstances, while the new regulations establish a permanent framework of the system of price transparency and protection of the economic interests of consumers,” Šušnjar explained.

He added that precisely for the further improvement of transparency and the long-term protection of consumers, on the basis of the Consumer Protection Act, new ordinances have been adopted. These are the Ordinance on the Display of the Base Price of Products and the Ordinance on the Method of Publishing Price Lists of Products. With their entry into force on the 16th of November, the application of the goals of the previous measures continues, but through a more systematic and permanent legal framework. For customers this means that the obligation of transparent price display doesn’t disappear, but the way in which traders and service providers will have to inform consumers is changing.

World.title: Qatar Airways Cuts 24,500 Seats on Zagreb-Doha Route
World.content:
November the 17th, 2026 – Qatar Airways is set to cut 24,500 seats on the Zagreb-Doha route, abandoning its previous plans for 7 weekly flights between the two cities.

Qatar’s national airline Qatar Airways has reduced the planned number of flights between Doha and Zagreb for the summer 2027 timetable. Index reports that instead of the originally planned daily flights, according to the latest changes the company will operate four times a week. This is the second unfavourable announcement for Zagreb Airport for next year, after Austrian Airlines decided to withdraw from the route between Zagreb and Vienna, reports the portal Croatian Aviation.

Qatar Airways will thus retain the number of flights it operates on this route during the current winter timetable, as well as in the recently completed summer one. That frequency was introduced after the outbreak of the conflict in the Middle East and the consequent disruptions in the company’s operations.

93 total cancelled rotations

Airbus A320 aircraft with 132 seats have been announced on the route between Doha and Zagreb. This means that each return rotation offers 264 seats. By reducing from seven to four flights a week, Qatar Airways is cancelling three weekly rotations, i.e. six individual flights. The summer timetable lasts 31 weeks, from the end of March to the end of October 2027, so this amounts to a total of 93 cancelled rotations. When the capacity of the announced aircraft is taken into account, with this decision Qatar Airways is withdrawing a total of 24,552 seats from sale on the route between the two cities.

a blow to zagreb’s connectivity with asia and australia

This is a significant reduction in capacity on one of the key routes from Zagreb. Through its hub in Doha, Qatar Airways enables passengers from Croatia to fly to numerous destinations in Asia, Australia, Africa and other parts of the world. The reduction in frequencies therefore does not only affect the direct link between Zagreb and Doha, but also the possibilities for onward travel.

In recent months the company has been adjusting its operations due to the security situation in the Middle East. Although it has gradually been restoring some capacity, limitations compared to the original plans still exist on certain markets. Zagreb will thus remain connected to Doha four times a week during the summer 2027 timetable as well, without a return to the daily operations that were on sale until a few days ago. Any increase in the number of flights will depend on the development of the situation in the region, the availability of the fleet and the strategy of the Qatari carrier.

World.title: Who Could Croatia Face in the Nations League Play-offs?
World.content:
Croatia will find out their opponent for the Nations League play-offs on Friday, November 20th, when the draw takes place at UEFA headquarters in Nyon, Switzerland, at noon. At stake is a place in League A, the competition’s top tier.

Croatia finished third in Group A3 behind Spain and England, missing out on the quarter-finals. Results in the other groups meant third place was not enough to guarantee their League A status outright, so they will have to fight for it over two legs against one of the runners-up from League B.

Who could Croatia face?

Croatia’s opponent will come from one of four League B groups. Bosnia and Herzegovina have already secured second place in Group B4, while the other three runners-up spots are still being decided: Slovenia and Scotland in Group B1, Hungary and Northern Ireland in Group B2, and Kosovo and the Republic of Ireland in Group B3.

That leaves seven teams in contention to become Croatia’s opponent. According to Football Meets Data, Bosnia and Herzegovina, the only side already guaranteed a play-off spot, are the most likely, followed by Slovenia, Kosovo, Northern Ireland, Hungary, the Republic of Ireland and Scotland.

Croatia hold the advantage

The play-off will be played over two legs in March 2027. The winner will compete in League A in the next edition of the Nations League, while the loser will drop into League B. Croatia will be seeded, which means they will play the second leg at home.

World.title: Minors in Croatia Will Soon be Unable to Order Energy Drinks in Cafes
World.content:
November the 16th, 2026 – Minors in Croatia will soon be unable to order energy drinks in cafes after shops banned their sale to under 18s back in June.

Energy drinks have not been allowed to be sold to minors in shops since June this year, and a ban on serving them in hospitality establishments is provided for in the Hospitality Activity Act. Poslovni reports that the Ministry of Health has launched the procedure for adopting the Act on Restricting the Use of Energy Drinks and Products Similar to Energy Drinks by persons under the age of 18.

The aforementioned Hospitality Activity Act will go before Parliament for a second reading. The new law will thus form a joint package of measures for the protection of children’s health together with those rules.

“Energy drinks are not harmless, and their effects can be more pronounced in children and young people whose bodies are still developing. That is why with the law we are not stopping at warnings on the packaging, but are also taking into account the composition of the products and their effect on the child’s body. We protect children best through prevention, timely information and clear rules, and with this proposal we are turning those principles into concrete measures, from expert risk assessment to clearly established responsibility of everyone who places these products on the market. In this way the Government continues to strengthen the system of child protection, providing support to parents and creating a safer environment for growing up,” said Minister of Health Dr Irena Hrstić.

Caffeine, other stimulants and sugar, with which energy drinks abound, can negatively affect the heart and blood vessels, the nervous system and mental health, and children are exposed to a greater risk of such consequences than adults. Although drinks with a high caffeine content already carry a mandatory warning that they are not recommended for children, pregnant women or breastfeeding women, research by the Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ) shows widespread consumption among schoolchildren, and some of them drink 750 millilitres or more on a single occasion.

That is why the Ministry of Health is going a step further and giving a health foundation to the bans from the areas of trade and hospitality. According to the draft, an energy drink will be considered a drink with more than 150 milligrams of caffeine per litre, from any source, with products based on coffee, tea and cocoa being excluded. The law will ensure the implementation of these bans, and minors will not be able to buy products that by composition or physiological effect correspond to an energy drink or are comparable to it, regardless of the form in which they come on the market or are used.

Protection does not stop at the point of sale. Advertising of all these products will not be allowed to be aimed at a minor audience, and in schools and other institutions where children stay it will be completely banned, as will their display. Educational institutions will also receive an obligation to promote knowledge about the harmfulness of energy drinks and similar products as part of preventive programmes, and monitoring of the impact on health is also envisaged.

The key expert role will be played by the HZJZ. It will keep a register of products to which the law applies, and entry into it will be mandatory for everyone who places them on the market. The Institute will also assess how much these products endanger the health of persons under the age of 18 and determine which product is considered similar to an energy drink. On the basis of that assessment a temporary ban order may also be issued, which will enable a rapid response to new risks.

The Ministry has submitted the Form of Legislative Activities to the Government’s Office for Legislation with a view to including the new law in the List of Laws outside the Plan of Legislative Activities for 2026. Public consultation on the Form will be conducted on the e-Consultations portal, the text of the Draft Proposal of the Act will be published in the next phase, and submission to the Government procedure is planned by the end of this year

World.title: Will Croatia Finally Get a Break From Price Increases in 2027?
World.content:
November the 16th, 2026 – Will Croatia finally get a break from price increases and constant pressure on the public’s bank accounts and wallets in 2027? A slowdown is on the cards…

The finance minister also spoke about whether citizens can expect a better standard of living and what the Government’s offer is for increasing salaries in public and state services. Poslovni reports that price growth could weaken already in the first months of next year, but the realisation of the Government’s forecasts will largely depend on the movement of energy prices and the geopolitical situation.

Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Tomislav Ćorić expects that inflation in Croatia will begin to slow significantly already in the first quarter of 2027. Appearing on the central HTV News, he assessed that the economic projections for next year are optimistic, especially in comparison with expectations for the European Union and the Eurozone. According to the Government’s projections, inflation in 2027 should fall to 2.7 percent on an annual basis, while economic growth of 2.1 percent is expected.

when can we expect a price slowdown?

Ćorić believes that the beginning of the year should bring a weakening of inflationary pressures thanks to the gradual disappearance of base effects from previous price increases and the expected calming of oil prices. These are factors that should contribute to slower price growth, although this does not mean that products and services will necessarily become cheaper. The minister considers the greatest risk to the realisation of these expectations to be a possible deterioration of geopolitical circumstances, primarily the continued escalation of the conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East.

If there are no new disruptions on international markets, he believes that the planned economic indicators could be achieved.

will quality of life actually improve in 2027?

Asked whether he expects that the general public will live better in 2027 than currently, Ćorić replied that he hopes so and believes in it. He bases such expectations on the reduction of inflationary pressures, an increase in the standard of living and the continuation of economic growth. He also believes that the investments envisaged in the new state budget should further strengthen the resilience of the Croatian economy.

The minister also commented on the negotiations on salaries for employees in state and public services. For 2027, the Croatian Government has offered an increase in the base for calculating salaries of a total of 3.5 percent and the gradual introduction of a meal allowance, which would reach 50 euros per month by the end of the year. Ćorić considers this a realistic offer, aligned with the possibilities of the state budget.

An agreement has not yet been reached, however. The public service trade unions rejected the offered increase in the base and initiated a mediation procedure, while the state service trade unions still need to consider the offer in their bodies.

further spending on defence

Speaking about increased defence expenditure, Ćorić said that economic results enable higher budget revenues and expenditures, which is why it was not necessary to reduce funds for other sectors in order to finance security investments. Around 1.5 billion euros is envisaged for defence in the budget proposal for 2027, and the minister confirmed that spending should continue to grow due to the obligations Croatia has assumed within NATO.

At the same time, the Government plans to keep the general government deficit at the level of 2.9 percent of GDP and to continue reducing the share of public debt. Ćorić emphasised that stable public finances and the rise in Croatia’s credit rating enable more favourable borrowing conditions. As an indicator of citizens’ confidence in government securities, he singled out the latest issue of one-year treasury bills, in which the desired amount of one billion euros was reached after only five days. The minister also expects that a budget rebalancing could follow after the summer of 2027, but he does not foresee major changes compared to the current plans.

World.title: Seismic Stations Cover All of Croatia for the First Time
World.content:
November the 16th, 2026 – Seismic stations cover all of Croatia for the first time ever, with 125 stations currently measuring earthquakes, and a further 55 planned.

As part of the much wider EU CROSSNET project, Croatia has installed 125 seismic stations and plans another 55, which would bring the network to around 180 stations. Zrinka Gabelica Toplek reports for Poslovni that project leader Tomislav Fiket emphasised that for the first time, the entire country is now covered from Ilok all the way down to Cavtat. He did however duly warn that further implementation depends on the employment of nine young experts.

rapid warning systems

CROSSNET modernises and significantly expands the system for monitoring seismic activity in Croatia. A dense network of stations enables more precise determination of the location and magnitude of earthquakes, faster data processing and better information for the public and the competent services. At the conference “From the 1880 earthquake to the modern seismic network – how we monitor ground shaking today”, held to mark the 146th anniversary of the great Zagreb earthquake, Fiket said that the general public, wherever they live, should now be able to receive equally high-quality information.

“For the first time in history, all of Croatia has been successfully covered by seismic stations. It’s extremely important to us that every single person, wherever they live, has the opportunity to receive equally high-quality information,” Fiket emphasised. Earthquakes can’t be predicted, but rapid warning systems can react after the arrival of the first, non-destructive wave. A dense network of stations makes it possible to send a warning to citizens before the arrival of the destructive second wave, which can reduce the number of victims and the extent of damage. Data from the stations arrives at the central system in near real time, and people can also follow 24-hour records of the seismic stations and an interactive earthquake hazard map.

a 13.6 million euro project

The CROSSNET project is otherwise worth around 13.6 million euros. Of that, 75 percent is financed by the European Union through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NPOO), and 25 percent comes from the state budget itself. It was launched back in November 2021 and was supposed to finish at the end of June, but has been extended until the 31st of December 2026 because the employment of nine young experts participating in its implementation has not been secured.

The problem arose after the financing of the Seismological Service of the Republic of Croatia was transferred from the state budget to programme contracts of the Faculty of Science (PMF) at the end of last year. “Those nine jobs were missed in the negotiations and were not negotiated,” Fiket said, emphasising that the Faculty of Science was supposed to ensure the employment of these experts, but this has not been done so far.

World.title: Estonian goshawk may have spent winters raiding Russian poultry farm
World.content:
While migrating birds in Estonia usually fly south for winter, one goshawk headed north-east to Russia, where GPS data suggest it may have found food near a poultry farm.

The unusual movements of the bird were documented in a study by Ülo Väli.

The female goshawk, tracked by researchers between 2022 and 2024, traveled approximately 280 kilometers from her breeding grounds in southeastern Estonia to the same wintering area in northwestern Russia, in two consecutive years. GPS data recorded the bird of prey near a large industrial poultry farm and on multiple occasions. So even while the planned closure of the border with Russia next month may work for humans, wildlife will perhaps pay it less heed.

The claim suggests the goshawk hunted at the poultry farm near Pervomayskoye, also known as Kivennapa, close to St Petersburg. Väli suggested that the bird may have fed on chicken carcasses or pigeons in the surrounding area.

According to the researcher, goshawks generally lead fairly sedentary lives. Males tend to remain close to their nests, while females are slightly more mobile and can expand their home ranges to an extent. However, for an adult bird to travel almost 300 kilometers from its breeding grounds is a truly exceptional thing.

There could be several explanations for this, Väli said. The bird may have originally hatched near Pervomayskoye and subsequently established its breeding territory in Estonia after dispersing south as a juvenile. Alternatively, it may have visited the area to explore it as a juvenile, a time when goshawks roam more widely, or perhaps reached it later in life while searching for food. The possibility that the Russian area was its original home is a particularly interesting one, as the availability of prey there may have encouraged the bird to return.

It is also unusual that the goshawk flew to Russia over the sea, across the Gulf of Finland, as she would likely have had to do, Väli explained. "Birds of prey generally do not like crossing open water, but there was no easier route to fly there," he said.

What makes this even more remarkable is the bird's build. Goshawks are roughly the size of ravens, with short wings and long tails. Their physical characteristics are adapted to life in forests, rather than long-distance migration across open landscapes, still less water. Nevertheless, GPS data suggest that the female crossed the Gulf of Finland during both winters, Väli said.

Ornithology is not untouched by the war in Ukraine either

The ornithologists tracked the goshawk's movements using a solar-powered GPS device attached to the bird like a backpack. The device weighed just 30 grams, approximately two per cent of the bird's body weight, and recorded its location at intervals of as little as 10 minutes.

According to Väli, fitting the device was relatively straightforward on this occasion. "A kindly farmer in Põlva County caught it in his chicken enclosure and, instead of killing it, as many people probably would have done, notified ornithologists," he said. This meant the researcher did not have to spend time catching the bird himself.

The GPS device transmitted the bird's location remotely, allowing researchers to follow its movements across national borders. Although the ornithologists tracked the bird during the first years of the full-scale war in Ukraine, Väli said he initially had no problems with this.

The situation has since changed, however, and the researcher confirmed that the war has also affected ornithologists' work. "GPS jamming [in Russia] is already quite serious; we can no longer even track birds' movements properly," Väli noted.

The device itself can also pose problems when tracking a bird. It is powered by solar panels, meaning that prolonged periods of poor weather can affect its operation. "When the weather is wintry and gray, the battery inside does not get recharged," Väli said.

The goshawk eventually died in Russia in 2024. According to the scientific study, the bird was captured in a dovecote near St Petersburg, severely injured, and transferred to a rehabilitation center. Väli said it was however challenging to obtain information about the bird's fate from a country waging a war of aggression. Here limited movement initially indicated that she had died, while a Russian ornithologist he knew also informed him of its death. There is no broader cooperation, however, he said, with Russian authorities, and universities have also ended cooperation with Russian counterparts.

An estimated 400 to 600 Eurasian Goshawks (Astur gentilis) breed in Estonia.

The article was originally published in the scientific journal Ringing & Migration.

World.title: Tallinn to increase road construction and cut officials in 2027
World.content:
Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) said Tallinn will continue investing in infrastructure next year while cutting jobs in the city administration.

Major projects will include the reconstruction of Pärnu maantee and Petrooleumi tänav, the continuation of the second phase of Peterburi tee, and the reconstruction of the Hipodroomi intersection.

The second phase of Peterburi tee will involve repairing uneven sections of road made of concrete slabs near Iru, which Järvan described as a roller coaster made of concrete blocks.

At the same time, the city government will continue to reduce the size of the public sector, Järvan said.

He said approximately 100 officials were hired every year in previous years, but expansion cannot continue at this pace.

The deputy mayor highlighted that the current coalition abolished the green transition department after coming to power.

"Today, almost a year later, we can ask whether the City of Tallinn has collapsed as a result. No, but costs are lower. Some jokers might claim that if the green transition department had not been abolished, we would already have snow on the ground in November. I doubt that," he commented.

Seven positions will be cut in the city's business service next year. "We have clearly demonstrated that we can do more with less," Järvan noted.
