World.title: Trump joins ‘Quad’ summit for first leaders’ meeting in two years
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Tuesday joined his three fellow “Quad” leaders for their first summit in two years, with the grouping expressing “grave concerns” about economic coercion and announcing a new maritime security initiative.

Trump joined Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Australian leader Anthony Albanese and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi for the four-way summit on the sidelines of Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meetings in Manila just hours after arriving in the Philippine capital.

In a joint statement released after the meeting, the leaders called the Quad “a force for good and a partnership of action, committed to peace, stability and prosperity.”

World.title: Japan to make teaching licenses easier to obtain
World.content:
A government panel released a draft proposal Tuesday to reduce the number of credits required to obtain teaching licenses in university programs and establish a new one-year licensing course for working adults.

The proposal, presented by the teacher training subcommittee of the Central Council for Education, which advises the education minister, is designed to make teaching licenses easier to obtain and increase the number of applicants.

The council expects to finalize its recommendations by year-end and submit a bill to revise the education personnel certification law to the ordinary parliamentary session next year.

Under the current system, students seeking a standard teaching license for elementary, junior high or high school must earn 59 credits in teaching-related common subjects through a university teacher-training program. The proposal would reduce the requirement to 36 or 37 credits.

Although the total number of credits required for certification would remain at 56 or 57, 20 credits earned in a student’s major field would be recognized as a new area of specialty and thus treated as credits that can be counted toward the total, making it easier for students from a broader range of faculties to obtain teaching licenses.

A new graduate school program would target working adults with a university degree or higher, allowing them to obtain a license for elementary, junior high or high school in one year.

Participants would receive compensation for practical training at schools to alleviate their financial burdens.

The draft additionally calls for a new license allowing teachers to teach only specific subjects at elementary schools, where homeroom teachers are currently supposed to teach all subjects.

Graduates of kōsen technical colleges would also be eligible to obtain licenses for elementary and junior high schools.

According to an education ministry survey, the competition ratio for the public school teacher employment examination conducted in fiscal 2024 fell to a record low of 2.9 applicants per opening, reflecting difficulties securing enough teachers.

World.title: Japan space probe changes target over engine trouble
World.content:
A Japanese probe that returned precious asteroid dust to Earth six years ago has changed course in its extended mission, officials said Tuesday, citing issues in its aging engines.

The unmanned Hayabusa-2 probe brought back pristine materials from the asteroid Ryugu in 2020, supporting discoveries linked to clues on the origin of life.

In July, the probe flew 400 meters (1,312 feet) from a near-Earth asteroid, making the closest approach ever recorded in such a mission, Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) has said.

It was then headed for its main target, an asteroid called 1998 KY26 that will be some 300 million kilometers away from Earth when the probe would have reached it in 2031.

However, 12 years since its launch, “the deterioration of the onboard equipment ... is becoming increasingly evident,” Yuya Mimasu, team leader of the extended mission, told reporters.

With the main engines suffering repeated malfunctions, “we decided to revise the plan to one that could be safely implemented,” he said.

The probe will now head towards an asteroid called 2015 BM510, aiming for a flyby — passing close to it at high speed — in April 2028, according to the team leader.

“Because it is a dark, small asteroid ... it will be one of the world’s most difficult flyby missions,” Mimasu said.

The new target is between 17 meters and 74 meters in diameter, completing a rotation every 49 minutes.

The revised operation can help “future planetary defense” missions aimed at deflecting asteroids that might otherwise collide with Earth, Mimasu said.

World.title: Mother bear on the loose prompts city in Gunma Prefecture to shut schools
World.content:
Authorities in the city of Maebashi in Gunma Prefecture ordered school closures as officials were looking for a bear on the loose on Tuesday, after media reports said at least one person had been attacked.

Officials in the city have captured a cub, one of two animals seen roaming in residential areas. The search for the bear believed to be its mother continues.

Bear sightings nationwide have sharply decreased from the last fiscal year, when a record 13 people were killed.

Still, experts say growing bear populations, declining human populations in rural areas and fluctuations in the availability of food in the wilderness have driven the animals into residential neighborhoods in search of food.

In a post on X, Maebashi Mayor Akira Ogawa urged residents to stay indoors, warning of “an extremely dangerous situation.”

“All residents, especially those living in the areas where the animals have been and the surrounding neighborhoods, are urged to refrain from nonessential outings such as walks and to act with safety as your top priority,” she said.

The mayor said one person was injured, without elaborating.

Local media said a man in his 50s suffered a non-life-threatening injury.

With the search ongoing, officials said the city’s schools will be closed on Wednesday as a precaution.

In September alone, 1,759 bear sightings were reported nationwide, sharply lower than the 4,766 cases recorded a year earlier.

World.title: New biography of WWII admiral sets out to show his life story as a whole
World.content:
Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto has always presented something of a puzzle. How did this Harvard-educated admirer of the United States, reluctant to go to war, become the mastermind of the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941?

Drawing on recently discovered Japanese sources, Ronald Drabkin’s riveting biography, coming out on Nov. 17, published by Tuttle, clarifies the conundrum: Much of Yamamoto’s popular image simply isn’t true.

World.title: Chiba zoo’s Futa gets Guinness award for being oldest living red panda in captivity
World.content:
More than 100 people turned up at a Chiba zoo Tuesday to celebrate 23-year-old Futa being recognized with a world record for becoming the oldest living red panda in captivity .

A representative of Guinness World Records, the international record-keeping organization, attended the ceremony to present a certificate for the award to Chiba Zoological Park.

The ceremony, attended by about 180 people, including the media, began with staff members from the zoo sharing their memories of Futa, who turned 23 years and 135 days old the same day.

“I mostly just feel amazed at how hugely popular he has become. During my time, we had no worries about his health at all — he has always been very well loved,” said former zookeeper Masahira Hamada, who looked after Futa for over a decade, from 2007 until 2019.

Futa was not present at the event due to the cold weather. His current zookeeper, Yasushi Ito, received the award on his behalf.

Ito reflected on the number of handlers Futa has had over the years.

“I am now holding the baton passed down through all their hard work and effort,” he said. “I sincerely hope Futa continues to live a long and healthy life.”

Zookeepers at Chiba Zoological Park in the city of Chiba accept the Guinness World Records certification for a red panda at the zoo named Futa becoming the oldest living one in captivity on Tuesday. | Maddie Baker

Kaoru Ishikawa, the vice president of Guinness World Records Japan, said, “For the fans, it’s a shame that Futa wasn’t here, but I was impressed by how much the staff here considered his (health) condition.”

One of the fans at the award ceremony was Chiyo Kurokawa, who attended the event with a group of friends, all wearing the same red panda ears.

“After (Futa) stood up on his hind legs, he became hugely famous. Back then, Chiba Zoological Park had very few visitors and was struggling. Futa became the spark that turned things around,” she reflected.

Another fan, Shiho Nakano, wore a red panda onesie to attend the event.

“I’ve been following (Futa) for 19 years so lots of memories came flooding back. I felt overwhelmingly happy, and at the same time, I felt emotional and like I might cry,” she said.

“It’s through taking things one day at a time that he was able to receive an award like this. I hope he continues to be remembered forever,” she added.

World.title: Odds improve on Trump-Kim meeting on APEC sidelines, analysts say
World.content:
The odds of US President Donald Trump meeting North Korean leader Kim Jong Un on the sidelines of the APEC summit have improved after the Kremlin said a meeting between Kim and Russian President Vladimir Putin was possible, analysts said.

Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in meeting Kim again and said Monday it might happen in China this week. However, previously mooted meetings have not taken place and U.S. and South Korean officials have said the chances were low.

But a report by Russia’s Interfax news agency quoting the Kremlin saying Putin could meet Kim if the North Korean leader attended this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen has shifted bets.

World.title: Nikkei 225 near bear market territory as AI boom cools
World.content:
The Nikkei 225 stock index has been trading in or near bear market territory for a week and is not expected to recover its highs until artificial intelligence and data center optimism returns.

It declined 6% on Nov. 6 to close at 57,434.77, down more than 20% from a record 72,366.34 hit on June 25. A 20% fall is considered to be a technical bear market, though analysts and academics warn that a decline alone does not make a true bear market.

A landslide victory in U.S. midterm elections by the Democratic Party earlier this month rattled investors, stoking fears of a slowdown in data center construction given that many candidates pledged stricter regulations for these projects.

World.title: Second-hand luxury stores in Hong Kong probed over HK$16.6m payment defaults
World.content:
Hong Kong police are investigating two second-hand luxury goods shops in connection with more than 40 complaints of suspected fraud totalling HK$16.6 million (US$2.11 million).

Vootic in Causeway Bay and Obsessplanet in Admiralty were closed abruptly on Tuesday. The two shops, which sell pre-owned high-end items on behalf of their owners, have been accused of defaulting on payments.

A notice posted outside the closed Obsessplanet store stated that police had sealed off the shop in relation to the suspected fraud and appealed to victims to contact the force.

World.title: Hong Kong plans first sustainable aviation fuel facility to meet 2030 goal
World.content:
Hong Kong has taken a major step towards building a cross-border supply chain for sustainable aviation fuel with the establishment of the city’s first blending facility in Tuen Mun, as it seeks to meet a clean-fuel target by 2030.

The Airport Authority, Hong Kong and China Gas Company (Towngas) and its incubated sustainable fuels company, EcoCeres, announced on Tuesday that they would establish a three-party framework to develop the facility in Tuen Mun Area 38.

The move follows EcoCeres’ HK$10 billion investment, announced in May, to build a sustainable aviation fuel production plant in Dongguan, Guangdong province, with backing from the Hong Kong and Dongguan governments. The plant is expected to begin production in 2030.

World.title: Hong Kong incinerator fire probably caused by smoking or welding, probe finds
World.content:
A blaze that forced the temporary shutdown of Hong Kong’s first waste-to-energy incinerator was probably caused by smoking or welding work, fire authorities have concluded.

The findings come months after authorities tightened anti-smoking rules at construction sites following the deadly Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po.

“The investigation has ruled out electrical faults, arson and spontaneous combustion of chemical substances as the cause of the fire, which is instead suspected to be related to welding works or smoking,” the Fire Services Department said.

World.title: ‘Nobody wins the future alone’: John Lee calls for collaboration at Apec
World.content:
Hong Kong’s leader has called on Apec delegates to “prosper and win together” to thrive in an increasingly complex global environment as he offered the city as a springboard for businesses seeking to enter the mainland Chinese market.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu told hundreds of business delegates at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum’s CEO Summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday that the Greater Bay Area, which combines Hong Kong, Macau and nine cities in Guangdong province, was a proven model of regional collaboration.

The city leader also attended a dinner with Hong Kong’s representatives to the Apec Business Advisory Council in the evening to discuss issues including the promotion of regional cooperation. The council is an advisory body established by Apec.

World.title: 2 hospitalised and 200 flee to safety after fire breaks out at Hong Kong flat
World.content:
Two people were taken to hospital and about 200 residents fled to safety after a fire broke out in a flat at a public housing estate in Hong Kong’s Lam Tin on Tuesday.

A man and a woman escaped from the flat in Kai Wong House at Kai Tin Estate on their own. The man suffered minor arm injuries and smoke inhalation, while the woman complained of discomfort after inhaling smoke.

Firefighters also rescued a cat from the flat and handed it over to staff from the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals for emergency treatment, but it later died.

World.title: Hong Kong driver flees police roadblock, hitting 4 taxis and injuring cabby
World.content:
Hong Kong police are searching for a motorist who rammed through a roadblock in Tsim Sha Tsui in the early hours of Tuesday, hitting four taxis and injuring one of the cabbies before fleeing.

The incident happened at about 1.10am as officers from the Kowloon West emergency unit were conducting an anti-crime roadblock operation near the junction of Nathan Road and Hillwood Road.

Police said a white Audi aroused suspicion as it emerged from Hillwood Road. Officers tried to stop the car for checks, but the car suddenly reversed before accelerating away.

World.title: Hong Kong organiser’s grant under review amid row over Yuja Wang’s concert change
World.content:
Hong Kong authorities have asked the organiser of the recent concerts of pianist Yuja Wang to provide an account of the row over programme changes that ended in full refunds to concertgoers, saying they would also review the grant to the group.

The Culture, Sports and Tourism Bureau was responding to the handling by Premiere Performances of Hong Kong (PPHK) of changes in the second of Wang’s two concerts last week, with the pianist and the organiser giving different accounts of the withdrawal of a piece. Concertgoers who felt short-changed later filed complaints to the Consumer Council.

“We note public comments made after the performance concerned as well as subsequent statements by the relevant parties. We have asked PPHK for an account of the incident, and will review the grant approved,” a bureau spokesman said in a reply to the South China Morning Post on Monday night.

World.title: Top Chinese cancer researcher calls on Hong Kong to deepen research ties with mainland
World.content:
A leading Chinese blood cancer specialist has urged Hong Kong to deepen research collaboration with mainland China, saying the city could play a unique role in connecting the mainland’s growing scientific capabilities with the international life sciences community.

Zhu Chen, a professor at Ruijin Hospital of Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s school of medicine, received the 2026 Shaw Prize in Life Science and Medicine last week alongside French molecular biologist Anne Dejean and French doctor and researcher Hugues de The for their work on a rare form of leukaemia, including the development of a highly effective targeted treatment.

Dejean and de The were recognised for discovering the molecular and cellular bases of acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL), a rare and aggressive form of blood cancer, while Chen contributed to translating their scientific findings into effective clinical treatments.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019275/China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
World.title: China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019275/China’s Basic Insurance to Cover CAR T-Cell Cancer Therapy
World.content:
China will include a CAR T-cell therapy in its national health insurance scheme for the first time, making a blood cancer treatment that once cost over 1 million yuan ($150,000) per dose more accessible.

The National Healthcare Security Administration announced on Nov. 14 that relmacabtagene autoleucel, or relma-cel, made by Shanghai-based biotech firm JW Therapeutics and sold under the brand name Carteyva, will be covered by insurance starting Jan. 1. The therapy has three approved uses for different types of lymphoma and costs 1.29 million yuan per dose.

CAR T-cell therapy is primarily used to treat types of lymphoma and involves extracting and genetically modifying a patient’s own immune cells to target cancer cells, before infusing them back into the body. China approved its first CAR T-cell therapy product in 2021.

Most of China’s population is covered by the country’s national insurance scheme: 1.33 billion were enrolled in basic medical insurance by the end of 2025. Only drugs listed in the national insurance catalog can be partially reimbursed through the medical insurance fund. For drugs not listed, patients must usually bear 100% of the cost.

For years, CAR T-cell drugs were excluded from the national insurance list because an unwritten industry rule held that drugs priced above 300,000 yuan rarely secured coverage, limiting patient access, according to Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper.

The rate of CAR T-cell drug use as a second-line treatment for large B-cell lymphoma in China is about one-sixth of that in the United States, while use as a third-line treatment is about one-10th of the rate in the U.S. and Europe.

Carteyva was one of five CAR T-cell therapies included last year in China’s first commercial insurance list for high-cost innovative drugs. This year, those drugs became eligible for national coverage. Two CAR T-cell drug manufacturers, including JW Therapeutics, entered insurance coverage negotiations on Sept. 6.

“Two or three years ago, we wouldn’t have dared to imagine this,” Tian Feng, JW Therapeutics chairman and CEO, told The Paper.

China records about 101,500 new lymphoma cases each year. Carteyva is available at more than 200 certified hospitals nationwide.

The updated national reimbursement list adds 107 drugs covering oncology, chronic diseases, mental illnesses, rare diseases, and pediatric medications. A separate commercial insurance list, which covers drugs outside the basic scheme, includes 12 new treatments.

“This is a historic moment for lymphoma patients in China,” Tian said, adding that when he and the company received the news, “everyone really felt that the treatment of lymphoma patients in China had entered a new, very exciting era.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG）

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019269/A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
World.title: A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019269/A Chinese Medical Drama’s Remedy for Big-City Blues: Go Home
World.content:
A TV drama about a doctor who returns to his small hometown after being fired from a prestigious city-based position has become a hit among young Chinese, who resonate with its message of finding purpose away from competitive urban areas.

“Small Town Remedy” has been hotly discussed since its Nov. 4 finale. Premiering Oct. 21, the show follows Liu Zhengliang, played by A-list actor Xiao Zhan, a young neurosurgeon who returns to his hometown in northeastern China — or Dongbei — from a major hospital following a botched surgery in which his patient dies.

The show’s popularity comes amid a broader shift in attitudes among young Chinese, who increasingly seek a more sustainable work-life balance and self-care amid growing fatigue stemming from relentless competition and conventional definitions of success.

Socially awkward and unfamiliar with local customs, Liu initially struggles to return to life at home after leaving his post in the southern metropolis of Shenzhen. The series depicts how his brother, childhood friends, and former hospital colleagues gradually help him overcome the trauma of his failed operation, among other personal struggles, such as the death of his mother.

Fans have reported being drawn to the drama’s lighthearted tone and the witty humor commonly associated with China’s Northeast, despite tackling heavy subject matter such as illness, death, and grief.

Its popularity has also sparked an online trend of learning the Dongbei dialect, with video lessons gaining traction on social media. One related hashtag — “‘Small Town Remedy’ Dongbei dialect listening test” — had amassed nearly 1.4 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Monday.

The 29-episode drama has earned an average rating of 8 out of 10 on review platform Douban and reached an audience of 148 million across all streaming platforms, according to data from domestic streaming platform iQiyi. Related hashtags on short-video platform Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, had also garnered more than 8 billion views.

Since the show’s finale, online users have been debating what Liu’s next move should be. Some suggest that as a talented young doctor, he should return to a major hospital to pursue better career prospects, while others say he’d be better off staying in his hometown, where he’d have the emotional space to continue recovering and potentially find greater purpose using his medical skills.

“Everyone wants to go to Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen, but if life away from home is too difficult, returning to your hometown is not a step backward, nor is it something to be ashamed of,” one user wrote beneath a post discussing the show on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. “One’s hometown can be a great choice, too.”

“As urbanization continues, more and more young people are facing the same dilemmas as Liu Zhengliang,” another Xiaohongshu user wrote in a comment under the same post, referring to Liu’s struggles with cultural identity and homesickness. “I think the theme of this show really suits the times.”

In one widely discussed scene, Liu and his girlfriend see off his younger brother as he leaves for Beijing in search of better job opportunities. Overwhelmed by the farewell, the female protagonist, played by Jiang Yan, questions the seemingly inevitable exodus from their hometown.

“Were we born in Dongbei only to leave it behind?” she asks. “The winters here may be cold, but people’s hearts are warm ... Will leaving Dongbei necessarily bring happiness? Don’t those who leave ever miss home?”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “Small Town Remedy.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019274/Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
World.title: Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019274/Shanghai Sacks Two Scientists Over Child’s Death in Gene Trial
World.content:
Shanghai authorities have dismissed two researchers after an investigation into a child’s death following experimental gene-editing treatment found unheeded safety warnings, failures in ethical review, and undisclosed payments and gifts from the family.

The child had Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, a rare neurodevelopmental disorder with no effective treatment, according to findings released Friday by the Shanghai investigation team. The family contributed 5.3 million yuan ($800,000) toward the research and separately gave researchers approximately 1.06 million yuan in money and gifts.

In July 2023, the family approached Qiu Zilong, deputy director of Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine’s Songjiang Research Institute, hoping his team could develop a customized gene-editing treatment, investigators said.

The child received an injection at the university’s affiliated Xinhua Hospital on March 24, 2025, and died seven days later.

At an emergency review April 2, the hospital’s ethics committee attributed the death to thrombotic microangiopathy, a complication of gene therapy, and ordered the study terminated.

The death went unmentioned in related preclinical research Qiu’s team published in Nature in February 2026, investigators said. The team reported using gene editing to correct a single error in the DNA code of mouse brain cells, restoring levels of a protein essential for normal brain development. The researchers said tests in monkeys also suggested the technique’s potential for use in humans.

Five months later, a joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch revealed the fatal human trial and reported that the Nature paper had also omitted evidence of liver and kidney damage in animal safety tests.

Shanghai authorities subsequently established a team to investigate the preclinical research, the hospital’s clinical study, and the data underlying the Nature paper.

Investigators found that Qiu’s team had failed to promptly share a safety report from experiments on nonhuman primates with the clinical study’s lead investigator, leaving warning signals unheeded.

Xinhua Hospital’s ethics committee approved the study despite insufficient toxicology and safety evidence, proceeding without additional material it had requested. The hospital also failed to independently and adequately assess the study’s scientific basis and safety.

Investigators said that although the consent form warned the family of serious complications and adverse events, it did not prominently communicate the risk of death.

Investigators found no data fabrication in the Nature paper but identified discrepancies between the research methods used and those described. Data from the same experimental batch had also been presented separately without explanation.

The Nature paper also failed to disclose financial conflicts involving four researchers. Qiu received expensive liquor and electronics worth approximately 100,000 yuan, while Xinhua Hospital associate researcher Yang Kan, the Nature paper’s first and corresponding author, received 900,000 yuan and expensive liquor. Two other members of Qiu’s team each received 30,000 yuan.

Investigators said the money and gifts had been returned or surrendered in accordance with regulations.

Qiu and Yang were both dismissed, and barred from participating in science and technology programs and awards for five years. Their names were entered into a database of serious research integrity violations.

The clinical study’s lead investigator, surnamed Yu, was removed as head of Xinhua Hospital’s research department and demoted. Yu was also barred for five years from being promoted, participating in science and technology programs and awards, and recruiting graduate students. Another official, surnamed Shi, was removed as head of the hospital’s ethics committee office and demoted.

Other officials responsible for the hospital’s ethics review and research oversight received disciplinary sanctions. Xinhua Hospital received an administrative penalty, which the investigation team did not detail.

The Shanghai Municipal Health Commission said it would soon launch special inspections of clinical research involving emerging biomedical technologies.

“As biomedical technologies advance rapidly, research institutions and practitioners must recognize the high risks associated with clinical studies involving emerging treatments such as cell and gene therapies,” the probe said. “While pursuing innovation, they must also adhere to professional standards.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: iStock/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019256/What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
World.title: What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019256/What Made Jade So Valuable in Ancient China and the Americas?
World.content:
Recent exhibitions at the Shanghai Museum and Beijing’s Capital Museum have introduced Chinese audiences to the civilizations of the ancient Americas. For Chinese visitors, the importance placed on jade may feel familiar. In both ancient China and Mesoamerica, finely worked jade adorned the powerful and accompanied them into the grave, a striking similarity that has long attracted scholarly interest.

How did jade come to carry such authority? One way to explore this question is to compare the jade traditions of Liangzhu and the Classic Maya lowlands, two societies from ancient China and the Americas. Liangzhu was an early regional state near present-day Hangzhou, capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, around 3300–2300 BC, with a walled capital, an extensive system of dams, and a pronounced social hierarchy. In the Classic Maya lowlands, spanning parts of present-day Mexico, Guatemala, and Belize, cities ruled by royal dynasties flourished around AD 300–900. Both Liangzhu and Maya cities hold UNESCO World Heritage status.

Thousands of years separated the two societies, and there is no evidence of direct contact between them. Yet both had complex social hierarchies in which powerful ritual authorities played important roles. By tracing jade from the selection of raw stone to its final resting place, we can see how control over labor, knowledge, and materials helped establish its authority in ways that were both similar and distinct.

Jade was valued in both ancient China and the Americas long before Liangzhu and the Classic Maya. The concept of jade encompasses several kinds of stone. Liangzhu’s finest ritual jades were made from nephrite, while Maya jade was principally jadeite. Both were prized for their appearance and could be polished to a lustrous finish. Craftspeople shaped jade using abrasives such as sand mixed with water. Working with different stones helped them recognize differences in hardness and toughness and determine which materials were best suited to particular objects.

In Liangzhu, material choice was closely tied to the form and status of the finished artifact. Other stones, such as serpentine, were generally used for small, less prestigious ornaments. Among the Maya, by contrast, the symbolic meanings of stones were more closely associated with their colors. Green and blue-green evoked water, cultivating maize, and renewed life. Jadeite remained highly prized, but a wider range of similarly colored stones could also be valued for their quality and craftsmanship.

Not everyone had equal access to these raw materials or the specialized skills needed to work them. This inequality helped establish jade’s association with power.

Workshops within and immediately outside Liangzhu city made prestigious ritual objects from nephrite. A short distance away, a large workshop complex specialized in small serpentine ornaments. Despite their proximity, the workshops used different materials and produced different types of objects. The fine finish of these serpentine ornaments, however, shows that their makers were skilled.

This contrast suggests that proximity and skill alone did not guarantee access to nephrite. Access appears to have depended on a workshop’s role and status within the production system.

Evidence from the Maya suggests broader access to raw jadeite, but tighter restrictions on the skills and knowledge required to produce elaborate royal artifacts. Near the jadeite sources in Guatemala’s Motagua Valley, in the country’s southeastern highlands, households of different social ranks shaped, sawed, and drilled the stone. At Cancuén, in the country’s center, much of the waste from the early stages of production was found in modest residences. Elaborately finished objects, however, were concentrated in elite buildings, alongside some tools used to polish ear ornaments.

While non-elite households carried out the early stages of jade production, finer carving, including sacred images and inscriptions that conveyed ritual and political meanings, appears to have been largely reserved for elites or specialist craftspeople working for them. Creating these details required skills and knowledge that were less widely shared. Access to raw jadeite did not necessarily mean access to the expertise needed to produce elaborate royal artifacts.

As jade artifacts took shape, their imagery became another critical means of expressing power. This is particularly evident in elite burials, where jade objects helped convey the status and ritual authority of those buried with them.

A jade cong, or ritual tube, from Fanshan, an elite cemetery within Liangzhu city, illustrates how craftsmanship and sacred imagery conveyed authority. Its surface bears an intricately carved human-and-animal-face motif known as the Sacred Insignia. The finest versions appeared on the most prestigious ritual jades, whose material and craftsmanship signaled status.

The cong also belonged to a prescribed set of burial goods. Within Liangzhu’s political center, elite burials followed established conventions that linked the types and placement of artifacts to rank and gender, leaving little scope for personal preference. Differences in the quantity and quality of objects expressed the deceased’s rank and ritual authority within this prescribed framework.

Maya rulers, by contrast, drew on shared beliefs but had greater freedom in how they arranged jade. One example comes from the tomb of Pakal the Great, ruler of the Maya city-state of Palenque, in what is now southern Mexico. His funerary mask is a mosaic of carefully fitted pieces of jade in different shades of green. Scholars interpret its youthful face as linking the ruler to the Maize God. A cube in one hand, a sphere in the other, a bead beside each foot, and a central belt figurine have been interpreted as forming a quincunx, a five-point arrangement representing the four directions and a center in Maya cosmology, with Pakal at its symbolic center.

Pakal’s jades derived meaning from their individual forms and their placement within his tomb. Shared beliefs could guide such arrangements without requiring the standardized sets found in Liangzhu elite graves. Maya sacred imagery also appeared on multicolored ceramic vessels, carved stone monuments, and buildings. Jade was one of several materials through which rulers expressed their place in the world.

The movement and final placement of jade objects also reflected their association with power in both societies.

In Liangzhu, the movement of prestigious jade objects appears to have reinforced relationships among elites. Similarities in carving between the political center and neighboring settlements suggest that these objects circulated primarily among elites, possibly through gift exchanges. Local production continued, but the most sophisticated carving techniques remained concentrated near the political center. When finished, Liangzhu jades were deliberately buried; prestigious ritual objects were typically placed in individual elite graves, while lower-ranking burials contained smaller, less elaborate ornaments.

Among the Maya, jade served purposes beyond elite ownership. Different forms of jade circulated in different ways. Some ornaments bore inscriptions linking them to particular people and events, while plain beads and axe-shaped objects known as celts circulated more freely and may have been used as payment by the Postclassic period (900–1521). Non-elite households acquired small jade beads that could express wealth and status. At Cancuén, jade-working households buried raw or partly worked jade during house construction, suggesting that even unfinished jade material held ritual value. At Copán, in western Honduras, jade and shell artifacts were buried together in a residential courtyard, showing how different materials could serve similar ritual purposes beyond royal burials.

These differences reveal how the two societies developed distinct ways of turning jade into a symbol of wealth and authority. In Liangzhu, the quality of the stone, specialized craftsmanship, sacred imagery, and rules governing its use were brought together in a tightly regulated system. Among the Maya, jade acquired authority through a wider range of materials and ritual settings, allowing for broader participation and more flexible exchange alongside restrictions imposed by elites.

Jade’s beauty may have made it desirable, but it was people who made it precious. Through craftsmanship, sacred rituals, and control over who could possess it, ancient societies transformed stone into a symbol of wealth and authority. The treasures displayed in museums today reveal a larger truth: The value of precious things lies not just in what they are, but in who gets to decide what they are worth.

Portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: Visuals from Lin Xin, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019262/China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
World.title: China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019262/China’s Short Dramas See Quality Shift With AI-Made Historical Hit
World.content:
An AI-generated short drama made by amateurs, including a former rideshare driver and a stay-at-home mother, has gone viral in China for its high production quality and historical accuracy, challenging the genre’s reputation for simple, brainless plots.

First released in August, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” already has 10 seasons and comprises roughly 1,000 3-minute episodes. As of Thursday, the show has amassed over 12 billion views across platforms including Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, and streaming site Bilibili, local media reported.

In the first nine months of this year, 490,000 micro-dramas were released in China, 13 times more than in all of 2025. AI is also reshaping the micro-drama industry, with AI-generated productions now accounting for more than 90% of all such content, according to a report the National Radio and Television Administration released in October. The report also found that China’s short-drama audience had surpassed 600 million active monthly viewers.

Adapted from a web novel published in installments beginning this April by a writer under the pen name Chagen’er, “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” follows five modern-day soldiers who unwittingly travel back to the late Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), bringing their weapons and military expertise with them.

The late Northern Song period is a popular setting for Chinese time-travel fiction, as it offers viewers an alternative reality to the dynasty’s end, when invading Jurchen tribes captured two of its emperors — widely remembered as a national disgrace.

Fans have praised the drama’s carefully crafted script, elaborate fight scenes, and rounded characters who grapple with everything from the imperial examination system to weapons, food, and military equipment shortages during invasions by northern nomadic groups.

The historical details have prompted some viewers to look up Song-era official ranks, military organizations, and historical records and compare them against the drama’s depictions.

The production team behind “Armed Into the Song Dynasty” reportedly comprises six members — including a former pharmaceutical sales representative, interior designer, rideshare driver, stay-at-home mother, and wholesale business owner — who met during an online course on how to use AI to make short dramas.

Zhang Hansheng, 54, the production team’s head, told domestic media that the series has so far cost roughly 1 million yuan ($150,000) to produce, but declined to disclose the team’s earnings. However, rumors of hefty returns have drawn fresh attention to AI drama production, which many see as a potential source of new opportunities for grassroots content creators.

In the comments on a video interview with Zhang by the domestic outlet Yicai, some viewers said the project had inspired them to learn AI tools and try making dramas themselves. Others urged caution, noting the rise of scams disguised as AI-related courses.

The show’s success comes as the genre shifts toward higher production values. Until recently, short dramas were widely considered mindless entertainment defined by exaggerated interpersonal conflicts, formulaic characters, and implausible plots.

Recently, multiple AI short dramas exploring Chinese history have changed this perception. They include “Assuming a Noble Identity,” which premiered last year, and “Inkstone Edge Green Plum,” released this fall.

Critics, however, have called for tighter scrutiny of how AI-generated content depicts China’s past. Last year, China’s National Radio and Television Administration launched a campaign against AI-generated videos that alter or distort classic literary, film, and television works, particularly those based on historical, revolutionary, and heroic themes.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “Armed Into the Song Dynasty.” From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019263/How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
World.title: How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019263/How ‘Anxious China’ Changed Its Mind About Psychotherapy
World.content:
Editor’s note: Zhang Li is a professor of anthropology at the University of California, Davis, and the author of “Anxious China: Inner Revolution and Politics of Psychotherapy,” which explores how a new psychotherapeutic culture is taking root in China amid profound socioeconomic change. A Chinese version of the book was released this summer. Here, Zhang, who grew up in Kunming, capital of the southwestern Yunnan province, talks with The Paper about her personal journey, trends in mental health care, and the potential impact of artificial intelligence.

The Paper: In your book, you say that returning home to Kunming to conduct research into the city’s mental and psychological landscape was a “deeply emotional experience” that sometimes left you feeling vulnerable. How did your personal connection with Kunming shape this project?

Zhang: The idea for the book first came to me when I learned that my best friend from middle school had become a therapist. I was quite surprised. This was around 2000, when interest in psychology was just beginning to take off in China and few people knew anything about mental health counseling. When I talked to my friend about her work, I realized that it touched on all kinds of everyday issues but was relatively unexplored. Most of the anthropological field research I’d come across had been conducted outside China.

As I worked on the project, I discovered how deeply it was connected to my family. My mother died 13 years ago. Looking back, I realized she’d lived with post-traumatic stress disorder for much of her life. She lost her mother when she was 8 years old. Her father remarried, and her stepmother treated her and her siblings very badly.

Growing up, we became accustomed to her extreme emotional reactions, but we had no idea they were symptomatic of a psychological disorder. Back then, people simply described this behavior as having “a bad temper.” It was only after reading up on the subject that I came to understand that my mother had suffered from chronic anxiety and depression, but she lacked the language to express it.

Seeing a psychiatrist is more normalized now; back then, mental health was a taboo topic. When I began my fieldwork, my mother was 80. I repeatedly urged her to see a psychiatrist, and eventually she agreed. After a complicated and rather haphazard diagnostic process, she was prescribed a short course of Prozac, which helped improve her condition. In the final three years of her life, she was relatively at peace, and we could have calmer, more constructive conversations.

I chose Kunming for my fieldwork because it allowed me to leverage personal connections and familiarity with the local environment. In addition, scholars were already conducting similar research in major cities such as Beijing and Shanghai, so I wanted to look at a medium-sized city. Kunming was experiencing many of the same problems as larger cities amid China’s economic reforms and social transformation. Rapid, large-scale change inevitably causes disruption, and the psychological disruption individuals experience manifests in all kinds of ways.

Another factor, as I discuss in the book, is Kunming’s place in the history of psychotherapy in China. In 1988, the city hosted the country’s first Advanced Sino-German Psychotherapy Symposium. This earned Kunming a reputation as the “cradle of Chinese psychotherapy.”

The Paper: Why do you consider anxiety a key indicator for the pulse of contemporary Chinese society, and what distinguishes the anxiety here from that elsewhere in the world?

Zhang: Over the years, through interactions with people from diverse backgrounds, I’ve come to feel that Chinese people are an exceptionally anxious population, or as we say, neijuan, “involuted.” Some people are depressed or “low energy,” while others are energetic and highly strung, but anxiety is pervasive across social classes and age groups.

At the same time, anxiety is a global phenomenon. With our digital devices always at hand, constant exposure to news about climate change, geopolitical crises, and the threat of artificial intelligence further exacerbates our anxiety. Anthropologists in other countries, including India, Russia, Japan, and the United States, have found that people in all of these places experience anxiety. But while a general sense of anxiety may be shared across populations, specific trigger issues closely reflect local political, economic, and cultural pressures.

The Paper: The localization of psychotherapy is a central theme of the book. Based on your observations and personal experiences, what similarities and differences do you see between China and the United States?

Zhang: Psychotherapy began to take off in China in the late 1990s and early 2000s. In the West, psychotherapy has a much longer history and has undergone a lengthy process of professionalization. To become a licensed therapist in the U.S., you must complete an undergraduate degree and a master’s in counseling or psychology, and then accumulate a certain amount of clinical experience.

In China, the profession is relatively immature and poorly regulated. With low barriers to entry, practitioners vary widely in competence, and this makes it difficult to find a reliable, qualified therapist. A one-hour therapy session can cost 500 to 1,000 yuan ($75 to $150), making trial and error an expensive process.

In terms of specific techniques and theoretical schools, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is the predominant approach in Europe and the U.S. In China, a wide range of therapeutic approaches are popular. In my book, I focus primarily on Satir-based systematic family therapy, CBT, and Jungian psychology-inspired sandplay therapy.

I have a great deal of respect for Jungian sandplay therapy because it resonates in many ways with traditional Chinese culture. However, many young urban Chinese tend to favor therapeutic methods they consider to be “scientific,” and have little interest in methods associated with traditional culture. The Satir model was influential in the U.S. in the ’70s and ’80s, but is no longer popular. However, its emphasis on family relationships resonates with Chinese cultural values and has helped make the Satir model hugely popular here.

Another difference is that Western practitioners emphasize language and narrative, with sessions generally taking the form of a conversation between therapist and patient. Chinese people are less comfortable with talk therapy approaches, and the popular models tend to use both nonverbal and verbal methods.

The Paper: In the book, you argue that Chinese therapists have not just absorbed and imitated Western therapeutic methods but rather selected and adapted approaches suited to the needs of the Chinese population. Where have these localization efforts worked, and what role has the market played?

Zhang: Whenever psychotherapy enters a new country, it always undergoes a process of localization. The efforts and experiments therapists undertook to adapt Western therapies to Chinese contexts were necessary, but also challenging. It’s difficult to say definitively how successful they’ve been.

Some have made a significant impact. However, some localization efforts failed to preserve the essence of the original approaches, instead veering into something resembling ideological indoctrination — not a desirable outcome. But China’s psychotherapy field is still young, and there’s ample room for development.

The market has played a crucial role, because therapy is extremely expensive. In China and the West, therapy is mainly accessible to the middle and upper classes; it’s a luxury for the working class. With the exception of some mental health counseling services provided through psychiatric departments that can be covered by medical insurance, most therapy in China is paid for out of pocket. As a result, individuals’ ability to pay is an important factor shaping the development of the profession.

The Paper: You observe that by 2008, more than 100,000 people in China had obtained certification to work as counselors, yet less than 15% went on to work in the field, with many pursuing psychotherapy training as a form of self-care. Can psychotherapy training that excludes the patient-therapist relationship have a therapeutic effect?

Zhang: I found this phenomenon very interesting. When I spoke with individuals who had completed training programs, I discovered that many were facing difficulties in their lives, or problems in their marriages or relationships with their children. They wanted help, but when they sought a therapist, they found the cost prohibitively expensive. They figured they might as well spend that money on a counseling certification that could give them tools to help themselves and support their loved ones, as well as skills they could apply professionally. About 90% of interviewees had full-time jobs, including as teachers, police officers, and government employees. None of them intended to pursue careers in mental health care.

The therapeutic relationship is central to mental health care, and the effectiveness of therapy often depends on the rapport between client and counselor. However, these certification programs also involve close interactions among instructors and participants. Role-playing exercises add to this dynamic. The training environment functions as a safe therapeutic space, and the courses can have some therapeutic value for people dealing with relatively mild emotional difficulties.

When participants return home to their children or partners, they may not necessarily assume the role of a therapist, but the knowledge they’ve acquired may give them a new perspective on how to understand and interact with them.

The Paper: Why is it predominantly urban middle-class women participating in such programs?

Zhang: The people I interviewed were almost all middle class. A counseling certification program can cost thousands of yuan in tuition, and there may be additional expenses down the line. Lower-income urban residents already have their hands full making ends meet — they don’t have the time, energy, or financial resources to invest in these kinds of things. There are exceptions, of course. I encountered two migrant workers who pursued certifications after their children experienced serious mental health problems.

In the training courses I attended, the ratio was roughly nine women to every man. This discrepancy is partly related to gender stereotypes. In one course, I spoke with the sole male participant, a police officer, who told me his family was baffled by his decision to study counseling. They thought that when he encountered problems, he should just grin and bear it. But he found the training extremely helpful.

Generally, looking after the emotional well-being of family members is considered women’s responsibility, particularly when it comes to children’s emotional problems. This may be changing among younger generations, of course.

The Paper: Your book mentions the late-night talk show Xinli Fangtan, or “Psychological Time,” in the 2000s. Through counseling sessions, its guest experts sought to destigmatize family and work problems, framing them as social rather than medical problems. But today, mental health issues are increasingly medicalized, with hospital psychiatrists booked solid, and social media awash with clinical terms like “trauma” and ADHD. What’s behind this reversal?

Zhang: The medicalization of mental health problems and the individualization of structural problems are not phenomena unique to China; they are happening around the world. In the West, where psychology is much more developed, there has been considerable criticism of this trend. One of the main arguments is that psychology turns many social problems into individual problems, thereby eliminating the impetus to address the underlying structural issues.

But this is one side of a two-sided problem. On the other side, you have what my mother’s generation experienced: people talked only about social problems, never psychological ones. Many people were suffering, yet no medical resources or treatments were available to them. Now we’ve swung to the opposite extreme, where it seems every problem can be solved through therapy or medication. I don’t think this kind of binary thinking is helpful. Rather than treating every problem as either an individual medical issue or a social one, we need to understand how these factors interact and adopt corresponding approaches.

The Paper: You observe that corporate psychotherapy and mental health initiatives, framed as “psychological care,” are becoming new tools of management and control. What does this mean for employees?

Zhang: This is not limited to Chinese companies. In Western capitalist societies, it is very common for businesses to use mental health care as a tool of management and control.

For individuals in China, this approach has some appeal. In my interviews, many employees told me they liked it. Companies have outside experts or human resources staff lead sessions with employees. Rather than simply issuing instructions from above, they take a more egalitarian approach, offering advice on managing family and workplace relationships, or leading group activities such as meditation.

On the other hand, this form of management has attracted considerable criticism in the West. The mechanisms underlying it are often invisible: control over employees may operate at an unconscious level, potentially making it even more effective than overt coercion. However, based on my observations, this approach has some merits and should not be dismissed outright.

The Paper: Your fieldwork for the book ended in 2018. Have you continued to follow developments in this “inner revolution”?

Zhang: I’ve observed three major trends. First, public interest in psychology and mental health has increased. Second, many therapists report that their client numbers have declined in recent years and that fees have decreased. Many people are turning instead to online counseling services, which are cheaper and anonymous.

Third, the emergence of artificial intelligence has had a considerable impact. When people encounter problems, many turn first to free AI tools. Some even feel AI is more trustworthy than a therapist. Therapists have found that many clients who have consulted AI come into sessions with a clearer understanding of their problems. However, in more serious cases, timely medical intervention and medication may be necessary, which is where AI cannot replace a professional.

Reported by Zhu Fan.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Visuals from the book cover of “Anxious China: Inner Revolution and Politics of Psychotherapy” and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019255/China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
World.title: China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019255/China’s Hospital Companions Learn Where to Draw the Line
World.content:
SHANGHAI — When prospective clients contacted Li Shuping’s medical companion agency in Shanghai, their first question often had little to do with the hospital visit they were arranging.

“Patients used to ask first whether we were individuals or a legitimate agency,” Li tells Sixth Tone. Patients hire her company, Qingbeihu, to send a trained companion with them to hospital, helping with appointments, consultations, and paperwork.

The agency opened in September 2025, when almost anyone could advertise the same service on social media. And with people aged 60 or older accounting for 23% of China’s population by the end of 2025 and 59 million forecast to need care by 2030, more families were turning to companions to guide elderly relatives through hospital visits.

But written contracts were often absent, leaving services and fees unclear. Some patients faced unexpected charges once a visit was underway, with little recourse if they disputed them, prompting calls for tighter oversight.

But since Shanghai announced new rules for medical companion services effective July 1, Qingbeihu has received more inquiries, Li says. “Orders are growing steadily, and prospective clients seem more willing to trust the service.”

The rules cover medical companion services for Shanghai residents aged 60 and older and set requirements for worker qualifications, pricing transparency, and written contracts. They also require companions to wear identity badges, provide public lists of qualified agencies, and define responsibilities that include helping patients communicate with doctors and offering psychological support.

More recently, a national standard that took effect Nov. 1 covers medical companion services for patients of all ages across China. It also sets limits on what companions can do, prohibiting them from giving medical advice or making treatment decisions on patients’ behalf.

Following Shanghai’s new rules, Li says Qingbeihu now uses written risk and privacy agreements with patients and companions, as well as accident insurance for companions. For elderly clients unfamiliar with digital services, the agency also provides paper consent forms before a visit.

“Elderly people are very willing to have young people accompany them to seek care — it is also a kind of emotional support,” Li says.

For Qingbeihu’s six full-time companions, all under 30, the working day often begins as early as 5 a.m.

Patient work

By the time Li Suyu, not related to Li Shuping, meets a patient at the hospital around 7:30 a.m., she has already asked about their medical history, drug allergies, and mobility. She then checks registration details and organizes medical records and examination reports before the hospital opens at 8.

Once consultations begin, the 22-year-old accompanies patients to see their doctors, records treatment plans and prescribed medications, and arranges any examinations ordered. She also keeps family members informed and, after the visit, helps patients keep track of follow-up appointments and medication reminders.

In the afternoon, she takes patients for blood tests or ultrasounds, then collects their reports and mails them out. She often handles about 28 bookings a month, with as many as four on a busy day, each lasting two to four hours. At Qingbeihu, a two-hour booking costs 188 yuan ($26), while four hours of surgery accompaniment costs 360 yuan.

Li previously worked in sales and became interested in medical companionship after accompanying a family member to hospital and struggling with some of the procedures herself.

“I had no medical background, so even understanding the doctors’ terminology was difficult at first,” she recalls. When she encountered unfamiliar terms, she consulted more experienced colleagues.

At Qingbeihu, training covers first aid, hospital procedures, and organizing patient records. Companions also attend training at a Red Cross first-aid center and must pass an assessment organized by the Shanghai Association of Elderly Care Services and Aging Industry to obtain a medical companion certificate.

Much of the initial training is theoretical. Even after certification, newcomers must shadow experienced colleagues before taking bookings on their own.

“Many elderly patients become anxious in crowded hospitals, especially when they don’t know their way around,” Li says. She learned to calm them through conversation or small gestures, such as offering a bottle of water or some snacks.

One elderly patient with mid- to late-stage cancer initially refused to engage with her. He believed his illness was incurable and saw little point in spending money on treatment.

Li began talking to him about his family, listening as he spoke about his grandchildren. As he grew more comfortable with her, she encouraged him to continue treatment, reminding him that his relatives wanted him to recover. Li says he eventually agreed to cooperate with treatment.

Ma Xunru, a 60-year-old Shanghai retiree, had reservations when she hired a medical companion while her daughter was away on a business trip. She needed to visit a hospital for dizziness and cervical spine problems but worried that the companion might not be professional.

The crowds at the top-tier hospital made her dizziness worse. But her companion arranged appointments with two departments so she could see the doctors and complete the necessary examinations. Ma says that if she had gone alone or with her daughter, they would have registered with only one department.

“It was such a relief to have the companion with me. Otherwise I wouldn’t have known where to go,” Ma says. She now plans to use the service again.

“I think in the future I’ll ask my daughter to book a companion as well, so that I don’t need to bother her, since she’s busy with her work and life.”

Doctor’s orders

When Wang, a rehabilitation doctor in Shanghai, needed someone to accompany her for a gastroscopy, she hired a medical companion. Most of her friends were doctors, too, and asking one of them to come along would have meant rearranging a hospital shift.

She expected help preparing for the procedure and someone to talk to while she waited. “When taking the order, they only asked what time and where. And they were on their phone the whole time,” she recalls.

The experience helped prompt Wang, 25, to establish Zhuoyu Health with Zhou, 30, a gynecology and reproductive medicine doctor. Both asked to be identified only by their surnames.

Both had seen elderly patients struggle with hospital equipment such as self-service machines. Zhuoyu now has more than a dozen part-time companions drawn from rehabilitation, gynecology, anesthesiology, and the medical device industry.

Wang and Zhou found that questions they considered straightforward could leave patients at a loss, from what to do if they lost their ID card at a hospital to how to prepare for a CT scan. During consultations, they also help patients ask questions they might otherwise overlook and, afterward, understand their doctors’ instructions.

Wang’s first booking, in early June, involved an elderly woman whose health had suffered, she says, from using folk remedies during a long illness.

Before the visit, Wang and the woman’s son-in-law reviewed her medical records and the remedies she had been taking. With heavy rain that day, Wang rented a wheelchair for her. During an echocardiogram, she helped the woman adjust her clothing and explained each step.

Wang admitted to the family that she was handling her first booking. “I was very nervous taking my first order, and the patient’s family comforted me instead,” she recalls.

Zhou encountered a different problem while accompanying an elderly woman with poor hearing and limited Mandarin for a contrast-enhanced CT scan. The patient struggled to follow instructions requiring specific movements, and her anxious daughter began scolding her.

Zhou took the woman out of the examination room and explained what she needed to do. The second attempt went smoothly. “She wasn’t being uncooperative. She genuinely didn’t understand what she was supposed to do,” Zhou recalls telling the daughter.

Yang Hanxue, 25, decided to become a medical companion after seeing elderly people living alone and out-of-town patients struggle through hospital visits while she was working as a nurse.

Now at Qingbeihu, she adjusts her approach to different patients, explaining delays to those who are anxious, listening to those who want to talk, and keeping small talk to a minimum with people wary of the service.

Yang recalls a family wanting an elderly relative to undergo a full set of examinations, although the patient might not have been able to tolerate them. In such situations, she says, companions should remain neutral, relay the doctor’s advice, help families raise questions during consultations, and work toward an arrangement that accounts for the patient’s condition and the family’s wishes.

“Many people don’t understand this profession and mistakenly think we are experts, consulting us on how to treat illnesses,” Yang says. She tells patients and families to follow their doctor’s advice rather than offering treatment recommendations herself.

Wang recalls a patient who fell into a deep coma. The family eventually decided to discontinue treatment. Wang and Zhou say companions should not influence such decisions, but can offer support to relatives struggling with the choices they face.

Despite being a practicing doctor, Wang believes the boundaries of medical companionship need to be more clearly defined, particularly when patients ask companions to weigh in on treatment decisions.

“Patients often ask me, ‘The doctor recommended this — should I do it? Should I keep taking this medicine?’” she says.

Contributions: Marianne Gunnarsson; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A trained medical companion explains prescribed medication to an elderly couple at a traditional Chinese medicine hospital in Beijing, May 22, 2025. Jade GAO/AFP/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.title: Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019254/Zero-Sum: Nanjing Noodle Shops Set a Price Rivals Can’t Match
World.content:
A pair of Chinese noodle shops serving free meals sparked debate this week after their popularity reportedly disrupted neighboring shops’ business.

“Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop,” which opened two outlets last month in the densely populated Jiangning and Yuhuatai districts of Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, offers only one dish: noodles with braised vegetarian chicken and shiitake mushrooms. Each restaurant has around 50 seats, and since opening have been frequented mainly by middle-aged and elderly customers, according to domestic media.

Jiangning is home to a large migrant worker population, while Yuhuatai has the city’s largest public housing project. Signs outside the restaurants read, “A bowl of pure intention, with no fixed price; three meals a day, offered with warmth to those in need.”

The owner, surnamed Zhang, told domestic media he opened the shops for two reasons: promoting vegetarianism and charity. He said he had previously donated to charities and operated low-cost vegetarian restaurants but found that offering free noodles was the most effective way to achieve his philanthropic goals.

The two shops have served more than 1,000 bowls of noodles each day, Zhang said. He added that he had initially planned to open 10 stores, each serving 500 bowls a day, but demand had exceeded his expectations.

“Our idea was simple: get more people to come eat,” he said.

The topic has garnered more than 10 million views on microblogging platform Weibo, with many questioning whether the measures can genuinely help those in need.

Asked what they thought about the initiative, a local resident told domestic media, “It’s both good and bad. The good thing is that people who are genuinely struggling can come here to get a meal and meet their basic needs. The bad thing is, how can you tell who has money and who doesn’t?”

Other users suggested requiring customers to show their ID cards to exclude locals and help migrant workers.

In an interview with domestic media, Zhang rejected the idea of screening customers. “We want to give people facing difficulties a sense of dignity and respect,” he said.

Domestic media reported that one nearby restaurant’s daily revenue had fallen from 3,000 yuan ($450) to just a few hundred yuan. Another shop owner said he was considering not renewing his lease over concerns about declining customer traffic.

However, some shop owners said customer traffic along the street had already fallen after the relocation of several nearby factories. Others said the free noodle shops had not significantly affected their business.

Zhang told domestic media that affected business owners could work at his stores if they were willing.

He added that the two shops could lose up to 10 million yuan a year. The stores do not have payment QR codes, and he has also turned down donation offers from friends.

The shops have reportedly recently installed barriers to keep lines orderly and stopped providing noodle refills and napkins to discourage those who don’t truly need help from taking advantage of the offer.

Authorities told domestic media they had found no evidence that the restaurants were providing free meals as a publicity stunt. Local authorities also said they had visited the shops to check food safety compliance and help maintain order among customers queuing outside.



Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Crowds gather at a “zero-yuan noodle shop” in Nanjing, Jiangsu province, October 2026. From Weibo)

World.title: 49th ASEAN Summit closes, Philippines turns over chairmanship to Singapore
World.content:
Watch the closing ceremony of the 49th ASEAN Summit here

MANILA, Philippines – Leaders wrapped up the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits with a closing ceremony at the Philippine International Convention Center in Pasay City on Tuesday, November 17.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. emphasized that challenges confronting Southeast Asian nations have become “increasingly intertwined,” as he delivered his closing remarks.

“Energy security is also economic security. Maritime stability sustains peace, trade, and livelihoods. Technology brings opportunity, but also new questions of security and governance, inclusion. And climate change knows no frontiers, testing the resilience of our communities,” Marcos said.

“Our institutions must therefore become as connected as the challenges that we face, and ultimately every member state must be able to count on ASEAN and ASEAN must be able to count on every member.”

During the ceremony, 2026 ASEAN chair Philippines also turned over chairmanship of the regional bloc for 2027 to Singapore.

“To Prime Minister [Lawrence] Wong and the people of Singapore, we have the utmost confidence. We offer our friendship and our full and complete support,” Marcos said.

In his remarks, Wong congratulated the Philippines “on a very successful ASEAN chairmanship,” and thanked Marcos “for steering ASEAN through a difficult year.”

Wong also announced that Singapore has chosen “Deeper Integration, Wider Partnerships” as the theme for its ASEAN chairmanship in 2027, the year the bloc turns 60.

“‘Deeper Integration,’ because we can do much more to realize the full potential of ASEAN. This includes strengthening our links in finance, digital technologies, and energy. We must take further steps toward a single ASEAN market, where businesses can set up and operate more seamlessly across borders, and where our people can enjoy more opportunities to work, invest, and prosper,” Wong said.

“‘Wider Partnerships,’ because ASEAN must continue to be open and and outward-looking. At a time when the world is becoming more divided, our response is to keep building bridges, to strengthen ties with our partners…and to ensure that Southeast Asia remains a region where all countries can engage and cooperate.”

The speeches were followed by musical performances from Julie Anne San Jose, Gary Valenciano, and P-pop group SB19.

Watch the closing ceremony in the video above. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: 49th ASEAN Summit in Manila
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The global energy crisis, food security, and transnational crime are among the top issues on the table as Southeast Asian leaders and their allies converge in Manila.

The Philippines, chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations for 2026, is hosting the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits from Sunday, November 15, to Tuesday, November 17.

Aside from leaders and representatives of ASEAN’s 11 members, other world leaders will be in attendance, including United States President Donald Trump, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, and newly reelected Brazil President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who is embarking on a state visit to the Philippines before the summit.

During the summit’s closing ceremony, the Philippines will also turn over the ASEAN chairmanship to Singapore, which will lead the bloc in 2027.

World.content:
Here are today’s headlines – the latest news in the Philippines and around the world:

US President Donald Trump arrives in Manila for a state visit and to participate in the ASEAN-US Special Summit, amid protests from groups opposing his policies, especially the war on Iran and Pax Silica.

After Manila, US President Donald Trump will head to China on Wednesday, November 18, where he will meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and possibly North Korean leader Kim Jong-Un.

Filipino climate advocates at COP31 call for an independent probe into the arrests of hundreds of protesters during the ASEAN Summit in Manila. They emphasize the link between the fight for the planet and for human rights and democratic freedoms.

All 11 ASEAN member states sign a preliminary agreement saying they will work towards integrating the region’s electricity grids by 2045. The agreement focuses on infrastructure planning, policy development, and financing.
