World.title: Trump meets regional allies in Manila ahead of China visit
World.content:
QUAD LEADERS MEETING. US President Donald Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi attend a Quad (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue) summit, Paranaque City on November 17, 2026.

It is Trump's first meeting of the Quad grouping and he says the leaders' discussions would include security and the development of artificial intelligence

MANILA, Philippines – US President Donald Trump met the leaders of regional allies India, Japan, and Australia in the Philippines on Tuesday, November 17, at the start of an Asian trip that also includes a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts.

Trump arrived in the Philippine capital at the tail end of a Southeast Asian summit, and began his three-day regional visit with the first meeting in two years of the Quad group of Indo-Pacific democracies.

“Our countries are the four corners of a free, open, stable, and prosperous Indo-Pacific,” Trump said in remarks ahead of the meeting. “We have outstanding relationships and coordinate closely on matters of regional security, economic security and diplomacy.”

Trump’s three-day trip to Asia, which also includes the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, comes after his Republican Party’s defeat in midterm elections, plus spy allegations and new US curbs on China’s access to AI chips that could complicate a fragile trade-war truce.

Demonstrators gathered in Manila for a fifth day of protests that have included the burning of Trump effigies, calls for an end to the Middle East war and the scrapping of the US-led Pax Silica supply chain initiative.

It was Trump’s first meeting of the Quad grouping — which his predecessor Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative — and he said the leaders’ discussions would include security and the development of artificial intelligence.

“We want to ensure that the future of this critical technology is dominated by nations that share our values and our common interests and make sure that it turns out to be as good as it can be,” Trump said, announcing the Quad would launch a new AI accelerator.

Trump arrived at the end of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit and after the Quad meeting will join a US-ASEAN “Special Summit” later on Tuesday.

It comes ahead of the APEC gathering hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, who has previously objected to the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing. Quad members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.

Quad meeting the ‘best possible signal’

At the ASEAN summit on Monday, Chinese Premier Li Qiang hailed what he called the “truly extraordinary” economic achievements of China and ASEAN in the face of global trade restrictions, expressing Beijing’s commitment to free trade and the need to “stand united, ward off interference, and work together”.

China is ASEAN’s largest trading partner and a key source of investment, but the biggest economies of the 11-member bloc — which has a combined GDP of more than $3.9 trillion — want to deepen ties with the US despite protracted trade and diplomatic uncertainty under the Trump administration.

Former US Deputy Secretary of State Kurt Campbell credited Washington’s top diplomat, Marco Rubio, with the timing and reconvening of the Quad, which he said had lost ambition under Trump.

“Part of what he (Rubio) is thinking is that this is probably the best possible signal if you’re going to go into a trilateral meeting,” said Campbell, co-founder of The Asia Group, referring to Thursday’s US-China-Russia talks.

“The linchpin of everything that we do in Asia is the US-Japan relationship, and a perception that this is not at the top of the president’s mind would concern me.”

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales on Friday said that under Trump’s leadership, the Quad had demonstrated it is “a partnership of action, tackling the region’s toughest challenges and driving opportunities to ensure a free and open Indo-Pacific.”

A Japanese foreign ministry official said it was expected that Quad leaders would try to show unity, with maritime security, export restrictions, critical-minerals supply-chain diversification and AI among potential discussion points.

Japan to play more proactive role, PM says

ASEAN’s leaders held meetings on Tuesday involving counterparts from Japan, South Korea, China, and India.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi pledged to work with ASEAN to boost regional economic and energy resilience, to address export restrictions and vulnerabilities from rapid AI development, and to strengthen supply chains, including on critical minerals.

“While the international order is experiencing a period of great instability, Japan will play an ever more proactive role,” Takaichi said.

Trump was due to sign a joint statement with Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul on Tuesday on an agreement on reciprocal trade. Thai media have reported the two would hold talks and the statement would be about progress on negotiations.

The US is Thailand’s largest export market, accounting for 24% of its total shipments this year. The US designated Thailand as a major non-NATO ally in 2003.

Trump will meet Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr on Wednesday, before heading to Shenzhen. – Rappler.com

World.title: Caloocan DPWH deals with Malapitan kin raise conflict-of-interest questions
World.content:
INAUGURATION. Mayor Dale 'Along' Malapitan delivers his remarks after the blessing and turnover of a covered court in Barangay 174 in Caloocan City's 1st District in November 2024. His father, Caloocan 1st District Oscar 'Oca' Malapitan, is seated behind him.

Mayor Along Malapitan is the son-in-law of a government contractor who had won DPWH projects in Caloocan City, mostly in the 1st District where his father, Oscar, is congressman

There are many government contractors in Caloocan City, but one, in particular, got the attention of locals because of its links to the city’s dominant political dynasty.

The contractor drew little attention outside Caloocan, even when it appeared on a list of alleged Malacañang-dictated budget insertions cited by fugitive resigned lawmaker Zaldy Co in November 2025.

After months in hiding following his implication in the flood control scandal, Co broke his silence with a series of Facebook videos. He tagged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and then-speaker Martin Romualdez as the alleged masterminds of P100 billion in insertions in the 2025 budget.

Co released a 20-page list of insertions that Marcos allegedly requested, through Palace officials, at the bicameral conference committee level. He claimed he never received a single centavo from government coffers. Malacañang and Romualdez denied the allegations and challenged him to submit them formally under oath.

Two projects on Co’s list, worth a total of P188 million, named Ave-Mira Construction and Trading as contractor.

Days after Co’s bombshell, concerned citizen Christopher Orongan, a former soldier, asked on Facebook: “Marami yatang projects sa Caloocan itong Ave-Mira Construction and Trading. Sino kaya ang may-ari nito? Kilala ba?”

(Ave-Mira Construction and Trading seems to have many projects in Caloocan. I wonder who its owner is? Are they known?)

Five days later, Orongan asked a more pointed question: “Sino si Avelino Narciso? Related ba sa asawa ng kasalukuyang Mayor ng Caloocan City (Who is Avelino Narciso? Is he related to the wife of the incumbent Caloocan City mayor)?”

Even after Orongan answered his own question, the posts gained little traction. Interest was localized, limited to Caloocan netizens or those aware of city politics. Public attention was focused on the top 15 flood control contractors Marcos had named months earlier, the resulting congressional inquiries, and the fugitive Co.

The government investigation into flood control corruption was already in full swing, after Marcos formed the Independent Commission for Infrastructure (ICI) in September 2025.

Ave-Mira

Ave-Mira was established in Orani, Bataan, and is named after owner Avelino Narciso and his wife, Edelmira. Their daughter, Aubrey, is the wife of Caloocan City Mayor Dale Gonzalo “Along” Malapitan.

The company’s General Information Sheet filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission in July 2025 lists the following:

Narciso as the corporate secretary with a 33% share

Son-in-law Rome Sicat as chairman with 33.5%

Sicat’s wife, Abba Narciso Sicat, as treasurer with 33.5%

Rome and Abba both served on the Orani Municipal Council. Rome was town councilor from 2010 to 2019, while Abba was first elected in 2019 and is on her third term.

Ave-Mira began getting Department of Public Works and Highways contracts in 2019, starting with a project in Orani. That year, it secured eight DPWH contracts: seven in Bataan and one in Caloocan. Its other contracts are as follows:

Bataan, 2019 to 2025: 49 contracts worth P727,956,762.16. 14 of them were in Orani.

49 contracts worth P727,956,762.16. 14 of them were in Orani. Bulacan, 2021 to 2024: P51,463,463 worth of road, building and flood control contracts under the Bulacan 1st District Engineering Office. Senator Panfilo Lacson highlighted that office in his August 2025 privilege speech on flood control corruption.

P51,463,463 worth of road, building and flood control contracts under the Bulacan 1st District Engineering Office. Senator Panfilo Lacson highlighted that office in his August 2025 privilege speech on flood control corruption. Quezon City: the company also secured government contracts here.

Malapitan political dynasty and Narcisos

The Malapitans’ rise to the dominant political dynasty in Caloocan City started with their patriarch, Oscar, who served as Caloocan councilor from 1992 to 1998, vice mayor from 1998 to 2001, and 1st District congressman from 2004 to 2013. He was mayor from 2013 to 2022, and has been congressman again since 2022.

Along was 1st District councilor when he married Aubrey Narciso in 2013. That year, he sought his father’s congressional seat but lost to then-outgoing mayor Recom Echiverri. He ran again in 2016 and won.

He was reelected in 2019, and by the end of his second term in 2022, his father was a term-limited mayor. The two won each other’s posts in the 2022 elections and were both reelected in 2025.

Along’s brother, Enteng, entered politics in 2019 as a 1st District councilor. He won a third term in 2025 and will serve until 2028.

Narciso was among Along’s donors in the last two elections. He donated P3 million to his son-in-law’s 2022 election campaign, and the same amount to his 2025 election campaign, according to Along’s Statements of Contributions and Expenditures (SOCEs) obtained by Rappler from the Commission on Elections (Comelec).

From 2019 to 2025, while Along and Oscar were either congressman or city mayor, Ave-Mira got 39 DPWH projects in Caloocan City worth P731,368,859.87. Two were joint ventures with Orani Construction and Supply Corporation.

In early November 2024, Congressman Malapitan and Mayor Along led the blessing and turnover of covered courts in Barangays 174 and 176, both in the 1st District.

A post on the congressman’s official Facebook page was accompanied by his photos with Along. It said in part, “Mula sa pondong inilaan ni Congressman Oca Malapitan sa mga proyektong ito, binuksan ito sa publiko partikular sa mga residente upang kanilang magamit at pagdausan ng iba’t ibang aktibidad.”

(From the funds allocated by Congressman Oca Malapitan for these projects, these were opened to the public particularly for the residents’ use and for their activities.)

The post added that the congressman will continue supporting the Caloocan government’s goals of building more infrastructure for the people’s welfare and community development.

The Barangay 176 covered court cost P4,876,621.09, and the Barangay 174 covered court, P6,805,023.78. Ave-Mira was the contractor for both courts.

Based on contracts on the DPWH website, covered courts in Metro Manila typically cost at least P4.8 million in 2024, but could cost double that, or more, depending on size and features.

Responses

Rappler asked the DPWH Metro Manila 3rd District Engineering Office, which implemented the projects, how Ave-Mira’s Caloocan contracts were procured.

In a letter, it replied: “Based on official records, the projects were procured and implemented in accordance with applicable procurement laws, rules, regulations, and DPWH procedures. Any variation orders, extensions, additional works, or other modifications, if applicable, were likewise processed in accordance with existing rules.”

District Engineer Maria Cristina Tacardon added: “No formal complaint from the concerned end-users regarding project implementation has been received or recorded by this Office. However, this does not cover concerns raised through other channels.”

On possible communications, endorsements, recommendations or interventions in choosing Ave-Mira, she said her office “can only confirm matters supported by official records.”

We reached out to Mayor Along’s office from September 21 to November 6 through his and city hall’s official emails, asking about possible conflicts of interest. A physical letter sent to city hall on November 4 was acknowledged and received the same day.

We also contacted Ave-Mira through the email addresses in their GIS on September 21, and followed up by text and Viber until November 7.

We will update this story once they respond.

Laws, bills on conflict of interest

The Philippine Constitution and various laws prohibit conflicts of interest. Politicians are barred from holding paid occupations other than their elective posts, and from having direct or indirect financial interests in government contracts.

The Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees, Section 4(c) states: Public officials and employees “shall not dispense or extend undue favors on account of their office to their relatives whether by consanguinity or affinity.”

The Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act, Section 4(a) also states: It is illegal for any person having a familial relationship with any public official to take advantage of it by directly or indirectly requesting or receiving an advantage from “any other person having some business, transaction, application, request or contract with the government, in which such public official has to intervene.”

Meanwhile, Section 89(a) of the Local Government Code prohibits local public officials and employees from directly or indirectly engaging in a business transaction in a local government unit where they serve.

Congress has proposed measures to address the problem of conflict of interest.

Senate Bill No. 1962 (Government Contracting and Procurement Act), approved on final reading in September: It would ban relatives of public officials within the fourth degree of consanguinity and affinity from all government contracts. The House version is pending.

(Government Contracting and Procurement Act), approved on final reading in September: It would ban relatives of public officials within the fourth degree of consanguinity and affinity from all government contracts. The House version is pending. House Bill No. 9142 (Electoral Conflict of Interest Prevention Act): It would require candidates to submit a sworn declaration that they and their immediate family have had no interest in government contracts in the five years before filing their certificate of candidacy.

(Electoral Conflict of Interest Prevention Act): It would require candidates to submit a sworn declaration that they and their immediate family have had no interest in government contracts in the five years before filing their certificate of candidacy. House Bill No. 9906 (New Party-list System Act): It would bar political dynasty members, incumbent elective officials, recent electoral candidates, and persons with direct financial interests in government contracts from being party-list nominees.

Power of the people

The push for more laws shows how difficult it is to address conflict of interest. This is magnified by the infrastructure corruption scandal and the proliferation of “politicontractors.”

Asked about Ave-Mira’s Caloocan contracts, People’s Budget Coalition national coordinator Mary Abigail Modales told Rappler: “Is there potential conflict of interest? Yes, there is potential conflict of interest. But before we reach a conclusion, we have to be careful because we’re accusing someone of conflict of interest.”

Modales said that to determine conflict of interest, these issues must first be addressed: beneficial ownership of the company, degree of relationship, receipt of undue benefit, and if the biddings were rigged or influenced by a public official to favor a contractor.

GoodGovPH chairperson Bryan Ezra Gonzales said ordinary citizens should know how to spot red flags in government projects and what to do about them.

He cited transparency watchdogs and government feedback mechanisms — Bisto Proyekto, Sumbong sa Pangulo, the Department of Budget and Management’s Project Digital Information for Monitoring and Evaluation (DIME), and the DPWH which, he said, has been “pro-active” on complaints under Vince Dizon.

He also acknowledged that many people are wary of becoming a whistleblower, underscoring the need for better government protection for them.

With the country nearing another election year, Gonzales offered a reminder: “One way wherein the public can collectively hold someone to account, someone in elective office, is to vote them out.” – Rappler.com

Eunicito Barreno is a 2026 Aries Rufo Fellow. He is a senior journalism student at the University of the Philippines Diliman, where he is also a news staffer at the Philippine Collegian, the university’s official student publication.

World.title: What will Gamaliel Cordoba, Marcos’ newest SC pick, bring to Padre Faura?
World.content:
CORDOBA. In this file photo, due to lack of time, the Commission on Appointments postponed the confirmation of then-COA chair Gamaliel Cordoba, on November 23, 2022.

Cordoba was the NTC commissioner when the Duterte administration launched a crackdown against ABS-CBN and Bulatlat. He also has ties with a big fishing company.

Gamaliel Asis Cordoba entered President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration in 2022 when Commission on Audit (COA) chairperson Jose Calida resigned just months into his post.

On November 13, Cordoba’s strong ties with Marcos became apparent again after the President picked him as his third appointee to the Supreme Court (SC). Cordoba replaced former associate justice Amy Lazaro Javier, an appointee of former president Rodrigo Duterte, who retired on November 16.

He is the latest Marcos appointee to the High Court after Associate Justice Raul Villanueva in 2025, and recently, Chief Justice Rodil Zalameda on November 5. He is the country’s 196th SC associate justice.

This brings the number of Marcos appointees to the High Court to three, compared with two appointed by the late former president Benigno Aquino III and nine by former president Rodrigo Duterte. Zalameda’s appointment as chief justice leaves another vacancy in the associate justice post.

Cordoba served for four years and a month in COA, the government institution mandated to audit government finances and purchases. In 2022 and 2023, he was external auditor of the International Labour Organization.

Under Cordoba, COA issued a notice of disallowance on Vice President Sara Duterte’s P73-million confidential funds for the Office of the Vice President (OVP), and P75 million for the Department of Education (DepEd)

While COA has already cleared the DepEd funds, it affirmed with finality the disallowance against the OVP. (READ: With finality: COA affirms disallowance of Sara Duterte’s P73-M confidential funds)

It was also under Cordoba in 2024 when the commission started delaying the publication of its Annual Audit Reports or AAR. Budget transparency advocates, journalists, and even politicians rely on AARs to check how agencies used their funds and if there are red flags from these transactions.

Advocates criticized the delay in publication, asserting that it neither indicated transparency nor established credibility.

ABS-CBN, Bulatlat crackdown

Cordoba was the longest serving commissioner of the National Telecommunications Commission (NTC) — from 2009 to 2022.

He was the NTC commissioner when former president Duterte waged a campaign against media giant ABS-CBN that ultimately led to the network’s shutdown.

At the height of the controversy, Cordoba said in one of the legislative inquiries in 2020 that the NTC would “most likely” issue a provisional authority so ABS-CBN could continue operating pending a franchise renewal. Cordoba also said at the time that ABS-CBN had no standing penalties with the NTC.

But ABS-CBN’s franchise expired and was not renewed during Duterte’s term. Its shutdown led to the retrenchment of around 5,000 personnel.

When Cordoba was still with the NTC, the website of alternative news site Bulatlat was also blocked.

Before the end of Duterte’s term in 2022, then-national security adviser Hermogenes Esperon Jr. wrote to Cordoba, requesting the commission to “order Philippine Internet Service Providers (ISPs) to block access to the following websites affiliated [with] and are supporting these terrorists and terrorist organizations.”

Esperon used the highly contested anti-terror law to justify the request. He also cited affiliations with terrorist organizations without providing substantial evidence.

After a legal battle, Bulatlat’s website was unblocked after the news site won against the NTC and Esperon in court.

But this was not the only issue that Cordoba got embroiled in.

A Rappler investigation in 2024 showed that the family of Cordoba’s wife, Monica Elena Cordoba, partly owns the commercial fishing company Mercidar Fishing Corporation. A copy of Cordoba’s 2023 Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth obtained by Rappler showed that he was also a shareholder of Mercidar in 2015 and 2019 — the years when he was already with the NTC.

To avoid conflicts of interest, Section 9 of the Code of Conduct for Public Officials requires officials to divest themselves of their shareholdings or financial interest within 60 days of taking office. Rappler found that during Cordoba’s time in the NTC, the commission stopped issuing service numbers for trackers that would prevent unregulated fishing.

Mercidar is central to the municipal waters issue. Originally, 15-kilometer municipal waters were exclusively for small fisherfolk.

But in December 2023, Malabon City Regional Trial Court Judge Zaldy Docena allowed Mercidar to operate within the 15-kilometer municipal waters except in shallow waters (less than 7 fathoms deep). A year later, in 2024, the SC affirmed this decision.

From Arroyo to Marcos

Although not a politician, Cordoba has proven to be somewhat of a political survivor, having served under four presidents: Gloria Macapagal Arroyo, Aquino, Duterte, and Marcos.

Arroyo appointed him in 2009, and the succeeding presidents kept him as part of their administrations until his appointment to the COA, an independent body.

His COA profile claimed that Cordoba’s stint in the NTC saw the improvement in the country’s internet connectivity. It also said that under him, the NTC broke the long-time duopoly in the country’s telecommunications industry.

“The country’s fixed broadband and mobile internet speeds remarkably improved globally under his leadership with Ookla Speedtest Global Index now ranking the Philippines 41st out of 180 countries globally for fixed broadband and 79th out of 140 countries for mobile,” said Cordoba’s profile.

“… The NTC broke the long-time duopoly in the telecommunications industry by successfully selecting a third telco through a most transparent bidding process under the guidance of the International Telecommunication Union,” it added.

Cordoba is a government official through and through. In 2010, Arroyo gave him the Presidential Medal of Merit “for his exemplary performance and service delivery to the Filipino people.”

He has also held the following positions in government:

director of the Office of Presidential Chief of Staff (2001-2002)

assistant executive secretary (2002-2003)

undersecretary, Office of the President (2003-2006)

appointments secretary, Office of the President (2006-2007)

member of board of directors, Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation (2008-2009)

Before joining government, Cordoba worked as an associate lawyer at Siguion Reyna, Montecillo and Ongsiako Law Offices. He also worked as a tax lawyer at accounting firm SyCip Gorres Velayo and Co.

The new SC associate justice joined the long list of High Court magistrates who are products of the Ateneo de Manila University. He earned his economics degree from the university in 1992, then his juris doctor four years later. Cordoba passed the Bar in 1997 with Roll No. 42213.

Like Zalameda, Cordoba is a member of the Fraternal Order of Utopia.

Play Video

Contribution to the SC

To secure his SC appointment, Cordoba had to beat other strong contenders.

Some of the shortlisted nominees for the post have been serving in the judiciary for decades, or are respected lawyers like Solicitor General Darlene Marie Berberabe, whom Marcos did not pick in the last two selections for SC justice.

Cordoba applied only once and got the job.

During his Judicial and Bar Council interview on October 13, Cordoba said he applied for the position because he felt like it was the “time” to seek higher office. He said he believed it was his chance to affect more people and have a lasting legacy in public service.

Given his experience with mainly executive offices, the new justice said he would bring to the SC en banc a different perspective in handling cases. He said he believed that while having judicial experience was an advantage for an associate justice, his executive experience was something that should be considered too.

“We’re bringing many facets and many fresh new ideas which we can inject into the decisions,” he said.

As an associate justice, Cordoba promised to support the SC’s Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations or SPJI. He said the program has to continue and be expanded even more, adding that the initiative brings the courts closer to people.

SPJI is the brainchild of former chief justice Alexander Gesmundo that introduced innovations in the judiciary, including digitalization. The project has been running since 2022 and will end in 2027.

Play Video

As an SC justice, Cordoba said he would be the type who would follow what’s written in the 1987 Constitution and existing jurisprudence. He said he would act according to the Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability.

Cordoba also said he would inhibit himself if cases he participated in under the NTC, COA, and related offices found their way to the Supreme Court. – Rappler.com

World.title: Japan proposes creation of ‘Asian’ IEA
World.content:
WOMAN PM. Japan's Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae arrives at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport to attend the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and Related Summits in Manila on November 16, 2026.

Under the initiative, Japan would also offer its unused oil storage facilities to other countries and help them develop own stockpiling systems

MANILA, Philippines – Japan on Tuesday, November 17, proposed the creation of a regional task force to strengthen cooperation on oil stockpiling and coordinate the release of supplies during emergencies.

Japan Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae announced the proposed Asia Oil Security Task Force during the fourth Asia Zero-Emission Community (AZEC) Leaders’ Meeting in Manila.

“We intend to promote as an equivalent of Asian version of the IEA (International Energy Agency),” Takaichi said.

The Middle East oil crisis exposed vulnerabilities in the global and Philippine energy security, driven by heavy reliance on fossil fuels and imports and critical shipping routes such as the Strait of Hormuz.

In a separate interview, Japan Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) Press Secretary Toshihiro Kitamura elaborated on the proposal, saying that Japan — under the initiative — would offer its unused oil storage facilities to other countries and help them develop their own oil stockpiling systems.

“We have suggested to utilize our crude oil stockpiling facilities in Japan, which is not utilized. By utilizing those unused stockpiling facilities, we can stockpile in advance the crude oil purchased in Middle East or other countries,” Kitamura told reporters. (Watch this video below on how Japan’s national petroleum stockpiling helps ensure its energy security:

Play Video

Kitamura said discussions on the proposed task force’s operational rules were still ongoing, including the possible fees other countries would pay to use Japan’s unused storage facilities.

“Under AZEC 2.0 POWERR Asia initiative, we are going to support Asian countries, especially ASEAN countries, to be more resilient by providing such a stockpiling system either individually, or jointly in the region,” he added.

Speaking at the AZEC summit, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said stockpiling alone would not be enough to ensure energy security. He said the Philippines is actively advancing its strategic petroleum reserve and welcoming “high-impact investments across our energy landscape, from renewables, grid modernization, and energy storage to natural gas, energy efficiency, and emerging technologies that contribute to overall regional energy security”.

“Sustainable and enduring energy security demands that oil-consuming and oil-producing nations act in unison. We must deepen information sharing and practical storage arrangements, as well as commit to upholding international law to keep sea lanes open and maintain fair, transparent markets,” Marcos said.

Apart from Japan and the Philippines, other AZEC partner countries include Australia, Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.

Japan, PH ink agreement on strategic petroleum reserve

In a related development, the Philippines and Japan signed a memorandum of cooperation (MOC) to advance the country’s strategic petroleum reserve and strengthen its preparedness against global oil supply disruptions.

Energy Secretary Sharon Garin and Japan’s Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry Ryosei Akazawa signed the agreement on Monday, November 16, which provides a framework for developing, managing, and releasing strategic reserves, while opening the door for Japanese participation in stockpiling projects led by the Philippine National Oil Company (PNOC).

“Japan will help us establish more storage facilities for fuel products, whether that is diesel, gas or crude oil,” Garin said.

The agreement also covers the development of oil storage facilities and the identification of financing arrangements. Japanese agencies will assist the Philippines through capacity-building, oil security assessments, and policy development, providing technical expertise and support in managing strategic reserves, Garin added.

“We can establish our own oil tanks, or ports and jetties. We do have our own storage facilities for oil. But we need to know how to manage all these strategic reserves,” she said.

“We will start on capacity-building, especially with PNOC,” Garin added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Trump arrives in Manila for state visit, ASEAN-US Special Summit
World.content:
STATE VISIT. US President Donald Trump disembarks Air Force One upon arrival at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport to attend the ASEAN-US Summit, in Pasay City, Metro Manila, Philippines, November 17, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) US President Donald Trump will also meet with fellow Quad leaders in Manila where protests against Pax Silica and the US war on Iran await him

MANILA, Philippines – US President Donald Trump arrived in Manila late Tuesday afternoon, November 17, for a state visit and to participate in the ASEAN-US Special Summit and the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue (Quad) leaders’ summit on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit.

Trump was personally welcomed by Executive Secretary Ralph Recto, representing President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.; House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, the President’s son; and Philippine Ambassador to the US Babe Romualdez.

The US leader received a grand welcome upon his arrival at the airport where there were over 80 cultural dancers, over 40 students waving small Philippine flags, and five beauty queens. A band played the Village People’s “YMCA” — Trump’s anthem — as the US leader made his way from Air Force One to the helicopter that would bring him and his delegation to the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC), where the 49th ASEAN Summit had just concluded.

“Thank you,” he said to the crowd at the airport, and pumped his fist before he boarded the helicopter.

Trump arrived in Manila amid protests from groups opposed to his policies, especially the US war on Iran and his administration’s vaunted Pax Silica initiative. Hundreds had been arrested in relation to the protests that began on November 15, the opening of the 49th ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.

Before Trump’s late afternoon arrival on Tuesday, ASEAN leaders held meetings with Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, Chinese Premier Li Qiang, and Indian President Narendra Modi, ahead of the annual East Asia Summit.

Trump skipped the East Asia Summit but will join a US-ASEAN Special Summit as well as the Quad leaders’ summit, both scheduled after the conclusion of the ASEAN Summit.

The meeting of the Quad — the US, Japan, Australia, and India — will be Trump’s first and takes place two years after the last gathering of the group, which his predecessor Joe Biden regarded as a signature foreign policy initiative.

It comes just ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping who previously objected to the Quad as an effort to encircle Beijing. Quad members have said the grouping is not directed against any one country.

On Wednesday, November 18, Trump will have bilateral meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in Malacañang, to be followed by a state luncheon in his honor before he departs for the APEC Summit in Shenzen.

Trump’s Asia trip, which also includes a much-anticipated trilateral meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts in Shenzen, comes after his Republican Party’s defeat in midterm elections and spy allegations that could complicate a fragile trade-war truce between the US and China. – With reports from Jelo Mantaring, Reuters/Rappler.com

World.title: Former Vatican envoy to PH, Archbishop Antonio Franco dies at 89
World.content:
Archbishop Antonio Franco, former apostolic nuncio to the Philippines —CBCP News/Diocese of Cerreto Sannita-Telese-Sant’agata De’ Goti, Italy

MANILA, Philippines — Archbishop Antonio Franco, who represented the Vatican in the Philippines for seven years and later served in diplomatic posts across Europe and the Middle East, died in Italy on Nov. 15. He was 89.

Franco died at Rummo Hospital in Benevento, Italy, after being admitted days earlier, according to the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) News.

Bishop Giuseppe Mazzafaro of the Diocese of Cerreto Sannita-Telese-Sant’Agata de’ Goti confirmed his death on Nov. 15.

Article continues after this 

Franco served as apostolic nuncio to the Philippines from 1999 to 2006, a period that included the 2001 Edsa II People Power uprising and changes in the country’s Catholic Church structure, including the creation of new dioceses following the reorganization of the Archdiocese of Manila.

READ: CBCP backs ‘genuine and effective’ anti-dynasty law

His diplomatic assignments later took him to Ukraine, Israel and Cyprus. He also served as apostolic delegate to Jerusalem and Palestine.

Franco had also been posted in Bolivia, Iran and France, and served at the Holy See’s permanent mission to the United Nations in New York.

Church leader remember Franco

Cardinal Pablo Virgilio David also expressed sadness over Franco’s death, remembering the former apostolic nuncio with affection and gratitude.

Article continues after this 

“I remember him with great fondness,” David said in a Facebook post, recalling Franco’s time as the Vatican’s representative in the Philippines.

David also credited the late archbishop for leaving a lasting impression on him, particularly through his encouragement when he was appointed auxiliary bishop of San Fernando in 2006.

Article continues after this 

READ: Cardinal David warns vs human, environmental costs of Pax Silica

He said the episcopal ring he received through Franco remains on his finger 20 years later, serving as a reminder of the nuncio’s generosity and encouragement to embrace his calling.

Franco was born in Puglianello, Italy, on March 24, 1937, and was ordained a priest for the Diocese of Cerreto Sannita-Telese-Sant’Agata de’ Goti on July 10, 1960.

He entered the Vatican diplomatic service in 1972 and spent more than four decades representing the Holy See before retiring in August 2012.

His remains arrived on Nov. 16 at the Parish of St. James the Apostle in Puglianello, where a wake was held. His funeral Mass is scheduled for Tuesday at the Church of St. Alphonsus Maria de’ Liguori in Telese Terme, Italy. /cb

World.title: CIDG seizes P2.42M worth of illegal ‘ukay-ukay’ in Bacolod City
World.content:
BACOLOD CITY, NEGROS OCCIDENTAL, Philippines — Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) operatives arrested a 39-year-old man and seized 60 bales of undocumented imported used clothing, locally known as “ukay-ukay,” valued at P2.42 million, during a joint law enforcement operation in Barangay Cabug here on Monday afternoon, Nov. 16.

Operatives from the CIDG Regional Field Unit–Negros Island Region, together with the CIDG Bacolod City Field Unit, the Provincial Intelligence Unit of the Negros Occidental Police Provincial Office, and Bacolod City Police Station 9, carried out the operation.

They apprehended the suspect, identified only as “Archie,” of Mabini, Bohol, while he was allegedly unloading and selling the assorted secondhand garments, the CIDG reported.

Article continues after this 

READ: Has thrifting lost its identity?

The CIDG said the suspect failed to present importation documents, customs declarations, import permits, or proof of payment of duties and taxes.

Aside from the confiscated garments, authorities also impounded the truck used to transport the contraband.

READ: ‘Reloving’ preloved

In a statement, Maj. Gen. Robert AA Morico II, CIDG Director, said that the commercial importation of used clothing and rags is strictly prohibited under Republic Act No. 4653, except for approved specific relief purposes.

Article continues after this 

The law was enacted to safeguard public health and maintain national dignity by preventing the entry of potentially unsanitary textiles into the country.

The CIDG warned the public that purchasing undocumented “ukay-ukay” poses health and hygiene risks, as smuggled garments bypass formal sanitation and quarantine inspections. Unwashed secondhand clothes may carry fungal infections, scabies, lice, bed bugs, or harsh chemical residues from warehouse fumigation.

Article continues after this 

The CIDG leadership commended the CIDG Negros Island Region Field Unit, headed by Colonel Dominick S. Poblete, for the successful operation, noting that it underscores the unit’s sustained campaign against illegal trade.

The agency assured the public of its commitment to consumer protection and urged buyers to choose safe, legal alternatives such as locally sourced thrift drives and homegrown Filipino apparel brands.

Citizens are also encouraged to report large-scale smuggling, illegal warehousing, and unauthorized distribution of imported used clothing in their communities, the CIDG said. /cb

World.title: Motorcycle rider killed in road crash in Ilocos Norte
World.content:
Inquirer files

SAN ILDEFONSO, ILOCOS SUR, Philippines — A motorcycle rider died after crashing into roadside barriers along the Piddig-Carasi Road in Barangay Abucay, Piddig, Ilocos Norte, on Monday afternoon, Nov. 16.

Police said the victim, a 40-year-old resident of Piddig, was traveling west on a white Yamaha Mio Gear motorcycle when he reached a curve and slammed into the roadside barriers at 3:30 p.m.

According to the investigators, the impact left the victim, with fractures to the right side of his ribs, severe abdominal injuries, and multiple wounds and abrasions on the right side of his body, according to the Piddig Municipal Police Station.

Article continues after this

World.title: Anti-Pax Silica banners removed minutes after posting in Isabela universities
World.content:
The anti-Pax Silica banner displayed at the Philippine Normal University-Isabela Campus in Alicia, Isabela, was taken down within minutes of being put up on Nov. 17. —Photos courtesy of PNU student publication The Torch Norluzonian

ECHAGUE, ISABELA, Philippines — Anti-Pax Silica tarpaulin banners displayed at two universities in Isabela were taken down within minutes of being put up on Tuesday, Nov. 17. This, amid farmers and youth groups voicing continuous opposition to the United States-led international initiative that will be set up in Capas, Tarlac, citing concerns over human rights, food security and the displacement of farming communities.

“The photographs speak about the possibility of agricultural lands being replaced by the Pax Silica industrial hub and the threats to food security, jobs and the lives of Filipinos—not only in Capas, Tarlac, but also in Isabela and other parts of the country,” militant farmers’ group Danggayan Dagiti Mannalon iti Isabela said in a statement in Filipino.

“Isabelinos should speak out and never be silenced. We are intensifying our calls and asserting our rights. Let us unite against foreign interests and big businesses that work against our own,” the group added.

Article continues after this 

READ: Magalong says Pax Silica needs better marketing

The farmers’ concerns came as anti-Pax Silica banners displayed at Isabela State University (ISU)-Echague and the Philippine Normal University (PNU)-Isabela Campus in Alicia were removed within minutes and less than an hour after they were put up on Tuesday.

The two universities have yet to issue statements explaining the removal of the banners.

Earlier, school leaders at PNU and ISU reportedly said they had secured permission from university administrators to display the banners on their respective campuses.

READ: Cebu archbishop questions PH participation in Pax Silica

Article continues after this 

Saddened

Farmer Mario Delos Reyes, 65, said he was saddened by reports that indigenous communities and farmers could be displaced by the proposed initiative.

“We should not sacrifice food, lives and the future of Filipinos for the rich and the interests of the few,” he said.

Article continues after this 

Delos Reyes also cited the continuing difficulties faced by farmers in Isabela, including low farmgate prices, high production costs and drought-related damage to crops.

“Farmers like us are losing money and our livelihoods. Yet, we only get the crumbs of assistance,” he added.

World.title: Baguio cracks down on vendors selling spoiled food
World.content:
THE BAGUIO CITY HALL Mayor Benjamin Magalong has warned vendors that establishments caught selling spoiled, contaminated, or unfit-for-consumption food will face immediate closure. —Photo by Maureen Matayew

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — Mayor Benjamin Magalong warned vendors that establishments caught selling spoiled, contaminated, or unfit-for-consumption food would face immediate closure, saying violators would not be given a second chance.

In a statement on Tuesday, Nov. 17, Magalong said the city government would continue its inspections and enforcement campaign following the recent seizure of spoiled fish at a local establishment.

He specifically warned vendors against selling double-dead meat and spoiled agricultural products, saying he would not give violators another chance or entertain appeals once their violations are established.

Article continues after this 

READ: Baguio sees tourism boost amid prolonged dry spell

“They have been in the business for a long time, so they know whether the products they are selling are rotten, spoiled or contaminated. There is no excuse,” Magalong said.

READ: Serving healthy food now mandatory in Baguio City’s public events

The mayor stressed that selling spoiled food poses a serious public health and safety risk because it could lead to food poisoning.

“There will be no second chance. If they try to do it again, I will have their establishments closed,” Magalong warned.

He said the city’s crackdown would continue to prevent irresponsible vendors from putting consumersÆ health at risk. /cb

World.title: Sumlang Lake Christmas village in Albay draws 8,000 visitors
World.content:
The Christmas Village at Sumlang Lake in Camalig, Albay, draws about 8,000 visitors during its opening on Monday (Nov. 16), featuring festive lights, colorful installations and fireworks against the backdrop of Mayon Volcano. —Photos by Michael B. Jaucian

CAMALIG, ALBAY, Philippines — About 8,000 people attended the opening of the Christmas Village at Sumlang Lake, where the majestic Mayon Volcano served as the backdrop to the colorful Christmas decorations and festive displays.

The lakeside attraction featured towering Christmas installations, colorful displays and a three-minute fireworks show during the opening ceremony on Monday, Nov. 16.

Visitors from Albay and Camarines Sur also had the opportunity to take photos with mascots dressed as Santa Claus, Frosty the Snowman and other Christmas characters.

Article continues after this 

READ: Cordova skips Christmas Village contest to prioritize El Niño preparedness

Children enjoyed stationary rides, while families could spend time at the expanded playground, which also provides space for recreation and picnics.

The opening ceremony also featured musical and dance performances by local talents.

READ: The magic of Christmas, the warmth of community

Municipal Tourism Officer Jed Villanueva said about 8,000 people attended the Christmas Village lighting, reflecting the attraction’s appeal to both residents and tourists.

Article continues after this 

Councilor Filipe Noe Napa Jr., chairperson of the municipal council’s Committee on Tourism, Culture and Arts, said the Christmas decorations were intended to bring happiness to the public amid the various crises and challenges facing the country.

“Beyond the dazzling lights and festive attractions, the Christmas Village at Sumlang Lake offers visitors an opportunity to celebrate the season, create family memories, and appreciate the natural beauty of Albay,” he said. /cb

World.title: Transport group brands Trump ‘king of wars,’ ‘king of oil price hikes’
World.content:
Members of transport group Manibela gather at their headquarters in Nagtahan, Manila, on Tuesday morning for a protest against rising oil prices and the US-led Pax Silica initiative, as the country hosts the 49th Asean Summit. INQUIRER / Bernadette Nicole Pineda

MANILA, Philippines—Transport group Manibela branded US President Donald Trump the “king of wars” and “king of oil price hikes” on Tuesday, Nov. 17, blaming his administration’s role in armed conflicts for driving up fuel prices in the Philippines. Manibela president Mar Valbuena made the remarks as the group staged a demonstration against Trump’s expected arrival in the country for the 49th Asean Summit.

“[He is] the reason why we are suffering today, especially the transport sector, where his war has provided a way for oil companies to take advantage and raise the prices of petroleum products,” Valbuena told the Inquirer.

READ: Trump arrives in Manila for Asean-US special summit, Marcos meeting

Article continues after this 

The group called on Trump to end the wars and pursue dialogue instead, saying armed conflicts have affected Filipinos, particularly transport workers who are vulnerable to fluctuations in oil prices.

Valbuena also said the Asean Summit presented an opportunity for the Philippines to assert its sovereignty and show China that the country would not allow itself to be controlled by foreign powers.

“This is also an opportunity for us to show China that we are fighting, and we are not letting our seas and our country become a puppet of someone else’s country,” he said.

He added that the Philippines should not allow powerful countries, including the United States and China, to influence its domestic affairs.

Valbuena also criticized the government’s preparations for the Asean Summit, questioning why authorities could only mobilize funds and resources to clean up the country when foreign dignitaries were visiting.

Article continues after this 

“We can do it, but why are we only doing it now? The funds are so big, maybe there are still some left and it will continue. Not only where the Asean delegates pass through, but all places should be clean,” he said.

On Pax Silica

Meanwhile, Valbuena questioned the lack of transparency surrounding the proposed agreement between the Philippines and the United States under the Pax Silica initiative, saying the group had yet to see its specific provisions.

Article continues after this 

“There is no transparency regarding the contents of the pact between the US and the Philippines, how it will affect the Filipino people, including our local drivers,” he said.

Valbuena urged the government to explain how the initiative would benefit Filipinos and what its long-term consequences would be, particularly for communities and the environment.

He also raised concerns over possible damage to the country’s natural resources and the displacement of residents in areas where Pax Silica projects may be established.

The group called on the government to develop long-term measures to shield Filipinos from the economic effects of armed conflicts, saying preparations should be made even in the absence of war.

Valbuena clarified that the protest was more of a suspension of operations than a transport strike, as drivers had already noticed a decline in passengers due to the holiday.

Around 500 Manibela-member jeepney drivers joined the protest nationwide, according to the group.

Valbuena said more drivers were supposed to join the mobilization, but some from Rizal were allegedly stopped at a checkpoint.

Police Lt. Col. Marlon Mallorca, commander in Sta. Mesa, said police personnel were on standby and would intervene if the demonstration turned unruly. No clashes between authorities and protesters were reported.

The protest came as the Philippines hosted the 49th Asean Summit and related meetings from Nov. 16 to Nov. 18. Trump was expected to arrive in the country on Tuesday to attend the summit.

World.title: Regime Minister Turns to Migrant Workers in Malaysia to Plug Foreign Currency Gap
World.content:
Regime Labor Minister Maung Myint, admitted while talking to Myanmar workers in Malaysia last week that the junta is increasingly relying on migrant workers to bring in foreign currency as sanctions and declining export earnings squeeze its finances.

“The world sanctions us,” Maung Myint said during his visit to the country. He also claimed that one of the reasons for the decline in Myanmar’s international revenue was that the regime had deliberately “reduced” exports of natural resources.

Following the 2021 coup, Western countries and blocs including the U.S., the European Union, the United Kingdom and Canada imposed targeted economic sanctions on senior Myanmar regime officials, including coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, as well as state enterprises and military-controlled banks.

The sanctions remain in place, leaving some foreign development assistance programs suspended and interrupting international banking transfers, fueling the country’s foreign currency shortage and exacerbating an economic crisis caused by the regime’s mismanagement.

While Maung Myint claimed the regime had deliberately reduced natural-resource exports for environmental reasons, a World Bank report suggests that natural gas exports to Thailand and China—one of Myanmar’s major sources of foreign income—dropped by US$200 million in 2025-26 due to “reduced output” from existing offshore operations.

As international sanctions began to bite, the regime imposed remittance rules and enforced tax laws targeting overseas workers in 2023, aiming to extract funds from them. Foreign remittance value reached US$5.6 billion in 2025, and Maung Myint is hoping to match that figure this year.

“We’re trying to cover the shrinking income with remittances from workers,” he said in a video posted on his TikTok channel on Sunday.

He added that the rules and restrictions targeting migrant workers would be only temporary, claiming that potential increases in revenue from rare earths and a major deep-water drilling project in the Andaman Sea would eliminate the need for them.

However, he cautioned that rare earth sites “are not under the government’s control,” and are a “prospect” for foreign revenue once the regime gains control of them.

The majority of Myanmar’s approximately 600 rare-earth mining sites are concentrated on the China-Myanmar border in Kachin State under the control of the Kachin Independence Army. The rest also lie beyond the Myanmar regime’s control in eastern Shan State, in territory run by armed groups over which China exerts a great influence, including the United Wa State Army (UWSA).

Its lack of control over these deposits deprives the regime of billions of dollars in potential revenue, as global powers like the U.S. and India court it for access to the critical minerals.

He said the deep-water drilling project in the Andaman Sea’s Block M-15 could earn $400-500 billion. According to the World Bank report, the project could produce up to 94.6 trillion cubic feet of usable gas “if confirmed”, but its output “is not expected soon.”

Maung Myint last week turned his focus to Malaysia, which hosts the second-largest population of Myanmar migrant workers, after his efforts to extract more foreign currency met with resistance from migrant workers in Thailand.

Since being appointed labor minister in October, he has been pushing hard for workers to comply with the new remittance and tax rules, particularly the Certification of Identity (CI) process.

The push sparked widespread boycotts in Thailand, where only 15,000 of nearly 750,000 undocumented Myanmar workers applied for the CI. Workers refused to apply for fear of funding the military’s war on civilians and exposing themselves to military conscription.

In Malaysia, he used flattery, calling workers national “heroes” and comparing them to soldiers who “sacrifice their time with families to serve the country.”

World.title: All Quiet in Northern Shan—and for Good Reason
World.content:
For several months, speculation has swirled over whether northern Shan State could see a return of resistance offensives on the scale of Operation 1027. But what is the likelihood of a resurgence of fighting?

The speculation appears to stem from signs of friction between Beijing and Myanmar’s military regime over how the ethnic armed organizations are to be managed, as well as the regime’s recent efforts to restore ties with the U.S. and Japan.

Yet the differences between China and the military regime are not fundamental—they do not amount to a strategic or ideological split.

China has not abandoned its long-held view that the military is a central pillar in maintaining stability in Myanmar. What has changed is Beijing’s growing recognition that the crisis cannot be managed through the military alone.

The fact that Beijing now acknowledges other forces has become a source of discomfort for the regime. But that is not a policy shift, only a tactical adjustment in how China seeks to implement its existing policy.

Beijing’s position on border stability remains unchanged. China does not want to see a return of armed conflicts to northern Shan, which shares a 200-km stretch of border with Yunnan.

All the rare-earth mines and other major investments operating in areas controlled by Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) in northern Shan involve Chinese capital. Given the technical requirements involved in rare-earth extraction, the companies operating these projects are more likely to be state-linked Chinese enterprises than private firms. The Chinese government is unlikely to allow such investments to be jeopardized.

One point of frustration for China has been the regime’s handling of border trade. Naypyitaw frequently claims that cross-border trade was disrupted by ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) that now control the major border trade routes. Yet Beijing is well aware that the military has also restricted border trade with Thailand, even though it fully controls the trade corridor there. From China’s perspective, regime policy puts up more barriers to trade than the MNDAA or TNLA.

Estimated at US$6 billion annually, that business is relatively small compared with the scale of the Chinese economy. The more pressing concern for Beijing has been online scam operations. Since the MNDAA and TNLA established control over large parts of the border, scam syndicates targeting Chinese citizens have been brought under much tighter control. The central military regime, by contrast, failed for years to address the problem.

Chinese policymakers may therefore calculate that restoring central military control across northern Shan could revive the criminal networks Beijing has made considerable effort suppressing. The financial and political costs of that scenario would surely outweigh the benefits of expanded border trade.

The EAOs themselves have little incentive to launch new offensives. The MNDAA and TNLA now control substantially more territory than before Operation 1027, and arguably more than they had dared to dream of. Having achieved those objectives, neither group has a pressing need to expend additional force.

Beijing may have a similar view and is therefore likely to restrain them from fighting the regime again. That means there is virtually no prospect of the MNDAA or TNLA initiating hostilities. The only realistic scenario under which fighting might resume would be if the military regime attacks first.

For its part, Naypyitaw expects China to pressure EAOs to return all the territories in northern Shan State to it. That is how the regime recovered the northern Shan capital of Lashio. Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun’s recent proposal of “high-level autonomy” for ethnic forces was therefore a bitter pill for the regime to swallow. And soon after Deng made the proposal, the regime dispatched reconnaissance planes to northern Shan.

Having survived the military disasters of 2023 and 2024 in large part because of Chinese intervention, the military’s top brass is now dreaming of eventually reclaiming all lost territory by force. Such thinking is hardly surprising for an institution that seized power by forced and continues to view military means as the answer to political problems.

But here dreams and reality collide. Before Operation 1027, the Northeastern Command was backed by roughly 20 infantry and light infantry battalions, in addition to artillery, logistics and support units. It was further reinforced by as many as seven or eight division-sized formations rotated through the theater.

That force no longer exists. Now only about 10 infantry and light infantry battalions remain under Northeastern Command, dispersed across Muse, Tangyan and Mongyai. The military now fields only a single major combat formation across the region, spread among Nantlan, Kyaukme, Hsipaw and Nawnghkio, while smaller units are deployed in Mongmit and Mogoke.

Indeed, since the ceasefire with the MNDAA and TNLA, the regime has moved an estimated seven division-sized formations out of northern Shan State to active fronts in Rakhine, Chin, Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay.

That mean it simply does not have the strength to maintain more than a presence in northern Shan and hold existing positions. The convoys that are regularly observed traveling between Taunggyi, Kho Lam, Mong Nawng, Mongyai and Tangyan do not represent substantial reinforcements: they mainly transport batches of new recruits to and from military training facilities.

The military’s ability to sustain operations elsewhere, then, depends heavily on the fact that northern Shan remains relatively quiet. To reopen that front, it would first have to withdraw troops from other battlefields, which would risk repeating the overstretch that contributed to the military’s earlier defeats.

In essence, the regime would be creating a new battlefield at a time when it can barely manage the existing ones.

No matter how much it resents the loss of northern Shan’s borders, there is nothing it can do about it. In addition, any attempt to violate the Beijing-brokered ceasefire could invite retaliation from China itself. Unlike Thailand, which has repeatedly shown restraint when fighting spills across its border, Beijing is unlikely to tolerate renewed instability along a frontier it regards as strategically vital.

In other words, the regime would be digging its own grave.

Moe Set Nyein Chan is a military analyst

World.title: Dozens of Civilians Killed in Myanmar Regime Strikes as ASEAN Leaders Meet
World.content:
The Myanmar regime has continued bombing civilian targets nationwide after its leaders were barred from attending the ongoing 49th ASEAN Summit for rejecting the bloc’s peace plan.

Rakhine State has borne the brunt of attacks, which have killed over a dozen civilians in the past week as the ethnic Arkan Army (AA) pushes to seize the state capital, Sittwe, and Kyaukphyu, home to China-backed mega projects.

Junta warplanes pounded residential areas in the AA-held town of Kyauktaw on Monday night, but casualty figures were unclear as of press time. The strike followed an Oct. 28 attack on the town’s busy market that killed 50 civilians including children and wounded 60, drawing international condemnation.

The AA also reported another deadly strike on a displacement camp in Ponnagyun Township on Friday evening. Twelve people were killed and 18 injured as blasts ripped through the Byar La shelter for war-displaced civilians. The attack came just weeks after two regime fighter jets bombed the same IDP camp, killing eight civilians and destroying homes and shops on October 4.

The airstrikes continued Sunday as ASEAN leaders gathered for their summit in Manila, with Myanmar’s crisis topping the agenda.

Blasts destroyed bridges in the Rakhine townships of Minbya and Ramree, according to the AA. The attacks followed a Nov. 1 airstrike on a Kyauktaw bridge that killed seven commuters and injured seven others.

Meanwhile, the regime’s Taung Maw Oo naval base used drones and artillery to destroy around 60 homes Kyaukphyu’s Sane town at the weekend, months after it was abandoned by civilians.

Former army captain Zin Yaw, who defected following the 2021 coup, said the regime is targeting bridges to cut supply lines of the AA, which is pushing to seize the regime’s last remaining toeholds in Rakhine.

“The regime has failed to meet its military objectives, so it is now attempting to destroy the enemy’s administrative and supply chains,” he said.

Wai Hun Aung, a prominent Rakhine writer and relief worker, said regime forces are destroying bridges to slow the AA’s advance.

The AA has seized 14 out of Rakhine’s 17 townships plus Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State since launching a major offensive in November 2023.

The ethnic army has also expanded offensives across the border into Magwe, Bago and Ayeyarwady regions.

World.title: UN Chief Backs Engagement With Myanmar But ‘Violence Needs to Stop’
World.content:
MANILA—UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed support Monday for fresh diplomatic efforts to engage with Myanmar’s post-coup government, but said that “violence needs to stop.”

Guterres made the remarks in Manila, where leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) agreed Sunday to pursue a “calibrated engagement” with the war-torn country.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level ASEAN meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021, but the regional bloc is seeking a path towards normalizing diplomatic relations.

“We have never opposed the idea that it is always necessary to engage with whoever is involved in a conflict,” Guterres told a press conference on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit.

While “engagement is not appeasement,” Guterres said the “intolerable violations of human rights in Myanmar” must end.

“Violence needs to stop, humanitarian access needs to be granted, and all those arbitrarily detained must be immediately released,” Guterres said.

“And these are the conditions that could allow for what everybody should will [to happen], which is that Myanmar will find a way to move… to a true democratic situation.”

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” in an effort to implement ASEAN’s long-languishing five-point plan to end the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders adopted that language on Sunday in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach,” according to the joint statement.

Guterres’s remarks came as the UN’s International Court of Justice prepares to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its marginalized Muslim Rohingya minority.

World.title: Yangon Condo Raid Reveals Myanmar’s Cyber Scam Sector Thriving in Commercial Capital
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime says it has arrested 106 suspected online scammers in Yangon, signaling the country’s cyber-fraud epidemic has spread from the lawless borderlands to its largest city.

The regime announced Saturday that its forces raided Golden River Residence Condo in Yangon’s Thaketa Township on November 12, arresting 52 Chinese naionals, eight Vietnamese and 46 Myanmar citizens from multiple apartments.

The arrests come as Naypyitaw and Beijing trumpet crackdowns on cyber-fraud syndicates in notorious border scam hubs.

Those reportedly detained included a high-profile target of China’s Public Security Ministry — the first arrest of a warranted Chinese scammer in Myanmar in months. Also seized from the condo were over 120 computers and laptops and nearly 200 mobile phones.

Authorities said the gang ran online investment fraud schemes targeting Chinese, Japanese, South Korean and Indian citizens, while separate Telegram-based operations targeted victims in Brazil and Colombia through fake e-commerce platforms.

The raid came shortly after Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi pressed Myanmar investment minister Aung Kyaw Hoe to intensify efforts to combat scams and prevent a “resurgence of chaos” in Karen State’s Myawaddy crime hub on the Thai border.

Analysts say the Yangon bust signals a growing shift of Myanmar’s online scam industry from border enclaves to urban centers.

After the 2024 collapse of notorious fraud compounds in northern Shan State’s Laukkai and crackdowns along the Chinese and Thai borders, many scam syndicates dispersed in small, mobile operations through remote eastern and southern Shan, according to regime arrest reports and independent monitors.

However, many that had fled to Myawaddy have since moved deeper into the country under the protection of regime-aligned militias and other armed groups.

In September, 28 foreign and Myanmar nationals were arrested in Mandalay — the country’s second city — over an online gemstone scam involving Chinese, Indonesian and Malaysian suspects. The gang was charged with selling fake jade products via livestream and transferring the profits to accounts in Indonesia and Malaysia.

While the Nov. 12 raid was the first of its kind reported in Yangon, former fraudsters told The Irrawaddy that scam operations have long established a foothold in the commercial capital, targeting overseas victims through operations based in condominiums, housing estates and companies registered as legitimate businesses.

Analysts say enforcement efforts target low-level operators while overlooking the networks and militias behind the multibillion-dollar industry. Among them is the regime-aligned Karen Border Guard Force, whose Western-sanctioned leaders remain untouched even as the regime hails the demolition of scam compounds in Myawaddy.

World.title: ASEAN Seeks ‘Calibrated Engagement’ With Myanmar: Statement
World.content:
MANILA, Philippines—Southeast Asian leaders agreed Sunday on pursuing a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar’s post-coup government, according to a joint statement, as the regional bloc seeks a path towards normalization.

Myanmar is still a member of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but it has been frozen out of high-level meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar in an effort to implement ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC) plan aimed at ending the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila adopted that language in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach, taking into account developments on the ground,” according to the joint statement.

“Subject to sustained and concrete progress in the implementation of the 5PC by Myanmar, ASEAN may consider the gradual restoration of Myanmar’s full political representation,” the statement said.

The five-point plan has yielded little in the half-decade since it was agreed to, with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos conceding at a May summit he had not seen “any progress in Myanmar.”

On Sunday, in opening remarks at an ASEAN leaders’ retreat in Manila, he repeated a question he had posed to the group six months earlier: “What more can we do for Myanmar?”

“I hope our session leads to practical and forward-looking discussions on how we can further advance the implementation of the Five-Point Consensus, make our efforts more responsive to the realities on the ground, and support a peaceful, inclusive, Myanmar-owned and Myanmar-led process,” he said.

The ASEAN bloc’s rotating chair will pass at the end of this year from the Philippines to Singapore, a city-state analysts say opposes normalizing ties with Myanmar.

In 2028, it will be the turn of Thailand, which shares a long border with Myanmar and is leading the charge for closer relations.

“We believe it’s crucial to have someone at the table who can really talk on policy issues because engagement requires that they have someone who can really convey to us the position of Myanmar,” Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told AFP in Singapore on November 5.

“This is not about… recognizing… upgrading their position. But I think in reality, what is important is that we need someone at the table who can speak on behalf of Myanmar.”

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean.
