World.title: Azerbaijan, US discuss expanding agricultural cooperation
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. As part of his visit to the US, a delegation of Azerbaijan led by Minister of Agriculture Majnun Mammadov met with a US delegation led by Deputy Secretary of Agriculture Stephen Vaden.

During the meeting, the sides discussed expanding agricultural cooperation between Azerbaijan and the US, increasing bilateral trade in agricultural products, and exploring prospects for cooperation in scientific research and innovation.

Minister Majnun Mammadov briefed the US side on measures underway to strengthen Azerbaijan’s scientific capacity in agriculture, modernize research institutes, and align their activities with international standards. He emphasized the importance of launching joint scientific research projects and field trials with the US Department of Agriculture’s (USDA) Agricultural Research Service (ARS) and the National Institute of Food and Agriculture (NIFA).

The minister also highlighted ongoing efforts to develop agriculture in the liberated territories using a modern, climate-resilient, and digitally enabled model. Noting that Garabagh and East Zangezur have been declared green energy zones, he stated that US scientific research expertise could make a significant contribution to developing agricultural production systems in these territories in line with international standards.

Stephen Vaden noted that work was underway to conclude a memorandum of understanding between the agriculture ministries of the two countries. He added that the draft memorandum prepared by the Azerbaijani side had been submitted to its US counterpart and was under discussion.

Vaden emphasized the US side's interest in expanding cooperation under the memorandum in biotechnology, as well as livestock breeding and selection. The sides also discussed studying Azerbaijan's experience in these fields and exchanging expertise.

They also discussed ways to expand trade in agricultural products and strengthen bilateral trade ties. They exchanged views on prospects for agricultural cooperation, the exchange of expertise, and the draft memorandum of understanding between the two ministries.

World.title: Azerbaijan expands logistics network to strengthen regional hub role
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. Azerbaijan’s transportation and logistics strategy is entering a new phase. The increase in freight traffic along the Middle Corridor, the expansion of port and ferry infrastructure on the Caspian Sea, the development of the Zangezur Corridor, the commissioning of the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable, and preparations for the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway line — the main missing link in the North–South International Transport Corridor — are all integral parts of a unified process that is expanding the country’s role in regional connectivity.

The significance of these projects is not limited to an increase in the volume of goods transported. It is about creating a broader infrastructure system that facilitates the flow of goods, data, investments, and services between Asia and Europe. Within this system, Azerbaijan seeks to strengthen its position both as a transit country and as a regional hub providing port, rail, logistics, and digital communications services.

At the same time, the development of the Middle Corridor is of parallel importance to the completion of the Rasht–Astara line along the “North–South” axis. The complementarity of these two routes can expand Azerbaijan’s capacity to receive cargo flows from various directions and redirect them to regional and international markets.

Target of 30 million metric tons for Middle Corridor and Azerbaijan’s growing role as transit hub

The development of the Middle Corridor has become one of the main priorities on the regional economic agenda in recent years. Increased risks associated with traditional transport routes following the Russia-Ukraine war, conflicts in the Middle East, changes in international trade, and the need to diversify supply chains have heightened interest in the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route.

According to a statement by Mariam Kvrivishvili, Georgia’s Minister of Economy and Sustainable Development, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Kazakhstan have approved a joint plan to increase freight traffic along the Middle Corridor to 30 million metric tons by 2029. This goal requires coordinated action by the three countries to increase the route’s capacity and improve operational efficiency.

Azerbaijan’s transit figures also indicate some progress in this direction. According to a statement by Rashad Hasanov, Deputy Minister of Digital Development and Transport, the volume of transit cargo through the country has roughly doubled over the past five years and is expected to approach 16 million metric tons by the end of 2026. In the medium term, the plan is to increase this figure to 30 million metric tons by 2030.

It is important to distinguish between two different figures here: the 30 million metric tons set by Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Kazakhstan for 2029 is a target for the total volume of cargo transportation along the Middle Corridor. The target of 30 million metric tons for 2030, announced by Azerbaijan, however, refers to the volume of transit shipments through the country’s territory.

On October 9, 2026, at a meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State in a restricted format held in Turkmenbashi, President Ilham Aliyev emphasized that Azerbaijan is consistently strengthening its position as one of the region’s major transportation hubs and ensuring reliable transit along the “North–South” and “East–West” international corridors. “In the first half of 2026, transit cargo volumes through Azerbaijan increased by 10 percent to nearly 8 million tons. Our medium-term objective is to increase cargo volumes along each of the East-West and North-South corridors through Azerbaijan to 15 million tons,” the head of state said.

These figures indicate that Azerbaijan’s transit strategy is not limited to the Middle Corridor alone. The country seeks to expand its participation in a broader regional logistics network by attracting cargo flows in both the “East–West” and “North–South” directions.

Azerbaijan’s statistics on transport corridors for January–September 2026 also demonstrate the economic significance of these routes. During this period, 14.74 million metric tons of cargo were transported along the “East–West” corridor, including 7.5 million metric tons via the TRACECA route. Freight volumes via the “North–South” corridor totaled 6.87 million metric tons, via the “North–West” corridor - 3.89 million metric tons, and via the “South–West” corridor - 447,000 metric tons. Rail transport carried 12.08 million metric tons of cargo, maritime transport carried 5.37 million metric tons, and road transport carried 8.49 million metric tons. Transit cargo accounted for 47% of rail freight and 46.6% of road freight. These figures reflect, on the one hand, the significance of transit in Azerbaijan’s transportation system and, on the other, the importance of coordinating various modes of transport for the development of transport corridors.

New Transportation Links Across Caspian Sea: Port, Ferry, and Intermodal Logistics.

The effectiveness of the Middle Corridor depends not only on the condition of the railways and highways. The throughput capacity of ports on the Caspian Sea, the regularity of ferry services, the number of vessels, cargo handling times at ports, and coordination between rail and maritime transport are also key factors determining the route’s competitiveness. In this regard, the expansion of the Baku International Sea Trade Port and the deepening of cooperation with Kazakhstan in the field of maritime transport are of particular importance.

As part of the current expansion program for the Port of Baku, plans call for increasing its annual cargo handling capacity from 15 to 25 million metric tons. A multi-phase development plan is in place for container transportation. According to a statement by port advisor Khudayar Hasanli, container throughput is expected to reach 123,000 TEU by the end of 2026. The forecast for 2027 is 130,000–140,000 TEU. Current operational capacity allows for the handling of approximately 150,000 TEU. As a result of the work being carried out at the port, container handling capacity is expected to reach 260,000 TEU in the second half of 2027. At this stage, plans include dredging, the restoration and reconstruction of berths, the purchase of new equipment, the expansion of rail tracks and the container yard, as well as the creation of additional connecting tracks. At a later stage, plans call for increasing container throughput capacity to 500,000 TEU.

The documents signed between Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan on October 15, 2026, may provide additional impetus for the expansion of this infrastructure. With President Ilham Aliyev and President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in attendance, AZCON Holding and Kazakhstan’s National Welfare Fund “Samruk-Kazyna” exchanged certificates confirming the acquisition of two dry cargo ships.

In addition, AZCON and Samruk-Kazyna have identified the main areas of strategic cooperation for the “Caspian Bridge” (“Super Ferry”) project, which involves organizing regular cargo shipments between the ports of Alat and Kuryk using high-capacity ferries. The main goal of the project is to improve the reliability of transportation across the Caspian Sea, reduce the time spent on port operations, create specialized terminals, and establish a unified transportation and logistics system.

At the same time, Azerbaijan Railways CJSC and Kazakhstan’s Temir Zholy have signed a document outlining the basic terms for the creation of an intermodal freight terminal at the Baku International Sea Trade Port. The project is intended to strengthen the integration of port and rail operations, as well as create conditions for attracting container and other cargo flows. A joint venture is also planned to support the terminal’s operations. The investment model and financing terms will be finalized based on the project’s technical and economic indicators.

These initiatives complement one another: the new vessels and ferry system expand the possibilities for transit across the Caspian Sea, while the intermodal terminal facilitates the more efficient transfer of cargo arriving at the port to the rail network. Thus, the goal is not only to increase the port’s physical capacity but also to ensure faster and more predictable cargo movement on both shores of the Caspian Sea.

Digital Phase of Middle Corridor: Trans-Caspian Cable

A new phase in Azerbaijan’s transit strategy began on October 15, 2026, with the presidents of Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan participating in the official opening of the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable line. The project, implemented as part of the “Digital Silk Road” initiative, involves laying a fiber-optic cable approximately 380 kilometers long along the bottom of the Caspian Sea between Sumgayit and Aktau. The line has a capacity of over 400 terabits per second. With the launch of this project, the first direct undersea digital connection between Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan was established. Cable laying was completed in August 2026, and the opening ceremony took place in October.

President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev described the significance of the project as follows:

“This is undoubtedly a very important project that will attract international attention. But most importantly, it represents a new type of corridor. It is truly not just a transport corridor, but an innovation that meets the needs of the modern era, the era of digitalization, and a completely new form of cooperation.”

President Ilham Aliyev, in turn, stated:

“Yes. It is also another step in strengthening cooperation between Central Asia and Azerbaijan. Everyone is well aware that in November last year, Azerbaijan was admitted as a full member of the Consultative Meetings, and already this year, I recently participated as a full member of the community. This is yet another contribution to strengthening our cooperation, because this cable will be utilized by both the countries of Central Asia and the South Caucasus, as well as across a broader geography. So today we have launched a global project.”

Tokayev briefly described the essence of the project as follows:

“Yes, this is the Middle Corridor in digital format.”

This statement clearly demonstrates the project’s significance in terms of regional connectivity. While the Middle Corridor has thus far been viewed primarily as a transport route for containers, raw materials, and industrial goods, the new cable line expands its capabilities in the field of digital communications.

The new route will enable data to be transmitted from China and Central Asia through Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, and Georgia, and then on to Europe via the Black Sea or Türkiye. This could diversify data exchange routes, enhance the resilience of digital communications, and strengthen the region’s role in the international digital infrastructure.

The economic significance of the project extends beyond telecommunications services. The high-speed connection creates additional opportunities for the development of data centers in the fields of artificial intelligence, cloud services, and computing infrastructure. This could strengthen the positions of Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan not only as markets for digital services but also as infrastructure providers serving international data flows.

The Zangezur Corridor: A New Link for the Middle Corridor

Another key priority of Azerbaijan’s regional transportation strategy is the development of the Zangezur Corridor. The completion of the Horadiz–Aghband highway, the continuation of construction on the railway line, and the modernization of the railway infrastructure in Nakhchivan are concrete steps in this direction.

The Horadiz–Jabrayil–Zangilan–Aghband highway is an integral part of the Hajigabul–Horadiz–Aghband highway and the Zangezur Corridor. The total length of the project is 149.9 kilometers, and the length of the main section of the highway is 123.6 kilometers. The road is built to technical category 1B standards and has four to six lanes. The project includes three tunnels, 28 bridges, eight interchanges, underpasses, and culverts. Although the completion of the highway is an important milestone, it is also crucial to complete the rail link and infrastructure toward Nakhchivan to fully realize the corridor’s transportation and logistics capabilities.

On November 6, 2026, the United States, Azerbaijan, and Armenia announced the creation of trilateral technical planning groups to accelerate the implementation of TRIPP. In the initial phase, two groups are planned—one for transportation and one for electricity transmission. The task of these groups is to resolve technical issues, move the project to the next stages of implementation, and integrate it into regional infrastructure networks.

According to estimates by the Ministry of Digital Development and Transport, the development of the Zangezur Corridor could create additional freight transport capacity of up to 15 million metric tons per year. The creation of a second western exit to Türkiye via Nakhchivan will not only diversify Azerbaijan’s international routes but may also expand the alternative connectivity options of the Middle Corridor. At the same time, it is important to note that TRIPP is currently in the technical planning phase. To realize the project’s full transportation potential, the implementation of agreed-upon technical mechanisms, the development of infrastructure, and the process of integration into regional networks must be completed.

Rasht–Astara Line: Missing Link in the “North–South” Corridor

Alongside the development of the Middle Corridor, the Rasht–Astara railway line is a key project capable of strengthening Azerbaijan’s position in the “North–South” International Transport Corridor. The goal of the North–South Corridor, established under an intergovernmental agreement signed on September 12, 2000, between Russia, Iran, and India, is to reduce transit times for cargo transported from India to Russia, Northern Europe, and Western Europe. The goal is to reduce transit times, which can take more than six weeks on existing routes, to approximately three weeks via this corridor.

The corridor’s significance for Azerbaijan stems from its direct connection to Iran’s railway network. On March 6, 2019, the 175-kilometer Qazvin–Rasht railway was put into operation. However, the fact that the Rasht–Astara section within Iran remains incomplete hinders the establishment of uninterrupted rail service along the western route of the “North–South” corridor.

The proposed 162-kilometer Rasht–Astara line is intended to bridge this gap. The project calls for the construction of nine stations. Under an agreement signed between Russia and Iran on May 17, 2023, Russia is set to participate in financing the project. In previous agreements, the project’s cost was estimated at 1.6 billion euro, and construction was scheduled to be completed within 48 months.

At the same time, Iran and Russia have finalized a budget of 1.36 billion euro for the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway line. The project will create conditions for expanding the transit and logistics capabilities of the Azerbaijani city of Astara and increasing freight volumes.

According to a statement made by Gilan Province Governor Hadi Haghshenas to Trend, of the 162 kilometers of land through which the line will run, property rights for approximately 120 kilometers have already been purchased from citizens, and the acquisition process is ongoing for the remaining 42 kilometers. He also reported that work to reinforce the railroad track had been carried out on a 60-kilometer section.

Subsequent statements regarding the project indicate that the preparatory process is moving forward. On November 4, 2026, the Iranian side announced that land parcels along the entire route, including the remaining 37-kilometer section of the line, had been transferred to the Russian side to ensure access for engineering and survey work. On November 8, it was reported that Iran’s Supreme National Security Council had approved the agreement on the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway. According to a statement by Russian Railways management on October 15, construction is expected to begin in 2027, with the line to be completed within three years. Thus, while the transfer of land plots and the approval of the agreement are important milestones for advancing the project, the start and completion of construction still lie ahead.

The commissioning of the Rasht–Astara line will connect Iran’s rail network, via Azerbaijan, to destinations in the Caucasus, Russia, and Northern Europe. For Azerbaijan, this means more than just an increase in transit cargo volumes. It could also expand the country’s opportunities to participate in logistics services, cargo transshipment, and rail and port operations along the “North–South” route.

The interconnection between the Middle Corridor and the “North–South” Corridor is of particular importance here. The former is aimed at facilitating freight transportation between China, Central Asia, and Europe, while the latter connects India and the Persian Gulf region, on the one hand, with Russia and Europe, on the other. The logistics capabilities of both routes, which intersect within Azerbaijan, can make the country’s transit system more flexible.

Expansion of Logistics Network

Azerbaijan’s transportation strategy is not limited to maritime and rail connections. The construction of an airport in the Alat Free Economic Zone also aims to expand the country’s multimodal logistics capabilities.

The main construction work on the airport, which began in April 2024, is expected to be completed by the end of 2026, and the facility is scheduled to begin operations in late March or early April 2027. In the initial phase, the annual cargo handling capacity is planned to be 500,000 metric tons. In the subsequent phase, the goal is to increase this figure to at least 2 million metric tons.

The airport’s location within the Alat Free Economic Zone, near the Port of Baku, could enhance its role in the logistics system. This creates additional opportunities for coordinating maritime, rail, road, and air transport within a single integrated space.

The construction of four container ships at the Baku Shipyard for AD Ports and Kazakhstan Railways also signals the expansion of the manufacturing component within Azerbaijan’s transportation infrastructure. This demonstrates the country’s potential not only in providing transit services but also in participating in the production of the technical equipment necessary for these services.

The project to build the Northern Railway Line in Istanbul (Türkiye) is also important in the context of broader regional rail connectivity between Europe and Asia. An agreement has been signed with the Islamic Development Bank to finance the project with 660 million euro, which includes the construction of approximately 127 kilometers of electrified track and modern signaling systems. The total cost of the project is estimated at approximately $8.1 billion, with international financial institutions providing 83% of the funding. Upon completion, the railway line’s annual freight capacity is expected to increase from 3 million metric tons to 50 million metric tons. Although this project is not located directly within Azerbaijan, it is part of a broader regional effort to develop railway infrastructure westward along the Middle Corridor.

Message from international financial institutions: infrastructure alone is not enough

The stance of international financial institutions toward the development of the Middle Corridor is also crucial for the route’s prospects. Representatives of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) emphasize the importance of institutional and operational reforms, alongside physical infrastructure, for unlocking the corridor’s potential.

Roberto Cardarelli, Assistant Director in the Middle East and Central Asia Department (MCD) at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), said that over the past four to five years, the volume of cargo transported along the Middle Corridor has more than tripled. In his view, for the corridor to become a more significant route alongside the Northern and Southern routes, it is important to develop infrastructure such as roads, railways, and pipelines.

However, Cardarelli emphasized that physical infrastructure alone is not enough.

“To reduce trade costs, it is necessary to harmonize customs and border procedures, simplify the process of preparing the documentation required to transport goods from one country to another, and leverage the opportunities offered by digitalization and new technologies,” he noted.

This position highlights one of the main challenges facing the Middle Corridor. Delays at borders, customs, and ports when moving cargo from one country to another directly affect the overall delivery times and costs along the route. Increasing the capacity of a railway line or port does not automatically solve these problems. This requires harmonizing procedures between countries, accelerating data exchange, and establishing unified operational mechanisms.

The coordination efforts between the railways of Azerbaijan and Georgia serve as a practical example in this regard. At meetings held by a delegation led by Rovshan Rustamov, Chairman of Azerbaijan Railways CJSC, at the stations of Boyuk-Kasik, Gardabani, and Tbilisi, issues were discussed regarding the acceleration of border clearance procedures, the coordination of technical inspections, the elimination of duplicate operations, and real-time data exchange.

According to Azerbaijan Railways, the new operational approaches implemented on the Boyuk-Kasik–Tbilisi–Boyuk-Kasik route have cut the time it takes for freight trains to cross the border in half. This result demonstrates that to improve the efficiency of the logistics system, it is important not only to build new infrastructure but also to make more effective use of existing infrastructure.

Nataly Mouravidze, Head of the EBRD’s Baku Office, also highlighted three key priorities for the development of the Middle Corridor: eliminating major “bottlenecks” at ports, on railways, and at intermodal facilities; strengthening digitalization and coordination; and developing economic activity beyond the transportation sector.

According to her, business representatives evaluate not individual sections of the route, but its reliability, predictability, and costs along its entire length. Mouravidze emphasized that the success of the Middle Corridor should not be measured solely by the number of containers transported.

“Success should not be measured solely by the number of containers transported along the corridor or out of the region. The volume of investment attracted by the corridor, the number of jobs created, and business activity must also be taken into account,” she said.

This approach brings to the forefront the issue of transforming the Middle Corridor from a transit route into an economic corridor. The mere passage of cargo through the country’s territory does not, in and of itself, generate maximum economic benefit. To achieve this, it is necessary to develop warehousing and logistics services, cargo handling and packaging capabilities, industrial production, and export-oriented enterprises.

The “EU Business Climate Report Azerbaijan 2025/26,” funded by the European Union, also cites Azerbaijan’s geographic location, investments in transportation infrastructure, and the development of the Middle Corridor as factors that enhance the country’s significance as a regional transit hub. At the same time, the report identifies operational coordination, logistics costs, and existing “bottlenecks” in the corridor’s operations as major challenges for businesses. Consequently, the main task for Azerbaijan in the next phase is not only to increase the volume of transit cargo but also to derive greater economic benefits from these flows within the country.

Regional Partnership and International Interest

The development of the Middle Corridor is not limited to cooperation between Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Georgia. Central Asian nations, Türkiye, the European Union, the US, and international financial institutions are also showing interest in the region’s transport and digital connectivity potential.

President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev noted the growing demand for the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, adding that the modernization of infrastructure will expand the region's economic opportunities. According to World Bank estimates, if the planned infrastructure projects are implemented, the volume of cargo transported across the Caspian Sea could increase fourfold by 2040.

Tokayev has also proposed discussing the integration of the Middle Corridor with TRIPP at the expert level. This suggests that various routes, while serving as alternatives to one another, could in certain instances become complementary components of a unified regional logistics network. Chargé d'Affaires at the US Embassy in Azerbaijan, Amy Carlon, said at the CAMCA Regional Forum that the Trans-Caspian route has the potential to significantly transform trade relations across Eurasia. According to her, the US has supported the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund with $201 million. Carlon described the route not merely as an infrastructure project, but as a bridge between economies and people.

Azerbaijan’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Jeyhun Bayramov, also emphasized, at an event held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, that transport and logistics connectivity can accelerate economic growth, strengthen the resilience of supply chains, and create investment opportunities. He noted that the TRIPP initiative, in addition to establishing unimpeded multimodal connectivity between Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan, also holds potential for regional energy ties and the diversification of energy sources.

The expansion of Azerbaijan’s economic relations with Central Asia is also a significant part of this process. According to a statement by Minister of Economy Mikayil Jabbarov at the CAMCA Regional Forum, a 2023 World Bank assessment indicates the potential for trade volume along the Middle Corridor to triple and transit times to be halved by 2030. He noted that Central Asia has become Azerbaijan’s fastest-growing trading partner region over the past five years.

According to Jabbarov, regional cooperation should not be limited solely to transport. Joint production, investment funds, and energy and digital connectivity between Azerbaijan and the countries of Central Asia could also become key pillars of economic integration.

Support for the development of the Middle Corridor is also explicitly addressed in the Joint Declaration on Strategic Partnership signed with the UK. The document notes that both sides recognize the importance of regional and international connectivity and will support transport, logistics, and infrastructure projects that facilitate cross-border trade and investment. This demonstrates that Azerbaijan’s Middle Corridor strategy has been incorporated into the economic agenda shared with its European partners. China’s Ambassador to Azerbaijan, Lu Mei, also said that there is significant potential for expanding cooperation between the two countries in the fields of transport, energy, trade, and investment. For China, the Middle Corridor serves as a gateway to European markets via Central Asia and the South Caucasus. Consequently, the development of transport and logistics cooperation between Beijing and Baku is crucial for the long-term prospects of this route.

Economic Test of Middle Corridor: From Transit to Value-Added

Director of the Middle East and Central Asia Department at the International Monetary Fund (IMF), Jihad Azour, noted that potential investments in the Middle Corridor offer countries in the region the prospect of deeper integration into the global economy. According to him, economic growth in many Central Asian and Caucasian nations has accelerated in recent years, driven by shifts in the direction of investment and trade flows. At the same time, Azour emphasized that for infrastructure investments to yield tangible economic results, it is essential to improve the institutional environment, enhance the role of the private sector, reform state-owned enterprises, and reduce the state’s footprint in the economy.

This stance highlights one of the key economic issues regarding the future development of the Middle Corridor: while transport links create new opportunities for the countries in the region, capitalizing on these opportunities requires a competitive business environment, high-quality human capital, and efficient public governance.

For Azerbaijan, this is particularly significant in terms of developing the non-oil sector and diversifying exports. Beyond transit revenues, the creation of new economic activities, such as logistics services, warehousing, processing, manufacturing, digital services, and high-tech sectors, can enhance the benefits the country derives from the corridor.

The fiber-optic cable, shipbuilding, and air cargo transport projects are not isolated initiatives. Together, they form a system of infrastructure and services essential for transforming transport flows into economic value.

New Regional Logistics Model for Azerbaijan

The projects that Azerbaijan has implemented or is planning indicate a shift in the country’s role within the regional transport system. While the primary focus in the earlier phase was on attracting transit cargo flows by leveraging the country’s geographical location and existing transport infrastructure, the current strategy encompasses a broader scope.

The 30-million-ton regional target for the Middle Corridor, the expansion of the Port of Baku, the establishment of the Alat–Kuryk ferry system, the intermodal terminal project, the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable, the development of the Zangezur Corridor, and preparations for the construction of the Rasht–Astara railway line all serve to enhance Azerbaijan’s connectivity along the East–West and North–South axes.

However, the economic impact of these projects will not be determined solely by their completion. Key indicators will include the speed and cost-efficiency of cargo transport, the extent to which border and customs procedures are simplified, the coordination of port and railway operations, the involvement of the private sector, and the value added within the country by transit flows.

As emphasized by representatives from the IMF and the EBRD, the success of the Middle Corridor depends not only on the expansion of physical infrastructure but also on digitalization, institutional reforms, and the deepening of regional cooperation.

Thus, the primary task facing Azerbaijan is to transform its geographical position into a broader economic advantage. To achieve this, the country must evolve beyond serving merely as a transit territory for cargo; it must develop into a regional hub that integrates international trade, logistics, digital communications, processing, and manufacturing. The parallel development of the Middle Corridor and the Rasht–Astara line, alongside digital and multimodal connectivity, provides a key opportunity to realize this objective.

World.title: German FM thanks President Ilham Aliyev for warm welcome in Baku
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. German Foreign Minister Johann David Wadephul thanked Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev for the warm welcome he received during his visit to Baku.

Wadephul shared the message on his account on the social media platform X.

“Thank you, President, for your warm welcome in Baku. Azerbaijan is a reliable partner for the EU & Germany. Together, we are deepening our relationship with our Strategic Agenda. Germany encourages peace & cooperation between Azerbaijan & Armenia. We stand ready to support peace in the region,” the post reads.

World.title: Azerbaijani artist proposes festival dedicated to French cinema and music
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. Shafiga Mammadova, chair of the Azerbaijan Cinematographers Union and People's Artist, has proposed organizing a special festival dedicated to French cinema and music, Trend's correspondent reports.

Mammadova made the proposal on Tuesday in Baku during the opening of the Francophone Film Festival, which features films from France, Belgium, and Switzerland.

She noted that new film projects could be developed as part of cooperation with the French and Belgian embassies.

Mammadova suggested organizing either a festival or a special film evening dedicated to French cinema and its music.

“Perhaps we should hold such a festival or organize an evening dedicated to French cinema and its music. That would also be wonderful, and we could hold it jointly with the Union of Cinematographers,” she said.

Mammadova also encouraged participants to actively attend the film screenings and explore new cinematic works, while wishing the French Embassy success.

World.title: Francophone Film Festival opens in Baku with four European films
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. The Francophone Film Festival opened in Baku on November 17, featuring four films produced in France, Belgium and Switzerland, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

The festival is organized by the Embassies of France, Switzerland and Belgium in Azerbaijan, in cooperation with the Azerbaijan Union of Cinematographers.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, French Ambassador to Azerbaijan Sophie Lagoutte noted that the festival aims not only to promote the French language, spoken by around 300 million people worldwide, but also to support cultural diversity, international cooperation and peace.

"Cinema, by transcending our differences, serves as a powerful tool for bringing people together. It has the ability to connect people, encourage the exchange of views and create shared experiences," Lagoutte said.

In turn, Belgian Ambassador to Azerbaijan Julien de Fraipont placed particular emphasis on the film "The Kid with a Bike" (Le Gamin au vélo, 2011), directed by Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne, which will be screened on November 24. He noted that the film was a major success in Belgium and received the Audience Award at a film festival.

Meanwhile, Erica Garcia, attaché at the Embassy of Switzerland, highlighted the particular importance of cultural and linguistic diversity for her country. According to her, Switzerland, with its four national languages – German, French, Italian and Romansh – regards this diversity as one of the country's greatest assets.

The festival's main objective is to introduce Azerbaijani audiences to the rich cinematic heritage of Francophone countries, promote intercultural dialogue and present outstanding works of world cinema to a wider audience.

The festival opens on November 17 with a screening of the French musical comedy-drama "The Marching Band" (En fanfare, 2024), directed by Emmanuel Courcol. The film tells the story of a world-renowned conductor who discovers that he has a brother he never knew existed. Having grown up in completely different social environments, the brothers attempt to find common ground: one conducts famous orchestras, while the other works in a school cafeteria and plays the trombone in a local brass band. The film explores family ties, social inequality and the unifying power of music.

On November 24, audiences will be presented with the Belgian film "The Kid with a Bike" (Le Gamin au vélo, 2011), directed by Jean-Pierre and Luc Dardenne. The story centers on a boy searching for his father's love and care. The film raises issues of family relationships, social responsibility and human solidarity.

On December 1, the French film "Le Beau Serge" (1958), directed by Claude Chabrol, will be screened. It was his first feature-length film. The work, which played an important role in the emergence of the French New Wave, explores friendship, moral responsibility and contradictions in human relationships.

The program will conclude on December 8 with the historical drama "Unrest" (Unrueh, 2022) by Swiss director Cyril Schäublin. The film is set in a small Swiss town in the late 19th century, known for its watchmaking industry. The protagonist, Josephine, works at a factory producing watch mechanisms. Against the backdrop of technological changes and new approaches to the organization of labor, time and monetary circulation, she joins a local movement of anarchist watchmakers, where she meets Russian traveler and cartographer Peter Kropotkin.

The festival brings together works of classical and contemporary European cinema, showcasing diverse artistic approaches and stories of people from different eras and societies.

Screenings will take place every Tuesday at 7:00 p.m. at the CineMastercard Azerbaijan cinema.

World.title: Azerbaijan Army holds events marking National Revival Day (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 17. Events were held across the Azerbaijan Army on the occasion of 17 November – National Revival Day, the Azerbaijani Ministry of Defense reported.

The events commenced with commemorating the bright memory of the National Leader Heydar Aliyev and martyrs who sacrificed their lives for the Motherland. The National Anthem of the Republic of Azerbaijan was performed.

Speakers highlighted the historic role of 17 November – National Revival Day, a pivotal milestone in the Azerbaijani nation's struggle for freedom and restoration of the country's independence. They spoke about the foresight and wise policy of the National Leader, his profound commitment to national revival and spiritual values, as well as the successful continuation of Heydar Aliyev’s political course by the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Mr. Ilham Aliyev.

It was also underscored that the restoration of the tricolor flag of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic at the session of the newly convened Supreme Assembly of the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic on November 17, 1990, marked the beginning of a historic path leading from national revival to national prosperity.

Participants noted with a deep sense of pride and honor that, owing to the liberation of the lands from occupation by the Azerbaijan Army during the 44-day Patriotic War under the leadership of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Victorious Supreme Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces, Mr. Ilham Aliyev, 17 November – National Revival Day is now celebrated by our nation across the entire Motherland.

The musical performances, cultural programs, and other activities presented as part of the events aroused great interest among the event participants.

World.title: Why recognition of sexual assault 'often clicks' years later
World.content:
'Text me when you get home'. A pretend phone call on a low-lit street. Sharing your location before a first date.

These small acts of solidarity have long been commonplace in female friendships.

But as the public conversation around sexual violence and consent has grown, another kind of exchange has emerged: confiding about past sexual experiences that didn't feel right.

Experts say consent education has given women the language to name what happened to them, and many are finally gaining a sense of validation and justice years later.

A 'realisation' among friends

It's something writer and broadcaster Dee Salmin knows well.

"I've had multiple instances with friends where we're all having drinks and sharing some really vulnerable stories," Salmin says.

Dee Salmin says she grew up in a culture where sexual assault was "normalised". (Supplied)

"That's where you start to have that reckoning and those realisations."

It was through these conversations that Salmin recognised her own teenage experience as sexual assault, years after it happened.

She says even though it "felt wrong" at the time, she internalised blame because she "froze" in the moment.

"I was gaslighting myself into thinking that I'd done something that told him it was OK," she says.

"It's only now in hindsight, with maturity and education that I see how messed up it was."

The consent void

Salmin believes a lack of consent education made her experience "almost inevitable" with her and her peers normalising unacceptable behaviour.

"If someone at that time had heard my story and been like, 'Oh, that's sexual assault,' that might have really changed the types of interactions I had with men," she says.

" Sex ed was literally just a condom on a banana. "

It was only in her 20s, through her work on the sex and relationships podcast The Hook Up, that Salmin was able to understand and process her own sexual assault.

"I speak with so many incredible educators, activists and therapists and I now have such a strong understanding of consent and boundaries," she says.

Stream Dustfall on ABC iview When a detective investigates a spate of sexual assaults, little does she realise how close to home her investigations will lead.

When the realisation 'clicks'

Chanel Contos, founder and chief executive of Teach Us Consent, says someone might not identify a sexual assault in the moment because they're shocked, confused or don't have the words for it.

"It often clicks after learning about consent and what constitutes sexual violence," she says.

Ms Contos says this delayed realisation doesn't make the experience any less real or any less valid.

Chanel Contos says believing victim-survivors means supporting them whenever they choose to talk about it. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

"In the moment, people might freeze, shut down or fawn ... that's a stress and survival response, not consent."

Because these responses aren't widely understood, Ms Contos says victim-survivors often carry the belief that they are at fault and tell themselves it was "just bad sex" or a "miscommunication".

" It is never their fault. Responsibility sits with the person who didn't seek or respect consent. "

Why now?

Criminologist and social worker, Professor Anastasia Powell, says victim-survivors often knew their experience felt wrong, violating or frightening at the time, but it's only later that they fully recognised the harm.

Professor Powell, whose work focuses on sexual violence, says consent education in schools and increased media reporting have contributed to more awareness in the community.

Experts say understanding of sexual violence has improved over time, due to prominent advocates such as Brittany Higgins and Grace Tame. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"Recently we've seen extraordinary survivor advocates who have spoken openly about sexual violence and the failures of our institutions," she says.

" It can be common for someone to see these stories and recognise the parallels in their own life experience. "

But Professor Powell says there are significant gaps in community knowledge with many people still having a "really narrow picture" of sexual violence.

"There is a really persistent stereotype ... that it's the stranger, it's very physically forced, that it's a victim who clearly says no and fights back," she says.

" In reality, sexual assault is very often committed by someone known to us, often a date or an intimate partner. "

Anastasia Powell says stereotypes of sexual violence do not reflect the reality. (Supplied)

Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data shows female victim-survivors knew the male perpetrator in 84 per cent of cases. It also shows that of those women who have been sexually assaulted, one in three of the incidents occurred in their own home.

Professor Powell says common scenarios can include being intoxicated or asleep, consenting to one act but not another, feeling pressured or intimidated or simply freezing.

Intentional language and labels

Labelling these experiences, where there is no active agreement or consent, helps the broader community understand what sexual assault actually is, according to Professor Powell.

"Naming that sexual violence really clearly is part of recognising its seriousness and holding perpetrators to account," she says.

However, Professor Powell acknowledges that words like rape and sexual assault can initially feel "very confronting".

"People do need to be able to find space to find the words for their own experience in their own time," she says.

In Salmin's case, she was reluctant to identify herself as a victim-survivor because she didn't want it to become a core part of her identity.

Dee Salmin discloses details of her sexual assault in her book It's Not Love, Actually. (Supplied)

But she says sharing her story of sexual assault publicly was an important decision.

"It was really about being honest and naming things that a lot of women and girls experience that isn't spoken about as much as it should be," Salmin says.

The path to recovery

It's this sense of solidarity gained by exchanging "awful experiences" that Salmin has found to be "deeply bonding" and "healing".

"There's something really cathartic in realising you're not alone," she says.

"Lots of people won't want to talk about their experiences publicly or even privately to people, and that's absolutely fine.

"[But] if I can prevent someone from experiencing what I did, then [me speaking up] has been worth it."

Dee Salmin says sharing her story publicly has created a safer space for podcast listeners to open up about their own experiences. (Supplied)

Professor Powell says it's important for victim-survivors to be in control of their own story and to choose a pathway that feels right for them.

According to the ABS data, 92 per cent of women who experienced sexual assault by a male did not report the most recent incident to police.

Their reasons included: feeling like they could deal with it themselves, not regarding the incident as serious, feeling ashamed or embarrassed, thinking there was little the police could do, or feeling they wouldn't be believed.

"We know that criminal legal processes so often fail victim-survivors," she says.

" Justice doesn't have to mean a criminal prosecution. It might be more of a felt sense of justice that's much more personal. "

This can come from having the support of friends, family or a counsellor, who believe you and recognise the harm, according to Professor Powell.

She says it is possible for victim-survivors to heal and recover, with some "having a stronger sense of themselves" over time.

"It's one experience, one of many different experiences we might have in our life. It doesn't have to define who we are as a person," she says.

Stream all episodes of Dustfall now on ABC iview.

World.title: Senate paraquat inquiry under fire over vote to skip public hearings
World.content:
Neurologists and Parkinson's disease advocates say they have been gagged from publicly criticising the pesticides regulator as a Senate inquiry closes its doors to public hearings.

The Senate committee tasked with reviewing the controversial chemical paraquat, which has been linked to Parkinson's, will not hold public hearings for the first time in a decade.

The inquiry has been set up to examine the use of paraquat in Australia, given concerns of its links to Parkinson's disease.

Farmers use paraquat to control weeds in a range of crops, from broadacre grains to orchards and vineyards.

The Senate Standing Committee on Rural and Regional Affairs and Transport has chosen to complete an "on paper" review of submissions to the "continued use and regulation of paraquat" inquiry.

The terms of reference include an investigation of the regulator charged with giving the chemical the green light, the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority (APVMA).

Experts call for transparency

The committee was set to hear from some of the country's leading Parkinson's Disease experts, who have heavily criticised the regulator's review of the chemical in their submissions to the inquiry.

David Blacker, a neurologist from WA and Parkinson's sufferer, is among them.

"For the public to have confidence in any decision, it has to have transparency," he said.

Professor Blacker said his cohort of dozens of neurologists from around the country were hoping to publicly raise issues with the regulator's final review of paraquat, which was released in June after a decades-long process.

"We wanted to raise that the report itself has a whole lot of flaws," he said.

"There are internal flaws of logic, there are contradictions, there are straight-out transcription errors of numbers in studies that lead to fairly substantial conclusions in the wrong way."

David Blacker is calling for a ban of the herbicide paraquat due to its link with Parkinson's disease. (Supplied)

Approval process needs scruinty

Professor Blacker said the APVMA had misinterpreted the AGVET code when making its decision on the continued use of paraquat in Australia.

"If we develop a new drug or treatment, before we give it to the general population, we have to definitively prove that it is safe," he said.

"Whereas the scenario that has evolved in Australia is completely the opposite of that, where the potentially hazardous chemicals are used and we've had to demonstrate harm before action will occur, which is completely the wrong way around."

After the harvest In this small rural community, Parkinson's disease is all too common. Many fear that farm chemicals could be behind it.

Independent ACT senator David Pocock sits on the Senate committee tasked with the inquiry and agrees the regulator needs serious scrutiny.

"There's some really fundamental questions about how our national pesticide regulator conducts scientific reviews, with many experts questioning whether its methods are actually transparent and replicable," he said.

"If other scientists can't independently scrutinise or replicate how the regulator assessed the evidence, then I think there is a serious problem and the Senate should be looking at that."

Mr Pocock said the major parties colluded to shut down hearings, and was worried it would impact the outcome of the committee report.

"If you're not willing to have a public hearing and actually hear from farmers, hear from experts, allow the APVMA to be questioned, it kind of shows that you don't want too much scrutiny," he said.

A senate inquiry investigating the use of paraquat on Australian farms will not hold public hearings. (ABC News: Jo Prendergast)

Industry pressure to forgo hearings

Mr Pocock put a motion to the Senate to call for public hearings, but it was defeated in what he calls a "very unusual" vote.

"Of the 35 reference inquiries this committee has conducted over the past decade, every single one held a public hearing," he said.

"So this is very unusual for the Senate, and it's the major parties voting against public hearings."

Mr Pocock pointed to public pressure on the committee from industry groups after the inquiry was announced in September as a reason for the backflip.

Australia approves restricted use of herbicide banned in 70 other countries The Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority concludes its nearly 30-year review of the controversial but popular herbicide.

"I can't speak for them. I'd love them to actually give us an answer on that because a number of senators on that committee in the past have really pushed for public hearings and have talked about the value of them and that isn't the case with this particular inquiry," he said.

" This raises serious questions about whose interests are being prioritised; farmers living with Parkinson's disease deserve to have their stories heard by the Senate. "

In a statement to the ABC, deputy chair of the committee, Nationals senator Ross Cadell, denied industry pressure came to bear on the vote.

"That's a personal view and industry has nothing to do with it," he said.

" It's a complicated topic where the science should be examined, which can be done by submission, as opposed to by emotions in a public enquiry. "

Farmers use paraquat to control weeds in their crops. (ABC: Bec Whetham)

Advocates 'disgusted'

CEO of Parkinson's Australia, Olivia Nassaris, said she was "disgusted" by the move to forgo public hearings.

"I was shocked and I felt deeply disgusted that there wasn't a public hearing because I had told people living with Parkinson's that they were going to be able to represent their truth to the Senate committee, and now they don't get that opportunity, and I don't think that's what our democracy is built on," she said.

Ms Nassaris said she believed the committee and the chemicals regulator had bowed to pressure from industry groups.

"I think that the APVMA has bowed to pressure from the farming industry," she said.

"I definitely think that they're not wanting to hear from people living with Parkinson's, and the saddest thing about being gagged is that you are gagging people who are living with a degenerative, incurable condition."

Loading...

In a statement, the APVMA said it "does not accept that its decision was shaped by farming industry pressure or that it failed to correctly apply the statutory criteria in the AGVET Code".

"The final decision did not allow paraquat use to continue unchanged. It introduced significant restrictions, including reduced application rates, strengthened worker protections and the removal of uses that did not meet the statutory criteria," the statement said.

The APVMA has made changes to usage requirements, and said if used according to guidelines — which are now stricter than ever — it does not believe paraquat is unsafe.

The company that first made paraquat, Syngenta, said there was no proof the chemical caused Parkinson's Disease and maintained the product was safe for farmers to use.

In September, when the inquiry was announced, WA Farmers grain council president Mark Fowler launched a broadside at the Liberals and Nationals.

"The Liberals and the Nationals are supposed to be connected to their rural roots," he said.

"This does not reflect that at all. Politicising one of our cornerstone chemicals for the system we depend on in Australia is not in grain growers' or farmers' interests."

Mr Fowler declined an interview.

Parkinson's Australia to launch case against regulator

Ms Nassaris said her organisation, the peak body for Parkinson's advocacy, is taking the APVMA to the Administrative Review Tribunal over its decision to allow the continued use of paraquat.

The tribunal has powers to set aside or vary the regulator's decision.

"Parkinson's Australia is running a parallel appeal with the Administrative Review Tribunal, and we're very lucky to be represented with pro bono solicitors and barristers"

"Parkinson's Australia will argue that APVMA did not properly consider the significant body of scientific evidence showing an increased risk of Parkinson's disease among people exposed to paraquat and so we're not stopping here; we're going to keep going," she said.

Olivia Nassaris says she is 'disgusted' people will not be able to share their stories in person at the senate inquiry. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

Dozens of neurologists wrote to the APVMA during their chemical review process in 2024.

Dr Blacker said he was disappointed when the regulator did not contact them for health advice and was hoping the public inquiry would be a chance to rectify that.

Parkinson's disease experts warn watchdog as deadline looms on paraquat decision Dozens of neurologists are concerned "real world" human studies linking paraquat to Parkinson's disease are being overlooked as the regulator weighs up the future of the controversial weed killer.

"Putting us in the corner and not listening to us runs a risk of us not making any further progress on this condition," he said.

"Although it's a terrible situation, the fact that we're honing in now on potential causes gives us an opportunity to actually start reducing risk exposures and potentially start turning around this rapid increase in people with Parkinson's disease." Dr Blacker said.

The ABC contacted the 26 senators who voted no to holding public hearings.

Apart from Nationals senator Ross Cadell, the Assistant Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, Senator Anthony Chisholm responded on behalf of the ALP senator and Liberal senator Matt O'Sullivan also replied, but the rest did not respond.

Assistant Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry, Senator Anthony Chisholm said in a statement on behalf of ALP senators:

“The Government supports a robust regulatory framework for agricultural and veterinary chemicals in Australia that puts science at the centre of decisions about our health and safety.

“The APVMA is an independent statutory authority that makes regulatory decisions based on scientific evidence and in accordance with the law.”

Liberal Senator Matt O'Sullivan said in a statement he: "respects the committee's decision and considers the APVMA is best placed to assess the scientific evidence and determine the appropriate regulatory response".

The inquiry has received submissions from industry groups and peak bodies representing Parkinson's doctors and sufferers. Submissions are open until November 18.

The committee will report on the first sitting day of 2027.

World.title: Bupa GP clinic urged doctors to bill costly Medicare items to lift revenue
World.content:
A GP clinic operated by health insurance giant Bupa encouraged doctors to lift their billing of more costly Medicare items.

The ABC has obtained an email from a Bupa clinic to its GPs in June, which told doctors to ensure "revenue is increasing".

The email asked doctors to do this by increasing the bookings of patients for costly Medicare checks known as "chronic condition management plans" (CCMPs).

It further encouraged doctors to re-book patients, if they were eligible for further checks but Medicare rules prevented them from being claimed on the same day.

CCMPs are personalised plans written by GPs, designed to create a structure to improve outcomes for people struggling with complex health conditions.

The plans can be used for conditions ranging from eczema to heart disease, and while often beneficial to patients, they may not be essential for everyone with a chronic condition.

The Medicare schedule fee for a GP to prepare a CCMP is $160.60, compared to $87.10 for a standard GP appointment lasting at least 20 minutes.

The federal government's spending on the plans is rising rapidly and it is now spending nearly $1.3 billion a year on these chronic care plans out of the $35 billion Medicare budget.

'Need to explain' why items not billed

In the email, Bupa told doctors their appointment books were closely scrutinised each day through the popular software portal Cubiko, for "possible service opportunities", and notes were left about what could be billed.

Bupa operates 33 medical centres. (ABC News: John Gunn)

The booking software includes a specific function to check for chances to bill patients for 'possible service opportunities', including the costly chronic care plans.

The email also detailed how the "ops team" had tasked the practice managers with "ensuring revenue is increasing by ensuring there is an uptick in billings of HA [health assessments]".

Cubiko spruiks that its "QuickCheck" function can help identify opportunities for billing patients more Medicare items. (ABC News: Screenshot)

Bupa's email then went on to list the Medicare item numbers for these health assessments, including chronic condition management plans and a nurse item.

GPs were reminded that practice managers need to "ensure" an increase in patients being charged for these more expensive Medicare items, otherwise practice managers "need to explain why these are not being billed".

In a statement, Bupa said the email was sent at one clinic and was an attempt to remind doctors to consider preventative care.

"Patient needs, clinical judgement and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first," it said.

" While technology solutions help provide prompts … decisions about a patient's care and eligibility always remain with the treating doctor. "

Bupa said practice managers provide "administrative support to our doctors. Patient needs, clinical judgement, and compliance with Medicare requirements always come first and we reinforce this through ongoing guidance and training".

Do you know more? Share it with us here.

If GPs coerced, 'it has to be stopped'

Health economist Terry Barnes was a senior adviser to two health ministers in the Howard government.

He told the ABC he was not surprised by Bupa's email, and it was a window into how much corporate owners of GP clinics "called the shots".

Terry Barnes says optional extras like chronic condition management plans should not become mandatory Medicare billings. (ABC News: Billy Draper)

"If corporates are putting pressure on their doctors to order health assessments or any other type of extra service, and the optional extras become mandatory, then there is a real problem there," he said.

"If they are actually putting pressure on the doctors, coercing them internally, to behave in a certain way in relation to billing services and generating services then that has to be stopped."

Are private health insurers moving to US-style model? Increasing partnerships among health insurers, GP centres, and telehealth services raise concerns about a potential two-tier system in which privately insured patients have more affordable access to GP consultations.

He said the GP sector was becoming increasingly corporatised and more guardrails were needed to regulate owners.

"It comes down to the fact that corporates actually rely on taxpayer-funded Medicare for their revenue streams.

"Legislatively, corporates do have responsibilities to their shareholders and investors. GPs have a responsibility to their patients. It's important that those two conflicting responsibilities are reconciled."

Questions about Bupa's management of practices follow the announcement in June of its biggest takeover yet, acquiring Partnered Health's 68 clinics nationwide.

'Clinical autonomy' in question

To comply with Medicare, GPs could only bill items like chronic care plans when they were "medically necessary", according to Royal Australian College of General Practitioners president Michael Wright.

He said the plans "were really designed" to encourage GPs to be more proactive with patients with complex conditions, and GPs should not be put under undue pressure to bill certain items.

Dr Michael Wright says GPs should not face undue pressure from corporate owners of medical centres to over-service patients. (ABC News: John Gunn )

"It's important that GPs know that they're available, but certainly they shouldn't be forced into any particular billing model."

"The financial autonomy of GPs is core to the successes of Medicare and our health system," Dr Wright said.

A Cubiko spokesperson said it respected the clinical autonomy of general practitioners, and its software helped practices meet strict Medicare eligibility rules "therefore reducing, not increasing, the risk of incorrect billing".

"Chronic disease is significantly under-managed in Australian general practice, and Cubiko's tools help practices identify patients who may have unmet care needs," they said.

Chronic care plans 'bugbear' of regulator

The potential abuse of the chronic care plans across the industry has angered Bill Coote, who headed the Medicare regulator, the Professional Services Review (PSR), between 2011 and 2016.

Doctors had long campaigned for the Medicare item to legitimately fund help for the growing burden of the population with chronic disease, said Dr Coote, a past secretary-general of the Australian Medical Association.

Dr Bill Coote says he was concerned at his time with the Medicare regulator that lucrative chronic condition management plans were open to potential exploitation. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

But during his time at the PSR, Dr Coote said he saw continued allegations of abuse of the billing items and said it was the "bugbear" of his existence at the regulator.

He said it had been "galling" to oversee cases of GPs submitting reams of plans and billed Medicare multiple times, but there was little or no information even written into the actual plans.

"There was certainly encouragement of practitioners to bill those items for anyone with a chronic illness," he said.

"So, the ones we saw tended to be the extreme ones … and their claiming numbers were really quite extreme."

Medical centres not registered for Medicare

In 2023, an independent review of Medicare Integrity and Compliance scrutinised the management of corporatised GP clinics.

The author of the report, health economist Pradeep Philip, noted "surprisingly" that medical centres do not need to be registered Medicare providers — even though they collect revenue from the scheme.

"Increasingly, practitioners note that they have less and less visibility and control over what is billed in their name," Dr Philip, of Deloitte Access Economics wrote.

Three years on, the Department of Health has confirmed that, despite recent law changes, there is still no requirement for medical centres and their operators to be registered with Medicare.

The Medicare regulator is called the Professional Services Review. (Getty: Lisa Maree Williams)

"Medical centres are private businesses and are required to comply with relevant legislation," it said.

In effect, it means GP employees can have their access to Medicare revoked for bad behaviour — but the centres themselves do not face the same risk for encouraging such conduct.

One penalty handed down

The PSR does have some powers to regulate body corporates like medical centres and hospitals.

However, it has handed down just one penalty to such an entity — only referred to in public documents as "a company", which was handed a $1.16 million fine in 2023 for "inappropriate practice".

It said the head of Medicare had referred other companies to the agency for investigation as well.

"However, these investigations have either resulted in no further action or have not yet been finalised," the PSR said in a statement.

The Department of Health said it was implementing key findings of the 2023 review and spending $147 million over four years to crack down on non-compliance and improve fraud detection.

Bill Coote said Bupa was clearly not giving due consideration to the legal and ethical position doctors were in, based on the email it sent.

"You get the impression it's written by someone who's much more focused on the bottom line."
