Distraught Thomas Embling Hospital staff remain caring for a high-risk patient in the unit where he allegedly raped one of their colleagues, despite having repeatedly flagged security concerns. Police, health authorities and WorkSafe continue to investigate the alleged rape of a nurse by a patient in the hospital’s Apsley unit on November 2, amid staff calls for immediate security upgrades and increased staffing levels. Thomas Embling Hospital’s Apsley unit. The nurse’s alleged attacker has been held in the forensic hospital for years under a court order, after he was found not guilty of sexual offences due to mental impairment. Three sources, who cannot speak publicly due to patient confidentiality provisions, have told this masthead the man is still being held in the Apsley unit despite staff pleas for him to be transferred to a prison-based psychiatric facility.



They said the man – who has not been charged by police – has a history of violence against staff and has been kept in seclusion within the unit since November 2. Related Article Healthcare Police investigate alleged rape of nurse at Thomas Embling Hospital Unions representing the Thomas Embling workers are in discussions with the hospital’s operator, Forensicare, demanding security and staffing overhauls and the immediate transfer of the alleged rapist. The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists (RANZCP) is also considering stripping Forensicare of its training positions over concerns Thomas Embling is too unsafe for young doctors. A university last week cancelled work placements at the hospital from its nursing course due to safety issues.



A patient room inside Thomas Embling Hospital’s Apsley unit. A Forensicare spokesperson said it had provided a range of supports to staff and consumers following the alleged sex attack, and was working closely with police and other agencies as they investigate. “We have taken immediate steps to ensure safety within the unit and continue to monitor and review those measures,” the spokesperson said. “We are also conducting a comprehensive serious incident review to understand the circumstances, identify any lessons that may be learned, and determine what further actions are required to strengthen safety and support across the service. “The serious incident review will consider all relevant contributing factors and inform any actions required to further strengthen safety and operations within the unit.”



The eight-bed Apsley unit houses high-risk patients who have committed security breaches in other areas of the hospital, or who are deemed too dangerous for less secure units. This includes at least two long-term residents considered particularly dangerous, who were each found not guilty of heinous crimes due to mental impairment, according to one person who recently attended the unit but is not authorised to discuss it. The alleged rapist is one of these men. Other patients are moved into Apsley for several months at a time over security issues, such as being caught with smuggled drugs or presenting a risk to themselves or others, the person who attended the unit said. But the Apsley unit was not designed as a long-term secure setting for complex patients when it was opened in 2019, and staff say its small rooms and tight confines are not suitable for its current use.



Information previously posted on Forensicare’s website – but now removed – stated the Apsley unit offered “short-term treatment for severely unwell prisoners”, and was intended as a stepping stone to reduce waiting times for prisoners on compulsory treatment orders. “Apsley is a state-of-the-art short-term unit that will provide a charming space to assist patients in their mental health recovery journey,” a record of its opening stated. Thomas Embling Hospital’s Apsley unit. “Apsley patients will be treated by an experienced team of specialist multidisciplinary clinicians, using positive behaviours support treatment programs.” Another article, celebrating the unit’s 2020 Mental Health Design Award category win at the European Healthcare Design Awards, remains on the website. It states the award recognised Apsley’s environment that supports ongoing therapy, care and recovery, as well as appropriate levels of safety, security and supervision.



However, the Australian Nursing Midwifery Federation’s Victorian branch secretary, Maddy Harradence, said she was extremely concerned about the ongoing psychological impacts and physical safety of nurses at the facility. The nurses’ union is demanding Forensicare act immediately to improve safety, including transferring the alleged attacker, reducing the number of beds in Apsley while maintaining current staffing levels, and returning the unit to its primary purpose as a short-stay unit. The latest violence comes amid a wider Victorian mental healthcare crisis, extensively reported on by this masthead, which Paul Healey, the Health and Community Services Workers Union Victorian branch secretary, said the state government had again failed to address. “Ultimately, this once again comes back to sector-wide underfunding, a failure to invest in community teams, understaffing across the board and severe lack of understanding from parliamentarians about the realities facing the mental health workforce,” Healey said. The RANZCP confirmed it remained in discussions with Forensicare about its training accreditation of Thomas Embling Hospital and the Apsley unit, including the safety, supervision and support available to trainees.



“The RANZCP is deeply concerned by reports of an alleged sexual assault at Thomas Embling Hospital and the broader concerns being raised about safety within the facility. Patients, staff and trainees must be able to receive care, work and train in an environment that is safe and supportive,” the RANZCP said in a statement. “The concerns being raised also highlight a much broader challenge across forensic mental health: workforce shortages. “Safe and effective services depend on having enough appropriately trained staff, yet chronic shortages continue to place significant pressure on both workers and services.” Staff working in the Apsley told this masthead it relied on high levels of international medical and nursing graduates, whose working visas are sponsored by Forensicare.



To fill its growing staffing gaps, Forensicare sent a delegation to London and Manchester in September as part of a “UK recruitment tour”, aimed at finding new psychiatrists, nurses and other staff. As of this week, Forensicare has 26 open jobs listed on British employment sites, seeking staff ranging from a $424,816-a-year director of clinical services, to clinical support workers with a starting salary of $67,724. Each position is advertised with a $10,000 resettlement incentive. The international recruitment drive also aims to attract psychiatrists of varying seniority, psychologists, nurses, a nurse unit manager, an occupational therapist and administration and support staff. “Forensicare is undergoing one of the largest expansions in its history. Over the coming years, Thomas Embling Hospital will expand from 136 beds to 218 beds, with the addition of six new inpatient units and 82 new beds,” the job ads state. “Rather than joining a mature service with limited growth opportunities, you will be part of an organisation at a transformational stage of development.



“Unlike many healthcare settings, you’ll be supported by a workforce of qualified mental health professionals working collaboratively to deliver outstanding clinical outcomes.” But two sources have confirmed the RANZCP is preparing to remove Forensicare’s remaining two training posts, which allow junior doctors to work while completing their forensic qualifications. The college first took the extreme measure of stripping Thomas Embling of its seven training posts in October 2025 due to violence and worsening staff conditions at the facility, before returning two positions in February. Forensicare’s 2025-26 annual report revealed it had paid a consultant $16,500 to review its medical workforce and find out the “root causes of workforce dissatisfaction, operational inefficiency, and sustainability risk”. A Department of Health spokesperson said adverse events in mental health care were rare, and every effort was made to reduce the risk of violence and aggression through staff training and workplace protocols.



The spokesperson said the Thomas Embling Hospital incident was especially distressing and the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist was working closely with Forensicare as it undertook its incident review and implements any necessary changes. “The Department of Health continues to work closely with health services, unions and frontline staff to address occupational violence and aggression,” the spokesperson said. World.title: ASX eyes more losses as Wall Street falls; Nvidia results ahead
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX eyes more losses as Wall Street falls; Nvidia results ahead Stan Choe November 18, 2026 — 5:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. More manic swings for Nvidia and other stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry are dragging the US market downward. The S&P 500 sank 1.1 per cent and at one point was on track for its first back-to-back losses of at least 1.5 per cent since March. The Dow Jones was down 779 points, or 1.5 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite was down 1.2 per cent. Nvidia’s results will land after the closing bell. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to slide, with futures at 4.47am AEDT pointing to a loss of 37 points, or 0.4 per cent, at the open. The ASX slumped 1.8 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was steady at US67.41¢. The centre of the action was again Nvidia, which resumed its whipsaw moves. After flipping between modest gains and losses in the morning, it veered lower and dropped as much as 3.7 per cent before paring its loss to 1 per cent. The chip company is scheduled to deliver its latest earnings report after trading ends for the day. It will be the first time interim CEO Colette Kress speaks to Wall Street since taking over for Jensen Huang, the leather-jacketed star who became one of the most famous faces of the AI boom.



The pressure is on Kress and Nvidia to show whether the company’s tremendous growth can continue following the stunning resignation of one of AI’s strongest influencers. Nvidia is creating a new board committee to oversee national security and global trade compliance following revelations that Huang had a relationship with an alleged spy for China. Related Article Gender equality Gender pay gap drops below 20 per cent, but women still fall short of the top job Huang said on the X social-media network Tuesday that he would come back as CEO if “the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America.” Other stocks in the AI industry likewise swung lower after giving up early-morning strength. Advanced Micro Devices went from an early gain of 1.6 per cent to a drop of 2.1 per cent. After an initial climb of 1.8 per cent, CoreWeave flipped to a loss of 1.3 per cent AI-related stocks have been shaky for months because of a rolling chain of worries. At first, it was concerns that AI stock prices had broadly shot too high in their frenzy. Then it was worries that high interest rates would mean less borrowed money to fund further growth. More recently, it was concerns that Democratic victories in this month’s U.S. midterm elections could mean tougher regulations and restrictions on AI data centres.



Such stocks can almost single-handedly set the U.S. market’s course because they’ve grown into some of Wall Street’s most valuable and most influential. Most of Wall Street was weak Tuesday, and Home Depot sank 2.3 per cent even though it reported profit for the latest quarter that edged past analysts’ expectations. The retailer has been hampered by a housing market chilled by expensive mortgage rates, which have climbed with Treasury yields because of high oil prices, high inflation and other factors. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed toward 5.15 per cent Tuesday morning from 5.12 per cent late Monday before later pulling back to 5.10 per cent. It erased its gains after the sharp drops for AI stocks pushed investors to herd into investments seen as safer bets. In the morning, yields got support from a report showing an underlying measure of spending at U.S. retailers was stronger last month than economists expected. Such spending, along with big investments in AI, has helped the U.S. economy continue to grow despite frustration with high inflation.



Elsewhere on Wall Street, stocks of banks were lower amid concerns about how much pain the broad U.S. economy will feel from any pullback in AI-related spending. JPMorgan Chase fell 2.1 per cent. A day before, a technical issue at the bank had slowed transactions for customers trying to use the Zelle payment system. United Airlines had its own operational struggles, as a system outage lasted more than 90 minutes and forced the carrier to delay departing flights Monday. The outage came just days after a malfunction in the Federal Aviation Administration’s network prompted a nationwide ground stop. United’s stock lost 3.3 per cent, but that may have been due more to a rise in oil prices. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil rose 1 per cent to $93.36. It’s been yo-yoing amid uncertainty about what will happen in the war with Iran.



The Walt Disney Co. helped limit Wall Street’s losses after rising 0.7 per cent. It reported stronger revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Related Article Opinion

AI Ousted Nvidia boss may have bigger problems than getting his job back Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Stock prices generally tend to follow the path of corporate profits over the long term, depending on how interest rates behave. The big businesses across the S&P 500 index are on track to deliver earnings per share for the summer that are nearly 32 per cent higher than a year earlier, according to FactSet. In stock markets abroad, indexes sank across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 2.6 per cent and dropped to its lowest closing level since February. World.title: Don’t want the age pension? These new tax rules might change your mind
World.content:
Analysis MoneyPlanning & budgetingPension Don’t want the age pension? These new tax rules might change your mind Sandy Wong and Chris Holloway November 18, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tax changes often have unexpected consequences, and the proposals to overhaul Australia’s capital gains tax (CGT) system announced in this year’s federal budget are no exception. One surprising implication is that for eligible retirees, the age pension may now be more valuable than many people realise. While the details of the proposed CGT changes are currently being debated, the budget announcement suggests capital gains on investments will be taxed at a minimum rate of 30 per cent, increasing potential tax liabilities. The rules are expected to apply to assets from July 1, 2027, meaning individuals may face higher taxes on their investment returns over time. Applying for the age pension takes some effort, but proposed changes to the CGT rules add to the existing benefits. Dominic Lorrimer The little-known exemption for pensioners Under the proposed changes, individuals who receive a means-tested support payment (such as the age pension) in the financial year of the realised capital gain, may be exempt from the new minimum tax CGT rules. This exemption can apply even if the retiree is eligible to receive only a partial payment.



Around 2.7 million Australians receive at least some level of income from the age pension. But some retirees who are eligible for the benefits choose not to apply, viewing it as unnecessary or a “status” issue if they can self-fund their retirement. The CGT changes may overturn this view. Receiving even $1 of age pension could potentially mean a significant reduction in overall tax on investments – particularly for retirees with a lower taxable income. Consider this common hypothetical example, fast forwarding to 2029 to show how the changed CGT treatment would play out. Adam is single and turns 75 in August 2029. He owns his home, which is valued at $800,000. His household contents and car are worth $40,000. He has $440,000 in a bank account and share investments worth $250,000, which he purchased at a cost base of $160,000 and which were worth $220,000 on July 1, 2027. Adam is conscious that his assets are near the assets test limit for the age pension. He did not bother to apply for age pension as he may need to inform Services Australia (Centrelink) if his shares increase in value and put him above limit.



Let’s say that Adam intends to sell his shares to fund a move into aged care while he prepares his home for sale. Since he does not receive the age pension, the share sale would trigger CGT and the capital gains from the share sales would be subject to the minimum 30 per cent tax. In this case, Adam would pay a total of $8,543 in tax on the sale of his shares. Should he receive a part aged pension in the financial year of the share sale, there would be no minimum 30 per cent minimum tax, but more favourable marginal tax rates applied to the overall capital gains. This would result in a total tax bill of $6,143 – which is a $2,400 tax saving compared to what he needs to pay without the age pension. The table below outlines the calculations. Although the income Adam is entitled to through the age pension may be small, the tax advantage of applying makes a significant difference to the amount he ends up with after the sale of his shares.



Age pension recipients can also unlock benefits such as the Pensioner Concession Card, which entitles them to lower cost health care, and the Energy Supplement to assist with specific household bills. Editor's pick Opinion

Hip pocket Worried you can’t afford aged care? Here’s what you could pay Dominic Powell Money Editor Applying for the age pension does take some effort, but the proposed changes to the CGT rules add to the existing benefits. Even a small entitlement can have significant value. Professional financial advisers can also help with these processes, so retirees do not have to tackle the task alone. For people who expect to realise capital gains on their investments in the coming years, now presents a good window of opportunity to reassess age pension eligibility and plan ahead as there are potential strategies that an individual may consider. In addition, there will be an increased need for individuals to maintain detailed records. This includes accurate cost-base information for assets – at their purchase date, as their value stood on July 1, 2027, and any adjustments arising from Dividend Reinvestment Plans.



Sandy Wong is the national manager, advice and Chris Holloway is the senior manager of tax at Equity Trustees. Advice given in this article is general in nature and not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: My mum died last year. Do we need to file her last tax return?
World.content:
MoneyTaxAsk an expert Opinion My mum died last year. Do we need to file her last tax return? Noel Whittaker Money columnist November 18, 2026 — 5:01am

November 18, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

I am 69 and co-executor of my mother’s estate with my sister, 64, and brother, 59. Mum died late last year aged 95, and her only substantial asset was the family home, now on the market for about $1.2 million. We opened an estate bank account, but funeral expenses, household bills and selling costs have exhausted her remaining cash. I’m getting conflicting advice about whether we need to lodge a final tax return for Mum or a separate return for her estate. Her only income was the age pension, and she hadn’t paid income tax for years. The ATO hasn’t been particularly helpful. What are our responsibilities as executors, and how can we settle the estate without unnecessary complications or delays? Even a straightforward estate can face an unexpected challenge. Simon Letch I think it’s well worth engaging an accountant and a solicitor to guide you through the process. If your mother’s only income was the age pension, it’s unlikely a final personal tax return will be necessary, but the ATO should be notified of her death and advised that no further returns are required. The estate is a separate matter and may need to lodge a tax return, depending on whether it earns taxable income or makes a taxable capital gain. The good news is that the sale of your mother’s home should be exempt from capital gains tax, provided it was her main residence and settlement occurs within two years of her death. Your accountant can confirm the exemption and deal with the ATO.



As executors, your practical duties are to identify and collect the assets, keep proper records of money received and expenses paid, settle outstanding bills and taxes, and distribute the balance according to the will. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m worried our super could get hacked. Is my money safer in the bank? Paul Benson Money contributor Keep the beneficiaries informed, retain enough money to cover any unexpected liabilities and don’t rush to distribute the proceeds until you’re satisfied all obligations have been met. Even a straightforward estate can face an unexpected challenge, which is why a solicitor’s guidance is valuable. Given what you’ve told me, the professional costs should be manageable, and a little advice now could save considerable expense and worry later. You recently wrote about a testamentary trust of David who named his three children as equal beneficiaries. Could the 30 per cent minimum tax and non-refundable offset be avoided by nominating the three children as equal beneficiaries under the “excluded election trust” option, provided they receive their shares as specified?



Estate lawyer Rachael Rofe tells me this option is available only to trusts existing on July 1, 2028. David’s trust, commencing in 2030, could not qualify. A testamentary trust established from July 1, 2028 can qualify for an exclusion from the 30 per cent minimum tax if its beneficiaries are limited to individuals, tax-exempt entities and special disability trusts. A will allowing companies or trusts to benefit may fail, even if they receive nothing. Earlier trusts are exempt from this condition. The exclusion covers only income from inherited assets. Get this right and a testamentary trust remains one of the most tax-effective and asset-protective vehicles. The legislation is still before parliament, but David should review his will. For existing family trusts, the election fixes each beneficiary’s share, changeable only on death or relationship breakdown. The trustee could no longer favour a lower-income child over a high-income one, losing much flexibility. I am 67, single and working full-time, earning $3432 a fortnight after tax. I hope to retire within two years. My superannuation balance is $239,000, and my employer and voluntary contributions total the maximum $32,500 a year. I owe $219,400 on my mortgage at 6.89 per cent, with repayments of $788 a fortnight. I also have $15,350 in redraw and $6400 in savings. Should I withdraw $100,000 from super to reduce the mortgage or leave it invested? I’m worried about retiring with a large debt but equally concerned about depleting my super.



The conventional wisdom was to focus on super because the returns should exceed your mortgage interest. But those days are gone. With mortgage rates approaching 7 per cent, reducing your debt may be just as beneficial as investing in super, particularly in these uncertain times. Editor's pick Opinion

Hip pocket Tax office breathing down your neck? Here’s how to make it stop Dominic Powell Money Editor I have no problem with you withdrawing money from super to reduce the mortgage, but keep making the maximum concessional contributions while working. Once your home is paid off, you’ll have a valuable retirement asset. As the years pass, you may even consider accessing some of that equity through a reverse mortgage or the government’s Home Equity Access Scheme to help meet rising living costs. My father, 63, recently inherited money following the death of his parents. He wants to give $20,000 each to my sister and me. He is still working full-time and plans to continue for at least another five years. We understand Centrelink has gifting rules and that the $40,000 could affect his future age pension entitlement. But are there any other financial or tax consequences? Would he pay tax on the gifts, and would my sister or I have to declare the money as income? Is there anything else we should consider before he transfers it?



Your father won’t be eligible for the age pension for another four years, and gifts exceeding Centrelink’s allowable limits are counted for five years from the date they are made. Given the timing, the impact on his future pension should be relatively minor. There are no tax consequences for either the giver or the recipient. However, once the money is in your names, any income earned from investing it may be taxable. Noel Whittaker is the author of Retirement Made Simple and other books on personal finance. Email: noel@noelwhittaker.com.au. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. World.title: Should I tell my boss’s wife he’s having an affair with a colleague?
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsGot a Minute? Should I tell my boss’s wife he’s having an affair with a colleague? Kirstin Ferguson November 18, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Each week, Dr Kirstin Ferguson tackles questions about workplace, career and leadership in her advice column Got a Minute? This week: a confrontation about a workplace affair, an uncomfortable uniform change and explaining a resume gap. Sometimes removing yourself from a situation is the best way to protect yourself. Dionne Gain My boss’s wife asked me outright whether he’s having an affair. I work closely with my boss and have met his wife many times. She called me privately and asked whether his relationship with a colleague is “something she should be worried about”. At that point, I had no reason to be suspicious and said so. Since then, I have seen enough to share her concerns. Do I protect my boss and say nothing or let his wife know her suspicions are correct? I think I need to write this answer in caps; I want to yell it as loudly as possible: DO NOT GET INVOLVED. This will undoubtedly end in tears and you do not want to be in the middle of it. Your workplace responsibility is to your boss. That doesn’t mean you are expected to facilitate him having an affair – if that is happening, and you feel compromised, you should speak to him directly or a trusted leader at work. Likewise, if he is making decisions to favour the colleague you believe he is in a relationship with.



Related Article Got a Minute? I overheard two execs making fun of employees’ accents and weight. What do I do? As hard as it may be, and even given the empathy you might feel for her, you do not owe his wife anything. You should not call her to give her new information, you should not listen to her concerns if she calls. I think you just need to politely say you are busy and not engage in conversations – with either the wife or the husband – about their relationship at all. Honestly, this has the warning signs of a “big mess” written all over it, and you do not want to be collateral damage. There are currently discussions at management level about female staff uniforms, switching from skirts to slacks. I am an older woman of stocky build and find trousers uncomfortable and unflattering. When I mentioned this to my manager, she said she was sure the company could purchase maternity slacks for me. I am sure she only meant to be helpful – I could detect no malice in her voice – but I was so stunned I didn’t say anything. I have no idea what to say if she makes this offer again. I don’t blame you for being stunned, or for not wanting to wear maternity trousers when you are not pregnant. The real issue is the lack of choice and lack of options for all body shapes. I am sure you won’t be the only person feeling the way you do, and even if you are – right now – there are sure to be all kinds of body shapes employed in the future.



I would go back to your manager, pull the foot out of her mouth, and ask to discuss this again. Let her know that while you appreciate her trying to think of a solution, you are not pregnant and maternity trousers are not the answer. I would ask about the decision itself – what is the reason skirts are being replaced? Will staff be consulted about the fit and comfort of any new uniform? Is there a way that skirts can be incorporated into the broader options since the new uniform plan assumes (mind the pun!) that “one size fits all”. Good luck! How do I re-enter the workforce after a five-year gap on my CV due to a psychological workplace injury? I’m a female approaching 50 and have spent most of my jobs working in admin support roles. I was seriously bullied by my supervisor at my last job, became too sick to return to work and lost my job. How can I explain the break with no referees from anywhere since 2020? Related Article Got a Minute? Is it unethical to look for a new job while I’m trying for a baby? While you will need to clarify the gap in your work history, you do not owe them a detailed explanation of everything that happened since your last job. In fact, I would avoid talking about the bullying incident at all, if possible. Try to keep things simple without being untruthful. For example, consider saying, “I took time away from paid work following a workplace injury and am now seeking a return to an administration role”.

World.title: This quick one-pan Greek chicken risoni gives comforting risotto vibes (without any stirring)
World.content:
RecipesCookbook extracts This quick one-pan Greek chicken risoni gives comforting risotto vibes (without any stirring) Four essential chicken recipes from cookbook writer Nicole Maguire, including a make-head marinade, a reliable rice one-pot, a meatball spin on a viral hit, and a weeknight risoni dish that soaks up flavour like a dream. Nicole Maguire November 18, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

To her legion of fans at online hub Simple Home Edit, Sydney recipe writer Nicole Maguire is known for doing more with less, and her fuss-free approach to family cooking. Her first book, The Simple Dinner Edit, was all about building a bank of reliable, delicious recipes using everyday ingredients. Her second book, Simple Dinners Every Day, focused on getting ahead, and the small things you can do to make weeknights easier and more manageable. Now Maguire has released Simple Weeknights, a collection of recipes for when even that feels too much. Most of the recipes are designed to be on the table in 30 minutes or less, with plenty of one-pan and tray-bake dinners that use supermarket ingredients and don’t compromise on flavour. Simple ingredients are at the heart of Nicole Maguire’s new book. Jeremy Simons “The reality is, sometimes you don’t have the time to get ahead. Sometimes you don’t have the energy,” she writes in the book’s introduction.



“And sometimes, you simply don’t want to spend any extra time in the kitchen beyond what you absolutely need to.” The best recipes from Australia's leading chefs straight to your inbox. Sign up Over time, she says, she’s noticed that the recipes people come back to most are built around the ingredients we’re already buying every week – chicken, mince meat, tinned beans and tinned tuna. They’re quick to cook, budget-friendly and suit all ages, and can also be versatile when you know how to use them well. Here, Maguire shares four essential chicken recipes to help make dinner feel simpler, lighter and easier to return to, even on the busiest weeknights. Risoni soaks up flavour like a dream. Jeremy Simons One-pan Greek chicken risoni



Risoni (orzo) is one of my favourite shortcuts for weeknight dinners. It soaks up flavour like a dream and gives you cosy risotto vibes without any stirring. Here it cooks with lemon, garlic and oregano while the chicken roasts on top. The smell when this comes out of the oven is ridiculous in the best possible way. Finish with plenty of feta and a squeeze of lemon and dinner is done. INGREDIENTS 5-6 boneless chicken thighs (skin-on or skinless)

crumbled feta, to serve (optional) Marinade 60ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil

60ml (¼ cup) fresh lemon juice

1 tsp freshly grated garlic

1 tsp dried oregano

1 tsp sweet paprika

1 tsp brown sugar (optional)

1 tsp sea salt flakes

¼ tsp freshly ground black pepper



Risoni 300g (1½ cups) risoni

875ml (3½ cups) hot chicken stock (see note)

2 tbsp fresh lemon juice

optional sliced lemon to serve

90g (2 generous cups) baby spinach leaves

100g (1 cup) freshly grated parmesan METHOD Preheat the oven to 180C fan-forced (200C conventional). Combine the marinade ingredients in a large bowl. Add the chicken thighs and toss to coat. Heat a large, deep oven-safe frypan over medium heat. Cook the chicken for 5-6 minutes, turning once halfway. (The chicken will not be fully cooked at this point.) Set the chicken aside on a plate. To the same pan, add the risoni, hot chicken stock and lemon juice, ensuring the risoni is mostly submerged. Return the chicken to the pan (skin-side up if using skin-on thighs). Bake in the oven, uncovered, for 18 minutes, or until the risoni is tender and most of the liquid has been absorbed. There may be a small pool of residual liquid on top of the risoni, which is normal (it gets absorbed in the next step). Remove the pan from the oven. Remove the chicken and set aside on a plate. Add the spinach and parmesan to the risoni in the pan. Gently stir the risoni until the cheese melts and the spinach has wilted slightly. Return the chicken to the pan. Let it sit for 2-3 minutes to absorb any remaining liquid and allow the spinach to soften fully. Top with crumbled feta and extra lemon slices (if using). Serve warm, straight from the baking dish with your favourite sides. Serves 4



Note: Combine chicken stock powder or cubes (use the ratio as per the packet instructions) and boiling water from the kettle in a large jug. Prepare it just before needed. Leftovers: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Not suitable to freeze. Cook this dish gently and don’t rush it. Jeremy Simons Mum’s chicken Mum has a batch of this chicken marinating in her fridge at all times. When I first made this recipe myself, I called her mid-cook to make sure I was doing it right. When I put it on the table for the first time, the kids took one bite and said, “This tastes exactly like Baka’s chicken”, and I knew I’d nailed it! The flour and marinade create a soft, glossy, intensely savoury sauce in the pan – not quite gravy, but rich enough to spoon generously over mashed potatoes. Cook it gently and don’t rush it – that’s the only trick to this deliciously tender, smothered chicken.



INGREDIENTS 1kg boneless, skinless chicken thighs, fat trimmed

75g (½ cup) plain flour

3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil Marinade 60ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil

2 tsp chicken stock powder

2 tsp sweet paprika

½ tsp freshly ground black pepper

1 tbsp brown sugar

1 tbsp freshly grated garlic

½ tsp bicarbonate of soda METHOD



Combine the marinade ingredients in a large bowl and mix well. Add the chicken and toss to coat evenly. Press the chicken pieces into the flour, shaking off any excess. Heat the olive oil in a large, heavy-based non-stick frypan over medium heat (not high – the sugars can catch). Place the chicken in the pan in a single layer and cook for 5-6 minutes on the first side until deep golden. Turn the chicken, reduce the heat to medium-low and cook for a further 4-5 minutes. Cover loosely with a lid for the final few minutes to ensure the chicken cooks through without burning. Pour 60ml (¼ cup) of water into the base of the pan – it will bubble immediately. Use tongs to gently turn the chicken in the pan juices, scraping up any caramelised bits from the base. Cook for 1-2 minutes until the liquid reduces slightly and becomes glossy. Place the lid on, turn the heat off and allow the chicken to rest for 3-4 minutes. The sauce will thicken slightly as it settles (see note). Spoon the chicken onto plates along with the pan juices, with extra freshly ground black pepper and your favourite sides. Serves 4 Note: This is not crispy crumbed chicken. The flour forms a soft, slightly sticky coating that absorbs the pan juices and becomes deeply savoury. The sauce may separate slightly – this is normal and full of flavour. Spoon it all over the chicken. Make ahead: The chicken can be marinated for up to 2 days in the fridge. Leftovers: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days.



This one-pot dish is comforting and reliable. Jeremy Simons One-pot garlic chicken and rice This is one of those dinners made from ingredients most of us already have on hand – chicken thighs, rice and a few pantry spices – but wow it’s good! The chicken cooks until golden while the rice quietly absorbs all that garlicky stock underneath. It’s comforting, reliable and goes with almost anything you’ve got in the fridge. INGREDIENTS 5 boneless chicken thigh fillets (skin on or off)

1 brown onion, finely diced

1 tsp freshly grated garlic

200g (1 cup) jasmine rice

375ml (1½ cups) chicken stock

fresh thyme sprigs, to garnish



Marinade 1 tsp sea salt flakes

1 tsp onion powder

1 tsp garlic powder

1 tsp sweet paprika

1 tsp dried thyme

½ tsp freshly ground black pepper

60ml (¼ cup) extra-virgin olive oil METHOD Combine the marinade ingredients in a shallow bowl. Add the chicken and use tongs or your hands to ensure it is evenly coated in the marinade. Heat a large, deep heavy-based pan over medium-high heat. Cook the chicken for 6-8 minutes, turning once halfway through, until golden. Remove the chicken from the pan and set aside on a plate. Spoon out any excess fat from the pan (especially if you used skin-on chicken), if desired – although this is not essential. Add 60ml (¼ cup) of water and use a spoon to scrape up any bits stuck to the bottom of the pan. To the same pan, add the onion and garlic. Cook, stirring, for 1-2 minutes until fragrant. Add the rice and stock to the pan, stir and bring to a simmer. Once simmering, reduce the heat to low and return the chicken to the pan (skin-side up if using skin-on chicken thighs). Cover and cook for 15 minutes. Once the chicken and rice are cooked, remove the pan from the heat and allow it to stand for 10 minutes, covered. Serve sprinkled with fresh thyme and your favourite sides. Leftovers: Refrigerate for up to 3 days in an airtight container.



Serves 4 The meatballs here are baked. No frying required. Jeremy Simons Marry me chicken meatballs with risoni This is my kind of meatball dinner – no frying, no standing at the stove, just everything working for you in the background. The meatballs bake in the oven (yes, on a tray – we’re bending the one-pan rules slightly here), while the risoni (orzo) cooks on the stove. INGREDIENTS



olive oil spray or 1 tbsp olive oil

200g (1 cup) risoni Chicken meatballs 500g minced chicken

90g (1½ cups) panko breadcrumbs

1 small brown onion, finely diced

1 tbsp freshly grated garlic

1 egg

50g (½ cup) freshly grated parmesan

2 tbsp full-cream milk

1 tsp sweet paprika

1 tsp dried oregano

½ tsp sea salt flakes

½ tsp freshly ground black pepper Sauce 2 tbsp olive oil

1 brown onion, diced

1 tbsp freshly grated garlic

135g semi-dried tomatoes, drained and chopped

1 tbsp red wine vinegar

2 tbsp tomato paste

500ml (2 cups) chicken stock

125ml (½ cup) thickened cream

1 tsp dried oregano

½ tsp chilli flakes, plus extra to serve (optional)

½ tsp freshly ground black pepper

100g (2 cups) baby spinach leaves

50g (½ cup) freshly grated parmesan, plus extra to serve



METHOD Place all the meatball ingredients in a large bowl. Use your hands to mix the ingredients together until just combined. Roll heaped tablespoons of the meatball mixture into balls just a little smaller than a golf ball. Wet your hands with tap water if the mixture feels too sticky. It should make roughly 12 meatballs. Preheat the oven to 200C fan-forced (220C conventional) and line a baking tray with baking paper. Place the meatballs on the baking tray ensuring they are not touching. Spray generously with olive oil. Bake for 10 minutes. Turn the oven grill to high and grill the meatballs for 3-4 minutes until slightly browned on the edges. Meanwhile, for the sauce, heat the olive oil in a large, deep heavy-based frypan over medium-high heat. Add the onion and garlic and cook, stirring, for 2-3 minutes or until softened. Add the semi-dried tomatoes, followed by the red wine vinegar and cook, stirring, for 30 seconds until most of the liquid has evaporated. Add the tomato paste and cook, stirring, for 1-2 minutes. Add the risoni to the sauce, then add the chicken stock, cream, oregano, chilli flakes (if using) and pepper. Cook, stirring regularly, for 5 minutes. Add 125ml (½ cup) of water and cook, stirring regularly, for an additional 5 minutes, or until the risoni is tender. Turn the heat off, add the baby spinach and parmesan and stir until the spinach has just wilted. Add the baked meatballs to the pan and stir to coat them in the sauce. Serve immediately with an extra sprinkling of chilli flakes (if using) and parmesan. Serves 4 Make ahead: Roll the meatballs ahead of time, refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 2 days or freeze for up to 2 months. Thaw overnight in the fridge before proceeding with the recipe. Leftovers: Refrigerate in an airtight container for up to 3 days. Not suitable to freeze.

World.title: The most beautiful bay on Earth is just an hour from Phuket
World.content:
InspirationSouth-East Asia The most beautiful bay on Earth is just an hour from Phuket John Borthwick November 18, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

“We don’t do anything normal,” jokes the chief guide, snowy-haired Uncle Aew, as our boat leaves Phuket heading for Phang Nga Bay and its magnificently “not normal” World Heritage-listed islands. Shape-shifters, at dawn they drift like ghost galleons. From the air, they might be the spines of sleeping dragons. At sea level, you understand why a local creation myth explains them as mammoth elephants that drowned when the sea rose. Among the 42 limestone karst islands are hollow ones known in Thai as koh hong, “room islands”, with an enclosed central lagoon. We’re out to explore them, but the only way in is by threading through dark, narrow caves at the waterline. Skywalk Nangshi, overlooking Phang Nga Bay. “So many phones get dropped here that we call our first stop iPhone Cave,” says Aew, as we reach Panak Island. The Thai crew launch 25 yellow inflatable canoes, and we head for the cave entrance, phones gripped tight. Flat on my back in the canoe, I press even lower as the cave roof drops alarmingly close. Our guide, crouched at the stern, paddles us through the subterranean gloom like Charon, the Underworld ferryman on the River Styx in Greek mythology. Suddenly, we emerge into sunlight on a small, central lagoon ringed by limestone walls. As more canoes arrive, we spread out to explore this once-lost realm of mangroves and hanging gardens. We’re an hour from the malls and cocktail shores of Phuket, and a million years distant.



On our return to the mothership there’s a hearty buffet lunch waiting. We cruise further on with brahminy kites and sea eagles swooping for scraps at the stern. The boat owner, John “Caveman” Gray, is a legend in these waters. Originally from Hawaii, he pioneered kayaking on Phang Nga Bay more than 40 years ago. Since then, his operation, John Gray’s Sea Canoes, has evolved to include intricately organised excursions like today’s Hong by Starlight cruise. 



Related Article Thailand Thailand’s 12 best islands, ranked and rated Having seen Phang Nga Bay in the past from kayaks, boats, planes and almost everything but a train, I should have known there’s always one more way. Next day we wake before dawn. A minibus collects us for the ride to Samet Nangshe mountain on the western shore of the bay. It drops us at the Beyond Resort on the peak. I’m not ready for what comes next – stepping into midair without falling. We’ve walked out onto a glass skywalk that soars 80 metres above the ground and directly faces the great bay. This Andaman bridge of sighs (the longest skywalk in Thailand) reveals the bay’s dawn parade of islands briefly taking shape before us as mammoths, haystacks, dragons or whatever. The morning mist clears and soon enough, each island is again just an island. Normal, but in the most beautiful bay on Earth. DETAILS John Gray’s Sea Canoe “Hong by Starlight” tour departs from Phuket, year-round. Hotel transfer, lunch and dinner included; from $170 a person. See johngray-seacanoe.com; The Beyond Skywalk Nangshi resort is 45 kilometres from Phuket Airport; skywalk entrance from $21. See skywalk-nangshi.beyondresort.com The writer travelled with the support of the Tourist Authority of Thailand

World.title: From 2D pixels to cinematic masterpiece: How Grand Theft Auto has evolved
World.content:
Grand Theft Auto VI is slated to be one of the biggest entertainment releases of the year.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If you thought Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour was a big deal, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI is just as momentous. The latest instalment in Rockstar North’s mega-popular video game franchise is stopping the world in its tracks, making other cultural phenomenons like The Odyssey and Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl look like small fish. Many of its biggest fans have reportedly taken time off work to play the game, and it became the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation and Xbox history, generating more than $US1 billion before launch. The Grand Theft Auto franchise has come a long way since 1997. Rockstar North This kind of cultural sensation doesn’t just appear overnight. It took nearly three decades, eight standalone games and an immense number of technological advances for the GTA franchise to become the behemoth it is today. From pixel-mania to cinematic masterpieces, here’s a look through GTA’s colourful (and controversial) history. Grand Theft Auto (1997) For the late ’90s, GTA 1 was groundbreaking. Not only did it help introduce free-form missions and open-world designs, but it also mastered offbeat humour, gratuitous violence and general urban chaos. In hindsight, however, it looks more like an ancient artefact than cutting-edge game.



GTA 1 adopted a 2D bird’s-eye view, displaying the character’s crimes across the fictional cities of Liberty City, San Andreas and Vice City from above. Players needed to earn a certain amount of money in each level by completing criminal tasks (delivered via payphones) before driving to an exit marker to advance to the next stage. Rather than the sprawling, cinematic open-worlds we know today, the first instalment was more akin to an arcade game or racing title, just with more hit-and-runs. Its use of 2D geometric shapes resulted in a Minecraft-esque world where everything, even the bushes, were square and highly pixelated. What does GTA have to do with watches? Gamers technically have a watch factory to thank for GTA’s creation. In 1987, Scottish entrepreneur David Jones was made redundant from a Timex watch factory in Dundee. Using his severance package, he bought an Amiga 1000 computer, which he then used to try his hand at video game development. After developing a few smaller-scale games under the studio DMA Design, Jones and his team came up with Race ‘n’ Chase, an open-world game where police chase criminals. However, realising that the latter’s activities were more enticing, the studio decided to flip the script, shifting focus to the criminals, and published it under BMG Interactive. The first GTA was thus born. Grand Theft Auto 2 (1999) Much of the first game’s aesthetic carried through to the second (which fell under the wing of Rockstar Games, a Take-Two Interactive subsidiary), including the top-down perspective and 2D pixelated concrete jungle. However, GTA 2 developed “noon” and “dusk” modes, the latter of which delivered slightly improved graphics. Suddenly, you could actually make out the heads of characters and details on cars. It also introduced rival syndicates, which complicated players’ interactions with different gangs. And while it was painfully easy to die in GTA 1, GTA 2 introduced a 10-point health bar, as well as smoother camera tracking, self-straightening cars and auto-aim support for weapons.



Grand Theft Auto III (2001) The franchise really exploded when GTA III introduced 3D graphics. The game began to feel more like a cinematic experience, showing layered narratives, cutscenes and gameplay in third-person perspective. Players embodied Claude, a silent criminal who embeds himself in ruthless crime syndicates to exact revenge on his ex-girlfriend, who betrayed him during a bank heist. The franchise was so popular at this point that celebrities such as Michael Madsen and Kyle MacLachlan joined the voice cast, further adding to its cinematic appeal. This was also the first iteration in which gamers could follow a map radar and fly a plane. Say hello to the tiny heads and freakishly long necks of Grand Theft Auto III. YouTube (GTA Series Videos) The graphics were still far from today’s standards, however. The characters’ proportions were way off, displaying tiny heads on giraffe-like necks and freakishly broad shoulders. Their fingers never separated, as if they were wearing pantyhose over their hands. Characters’ dialogue also didn’t sync up with their mouth movements, making for a clunky experience. Australia’s Office of Film & Literature Classification deemed the game too “sexually explicit” for sale thanks to its implied violence against sex workers. It was refused classification, which effectively made it illegal to sell or distribute down under. Rockstar Games released an edited version in 2002, securing an MA15+ rating in Australia (there was no R18+ rating at the time).



GTA’s iconic ‘comic-book’ covers Graphic designer Stephen Bliss joined the fray for GTA III, designing the original game cover released in Europe. However, following 9/11, Rockstar Games asked Bliss to design a less violent cover for the American release. Instead of designing an entirely new cover, Bliss arranged some of his existing designs into panels, similar to comic-book layouts. The studio liked the new design so much that it inspired every following iteration. The style has become synonymous with GTA, so much so that Bliss is still asked to sign the covers of GTA V, even though he technically didn’t work on it. Grand Theft Auto: Vice City (2002) Vice City was essentially GTA III but set in a fictional ’80s Miami with more missions, motorcycles and helicopters (think Scarface or Miami Vice). The tiny heads on bizarrely long necks, however, remained. The characters may not have been awe-inspiring, but the landscapes were – palm trees, neon lights and retro diners all rendered in beautiful detail. Players embodied mobster Tommy Vercetti, who must track down those who ambushed him in an earlier drug deal gone wrong, and build his own criminal empire. Voiced by Ray Liotta, Vercetti was the game’s first-ever speaking protagonist. The soundtrack was also one of the most iconic in the franchise, including songs from INXS and Mötley Crüe. Players could finally jump out of moving cars, shoot out tires and even change their character’s clothes. What’s going on with your neck there, pal? YouTube (GTA Series Videos)



Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas (2004) Gamers landed in 1992 San Andreas, a far larger world-map that fictionalised California and Nevada. Given the wider scope for travel, Rockstar introduced trains and planes, as well as bicycles, and for the first time players could swim (falling into water in Vice City meant immediate death). The landscapes were popping. The people not so much. YouTube (GTA Series Videos) Filled with hip-hop references, San Andreas followed former gang member CJ who returned to the city following his mother’s death. There, he’s blackmailed by shifty cops and betrayed by his friends, sending him on a mission to reclaim his family’s gang territory. Players suddenly had to take care of their character’s bodies. Deep role-playing (RPG) mechanics meant characters could lose or gain weight based on what they ate and how often they exercised. The ‘Hot Coffee’ debacle Some players discovered a hidden interactive sexual minigame inside San Andreas’ code. Although Rockstar Games initially blamed hackers for creating the explicit content, investigations proved the developers had simply disabled the files rather than deleting them before releasing the game to the public. As a result, the game’s Mature rating was reclassified as Adults Only, forcing major retailers to pull it from shelves, including in Australia. This triggered massive product recalls, federal investigations and more than $US20 million in financial losses and legal settlements for publisher Take-Two Interactive.

World.title: Distressed staff forced to care for colleague’s alleged rapist
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaMental health Distressed staff forced to care for colleague’s alleged rapist Grant McArthur November 18, 2026 — 5:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Distraught Thomas Embling Hospital staff remain caring for a high-risk patient in the unit where he allegedly raped one of their colleagues, despite having repeatedly flagged security concerns. Police, health authorities and WorkSafe continue to investigate the alleged rape of a nurse by a patient in the hospital’s Apsley unit on November 2, amid staff calls for immediate security upgrades and increased staffing levels. Thomas Embling Hospital’s Apsley unit. The nurse’s alleged attacker has been held in the forensic hospital for years under a court order, after he was found not guilty of sexual offences due to mental impairment. Three sources, who cannot speak publicly due to patient confidentiality provisions, have told this masthead the man is still being held in the Apsley unit despite staff pleas for him to be transferred to a prison-based psychiatric facility.



They said the man – who has not been charged by police – has a history of violence against staff and has been kept in seclusion within the unit since November 2. Related Article Healthcare Police investigate alleged rape of nurse at Thomas Embling Hospital Unions representing the Thomas Embling workers are in discussions with the hospital’s operator, Forensicare, demanding security and staffing overhauls and the immediate transfer of the alleged rapist. The Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists (RANZCP) is also considering stripping Forensicare of its training positions over concerns Thomas Embling is too unsafe for young doctors. A university last week cancelled work placements at the hospital from its nursing course due to safety issues.



A patient room inside Thomas Embling Hospital’s Apsley unit. A Forensicare spokesperson said it had provided a range of supports to staff and consumers following the alleged sex attack, and was working closely with police and other agencies as they investigate. “We have taken immediate steps to ensure safety within the unit and continue to monitor and review those measures,” the spokesperson said. “We are also conducting a comprehensive serious incident review to understand the circumstances, identify any lessons that may be learned, and determine what further actions are required to strengthen safety and support across the service. “The serious incident review will consider all relevant contributing factors and inform any actions required to further strengthen safety and operations within the unit.”



The eight-bed Apsley unit houses high-risk patients who have committed security breaches in other areas of the hospital, or who are deemed too dangerous for less secure units. This includes at least two long-term residents considered particularly dangerous, who were each found not guilty of heinous crimes due to mental impairment, according to one person who recently attended the unit but is not authorised to discuss it. The alleged rapist is one of these men. Other patients are moved into Apsley for several months at a time over security issues, such as being caught with smuggled drugs or presenting a risk to themselves or others, the person who attended the unit said. But the Apsley unit was not designed as a long-term secure setting for complex patients when it was opened in 2019, and staff say its small rooms and tight confines are not suitable for its current use.



Information previously posted on Forensicare’s website – but now removed – stated the Apsley unit offered “short-term treatment for severely unwell prisoners”, and was intended as a stepping stone to reduce waiting times for prisoners on compulsory treatment orders. “Apsley is a state-of-the-art short-term unit that will provide a charming space to assist patients in their mental health recovery journey,” a record of its opening stated. Thomas Embling Hospital’s Apsley unit. “Apsley patients will be treated by an experienced team of specialist multidisciplinary clinicians, using positive behaviours support treatment programs.” Another article, celebrating the unit’s 2020 Mental Health Design Award category win at the European Healthcare Design Awards, remains on the website. It states the award recognised Apsley’s environment that supports ongoing therapy, care and recovery, as well as appropriate levels of safety, security and supervision.



However, the Australian Nursing Midwifery Federation’s Victorian branch secretary, Maddy Harradence, said she was extremely concerned about the ongoing psychological impacts and physical safety of nurses at the facility. The nurses’ union is demanding Forensicare act immediately to improve safety, including transferring the alleged attacker, reducing the number of beds in Apsley while maintaining current staffing levels, and returning the unit to its primary purpose as a short-stay unit. The latest violence comes amid a wider Victorian mental healthcare crisis, extensively reported on by this masthead, which Paul Healey, the Health and Community Services Workers Union Victorian branch secretary, said the state government had again failed to address. “Ultimately, this once again comes back to sector-wide underfunding, a failure to invest in community teams, understaffing across the board and severe lack of understanding from parliamentarians about the realities facing the mental health workforce,” Healey said. The RANZCP confirmed it remained in discussions with Forensicare about its training accreditation of Thomas Embling Hospital and the Apsley unit, including the safety, supervision and support available to trainees.



“The RANZCP is deeply concerned by reports of an alleged sexual assault at Thomas Embling Hospital and the broader concerns being raised about safety within the facility. Patients, staff and trainees must be able to receive care, work and train in an environment that is safe and supportive,” the RANZCP said in a statement. “The concerns being raised also highlight a much broader challenge across forensic mental health: workforce shortages. “Safe and effective services depend on having enough appropriately trained staff, yet chronic shortages continue to place significant pressure on both workers and services.” Staff working in the Apsley told this masthead it relied on high levels of international medical and nursing graduates, whose working visas are sponsored by Forensicare.



To fill its growing staffing gaps, Forensicare sent a delegation to London and Manchester in September as part of a “UK recruitment tour”, aimed at finding new psychiatrists, nurses and other staff. As of this week, Forensicare has 26 open jobs listed on British employment sites, seeking staff ranging from a $424,816-a-year director of clinical services, to clinical support workers with a starting salary of $67,724. Each position is advertised with a $10,000 resettlement incentive. The international recruitment drive also aims to attract psychiatrists of varying seniority, psychologists, nurses, a nurse unit manager, an occupational therapist and administration and support staff. “Forensicare is undergoing one of the largest expansions in its history. Over the coming years, Thomas Embling Hospital will expand from 136 beds to 218 beds, with the addition of six new inpatient units and 82 new beds,” the job ads state. “Rather than joining a mature service with limited growth opportunities, you will be part of an organisation at a transformational stage of development.



“Unlike many healthcare settings, you’ll be supported by a workforce of qualified mental health professionals working collaboratively to deliver outstanding clinical outcomes.” But two sources have confirmed the RANZCP is preparing to remove Forensicare’s remaining two training posts, which allow junior doctors to work while completing their forensic qualifications. The college first took the extreme measure of stripping Thomas Embling of its seven training posts in October 2025 due to violence and worsening staff conditions at the facility, before returning two positions in February. Forensicare’s 2025-26 annual report revealed it had paid a consultant $16,500 to review its medical workforce and find out the “root causes of workforce dissatisfaction, operational inefficiency, and sustainability risk”. A Department of Health spokesperson said adverse events in mental health care were rare, and every effort was made to reduce the risk of violence and aggression through staff training and workplace protocols.



The spokesperson said the Thomas Embling Hospital incident was especially distressing and the Office of the Chief Psychiatrist was working closely with Forensicare as it undertook its incident review and implements any necessary changes. “The Department of Health continues to work closely with health services, unions and frontline staff to address occupational violence and aggression,” the spokesperson said. World.title: Wife of forestry worker fatally crushed by falling tree calls for manual felling to be abolished
World.content:
The wife of a forestry worker who was crushed to death by a falling tree is calling for manual tree felling to be abolished.

Thirty-nine-year-old father of two Mykhailo Tremel was struck by a falling tree while working on a forestry block in Auckland in 2022.

His wife Brownyn wants urgent change to save others.

Her plea comes in response to a coroner's report last month that found Tremel's death could have been prevented had a logging machine been used.

While initially conscious, he radioed his colleagues for help. First aid was given, but he quickly deteriorated. He was pronounced dead on the scene.

Bronwyn Tremel told Morning Report the coroner's recommendations needed to be followed up with real action to save lives.

"It can't just be words on a page ... we need to make the people responsible accountable. We need answers and we need to know what's going to change. We need manual tree felling abolished," she said.

The coroner also urged WorkSafe to look at strengthening safety regulations in the forestry sector.

Manual tree fellers were 300 times more likely than the general population to die at work, the report said.

Knowing that Mykhailo's death could have been prevented made it harder to comes to terms with, Bronwyn said.

But she was adamant it should result in changes that meant it never happened again to anyone else.

World.title: 'Not the way MMP was supposed to work': Experts urge politicians to act on overhang
World.content:
A group of 46 experts wants politicians to urgently consider improving the MMP electoral system, to avoid undemocratic elections in future.

Their open letter - led by Andrew Geddis, Lara Greaves and Max Rashbrooke - is titled "Keep the 'P' in MMP" and points to the 11-seat overhang indicated by the initial results putting the proportionality the 'P' stands for at risk.

"I don't think it's how people want MMP to work," Rashbrooke told RNZ. "People should be speaking out on it and trying to underline for MPs the urgency of tackling it, and try and find a bipartisan solution."

Geddis said the four-seat overhang for Te Pāti Māori was the result of a deliberate campaign to expand influence well beyond its party vote entitlement, and despite campaigns calling for the same thing National's seven overhang seats were "more like an organic result of the National Party continuing to do reasonably well in individual electorates, while its party vote fell off".

Overall, the result distorted representation in Parliament, and he pointed to the '78 and '81 elections that delivered National governments despite Labour winning more votes. That mismatch was "one of the reasons we actually shifted to MMP".

"The overhang could well deliver the same outcome, where you have three parties that have a majority of the seats in the House, but receive fewer votes across the country than the other four parties in Parliament.

"Not really the way democracy is supposed to work, and it's definitely not the way MMP was supposed to work".

Andrew Geddis. Supplied

Rashbrooke warned it could also become the norm in future.

"Now that people have seen that it is at least possible to engineer an overhang the very real likelihood is that next election that will just become an arms race," he said.

The open letter warned this could lead to disillusionment and lower trust in democracy, and suggested setting up a dedicated select committee to tackle the problem and put solutions in place.

Geddis said while some would argue politicians should not be the ones designing electoral systems - "like allowing panel beaters to design intersections, they are going to do so with their own best interests in mind" - there was a need to get the problem fixed before the next election, leaving little time for a broader discussion.

"We've only got three years ... if we get a Parliamentary select committee doing the thinking about it, it'll help MPs come to realise what the best solution is rather than having an external examination which then has to go to Parliament."

The letter suggested options for fixing the overhang problem:

Add more list seats so that Parliament would get bigger, to make up for any overhang

so that Parliament would get bigger, to make up for any overhang Reduce the number of electorates which would reduce the number of possible overhang seats

which would reduce the number of possible overhang seats Remove electorate seats from parties that win too many overhang seats by (in line with Germany) requiring parties to have enough party votes to cover their overhang wins, perhaps allowing one or two overhang seats per party

by (in line with Germany) requiring parties to have enough party votes to cover their overhang wins, perhaps allowing one or two overhang seats per party Only have one vote , so that electorate-based votes also count as party votes, electing both a local MP and contributing to a party vote that could bring in additional list MPs

, so that electorate-based votes also count as party votes, electing both a local MP and contributing to a party vote that could bring in additional list MPs Change how votes in Parliament work so that it's based on the proportion of party vote, rather than the number of MPs

One campaign for such a strategy at the election led by billionaire Harry Mowbray explicitly aimed to undermine MMP, which he called a "complete dog" because it ensured power for minority voices.

Harry Mowbray. Supplied

However, Mowbray himself preferred something resembling the supplementary member system, which would be less representative and guarantee outsized influence from electorates.

"There's an irony there," Rashbrooke said, "that some of the people who are trying to engineer a situation where MMP becomes less proportional, and then argue that's a weakness in the system, are also people who want an electoral system that is much less proportional than MMP."

Geddis agreed.

"Harry Mowbray's criticism of MMP seems slightly confused ... he thinks it gives smaller parties too much power, and the way that he sought to undermine MMP was to show smaller parties how they could get more power."

He said he was not sure such campaigns were successful, but the real risk was future elections would become less policy, more about tactical voting strategies.

"There's no such thing as a perfect electoral system. There's always going to be pros and cons to any change."

The open letter also highlighted the three public referendums New Zealand had held on the electoral system - in 1992, '93 and 2011 - all favouring MMP.

Rashbrooke said there was no need to throw the proverbial baby out with the bathwater.

"The problem with any system other than MMP is it will be less proportional, it will do a worse job of translating what people actually want into seats in Parliament ... we have discovered there is a weakness in it, that weakness needs to be fixed.

"A bit like the case of: you've got a perfectly solid house, it's a really good house but you've just discovered that there's a little vulnerability in it ... something that needs to be patched up, something that needs to be mended - but the foundations are all totally secure."

Max Rashbrooke. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

An independent review following the 2011 referendum had also called for overhang seats to be abolished, and despite changes to the electoral system - including in both the most recent terms of Parliament, one led by National and one by Labour - politicians have never tackled that or a number of other recommendations.

Neither Geddis nor Rashbrooke believed the major parties could be blamed.

"The fixes that were proposed in the past were fixes for a much smaller problem that you know wasn't quite as pressing. This time around, we can see what the problem is, we can see its magnitude, and we can predict that it's likely to reoccur in the future," Geddis said.

Rashbrooke pointed to the 1986 Royal Commission on Electoral Reform's finding that "accidental deviations [from proportional results] are most unlikely, and that any attempt to deliberately manipulate the system would be both difficult to implement and likely to attract an electoral backlash".

"I didn't see this coming ... it's crept up upon us," Rashbrooke said. "I'm not sure that I would blame anyone very strongly for not seeing that coming, I think the point is just now that the problem is staring us in the face. We have to do something about it.

World.title: Category 5 cyclone with gusts up to 295km/h slams Cook Islands
World.content:
Severe Tropical Cyclone Xavier is now a category 5 system as it continues to swirl around in the Northern Cook Islands.

Warnings for gales and strong winds are in place.

Emergency Management Cook Islands is urging communities across the Northern Cook Islands to remain on high alert.

It said damaging gale-force winds, heavy rainfall, dangerous seas and coastal inundation remain significant threats, particularly for Pukapuka and Nassau.

"Residents are strongly urged to remain in safe shelter, stay away from coastal areas and follow instructions from local disaster risk management teams," it said.

The Fiji Meteorological Service, which has jurisdiction for this area of the Pacific, said in its latest update that Xavier was moving west-southwest at about 7km/h.

It said the storm had maximum sustained winds of about 220 km/h close to the centre, with gusts up to 315 km/h.

A resident on Manihiki in the Northern Cook Islands said the "worst is over" for his island as Xavier moves away.

However, a strong wind warning remains in place for Manihiki on Tuesday morning Cook Islands time, with Xavier now nearing Pukapuka and Nassau.

Those two islands are under a gale warning.

Jean Marie Williams told RNZ Pacific Waves Manihiki locals have been well prepared for the conditions, but power is the main concern.

He said electricity has been an issue for more than a year.

Audio player for " Manihiki residents ready for cyclone impact " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/pacific/2648447%2Fcategory-5-cyclone-xavier-batters-northern-cook-islands-with-gusts-up-to-315km-h

Manihiki residents ready for cyclone impact Pacific Waves Download MP3 4m

"Since we had our power that went down over a year ago we never got it replaced, and we only have power when the sun comes out, charges our solar system, and then we can only use maybe four, five hours' power, and then shut it down. Only use it for the night time," he said.

"Some of the families have their own generators that we do run to keep our freezers frozen, but otherwise, that's our biggest concern is our power.

"At the moment we have some damages on wharves."

Williams said Manihiki Island residents have been preparing for cyclone season since October, rather than waiting for official weather warnings.

"Here in Manihiki, on October the 25th, we activate our awareness and preparation for the cyclone season.

"Manahiki Island Council have their team, their workers, that go around almost 24 hours, just making sure that people are safe and the families are safe.

World.title: RNZ's election results analysis reveals a complicated, moody electorate
World.content:
Analysis - Anyone who tells you there was a singular "national mood" that defined the election result is wrong. There were many moods. It was the moodiest election we've seen in decades.

Votes split between candidates and parties en masse, and the party vote diverged starkly between even nearby polling booths.

There was also an historic high tide for the so-called "minor parties". Combined support for National plus Labour - the so-called purple vote - cratered all across the country, replaced with a vote of almost 40 percent for four smaller (but now all bigger than before) parties.

To get a grip on all of these different goings on, RNZ has conducted a deep analysis of the results. It examines the votes of communities of roughly 1000 to 4000 people who live around polling booths.

To paint a picture of each neighbourhood in the country, we looked at its defining features using information from the 2023 census. Are residents older and retired or younger? Do they rent, or do they own their home? How much do they earn?

We grouped the "statistical area 2" (SA2) areas using 13 census measures, including age, household income and ownership, household make-up and population density into seven types of neighbourhoods. We've named these by their most defining characteristic.

For example, in Auckland's Tāmaki electorate, Glendowie North falls into 'higher income areas' and Glen Innes West into 'young renting families'. These two neighbourhoods are only a few kilometres apart but are strikingly different in their profile - and the way they voted. Glendowie North's residents are older and richer - they increased their support for ACT and decreased it for National. People living in Glen Innes West are younger and earn less, they increased support for the Greens.

The voter patterns of Glen Innes West are clearer when they're combined with the same sorts of neighbourhoods nationwide - our analysis identified 249 others that were most characterised by 'young renting families'. We also found 572 'higher income areas' like Glendowie North, with 1.5 million people.

What follows is a rough sketch of how the country voted, broken out by these types of neighbourhoods.

There are some caveats. These borders aren't perfect. Some neighbourhoods teeter on the cusp of two different 'types' we have assigned.

It should also be noted that the census data is more than three years old and what was true then may be a little different now. When it was conducted in March 2023, for instance, the unemployment rate was at 3.5 percent. September's figure is 5.7 percent.

The voting data is preliminary, as counting of special votes is ongoing. When we've compared results to previous elections we've removed that election's special votes so it's a fair comparison.

The Mowbray twist

The biggest story of the election night results was the impact of vote splitting.

Calling the MMP system a "complete dog", businessman Harry Mowbray said he set out to "show people how bad it is".

His campaign called for National supporters to give their candidate vote to National and party vote to a coalition partner. The goal was to engineer overhang seats that would work in the coalition's favour.

Whether it was a result of Mowbray's direction or something that would've happened anyway, vote splitting did occur in large numbers. It resulted in seven overhang seats going to National, putting the coalition in the lead.
