RNZ's analysis shows this happened most powerfully in rural areas and small towns. People living in these areas are mostly of European descent (86 percent compared to the nation's 68 percent). Just over 60 percent own their homes, and around half are in full-time employment.

In this type of neighbourhood National's candidate vote grew by the tiniest amount, but its party vote plummeted 9.5 percentage points, while ACT and NZ First's combined party vote grew an almost identical 9.8 points.

During the campaign, ACT's David Seymour made an explicit vote splitting appeal to a gathering of voters in West Melton, near Christchurch.

"Those [ACT] MPs count just as much as extra National MPs. It's the size of the coalition that matters. So there's no risk to putting your party vote with ACT. You're still helping re-elect the coalition."

In Bankside, a small township close to West Melton, National's party vote dropped from 52.7 percent in 2023 to 43.3 percent. ACT's party vote climbed to 18.1 percent, up 5.1 points.

NZ First also benefitted in these neighbourhoods. Nearby, in Darfield, most of National's losses shifted to NZ First, which grew its vote share by 7.9 percentage points.

The pattern was repeated in rural and small town polling booths all across the country. ACT and NZ First's party vote increased in these areas far more than it did across the rest of the country. Rural and small town voters gave ACT 18 percent of the party vote, putting it a whisker behind Labour's 18.4 percent. NZ First received 13.8 percent.

Part of Mowbray's case for creating a National Party overhang was to cancel out the one Te Pāti Māori was encouraging its supporters to spin up on the left.

"There's one plan, two votes; our plan has to be to focus on the candidate votes. We trust you with the party vote we trust and we see your love for our people, for our taiao. We trust that you will choose what is right," co-leader Debbie Ngarewa-Packer told supporters.

"You have the power to bring this government to its knees."

The split in Te Pāti Māori's votes was seen across all neighbourhood types, including rural areas and small towns.

In Waipaoa, in the Gisborne District, Te Pāti Māori's candidate received more than half the candidate vote, while the party only secured 7 percent of party vote. In Whatawhata East in Waikato its party vote dropped even lower to 2.3 percent compared to a candidate vote of 72.4 percent.

Te Pāti Māori secured a four-seat overhang for the left bloc, with the Greens benefiting most.

Greens new heartland

The Greens had their best election result ever, gaining 13.3 percent of the party vote.

"[Voters] have given us the most historic support that we have ever seen. The Māori vote is quite phenomenal in terms of its increase even just from 2020, almost doubled. That may go up with specials. That is historic," said Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson.

Compared with 2023, its vote grew 26.6 points among voters on the Māori roll, while Te Pāti Māori's party vote dropped 23.6 percentage points.

Of the seven types of neighbourhoods RNZ looked at, the Greens grew most in areas where young renting families live. Roughly one in five votes in these suburbs came from voters on the Māori roll, more than double the national rate.

Just over a third of people in these neighbourhoods own their own homes, well below the national average of 50 percent, with almost 40 percent living in social housing. The median personal income is $36,000.

Voters here continued to support Labour, which secured 47 percent of the party vote, and they turned away from National, whose party vote fell to 17 percent. Te Pāti Māori's party vote also fell.

The Greens vote grew 6.8 percentage points from their 2023 result, rising to 15 percent in these neighbourhoods.

In Kaikohe, support for Labour, National and Te Pāti Māori dropped, while the Greens got 28 percent of the party vote, up from 5.7 percent in 2023 - a fivefold increase.

The party had similar growth in Moerewa in the Far North and Ōtāngarei in the Whangārei district as well as in Tauranga's Matapihi and Whakatāne's Waingarara-Waimana area.

It wasn't all clear sailing for the Greens. In some places their upwards trajectory stalled, with Opportunity's share of party vote growing.

In the wealthiest areas of the country, where 38 percent of people have a degree, close to 60 percent work fulltime and more than half the residents own their own home, the Green vote grew just 0.1 percentage points from 2023.

These neighbourhoods favour National, which secured a third of the party vote, despite falling 11 percentage points.

Opportunity was the biggest gainer in higher-income suburbs, winning 7.8 percent of the party vote in these areas here. Nearly a third of all Opportunity's party votes were cast in these suburbs.

In Wellington's Wadestown and Karori East, about one in five party votes went to Opportunity.

Opportunity's rise

For a party that more than doubled its tally of votes, it's unsurprising that Opportunity grew its share of support across all seven types of neighbourhood. It cleared the 5 percent threshold everywhere except rural and small towns, and young family renting areas, but one neighbourhood type stood out from the rest.

Student-heavy neighbourhoods threw the most support behind Opportunity, nearly doubling its party vote share from 5.7 percent in 2023 to 11.7 percent.

The party vote share for National, Te Pāti Māori and ACT dropped in these areas, with Opportunity growing more than Labour. NZ First and the Greens had very small increases.

The Greens remained strong in this neighbourhood, winning 34.9 percent of the votes, ahead of Labour (28.9 percent) and National (14.6 percent).

Student areas are the smallest type of neighbourhood RNZ tracked, with just 29 neighbourhoods, compared to other types with hundreds. While Opportunity did well here, it was only worth 6400 of its 144,298 votes.

Higher income areas were responsible for 30 percent of the party's votes, middle New Zealand 21 percent and retirement areas 17.6 percent.

Boomers versus millennials

Older and younger areas both moved away from National, but in different ways. Retirement areas split their party vote while younger areas shifted it.

The support that went away from National (down 9.4 points) was fairly evenly divided up between the smaller parties of the left and right blocs in retirement areas.

Opportunity grew its vote the most, up 3.8 points, despite claims its land tax policy would turn off these communities, which have the highest rate of home ownership in the country (63.6 percent against the 51.2 percent average).

NZ First got 11.7 percent of the party vote in these areas, its best result in the past four elections. Retirement areas matter to the party, roughly one in every four of its party votes come from these neighbourhoods.

Nationwide NZ First received 9.8 percent of the party vote, its best result since 2002 but on election night leader Winston Peters, called the election campaign "difficult".

Peters may have been hoping for more of the votes in these areas that went to ACT (up 2.7 points) and even the Greens (up 2.6 points), which also both got their biggest share of the party vote here since 2017.

Labour barely moved, rising to 25.8 percent, but this still represented its second lowest result among retirement neighbourhoods since 2017.

Across a fairly underwhelming map for Labour, the one area it did make meaningful ground was in neighbourhoods with a lot of young renters with few children.

Residents in these areas have a median age of 34, and only 28 percent own their own home. Fulltime employment rates are the highest in the country, at 59 percent, and the median household income is $101,000.

Here the vote shifted, rather than split, with Labour increasing its share of both the party and candidate vote.

National dropped from 37.1 percent of the party vote to 26.5, while Labour gained 5.1 percentage points to 31.9 percent.

Labour edged ahead on candidate votes across these neighbourhoods too, with a gain of nearly 5 points, putting it narrowly ahead of National.

Opportunity gained strongly here too, increasing its party vote share from 2.8 percent in 2023 to 7.3 percent.

The neighbourhoods that moved like the country did

Home to roughly a quarter of the population, middle New Zealand neighbourhoods almost mirrored how the country vote.

Voters here are close to the country's median age of 39, with around half owning their own home. The median personal income is $39,000, slightly under the national average of $43,000 with a household income of $84,000, again below the country's median. Roughly 10 percent live alone and 57 percent are families with children.

National's vote share dropped 8.7 points here, with NZ First and ACT picking up 5.5 points between them. The Greens and Opportunity picked up 6.9 points.

Labour got the biggest share of votes in this type of neighbourhood - around 30 percent compared to National's 28.3 percent - but its increase from 2023 was only 1.4 percentage points.

"Tonight New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out what exactly it is that you've said," Labour's Chris Hipkins said on election night.

"Every vote matters and every vote must now be counted."

The official count, which includes special votes, is due Friday 27 November.

Methodology

RNZ grouped Stats NZ's SA2 areas into seven types using 13 measures from the 2023 Census including age, home ownership, income, education, work, household make-up, social housing and population density. We tested between four and 12 types and repeated the grouping hundreds of times on resampled data. The seven neighbourhood types reappeared consistently, and the main vote findings held when neighbourhoods on the edge between two neighbourhood types were left out.

We named each type after what most sets it apart from the New Zealand average, such as a high share of young adults, older residents or families with children. Votes are those cast at voting places, linked to the neighbourhood the voting place is in.

Neighbourhoods with fewer than 100 residents, such as city centres, industrial areas and airports, were not given a type, because their census figures are unreliable. Votes cast there are included in national totals but not in the figures for any neighbourhood. Votes with no location, such as mobile and hospital voting were treated the same way. Combined these represent about 2.7 percent of the vote.

World.title: Mum of son who gained weight on anti-psychotics calls for wider Wegovy funding
World.content:
A West Coast mother is calling for weightloss drugs to be funded for people who gain weight on anti-psychotic medication.

The woman, who RNZ has agreed not to name to protect the family's privacy, says her 47-year-old son started taking olanzapine more than two decades ago, after he was hospitalised following a psychotic episode in his twenties.

The drug had stabalised him and allowed him to live a relatively normal life - but a side effect had been food cravings and weight gain of more than 20 kilograms.

It had also contributed to gallbladder problems leading to an emergency hospital trip for its removal.

Then, earlier this year, a family friend had offered to fund weightloss drug Wegovy for him for a year, at the cost of about $500 a month.

But his mum said that kindness couldn't be relied on forever, and the family couldn't afford to cover that ongoing cost themselves.

On Wegovy, his weight had dropped from 120kg to 98kg - his mum called the change "a revelation".

"He no longer raids the fridge at night, he looks great and he takes the dog for long walks every day," she said. "Best of all, his social confidence has improved and his sadness has lifted. The drug has given him back his hope and self respect."

But, they were both anxious about what would happen next year when he came off it. "Regaining the weight would plunge him into despair," she said.

She would love to see Wegovy funded for weight loss for people who gained weight after starting anti-psychotics.

In response to questions from RNZ, Pharmac said it had not received an application for Wegovy specifically to treat people on anti-psychotic medication.

What does the science say?

Professor Susanna Every-Palmer, a psychiatrist and head of the Department of Psychological Medicine at the University of Otago in Wellington. Otago University Wellington

Research has shown some antipsychotic drugs can make people hungrier, and likelier to eat more.

According to WebMD, "people often quickly put on weight after they start antipsychotics and keep gaining over time. Children are more likely to gain weight. Being overweight raises your risk of diabetes, heart attack, stroke, high blood pressure, arthritis, sleep apnea, and some cancers."

It said the risk was highest with the drugs clozapine, and olanzapine - the drug this man relied on.

Professor Susanna Every-Palmer, a psychiatrist and head of the Department of Psychological Medicine at the University of Otago in Wellington, said it wasn't just a willpower issue.

"The medications actually can increase appetite, often within weeks. So it's not that people who gain weight on these medications have failed in any way. It's a known biological effect, a very well recognised side effect."

What affect does it have on people already struggling?

Dan Goodwin, community support manager at Changing Minds. supplied

Dan Goodwin, community support manager at Changing Minds, a national mental health not-for-profit, said weight gain was one of the big reasons people stopped taking psychiatric medication.

"On top of the experiences that the anti-psychotics might be treating [...] now you also have a changing physical body as well, which might be causing you distress or it might be causing its own sense of shame."

Because the priority for healthcare services would be treating the primary issue - that is, the mental distress - weight gain was not often treated as a priority, which could compound that sense of shame, Goodwin said.

Weightloss drugs were growing in popularity, and it raised questions for doctors on how they approached and treated someone with a psychiatric disorder - in more ways than just their brains.

"It's going to become a more common request as those drugs kind of get developed and grow," Goodwin said.

Professor Every-Palmer said it also impacted physical health.

"People who are living with conditions for which we prescribe antipsychotic medications, so conditions like schizophrenia, they may die well over a decade earlier [than] the general population, mostly from heart disease and diabeties."

World.title: New Zealand-made superconductor returns from trip to space
World.content:
By Milly Matthews, student journalist

When scientist Randy Pollock opened the box containing his superconductor, fresh from a 10-month trip to space, it looked the same as when he'd sent it to the stars.

That is, other than some slight browning of the plastic covers on some of the cables from being exposed to the hard UV of space travel.

"They rolled it in on a cart in its container, and no one had opened it since it had been on the ground. It was really neat to be able to open it and see it again. It looked almost identical to the last time we had seen it."

It was a part of Victoria University's Hēki Space Mission, which was testing superpowered magnets that could eventually be used in a system to propel spaceships.

The mission was run by Paihau-Robinson Research Institute - part of Victoria University - in collaboration with domestic and international partners, and launched on 15 September 2025 aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 as part of Northrop Grumman's NG-23 resupply flight to the International Space Station (ISS).

It marked the first time a high-temperature superconducting magnet of this class was tested in orbit.

And, it was the first time in the professor's 30-year-long space career where he saw his work return home when it landed in June. He had to fly to Houston, Texas, to retrieve it.

The magnet, shaped like a thick CD disk, had arrived at the ISS on an uncrewed flight and undergone six months of testing.

Pollock, the institute's chief scientists and engineer for space research, showed RNZ a video of astronauts unboxing his invention, preparing to install it to an outside platform.

"One of the things that is bizarre watching this is it's relatively heavy. When we'd handle it in the lab, it was two people very carefully and gently lifting it up, whilst the astronauts use one hand, just spinning it around however they need because it's in zero gravity."

Hēki means egg in te reo, and the magnet's protective cover was adorned with art by Māori artist Reweti Arapere (Ngāti Raukawa ki te Tonga, Ngāti Porou and Ngāti Tūwharetoa).

"He came up with this design to tell the story of how the kōkako got its blue wattle in his design. It ties into Hēki because Kōkako is the name we were gifted by the Vice Chancellor Māori at the university, because our thruster puts out this dark blue glow.

"So this was the thing that would hopefully one day grow into a kōkako."

A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket soars upward after its liftoff from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida in March 2025. NASA/Glenn Benson

The magnet used a high-temperature superconductor, a material that could carry electrical current without resistance when cooled below a critical temperature, and known as "high-temperature" because it worked at warmer temperatures than conventional superconductors - although it still needed to be kept extremely cold.

The mission was extended from three months to six. Even so, that was far shorter than the 10 or 15 years expected of equipment used on a long-duration spacecraft mission.

"If you were going to fly on one of these missions where this was a critical part of a subsystem, you'd want to know that it could last for 10 or 15 years.

"We weren't able to show that it could work long-term, and that was the importance of getting it back on the Earth, was allowing that test to continue," he said.

However, he said that overall, they accomplished everything they set out to do.

"Once we got into space, we were able to show that we could operate, that we could manage our magnetic field, we could do it on the amount of power we were allowed, and we could handle the experiment going in and out of the shadow of the Earth."

The next step, according to Pollock, was to look at commercial sponsors.

"It is an expensive thing to put anything into space. These thrusters really come into their own with a very high-power system, so very expensive spacecraft. It is beyond a university research budget to fly a demonstration mission."

But there was no shortage of interest in the project.

"We have talked to people from Europe. We've talked to people from the United States. We've talked to people from Japan who view this as a big step forward in getting this out of the laboratory and into real applications."

In the meantime, Pollock said the team behind Hēki Space Mission has returned to its simulator with promising results.

World.title: There's Silicon Valley - but ever heard of Superconductor Valley?
World.content:
There's Silicon Valley - but ever heard of Superconductor Valley?

Since the late 1980s, scientists in the Hutt Valley have been working on superconducting technology - the phenomenon where electricity can flow with almost no resistance and can produce powerful magnetic fields.

On Tuesday, academics and industry leaders gathered in Wellington for the Superconductor Valley event - a series of panel discussions that canvassed where such technology was at and where it's going.

Hosted by Victoria University's Paihau-Robinson Research Institute, its director, professor Nick Long addressed the convention's name head on.

"Of course, it's a little bit of a riff on Silicon Valley and references the Hutt Valley where our team has lived and done its work.

"But, like Silicon Valley, we hope it's more of a state of mind than a place."

He said Superconductor Valley was Robinson's vision for an ecosystem across New Zealand working on superconductivity, cryogenics and related technologies.

Panel discussions covered aviation, magnets, fusion, and cryogenics and featured speakers from the university as well as tech companies, including OpenStar Technologies and Fabrum.

Among the aviation panellists was Dana Goodwin, the co-founder and chief executive of Crux Aerospace - a tech start-up hoping to harness the power of hydrogen for flight.

The Whakatane and Auckland-based company was building a hydrogen electric powertrain and had big plans for next year: "The first crewed hydrogen electric flight in the Southern Hemisphere, which is pretty cool."

Crux Aerospace hopes to harness the power of hydrogen for flight.

Following the demonstrator flight, the company expected the first larger aircraft to roll off the production line in 2031, she said.

"That aircraft will go straight into commercial operations and do real commercial work earning revenue for an operator."

Goodwin said passengers would hardly notice - except a hydrogen powered flight might be a slightly quieter.

"So from an outsider's perspective, it's very similar to what you would normally see. In fact, if you had a hydrogen aircraft sitting next to a fossil fuel aircraft, you probably wouldn't know the difference."

She also emphasised safety, maintaining the regulator didn't allow for a "backslide": "So if you're happy to fly in a fossil fuel aircraft today, you'll be happy to fly in a hydrogen aircraft tomorrow."

The technology would help the aviation industry reach its stated net-zero carbon goal by 2050, Goodwin said, but time was ticking.

"The sooner we can do this, the sooner we can start decarbonising flight. I'm not the climate scientist so I can't give you the numbers ... but the difference between five years of delay on this is significant to the environment."

She said the delay could also cost the country if it didn't get regulation and funding right.

"If we don't solve the problem here, we're going to be following the world and we're going to be paying for it both in time, in energy, in our money.

"We don't want to do that. New Zealand is so good at solving problems, we need to solve it first and have the rest of the world come and pay us to solve their problems as well."

Co-founder and chief executive of Crux Aerospace Dana Goodwin. RNZ / Mary Argue

Also helping to solve some of the world's problems was Robinson's chief scientist and engineer for space, professor Randy Pollock - but his eyes were on issues slightly further afield, such as space junk.

"If you can be much more efficient in fuel, you can have your space craft last longer," which saved operating costs and the environment, he said.

"It minimises space debris, minimises the amount of material that reenters the atmosphere. So it makes using space for all sorts of activities much more sustainable."

The technology underpinning fuel efficiency was something the Robinson group was researching, Pollock said, explaining that electric propulsion was a "kind of plasma rocket that gets used in space".

"It can't overcome the force of gravity, but it uses just an infinitesimal amount of fuel.

"So once you're in space and you have no friction, if you're willing to run your thruster for a long time, you can move your spacecraft without using nearly as much fuel as you would with traditional rockets."

Ultimately, it would allow for launches that were more space craft, less fuel tank, he said.

And the team's "low-level" superconducting technology had just proved it could work in orbit, with the return of Hēki - a powerful superconducting magnet - after six months of being on the International Space Station.

Pollock said many applications for superconducting technology were about five to 10 years away, but people had taken notice of Hēki.

"We accomplished everything we set out to do. We have gotten interest from people all over the world who had sort of looked at this as a technology that was promising but too hard," he said.

World.title: The economy is growing, you're just not feeling it yet, Westpac says
World.content:
Audio player for " Is it time to get my money out of AI? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2647983%2Fthe-economy-is-growing-you-re-just-not-feeling-it-yet-westpac-says

Is it time to get my money out of AI? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

No really, the economy is improving, Westpac economists say.

They have released their latest economic overview, noting that while the economy is growing, not everyone is feeling it yet.

Activity grew 2.6 percent in the year to June and Westpac's economists said they expected further moderate growth to have happened in recent months.

The export sector was strong, with good levels of earnings for commodities and an increase in tourism and other service-based exports. They expected economic activity to grow 2.8 percent next year and the year after.

But domestic parts of the economy were softer and the labour and housing markets were weak. Inflation meant many households had experienced drops in their real wages in recent years.

Audio player for " Kelly Eckhold on New Zealand's uneven economic recovery " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2647983%2Fthe-economy-is-growing-you-re-just-not-feeling-it-yet-westpac-says

Kelly Eckhold on New Zealand's uneven economic recovery Morning Report Download MP3 7m

"The New Zealand economy is moving forward, but it doesn't feel like a recovery everywhere. Exporters and many regional economies are performing strongly, while households and businesses exposed to the domestic economy are still grappling with high inflation, a soft jobs market and weak house prices," chief economist Kelly Eckhold said.

Westpac estimated merchandise export volumes would grow by more than 4 percent this year, while services exports were on track to increase 9 percent, helped by the continuing recovery in international tourism. Agricultural returns remained elevated.

"For now, exports are the economy's sunny side," Eckhold said.

Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / Westpac

"A competitive exchange rate, strong global demand and tight supply conditions across several commodity markets are generating very strong returns for New Zealand. Over time, we expect that strength to flow more broadly through incomes, employment and spending."

He said it would probably be the middle of next year before the recovery was felt more broadly.

"One indicator of that is when it's clear that the unemployment rate is falling and our forecasts have that remaining at 5.7 percent this year and then falling as we go through the middle part of next year."

The housing market was unlikely to provide much stimulus.

"House prices have fallen through 2026 and we think will only rise by about 1.75 percent in 2027, which is pretty low level of growth. So, therefore, we're not really expecting much out of the bits of the economy that are particularly housing focused."

But he said the weak housing market could also be good for the economy in the longer-term.

"Higher interest rates - both domestically and globally - are prompting changes in housing and related sectors. Resources will ultimately move from uncompetitive housing-dominated sectors such as residential construction and consumption to the stronger more competitive external sector. If sustained this will be very positive for New Zealand over the long term even though the transition is painful right now," Eckhold said.

He said the low New Zealand dollar had been helping exporters but Westpac expected it to increase to US62c by the end of next year as the USD fell and New Zealand interest rates lifted towards global norms.

"NZ is currently on special now when measured in foreign currency terms," Eckhold said. "That's a boon for exporters but tough for domestic consumers and a challenge to the RBNZ.

"We do continue to expect that interest rates are going to have to rise over the course of the next year. So we still expect that the OCR is going to rise to 4 percent in the second half of next year and that's reflecting that inflation is currently way too high, over 4 percent right now, and is going to take a while to fall back. And we certainly don't think that it's very likely that a 3.25 level type interest rate, which is what the Reserve Bank currently forecasts to be the peak in the OCR, is probably going to be sufficient to get core inflation back at anywhere near 2 percent. I'd also argue that that sort of interest rate would probably not be supportive of the exchange rate either.

"So you'd probably see a lower exchange rate than what we have in our forecasts, should that be the actual outcome for 2027."

World.title: Nine-month wait leaves Australia in a Cricket World Cup conundrum
World.content:
Australia's bid to lock in a revamped batting line-up ahead of next year's ODI World Cup defence is set to face a nine-month stumbling block, with a dearth of 50-over cricket on the horizon.

This month's three-match series against England has become something of a sideshow in Australia, given the Sandpapergate saga and debate over the Test squad make up.

But there will be serious consequences ahead of Wednesday's decider in Hobart.

Australia's heavy run of Test series and the IPL in April and May means the side's next ODI is not until next August, where they will face New Zealand in a top-end series.

The team is then likely to play three warm-up matches in Zimbabwe, before their World Cup opener against India in Cape Town on October 7.

Almost every other country is scheduled to play ODI matches in the coming nine months, but the Test team's busiest year threatens to leave Australia at a disadvantage.

Australia crashes to record ODI loss to England Australia's top order has collapsed dramatically to hand England its biggest ODI win on Australian shores, a 135-run triumph in Adelaide.

Since Australia's 2023 triumph win in India, David Warner, Steve Smith, Glenn Maxwell and Marcus Stoinis have all retired from the format.

Marnus Labuschagne is also no longer in the team, with only the bowlers missing from Australia's first-choice squad in the current matches against England.

Australia at least appear set on Travis Head and Mitch Marsh as openers, while Matt Renshaw, Cameron Green and Josh Inglis look solid in the middle order.

The number three role remains one of interest.

Cooper Connolly made two half-centuries against Zimbabwe on being moved there in September, but has since had a top score of 38 in six innings.

"It's obviously nice to get some consistency in one role," Connolly said on Tuesday.

"I like to pride myself on being versatile and being able to sort of bat anywhere.

"But I'm enjoying that role at number three, especially behind Heady and Bison (Marsh). They get us off to a flyer.

"Any chance you get to lock down a position in the Australian side, you're looking to do that. Whether that's at the top or in the middle, I'm happy with either."

Selectors may be able to use an Australia A tour of England that runs alongside next year's Ashes to experiment somewhat, but Test players will naturally be unavailable.

Australia have been able to play with a largely settled top and middle order in recent ODIs, with reasonable success.

But chief selector George Bailey conceded last week some roles were still yet to be settled on, including finding a finisher to replace the likes of Maxwell and Stoinis.

"Maxi and Stoins's ability to navigate through certain situations and then finish with real strong power is a pretty niche role," Bailey said.

Bailey pointed to Ollie Peake as one option, while long-time T20 specialist Tim David is also now back playing domestic one-day cricket and could be another.

A back-up spinner and another pace-bowling all-rounder option outside of Cameron Green were other roles of importance suggested by Bailey.

Meanwhile Mahli Beardman is expected to return for Wednesday's decider, after he was rested in Adelaide following his 6-24 on debut in Perth.

AAP

World.title: Power player banned for six AFL matches for betting on games
World.content:
Port Adelaide footballer Josh Sinn has been suspended for six AFL matches for betting on league games, one of which involved his own club.

The AFL said Sinn placed bets totalling $195 on four matches, including one involving the Power.

But Sinn, who missed the season due to injury, did not play in the game.

The four bets were uncovered by an AFL Integrity Unit investigation and were placed between April 25 and May 2.

All were unsuccessful, according to the league, which said Sinn was "not found to have used any inside information in placing the bets".

Sinn has been banned from the opening six rounds of next year's AFL season, but will be allowed to play in practice and pre-season matches, as well as SANFL games that coincide with the AFL's rounds five and six.

Alcohol and gambling ads 'deeply embedded' in AFL Every NRL and AFL club has an alcohol sponsor this season while every NRL and five AFL clubs are sponsored by gambling companies, a new report has found.

The league said Sinn had admitted to the breach and apologised to both it and the Power.

AFL chief operating officer Tom Harley said that, in determining the penalty, the league had "taken into account that [Sinn] did not play in any of the matches involved and was not found to have used inside information".

"Josh has admitted the conduct, accepted responsibility and expressed remorse," Harley said in a statement.

"Players know they cannot bet on AFL matches. Betting on a match involving your own club and teammates is particularly serious and, in this case, materially increased the sanction."

At a media conference this afternoon, Power CEO Matthew Richardson said the club was "extremely disappointed in Josh".

He said the club was first informed of the matter halfway through the year.

"We were first advised late in June, and that investigation was completed late last week," Richardson said.

"Josh is a young man who has made a very poor decision. Josh appreciates that, he's owning that.

"Our focus will be absolutely on supporting Josh as he now undertakes further education around gambling, and we'll support him in rebuilding his trust with our playing group, with our football club and with the community more broadly."

The league said Sinn would be required to undergo additional education to the gambling harm training that players received.

Richardson said the AFL had conducted a "really detailed investigation" into the breaches, which he described as "disappointing" and "stupid".

"What I do know is that the AFL have got really sophisticated tracking mechanisms," he said.

"The integrity of our game is paramount, but people make mistakes, and that's what's happened here. It's a serious mistake, hence the penalty."

World.title: The longer-term thinking driving Swimming Australia's newest event
World.content:
Swim GP's Melbourne debut ticked plenty of boxes at the weekend.

A whole bevvy of happy swimmers and cheery coaches who were clearly fully invested in the contest, competing in front of packed stands, with plenty viewing at home too.

But Swimming Australia chief executive Rob Woodhouse says this is only the start.

"Overall, [we're] really pleased," Woodhouse told ABC Sport, post the inaugural event.

"The two most pleasing aspects were the reaction and the buy-in from the athletes and coaches themselves … and the crowds.

Cheering fans were fully invested in the teams during the inaugural Swim GP. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"It's pretty rare that we can encourage and get young fans of swimming … getting them in the stands so they can watch the races and they can cheer and they can have their favourite team and favourite colours and things like that.

How Swim GP may have given a glimpse of the future of para-sport Swim GP's all-action, high-octane racing is designed to provide a boost for Australia's swimmers in the lead-up to LA28 and Brisbane 2032, and puts para-swimming front and centre.

"The reaction in the actual venue of the crowd, and a really good young crowd, was terrific. That's what we're aiming to do."

More than 3,500 supporters enjoyed the inaugural event live at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatics Centre in Albert Park, with Saturday night's session a complete sellout.

The made-for-TV event was also a boost for Channel Nine, who helped to develop the event, with Swimming Australia saying it achieved a peak reach of 1.13 million people, and an average audience of 237,000 for Friday night's offering.

In the currency of the modern media landscape, almost 3 million social media views sealed the deal for what was a productive evening all round.

It certainly went some way to help cement the current crop of Dolphins as celebrities in their own right, ahead of a huge six years of sport that culminates with the Brisbane 2032 Olympics.

A ready-made fan base

The fans embraced the swimmers in Melbourne. ( Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swimming Australia made no secret of its aim to targeting a younger age group, between five and 15 years of age, to build its athletes' brand — and it has a ready-made fan base that already exists in plain sight.

Three of the four teams: Kingtide, Wahoo and Kraken were partnered with swim-school providers Carlile, Rackley and GoSwim/Belgravia respectively, who have around 200 learn-to-swim schools around the country.

Woodhouse confirmed that integrating the estimated 600,000 families and 1 million kids who are involved in learn-to-swim programs with the Dolphins was a key part of the organisation's wider strategy leading into Brisbane 2032.

Swimming Australia wants its learn-to-swim participants to learn to love the sport. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"The wider message is about the industry and us and our athletes, Paralympic and Olympic athletes, engaging all the way down to learn-to-swim level," Woodhouse explained.

"If you get kids picking up a ball at four or five years of age then they're probably going to get hooked and join [a football team].

"In swimming we should be in the retention game, not the recruitment game.

"These providers like Rackley and Carlisle and Belgravia, getting them involved with this event they'll start, through those respective teams, to build a far greater awareness of Swim GP, of the teams and of the athletes, which brings in the younger fans.

"If we can build all of that fandom in the lead up to Brisbane '32, then we're going to be in a lot better position in five or six years."

Swim GP shone a spotlight on Australia's Dolphins. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Then there's the question of keeping athletes in the sport for as long as possible to spread important water safety messages.

"Certainly we have a long-term vision of Swimming Australia to be able to have athletes on contract where we're able to pay them to be ambassadors for, not just for the sport and swimming for Australia at Paralympics and at Olympics, but to actually be the custodians of those really important messages of drowning prevention and swimming safe," Woodhouse said.

"If we start doing that and keep kids in the sport longer, not about racing or anything like that, but just that fun element, then we're going to get the natural flow of all kids joining clubs and then going potentially into that pathway of competitive swimming and building up into higher performance pathways.

"It's a big flow-on effect, but it's a system-wide integration … being able to engage with everyone in the industry for the benefit of everyone, particularly for the kids."

Learnings from the ISL and ahead to LA28

Swimming Australia wants its swimmers exposed to big crowds in the lead up to LA. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

Swim GP is not a new concept, with Woodhouse leaning on his experiences with the International Swimming League (ISL), where he was chief executive of the London Roar franchise.

Woodhouse said there were discussions to get an Australia-based franchise into the league before it ran into a litany of problems, headlined by COVID.

That was enough to suggest Australia was ready for its own version of the competition, that and the prospect that Australia will become the centre of the swimming world in the coming years.

"I'm very confident, and our team are very confident, that Australia will become the centralised location for elite swimming between 2028 and 2032," Woodhouse said.

"Just as we want our athletes to go and get experience in California and race in LA, as they've done this year and last year ahead of the 2028 Olympic and Paralympic Games, a lot of the other athletes from around the world are going to want to come to Australia to compete, to acclimatise, to train and things like that.

Australia is primed to be the centre of the swimming world in the coming years. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"So we've got two or three years to build the models from Swim GP, but I actually believe we've got enough talent and big names here in Australia to build it without any international athletes.

"Then, if internationals do want to come after the '28 Olympics and Paralympics and compete with us, then obviously they'd be welcomed.

"But we've got a strong enough base of athletes here to make it a big success."

Part of that involves moving the competition around to different cities, perhaps by having a series of two or three meetings take place around the country.

And although this was "pressure-free" competition, with no emphasis on times of making squads, there is also a high performance element at play.

Although Swim GP was fun, coaches want to up the pressure. (Supplied: Swimming Australia/Delly Carr)

"Both our head coaches, [Paralympic head coach] Mel Tantrum and [Olympic head coach] Rowan Taylor [said] they absolutely want a packed stadium for our trials," Woodhouse said.

"The [LA28] Olympic team, they're competing at SoFi Stadium, 40,000 screaming Americans, while the Paralympic team will be down at Long Beach with 4,000 or 5,000 fans.

"Particularly for the Para-athletes, some of those athletes do have sensory issues, so for them to have some experience coming out to all of that noise and those bright flashing lights and all those sorts of things is really, really important.

"[The crowd in LA] will make a hell of a lot of noise and it's very intimidating," Woodhouse, who has experience to lean on as a bronze medallist in the 400m IM at the last LA Games in 1984, continued.

"There are different pressures, of course; this was all about fun and entertainment. But there are those really important experiential benefits for them as well."

World.title: Melbourne Cup runner So You Are found in Sydney skip bin
World.content:
Melbourne Cup runner So You Are has been found in a Sydney skip after it died from a severe bout of colic.

Sydney man Gregg Jowett released a video on social media on Monday after he discovered a horse in a skip at Lucas Heights. The horse appeared to share the markings of So You Are, which finished eighth in this year's Melbourne Cup.

On Tuesday REC Equine Specialists confirmed the horse in Mr Jowett's video was So You Are, who died on Monday.

Trainer Bjorn Baker said he expected a full explanation from REC Equine Specialists about how and why the horse's remains ended up in a skip bin.

"Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," Baker said.

"He was a much-loved horse, and he deserves to be treated with respect and dignity after his death.

"I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances, and I expect a full explanation of what occurred.

"My thoughts remain with the Ramsey family [owners], and with all my staff, for whom this has compounded an already devastating loss."

Video of So You Are in a skip bin, filmed by Sydney resident Gregg Jowett, has rocked the racing industry. (Facebook: Gregg Jowett)

REC Equine Specialists released a statement extending its deepest sympathy to the owners, trainer, and connections of So You Are, unreservedly apologising for the distress the video caused.

"On Monday 16 November, So You Are was brought into our hospital for emergency treatment of severe colic," REC Equine Specialists said in a statement.

"Despite the best efforts of our veterinary team, he could not be saved and was humanely euthanased under anaesthesia.

"After his death, So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried," it said.

"What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone else who cared for him. We are deeply sorry."

REC said it was not responsible for the burial of So You Are, but said it should have known how the horse was handled after leaving its care.

"So You Are was in our care. We did not carry out the burial ourselves, but we chose the provider and the arrangements, and we take full responsibility for that," it said.

"We should have known exactly how horses were handled after leaving our hospital, and we did not. That process is not good enough, and it must change.

"We have spoken with So You Are's owners and trainer to apologise personally. We are working with our service provider and the facility operators, together with Racing NSW, to establish how this happened and to put in processes to ensure it never happens again."

So You Are died from colic 13 days after running in the 2026 Melbourne Cup. (Getty Images: Racing Photos/George Sal)

So You Are had a successful spring, winning four times including a trio of Group 3 races at Rosehill, Randwick and the Bendigo Cup.

The five-year-old finished eighth in the Melbourne Cup, won by Point Of Law.

REC said it would no longer use the service provider and was reviewing how service providers it contracted cared for horses after death, from collection to final burial.

It said it would share the findings with Racing NSW.

Waste management company Cleanaway, which runs the Lucas Heights landfill, said So You Are's body had been moved to a skip bin in a permitted area of the site.

"Cleanaway's Lucas Heights landfill is licensed to accept and dispose of animal carcasses," a spokesperson said.

"The horse carcass delivered to the facility arrived in a small tipper truck, which is not permitted on the landfill tipping face for safety reasons.

"In accordance with established procedures, the carcass was transferred into a skip bin to enable its safe disposal at the landfill."

'Distressing and completely unacceptable'

The fallout from the distressing footage of deceased Melbourne Cup runner So You Are in a skip bin has been immediate.

ABC Sport understands that interim Racing NSW boss Graeme Hinton is working to create new industry standards to ensure animals are provided with dignity and respect after their death.

It is understood the new standards will be released at the end of the month.

Racehorse So You Are dies of colic Trainer Bjorn Baker says the five-year-old horse, which finished eighth in the Melbourne Cup, was rushed to hospital but died following a severe bout of colic.

Racing NSW released a statement saying So You Are was awaiting burial when the video was recorded, and that it would conduct an investigation.

"The way in which So You Are's body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable. So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect," the statement said.

"Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process.

"That burial, however, should have occurred in a timely and respectful manner.

"If through the course of our ongoing investigation any wrongdoing is found, Racing NSW will not hesitate to take appropriate action."

Animal Justice Party NSW Upper House MP Emma Hurst held a press conference in Sydney following the treatment of So You Are.

She said the news was "absolutely heartbreaking", but not surprising.

"This horse has been treated as though he is nothing more than a piece of rubbish," she said.

"To be completely honest, I'm not entirely surprised. We've had complaints about the racing industry for the entire eight years that I have been in parliament," she said.

"There are serious questions around the entire racing industry, and this most recent incident just raises more questions."

She called for greater transparency and accountability within the racing industry and called on the state government for further action.

World.title: Wallabies in danger of missing 'big three' target
World.content:
Coach Les Kiss is determined to ensure Australia finishes among the top three Southern Hemisphere teams in the Nations Championship after a rare weekend blowout for the Wallabies, All Blacks and Springboks.

For only the second time in rugby history, all of the "big three" were turned over on the same weekend by Northern Hemisphere opposition as South Africa lost 21-19 in France, New Zealand were sensationally beaten 35-28 in Wales and Australia lost narrowly 15-12 to Scotland at Murrayfield.

That had only previously occurred in July 2022, when all three suffered home defeats: New Zealand losing 23-12 to Ireland in Dunedin, South Africa going down 13-12 to Wales in Bloemfontein and Australia falling 25-17 to England in Brisbane.

Now, Australia has fallen to fourth in the Southern Hemisphere table of the Nations Championship, leapfrogged by Argentina, and should the Wallabies succumb to a fifth-straight Test defeat against Wales on Saturday, it will finish in that position.

Should Argentina upset France, even a Wallabies win would not be enough to claw them back to that third spot.

Wallabies attacking woes The Wallabies once again show precious little in an attacking sense, as Scotland edge a "turgid" encounter at Murrayfield.

But Kiss made it clear this would represent failure for a team that had come on its British sojourn seeking a top-three finish.

"We were aiming for the top-three when we came here, New Zealand and South Africa already being up there and going to be hard to reel in," Kiss said.

"So we were aiming for the top-three for sure, and that's what we'll measure ourselves on."

It is still only halfway through the tour, but the grim scenario of a second-straight European wipe-out looms following defeats in England, Italy, Ireland and France last year, the first time in 67 years that such a whitewash had occurred.

Les Kiss has watched his Wallabies side lose four Tests on the trot. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

Asked if the Wallabies had lost their confidence, Kiss mused: "Yeah, you do want a team with a bit of swagger. There's been losses throughout the last few years that have seemed to hang on, that's for sure.

"I wouldn't say it's confidence, I wouldn't say it's just belief. I think it's a mixture of those things coming together and it's just down to them believing that they can now win those big moments."

He referred to that last-second burst down the right touchline on Sunday, when Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Max Jorgensen and Tom Wright could not quite turn the break into a match-winning moment.

"The losses obviously takes its toll but, mate, they're hardy and they're going to continue to work hard," Kiss said.

It all gives Saturday's Test against a Welsh side currently residing on cloud nine even more of a "must-win" feel.

Wales beat All Blacks Wales has pulled off one of the greatest wins in its recent history, beating the All Blacks for the first time in 73 years in a Nations Championship boilover.

Captain Harry Wilson counters: "Every Test match is must-win. We're going to go into the Wales game with the same attitude we do every time. We need a win. We're going to do everything in our power to make sure we can."

But Kiss admitted the incredible Welsh win over the All Blacks, their first in 73 years, had "changed everyone's minds" about Steve Tandy's reinvented team.

"Honestly, it was compelling. It was phenomenal what they did. So we're going to need to be good to go there on a short turnaround."

But could Australia be facing a side with energy levels zapped from their legs after throwing themselves into a record-breaking 346 tackles against New Zealand? Kiss just smiled: "Nah, they'll be energised. That's inspiring what they did, isn't it?

"We've just got to make sure we've got our reason to be up for it too, which is that it's a bloody important Test match to win."

AAP

World.title: Khawaja avoids sandpaper questions on first TV appearance since 7.30
World.content:
Usman Khawaja has avoided being asked about Sandpapergate in his first television appearance since last week's refusal to fully answer questions on the ABC.

After cancelling some interviews with mainstream media outlets last week during his tour to promote his autobiography Sabr, Khawaja appeared on Channel 10's Sam Pang Tonight on Monday.

The Gold Logie-winning host asked the former opener about everything from his relationship with David Warner to how he proposed to wife, Rachel.

Khawaja opens up on racism, mental health Usman Khawaja speaks about the racist stereotyping he faced and his early mental health struggles coping with cricket failures.

But conspicuously absent were any questions about the 2018 ball-tampering scandal, Khawaja's claims the entire team knew of the plot, or Pat Cummins's denial and 70-minute response last Friday.

Instead, the closest the conversation veered towards ball tampering came when Pang flashed the first page of the sandpaper book chapter, then asked about Will Smith references in it.

Other topics covered included growing up in Pakistan, perfecting the pull shot, and Khawaja feeling Adam Zampa's behind during the national anthem in 2016.

On the topic of his friendship with Warner, Khawaja said the pair were "yin and yang".

"Me and Davey are very different people," Khawaja said. "But when it comes to a lot of things like family, values and how we look after everyone …

"People don't see that side of him, and that's the side that connects us."

Khawaja spoke about his friendship with David Warner. (Getty Image: Alex Davidson, ICC)

Khawaja has previously stated that his Sandpapergate revelations came as a result of promising Warner he would tell the full story of the 2018 saga, which Cricket Australia initially deemed only Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft knew about.

Monday night's interview was in contrast to Khawaja's 12-minute grilling from Sarah Ferguson on ABC's 7:30 last Tuesday, when the opener dodged questions on the matter.

Pang and guest co-host Dave Lawson joked later in Monday's show that he "probably should have gone harder on the whole sandpaper gag thing".

Khawaja is still yet to fully respond to Cummins's denials, but did admit on a podcast recorded last Wednesday and released on Monday that he had to weigh up the damage his claims may cause to ex-teammates.

"I have stood up for three guys I feel like were treated unfairly," Khawaja said on the They Used To Be podcast, referring to Warner, Smith and Bancroft's 2018 suspensions.

"But there are other guys that are still playing in the team right now that there might be some sort of cost. I have tried my best to balance that out."

Khawaja is due to go on The Grade Cricketer podcast on Thursday, before an awkward reunion looms with former coach Darren Lehmann at the Gold Clash celebrity cricket match in Cairns on Sunday.

Lehmann last week rejected any suggestion he or his entire team knew about the use of sandpaper and suggested Khawaja was "trying to sell a book".

Usman Khawaja during his interview on 7.30. (ABC News)

The issue also appears unlikely to fade away quickly, with Bancroft considering speaking publicly in the coming days for the first time since Khawaja's revelations.

Khawaja spoke to Bancroft before the release of his book, which contains claims a coach told Bancroft to ramp up his ball management before Khawaja saw Bancroft place sandpaper in his pocket.

Warner has labelled Khawaja's claims about the scandal "100 per cent accurate". Paceman Mitchell Starc is aligned with Cummins's version of events.

Meanwhile, Steve Smith is now no longer expected to speak on the matter before Sunday's return from a neck injury in the Sheffield Shield, ahead of next month's first Test against New Zealand.

AAP

World.title: Popovic admits Socceroos future uncertain after Asian Cup postponement
World.content:
Tony Popovic has suggested his time in charge of the Socceroos is not over, saying he would be hard pressed to find a job that gives him as much satisfaction as coaching Australia.

Popovic's future has been a topic of hot debate since the delay of January's Asian Cup by 11 months due to the conflict in host nation Saudi Arabia.

The 53-year-old is without a contract beyond Wednesday's (AEDT) friendly with Jordan, which was relocated to Doha after Socceroos players raised security concerns.

"I don't expect it to be the last game, but you never know," Popovic said.

"As it stands, it is, with the Asian Cup postponement."

Popovic turned down a new four-year deal with Football Australia (FA) on the eve of the World Cup this year.

He instead committed to a short-term deal that ran until the end of the Asian Cup. But the tournament's delay has prompted a stand-off over which way the federation goes next.

Tony Popovic is yet to discuss a new contract with FA. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

The initial signs according to FA sources are that the governing body wants Popovic to stay, despite fellow coaches Kevin Muscat being off contract and John Aloisi being out of a job following his sacking by Chinese Super League side Chengdu Rongcheng.

FA chief executive Martin Kuegeler has been in the Middle East in the past week but has yet to sit down with Popovic and go through further details.

Socceroos crush Qatar The Socceroos have enjoyed an emphatic victory in the stronghold of the Asian champions, defeating Qatar 3-0 in Doha.

"We never had any plans to discuss my future during this period," Popovic said.

"So the Asian Cup postponement doesn't change that and I'm sure that'll all happen in the next couple of months."

Popovic, who boasts a record of 12 wins, six draws and seven losses in charge of Australia, had never coached a national team before succeeding Graham Arnold in 2024.

"I don't think I could ever have a job that would be as good as the one I have now," he said.

"I'm in such a privileged position, I don't take it for granted and I'm very grateful.

"I'm coaching my country, the Socceroos, and it doesn't get better than this, so I don't think I'll ever have something that feels as special as this.

"But I also know football things change, whether you have a contract or not."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Arrest over Melbourne Cup theft but trophies still missing
World.content:
A man has been arrested over the theft of three Melbourne Cup trophies won by racehorse Makybe Diva, but the trophies remain missing.

The three cups were stolen from a cabinet at Flemington Racecourse about 6:30am yesterday.

It is believed two men dressed in high-vis broke into the racecourse and stole the trophies from a cabinet where they were displayed.

Victoria Police said a 36-year-old man from Malvern East was arrested after police raided a property at Mount Waverley last night.

The man has been interviewed and released pending summons.

The trophies are yet to be recovered and the investigation is ongoing.

The three Melbourne Cup trophies are valued at $1 million each.

The trophies were stolen from a cabinet at Flemington Racecourse. (ABC News)

Yesterday, Tony Santic, who owned Makybe Diva, said he was "totally devastated" by the theft.

"They were irreplaceable … I just want them back in one piece," Santic said.

" Please just give the cups back. Put them somewhere and let the police know where they are and all's forgiven on my part. "

In a statement, Victoria Racing Club said it was "devastated by the incident".

The cups had been on display at the racecourse for the Spring Racing Carnival since September.

Makybe Diva is the only horse to have won the famous race in three consecutive years, each time being ridden by jockey Glen Boss.

The champion racehorse died earlier this year at the age of 27 after a short battle with the gastrointestinal condition colic.

Tech.title: YouTube found a new way to inflate view counts
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

YouTube’s view counts will now include the number of people that it estimates are watching a video together on TV. In an update on Monday, the platform says it’s bringing “co-views” to public view counts across long-form videos, Shorts, and live content to provide a more “complete picture” of how people are using its platform.

YouTube, which has become even more popular on TVs than phones, also says the change will help it align with “TV industry standards,” which similarly record views by estimating the number of people watching shows. The company says it doesn’t use devices, like cameras or microphones, to estimate how many people are watching a video on TV. Instead, it estimates co-views using a “privacy safe statistical model” that takes into account “demographic patterns and viewing times.”

This marks yet another update to YouTube’s view count system. In August, the platform began counting a view as soon as a video starts playing. The company said at the time that creators will notice their view counts increasing faster as a result of this change, and it seems like adding co-views could boost these numbers as well.

YouTube notes that it will only apply co-views to new views on TV going forward, and that they won’t appear retroactively. Co-views also won’t affect a creator’s ad revenue, YouTube Partner Program eligibility, or revenue.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo feels far more intuitive with Apple’s new face unlock
Tech.content:
Apple is testing adding face unlock to the iPhone Duo — not true Face ID, but something a little simpler and less secure. So far, it works great, and even with a few Apple-imposed security limitations, it makes the Duo quicker and more comfortable to use than relying on Touch ID every time. That’s one of my gripes with the phone taken care of.

The Duo’s foldable architecture means that Apple couldn’t fit in the full Face ID sensor array found on the rest of the iPhone lineup (though it reportedly hopes to change that by the second generation). Instead, it simply has two selfie cameras — one on the outer display, and another hidden under the inner one. Neither supports full Face ID, but after enough grumbling from reviewers and early adopters that using Touch ID alone feels cumbersome, Apple has relented.

The latest developer beta of iOS 27.3 introduces a new option to “Unlock with Front Camera” — Apple is careful not to call it Face ID. Setup is similar, though instead of rotating your head in a slow circle, you simply have to turn it left, right, up, and down. It takes five seconds or so, and I even managed it under the jerky conditions of a moving London bus.

Setup takes only a few seconds and is similar to Face ID.

The new face unlock brings convenience, taking just half a second to unlock, but Apple warns during setup that it “isn’t as secure as Touch ID or Face ID” because it lacks the infrared depth map of the TrueDepth cameras. That means it’s possible to spoof with a photograph or video clip, but I managed that only once in over 20 attempts. Crucially, after each failed attempt to trick the system with a photo, the phone demanded I use Touch ID for my next login — which it doesn’t require if it simply doesn’t detect any face in the frame. That means getting past this would require any would-be thief or spy to get the fake face right the first time.

Lacking TrueDepth also introduces limits in low light, though performance is better than I expected. Walking around after sunset, I had to seek out especially dark spots before I could find anywhere where unlocking failed, like huddling behind a truck on a leafy street where the streetlights couldn’t reach me. It will fail eventually, but it does have to get quite dark for that to happen.

Apple has imposed a few other limitations to reflect the lower security of the new system. You can only use it to unlock the phone from the lockscreen, so you will have to revert to Touch ID or a passcode to use Apple Pay, install or log in to an app, or get past any other screen where the phone requires security credentials.

That’s similar to most Android phones with camera-based face unlock. Only Google’s Pixel phones allow you to make purchases or log in to apps using Face Unlock, thanks to software tricks that make the system more secure than other Android alternatives, Google says.

You’ll have to use Touch ID or a passcode whenever you install an app. But also every time you try to unlock from the inner screen.

The iPhone Duo’s more annoying limitations reflect when you can use the feature. Face unlock works only for 45 minutes at a time, after which you’ll have to verify with Touch ID or your passcode the next time you unlock. Worse, it doesn’t work at all with the inner screen’s under-display selfie camera. Apple hasn’t said why, though presumably it felt the lower resolution and quality of that camera made face unlock unsuitable.

I’d love it if Apple loosened its restrictions just a little — 45 minutes isn’t a very long time before requiring Touch ID again, and I’m sure I’ll regularly forget that the inner screen requires a fingerprint. But the Duo already feels more comfortable to use, letting me get straight into the phone rather than fumbling for the fingerprint sensor. It’s small, but it’s a welcome sign that Apple is listening to the Duo’s early users and is willing to adjust its grand vision to meet the world where it is.

For now, face unlock is limited to the developer beta, but it could roll out to a public beta within a few days, and with luck will get a full launch along with the rest of iOS 27.3 in December. Now can we get the same option for MacBooks and iPads?

Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

Tech.title: Inside Microsoft’s giant Outlook outage
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

At 9AM last Thursday, everything seemed normal. Microsoft employees were arriving on campus, ready for a regular day of emails and meetings. But barely an hour later, one of Microsoft’s worst outages in history started to unfold, leaving employees, businesses, and many governments without access to Outlook emails for nearly 24 hours.

It all started in Switzerland, according to a source familiar with the outage. Exchange Online servers that power Outlook started to fall offline. The problem quickly spread to Mexico, and then to other countries around the world, as Microsoft’s failover systems tried to shift email traffic elsewhere. Within a couple of hours, more than 80 percent of Exchange servers were unresponsive.

Sources tell me that Microsoft marked the outage as “sev0” in its internal incident tracking system, the highest level, which indicates a catastrophic level of service disruption. Hundreds of engineers began trying to figure out what had gone wrong, and how to restore service. It’s not unusual for servers to fail under certain circumstances, but Microsoft has a variety of systems that are supposed to route traffic toward healthy servers to keep the broader system online. In this case, the failover systems did their job, but they also spread the problem.

In the early hours of the outage, engineers were analyzing crash reports, trace logs, and kernel dumps to try and find clues to the giant outage. Some servers had entered into maintenance mode and became unresponsive due to unusually high CPU loads. Engineers tried to bring servers back online, but they were almost immediately overwhelmed by traffic waiting to access the servers.

Exchange servers boot up and run an OS over a network (Preboot Execution Environment), a process that allows Microsoft’s support staff and engineers to manage OS updates remotely. I understand that the sudden burst of traffic from servers being rebooted was overwhelming the systems monitoring them, causing a form of reboot loop where they kept trying and failing to come back online.

As engineers continued to hunt for the root cause, Microsoft was even struggling to roll back servers to a healthy state using its usual processes of reverting recent changes. As the outside world began to wonder if this outage was related to a cyberattack or sloppy AI coding, Microsoft’s engineers were already investigating potential attack vectors and liaising with DDoS specialists to understand whether this could have been an attack.

I’m told crash reports and logs quickly ruled out the possibility of an attack, and after recent rollbacks failed, Microsoft’s engineers began to take a closer look at the networking stack of the servers and discovered an unusual bug. It was unusual because the bug had been sitting on Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers since July without any impact to servers.

“A latent defect caused servers to become overwhelmed and unresponsive under certain load conditions,” wrote Charles Lamanna, the leader of Microsoft’s Copilot, Agents, and Platform (CAP) team, in a post on X. The teams behind Office, Outlook, and Microsoft Teams all started reporting to Lamanna last month after the head of Office and Teams, Ryan Roslansky, left the company.

Microsoft’s preliminary post-incident report describes the bug as one affecting select Windows servers “due to lock contention inside an internal Windows process.” The bug doesn’t affect regular versions of Windows since it was the result of a fix that was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 networking gateway servers.

Microsoft didn’t find the bug until this major outage, and it admits that was because of the traffic mix and hardware used in its testing labs. “The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware; whereas our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores,” Lamanna wrote.

The bug became obvious because of two other incidents that increased load and reduced server capacity. Fifteen hours before this Outlook outage began, Microsoft Teams failed over from an alternative networking gateway to the main gateway that supports Exchange Online. “This increased the load on the networking gateway and changed its traffic patterns,” Lamanna wrote. Ordinarily this wouldn’t have been a problem, but at the same time around 14 percent of server capacity for this gateway was “out of service due to an unrelated issue from the previous day.”

The trifecta of a bug, Microsoft Teams failing over, and reduced server capacity all caused the network gateway to trigger the problem that had been lying dormant since July. It took Microsoft nearly 24 hours to get its Exchange servers stable again, and I’m told overlapping interventions from teams trying to fix issues complicated coordination at times.

Microsoft engineers had a running bridge call the entire time, and at one point it hit the maximum of 1,000 participants. That shows you how many teams were involved with trying to find the root cause of this huge outage, which started at the peak window of traffic in the US.

“Recovery took longer than usual because as servers returned to service, they were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and became unresponsive again,” Lamanna wrote. “Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state. Additionally, since the main code defect was a latent bug from several months previous, our normal rollback, flighting, and feature flags were unable to quickly revert the change.”

Microsoft is now working on a final post-incident review that will be published later this week. Even without that full review, it’s clear that the company will need to invest more into its testing processes to ensure that when something like this happens again, it can catch the problem a lot sooner. Outages happen daily, but this kind of cascading failure is a rare moment for Microsoft to learn from its mistakes and make sure the same sequence of events doesn’t bring down Outlook for millions of people again.

Notepad will return in December after next week’s Thanksgiving break.

I’m always keen to hear from readers, so please drop a comment here, or you can reach me at notepad@theverge.com if you want to discuss anything else. If you’ve heard about any of Microsoft’s secret projects, you can reach me via email at notepad@theverge.com or speak to me confidentially on the Signal messaging app, where I’m tomwarren.01. I’m also tomwarren on Telegram, if you’d prefer to chat there.

Thanks for subscribing to Notepad.

Tech.title: The DOJ says it’s investigating Megaspeed
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The Justice and Commerce Departments said that they are investigating Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company intertwined with the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, after reporting suggested an investigation had been halted last year.

“While we don’t typically comment on ongoing investigations, it is in the public interest to provide the facts and address inaccurate information circulating in public reporting,” the departments said in a statement issued Monday evening. The departments acknowledged there’s been “significant public attention” on Megaspeed.

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO last week after reports he had an affair with former Megaspeed executive and alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, who Megaspeed says left the company in August 2025. The scandal has raised questions about national security, and sparked scrutiny of Nvidia’s handling of exports of its chips to China and Megaspeed’s possible role in moving along Nvidia’s chips.

Earlier this month, the New York Times reported that a Commerce Department investigation into Megaspeed “came to a sudden halt” late last year after its investigators received an email from Nvidia’s general counsel, claiming Commerce Department official Jeffrey Kessler gave Nvidia permission to reach out. The case was then “quickly” handed over to the DOJ, according to the Times.

The announcement today says the DOJ took the “lead role” in the investigation last year:

After identifying suspicious activity through proactive monitoring of potential sensitive semiconductor diversion, the Department of Commerce initiated an investigation into Megaspeed in 2024 for potential export control violations. In May 2025, Department of Commerce investigators requested records from Nvidia concerning direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed. In June 2025, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its “no sell” list. Based on the Department of Commerce’s investigation, agents from the Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, in conjunction with Singaporean law enforcement officials, conducted an on-site, in-person, end-use check at Megaspeed in June 2025 and interviewed CEO Alice Huang.

Following this enforcement action, the Department of Justice took the lead role in the criminal investigation of Megaspeed.

The statement doesn’t go into detail about the current status of the case, but it says the DOJ and Commerce Department “will bring the full extent of the law against Megaspeed for any criminal conduct that may have occurred.”

Tech.title: Banning phones really does help kids learn, researchers say
Tech.content:
A new nationwide study found that in-school cellphone bans can lead to modest improvements in learning. Now, researchers want to understand whether kids’ phone use outside the classroom might contribute to the rest of students’ learning loss — using the conditions of Meta’s multibillion-dollar settlement from earlier this year.

Banning cellphones in schools has the equivalent effect of adding one to two weeks of school to the academic year, accounting for about half of the learning loss students experienced in the US between 2013 and the 2020 covid-19 pandemic, according to the study carried out by researchers from Harvard University and Dartmouth College in partnership with academic assessment group NWEA. The group analyzed testing data from 3.3 million students across 4,600 schools between the 2021–22 school year and 2025–26, including schools with and without phone bans. Though modest, such a finding is exactly the kind of effect researchers were seeking, says Tom Kane, faculty director of the Harvard University Center for Education Policy Research.

While previous studies about cellphone bans in school found positive effects on academic outcomes, many of them examined schools outside the US. An earlier nationwide US study looked at academic outcomes based on averages within schools, whereas this latest study looked at student-level data, which the researchers said allowed them to control for more factors and observe the effect of the bans on students who were experiencing the most or least learning loss.

In addition to potentially answering questions about the impact of a major new technology on learning, the findings show that cellphone bans can be a cost-effective way to improve student outcomes. While purchasing lockable pouches for a class of 17 students would cost an estimated $425 per teacher, the researchers found, paying an average teacher’s salary for an extra week would be $2,080.

The findings show that cellphone bans can be a cost-effective way to improve student outcomes

Many parents and teachers already have a hunch — popularized by academics like social psychologist Jonathan Haidt — that cellphones and social media have impacted their kids’ learning and mental health. But Kane says it’s still important that scientists get the chance to actually test that hypothesis. Prior to his in-school cellphone ban study, Kane believed that a de-emphasis on test-based accountability in US schools was largely to blame for learning loss. But as he looked into it further, he changed his mind after seeing that kids outside the US were also experiencing learning loss. Through this recent study, Kane found much of it is attributable to in-school cellphone use.

Kane was surprised by some of the findings in this latest study.
